concepts.title: Profit = Opponent Mistakes Minus Our Mistakes
concepts.summary: All poker profit derives from the gap between the mistakes opponents make and the mistakes we make; maximizing this gap is the fundamental goal.
concepts.details: Profit comes from two components: opponent errors (largely outside our control except via game selection) and our own errors (fully controllable). In softer fields you can play poorly and still win; in tougher fields edges shrink because opponents exploit you while you exploit them, forcing you to minimize your own leaks.
concepts.actionable_rule: Continuously minimize your own strategic leaks while identifying and exploiting opponents' mistakes; when opponents are strong, prioritize tightening your own game and select softer games.

concepts.title: GTO as a Base Strategy, Adapted Exploitatively
concepts.summary: Use unexploitable GTO ranges as a baseline, then deviate to exploit observed opponent frequencies; knowing equilibrium makes deviations easy to spot.
concepts.details: Elite players rarely play exact GTO; they use solver-derived equilibrium ranges as reference points and widen, tighten, or switch models based on opponent tendencies. Knowing the unexploitable frequencies makes it much easier to identify when opponents deviate in exploitable ways. Poker remains a game of playing the player.
concepts.actionable_rule: Default to GTO baseline ranges, but when an opponent's frequencies deviate from equilibrium, adjust your strategy to attack that imbalance.

concepts.title: Math Improves EV Estimation Precision
concepts.summary: You can win without explicit math, but understanding the underlying math makes your EV estimations more precise and your mastery more complete.
concepts.details: Even players who avoid math are doing it implicitly when trying to make +EV plays. A strong mathematical foundation sharpens the accuracy of EV approximations. Off-table study builds pattern recognition that eventually becomes instinctive at the table.
concepts.actionable_rule: Invest off-table study time learning the math behind decisions so that accurate EV estimation becomes automatic and instinctive during play.

concepts.title: Positional Order of Action
concepts.summary: Table seats are grouped into early, middle, and late position, with later positions acting last post-flop, conferring an informational advantage.
concepts.details: At a 9-handed table: EP = UTG, UTG1, UTG2; MP = Lojack and Hijack; LP = Cutoff and Button. The Button acts last on all post-flop streets and the Cutoff next-to-last, giving late positions superior information and control. With fewer players, early positions are removed first.
concepts.actionable_rule: Open wider and play more hands from late positions (CO, BN) where you act last, and play tighter from early positions where many players act behind you.

concepts.title: 80/20 Play-to-Study Ratio
concepts.summary: Allocate roughly 80% of poker time to playing and 20% to studying to balance theoretical growth with practical experience and metagame awareness.
concepts.details: Off-table work seems detached from real play since you rarely consult charts at the table, but accumulated study builds pattern recognition that becomes unconscious and instinctive. Playing volume keeps you current on the evolving metagame, so neither pure study nor pure play is sufficient alone.
concepts.actionable_rule: Maintain roughly an 80% play to 20% study ratio, ensuring continued play volume to stay current with the metagame while reserving meaningful time for theory work.

concepts.title: Effective Stack Determines Maximum Risk
concepts.summary: In any pot, the effective stack (the smallest stack among active players) caps how much either player can win or lose in a heads-up confrontation.
concepts.details: Stack depth is measured in big blinds. When two players have different stacks, the smaller stack is the effective stack because no one can win more than the shorter stack can put in. This governs SPR and all-in decisions.
concepts.actionable_rule: Compute the effective stack as the smaller of the two active stacks (in bb) and base all commitment and bet-sizing decisions on that number, not your own stack.

concepts.title: Assign Ranges, Not Single Hands
concepts.summary: Strong players never put an opponent on one hand; they assign a range of holdings and narrow it street by street based on actions.
concepts.details: Hand reading proceeds by asking which hands are consistent with the villain's actions and building the range combo by combo. Advanced players also evaluate their own range versus the opponent's in terms of equity, polarization, balance, and nut advantage.
concepts.actionable_rule: Whenever an opponent acts, update a weighted range of all consistent holdings rather than guessing one hand, and continually narrow it as new actions occur.

concepts.title: Avoid a Split Limp/Raise Range
concepts.summary: Raising only premiums while limping medium hands is highly exploitable because it telegraphs hand strength.
concepts.details: If a villain raises strong hands and limps medium ones, opponents can raise the limps (knowing they're weak) and fold to the raises (knowing they're strong). It also makes post-flop reads trivial — e.g., a raiser who never opens T9s or middle pairs cannot have straights/sets/two pair on low connected boards.
concepts.actionable_rule: Enter pots by raising a single unified range rather than splitting into raise-premiums/limp-mediums; and attack opponents who split by raising their limps and folding marginal hands to their raises.

concepts.title: Enter Pots by Raising for a Disguised Range
concepts.summary: Playing all the hands you want to play by raising (rather than limping some) keeps your range balanced and hard to read.
concepts.details: A unified raising-first-in strategy from a given position prevents opponents from deducing hand strength from your action, unlike a transparent limp/raise split. This is the foundation of solid early-position play.
concepts.actionable_rule: When first in, fold or raise — do not limp — so your opening range stays unified and unexploitable from each position.

concepts.title: Combinatorics of Starting Hands
concepts.summary: There are 1,326 starting combos: 6 per pocket pair (78 total), 4 per suited hand (312), and 12 per offsuit hand (936).
concepts.details: For pocket pairs use X*(X-1)/2 combos where X is available cards (6 for a fresh pair). Unpaired hands have X*Y combos (16 fresh; 4 suited + 12 offsuit). Counting combos rather than naming hands lets you weight ranges accurately.
concepts.actionable_rule: Count ranges in combinations: 6 combos per unblocked pair, 4 per suited holding, 12 per offsuit holding, then adjust for card removal.

concepts.title: Card Removal / Blockers Shrink Opponent Combos
concepts.summary: Cards in your hand and on the board remove specific combos from the villain's range, often dramatically reducing strong holdings.
concepts.details: In the example, the A♦3♦ in hand plus the A♣J♥9♥ board reduce villain's 306-combo range to 225 combos, with only 6 pure-air combos remaining. Sets, two pairs, and flush draws are all cut by the cards that are visible or held.
concepts.actionable_rule: Before estimating how many value or bluff combos an opponent holds, subtract every combo blocked by your hole cards and the board.

concepts.title: Estimate Then Refine Opponent Opening Ranges
concepts.summary: Since you rarely know an opponent's exact range, start from a standard positional opening range (e.g., ~23% from the hijack) and adjust to reads.
concepts.details: A reasonable hijack open of ~23% breaks into all pocket pairs, ~30 suited hands, and ~9 offsuit hands. Using a baseline percentage range lets you do combinatoric analysis even with incomplete information.
concepts.actionable_rule: Default each opponent to a standard position-based opening percentage, then widen or tighten it based on observed tendencies before doing range math.

concepts.title: Categorize the Board's Range Breakdown
concepts.summary: On a given flop, decompose the opponent's range into made-hand tiers (sets, two pair, top/middle/bottom pair, over/underpairs) and draws to assess equity distribution.
concepts.details: On A♣J♥9♥, the example range yields 157 made-hand combos and 72 drawing combos, separating flush draws, straight-flush draws, OESDs, gutshots, and air. Knowing how many strong vs weak combos exist drives betting and bluff-catching decisions.
concepts.actionable_rule: On each flop, bucket the opponent's range into made-hand strength tiers and draw types by combo count to gauge who holds the nut advantage.

concepts.title: Effective Nuts and Bluff Catchers
concepts.summary: Treat hands strong enough to never fold as effective nuts, and recognize bluff catchers that can only beat a bluff when deciding to call.
concepts.details: 7♣7♥ is the effective nuts on 8♥7♦2♦. A bluff catcher beats only bluffs, so its call profitability depends entirely on the opponent's bluff frequency. Air can win only by bluffing.
concepts.actionable_rule: Play effective-nut hands as the nuts for maximum value, and call with bluff catchers only when the opponent's estimated bluff combos make calling profitable.

concepts.title: Pot Odds as Reward-to-Risk Threshold
concepts.summary: Pot odds express the ratio of what you can win to what you must risk, converting to a minimum win percentage needed to justify a call.
concepts.details: Pot odds = amount to call / (pot + amount to call) gives the breakeven equity. Risking $100 to win $200 means you must win at least 33.3% of the time. In ratio form (odds against), your hand odds must be lower than pot odds to call; in percentage form, your equity must be greater than the required pot odds percentage. Ignores ICM/bankroll adjustments.
concepts.actionable_rule: Compute required equity = call / (pot + call); call only if your estimated equity exceeds this percentage.

concepts.title: Counting Outs and Converting to Equity
concepts.summary: Count cards that improve you to the best hand and convert to win probability using deck math or the rule-of-thumb multiplier.
concepts.details: With 47 unseen cards on the flop, one card to come gives roughly outs/47; for two cards to come (facing all-in) the probability is higher. Approximate: multiply outs by 2 per remaining card (×4 for two cards) to estimate equity percentage. A flush draw with 9 outs has ~35% to hit by the river. Adjust outs for dead cards and opponent holdings.
concepts.actionable_rule: Count clean outs, multiply by ~4 with two cards to come (or ~2 with one card), and compare the resulting equity to your pot odds.

concepts.title: Backdoor Draws Worth ~One Extra Out
concepts.summary: A backdoor flush or straight draw on the flop has roughly the value of one additional out (~4.26%).
concepts.details: Completing a runner-runner draw requires hitting two specific cards. The probability of completing a BDFD or a three-card-rundown BDSTD is close to 4.26%, the same as a one-out draw completing across turn and river. This lets you add roughly one out of equity when evaluating flop hands with backdoor potential.
concepts.actionable_rule: When evaluating a flop hand, add roughly one out (~4%) of equity for each live backdoor flush or straight draw.

concepts.title: Dead Outs and Drawing Dead
concepts.summary: Discount outs that also improve the opponent to a better hand, and recognize when you have no live outs at all.
concepts.details: An OESD nominally has 8 outs, but if Villain holds a flush draw, two of those cards complete his flush, leaving only 6 live outs. A player is drawing dead when every card that improves him still loses. Always evaluate outs relative to the opponent's likely range, not in a vacuum.
concepts.actionable_rule: Subtract any outs that also make the opponent a winning hand before computing your effective equity, and fold if you are drawing dead.

concepts.title: Implied and Reverse Implied Odds
concepts.summary: Account for money you expect to win on later streets when completing a draw, and money you may lose when you complete but are still beaten.
concepts.details: Implied odds increase the value of a draw because pot odds alone may not justify a call but future winnings can. Reverse implied odds reduce a draw's value when hitting it can lead to losing a larger pot (e.g., low flush vs higher flush). Adjust the breakeven equity downward for good implied odds and upward when reverse implied odds are significant.
concepts.actionable_rule: Call draws that miss direct pot odds when implied odds are strong, but tighten when reverse implied odds threaten to cost you a big pot if you complete second-best.

concepts.title: Pot Committed
concepts.summary: You are pot committed when the pot odds your remaining stack offers exceed the odds against winning, making any fold incorrect.
concepts.details: When the remaining stack relative to the pot gives you better odds than your chance of winning, folding to any bet or raise is a mistake. Recognizing commitment prevents folding in spots where calling is mathematically forced.
concepts.actionable_rule: If the pot odds from your remaining stack exceed the odds against your hand winning, do not fold to any bet or raise.

concepts.title: Hand Strength Is Relative (No Absolute Ranking)
concepts.summary: Poker hands cannot be ranked in a vacuum because equity is intransitive — each hand's strength depends on the opponent's specific holding or range.
concepts.details: AKo beats JTs and 22 beats AKo, yet JTs beats 22 — a rock-paper-scissors relationship. Therefore you must evaluate hands against the actual opposing range rather than by some fixed strength order.
concepts.actionable_rule: Evaluate every hand by its equity against the opponent's specific range, never by an absolute hand-strength ranking.

concepts.title: Equity vs Range Drives Preflop All-In Calls
concepts.summary: Assign the opponent a range based on their tendencies, compute your equity against it, and call only if equity exceeds the required pot odds.
concepts.details: Facing a 10bb shove getting odds requiring 45% equity, QTo had only 43% vs a tight player's jamming range, so it is a fold. Against a looser range the same hand might have enough equity to call. The opponent's tightness directly changes the range and thus the decision.
concepts.actionable_rule: Assign the shover a range matched to their tightness, calculate your equity against it, and call only if that equity beats your required pot odds.

concepts.title: Range vs Range Equity Shifts by Board Texture
concepts.summary: Preflop range advantage can flip on certain flops; play cautiously when the texture favors the caller's range even if your specific hand is strong.
concepts.details: A CO range with 58.5% preflop equity dropped to 49.67% on 875ss, which connects strongly with the BB's calling range (straights, two pair, combo draws). On such boards, high-frequency c-betting invites check-raises and checking back lets the opponent attack later streets. Even AA should check back at high frequency on dynamic low boards to bluff-catch and call across turns and rivers.
concepts.actionable_rule: On boards that shift range equity toward the caller, reduce c-bet frequency and check back strong-but-vulnerable hands to bluff-catch rather than overcommitting.

concepts.title: Bluff-Catching with Unblocked Boards
concepts.summary: A bluff-catcher is stronger when your hand does not block the opponent's likely bluffs, making it more probable they are bluffing.
concepts.details: Holding AA on 875sJ2 with no hearts or spades means you don't block missed flush draws, so Villain is more likely to be bluffing missed draws. Not blocking obvious bluff candidates increases the value of calling a river bet.
concepts.actionable_rule: When deciding to call as a bluff-catcher, prefer calling with hands that do NOT block the opponent's missed draws, since this makes a bluff more likely.

concepts.title: Expected Value Decision Rule
concepts.summary: EV = (%win × $won) − (%lose × $risked); always choose the highest-EV action, and note folding is always 0 EV.
concepts.details: EV sums each outcome's probability times payoff. The EV calculation begins from the decision point — money already in the pot is not yours, so folding is always exactly 0 EV. With A5s having 43.31% equity for an 18bb win risking 13bb, calling yields +0.4bb versus 0 for folding, so call. These small repeated edges compound over thousands of hands.
concepts.actionable_rule: Compute EV = (equity × amount won) − ((1−equity) × amount risked) for each option and pick the highest; remember folding is always 0 EV.

concepts.title: Fold Equity in Bet/Shove EV
concepts.summary: Fold equity is the extra value gained from the chance an opponent folds; solve for the minimum fold frequency needed to make an aggressive line break even.
concepts.details: Set EV = 0 and solve for the required fold frequency using the pot won when they fold versus the equity and risk when called. With T5o shoving over a wide aggressive opener, the breakeven fold equity was 47–51%; estimating Villain folds 52% makes the shove barely +EV. Wide opening ranges are hard to defend and often over-fold to re-raises.
concepts.actionable_rule: Estimate the minimum fold frequency that makes a bet/shove breakeven, then take the aggressive line only when you believe the opponent folds at least that often.

concepts.title: Equity Realization Determines True Hand Value
concepts.summary: Raw equity overstates a hand's value out of position because not all equity is realized; multiply by an equity realization factor to get true EV.
concepts.details: EV ≈ Eq × EqR × Pot. Hands over-realize when they capture more than their equity share and under-realize otherwise. 95o had 29.5% raw equity (beating pot odds) but only ~58% EqR vs an UTG range, below the 61% needed to break even, making the call −EV. Out-of-position, multiway, and weak unpaired hands tend to under-realize; position and initiative increase EqR.
concepts.actionable_rule: Before calling, multiply raw equity by the hand's equity realization factor; call only if Eq × EqR captures more of the pot than the required pot odds, even when raw equity alone seems sufficient.

concepts.title: Position Improves Equity Realization
concepts.summary: Acting later in the hand lets you realize more of your equity, raising the EV of marginal hands.
concepts.details: Position is a primary driver of hand playability and equity realization. Hands played in position over-realize equity because you get more information and control the pot, whereas out-of-position hands under-realize. This is why identical equity can be a call in position and a fold out of position.
concepts.actionable_rule: Widen your continuing range when in position and tighten it out of position, since position raises the equity realization factor.

concepts.title: Value of Position via Last Action and Free Cards
concepts.summary: Acting last on every street lets you react to opponents and guarantees a free card when checked to, dramatically improving equity realization.
concepts.details: In position you observe the opponent's action before deciding, and if checked to you can check behind to see a free card. OOP you often check and then face a bet you must fold to, denying your equity. This is why marginal hands realize far more equity IP.
concepts.actionable_rule: Prefer playing more hands in position; OOP tighten ranges because you realize less equity, and check behind marginal made hands IP to guarantee showdown when appropriate.

concepts.title: Hand Strength Drives Playability
concepts.summary: High-equity and very low-equity hands are easy (bet/call or fold); medium-strength hands are hardest because they want showdown but fold to pressure.
concepts.details: High raw equity hands happily play big pots and can call or raise. Very low equity hands simply fold. Medium hands struggle: they want free cards or cheap showdowns but cannot withstand aggression, making equity realization difficult.
concepts.actionable_rule: With high-equity hands, build the pot via bets/raises; with very weak hands, fold; with medium hands, prioritize pot control and cheap showdowns and avoid bloating the pot.

concepts.title: Suitedness and Connectedness Boost Equity Realization
concepts.summary: Suited hands realize ~16% more equity than offsuit due to flush draws; disconnected offsuit hands like Q2o realize the least.
concepts.details: Suited hands gain front- and backdoor flush draws, enabling more effective semi-bluffs and better implied-odds calls. Offsuit hands with no connectivity flop weak pairs with poor kickers and limited draws, making equity realization poor.
concepts.actionable_rule: Weight hand selection toward suited and connected holdings for their superior equity realization, and downgrade disconnected offsuit hands.

concepts.title: Range Advantage Protects Weak Hands
concepts.summary: When your range is stronger than the opponent's, they cannot bet aggressively, allowing your weak hands to realize equity via free cards.
concepts.details: A range vs range equity advantage caps the opponent's aggression because over-betting risks running into your strong hands. This lets the weaker portion of your range see cheap cards it otherwise could not defend.
concepts.actionable_rule: Identify whether you hold the range advantage; if so, bet/apply pressure liberally and protect weak hands, since the opponent cannot aggressively attack your strong range.

concepts.title: SPR Determines Hand Class Value
concepts.summary: Low SPR favors top-pair/overpair made hands; medium and high SPR increase the value of speculative and 'nutty' hands.
concepts.details: SPR = effective stack / pot. Low SPR (0-5): made hands like top pairs/overpairs win, speculative hands lack fold equity and implied odds. Medium SPR (6-11): top pair value demoted, suitedness/connectedness matter more. High SPR (11+): nuttiness dominates—sets, nut draws, high flushes/straights gain value; single pairs struggle to reach showdown.
concepts.actionable_rule: Compute SPR and tailor bet sizes to reach a favorable SPR: commit with top-pair-type hands at low SPR, and favor nut-potential hands while pot-controlling single pairs at high SPR.

concepts.title: Range Morphology Classification
concepts.summary: Ranges are linear (top equity, no gaps), polarized (nuts + bluffs), or condensed/depolarized (middle equity, extremes removed).
concepts.details: A linear range is the highest-equity hands contiguously. A polarized range pairs strong value with low-equity bluffs (perfectly polar = only nuts and air). A condensed range removes the top and bottom, leaving medium-equity hands. These shapes dictate optimal betting and sizing.
concepts.actionable_rule: Classify your range shape before betting: bet polarized ranges large, bet linear/condensed ranges smaller for thin value and protection.

concepts.title: Capped vs Uncapped Ranges
concepts.summary: A capped range lacks the strongest hands; an uncapped range contains all the nuts. Capped ranges can be attacked aggressively.
concepts.details: On A J T, a preflop caller's range often lacks straights, sets, and top two pairs (capped), while the preflop raiser retains them (uncapped). A condensed range is always capped, but a capped range need not be condensed (e.g., 543 board where caller still has straights/two pairs).
concepts.actionable_rule: When your opponent's range is capped on a board favoring the nuts, apply heavy pressure including overbets; when your own range is capped, defend cautiously and avoid bloating pots.

concepts.title: Each Hand Played for Maximum EV (No Loss-Leaders)
concepts.summary: Both GTO and maximally exploitative play evaluate each hand independently for highest EV; there are no sacrificial 'balance' plays.
concepts.details: A maximally exploitative strategy is the most profitable response to a fixed opponent, found by playing each of the 1,326 combos in its highest-EV way. GTO inherits this: a hand is only played two ways (mixed) if both actions share identical EV. No hand is ever played less profitably 'for balance' or to protect range.
concepts.actionable_rule: Evaluate each hand combo independently; take the highest-EV action, and only mix a hand between actions when those actions have exactly equal EV.

concepts.title: Maximally Exploitative Strategy Against Fixed Opponents
concepts.summary: Against an opponent with a known fixed strategy, call/play every hand that is independently +EV and fold every -EV hand.
concepts.details: Versus a BN who shoves 100% for 10bb, the BB MES is to call all hands with at least ~45% equity (66.21% of hands), capturing 92% of the pot. The MES requires knowing the opponent's full strategy; it maximizes EV but is itself exploitable by counter-adjustment.
concepts.actionable_rule: When you know an opponent's fixed strategy, compute each hand's EV against it and call/shove all +EV hands and fold all -EV hands, ignoring balance.

concepts.title: Counter-Exploitation and Convergence to Nash
concepts.summary: Adaptive opponents counter your MES; iterating best-responses converges to Nash Equilibrium where neither can improve.
concepts.details: After BB adopts its MES, the BN can shove tighter (46.61%) to exploit it; BB then re-adjusts (30.3%), and so on. Iterating these best responses (or taking partial steps if oscillating) converges to Nash, where every strategy is simultaneously a best response and no unilateral change improves EV.
concepts.actionable_rule: Against thinking opponents, anticipate counter-adjustments; deviate from GTO to exploit but retreat toward equilibrium if the opponent counters your exploit.

concepts.title: GTO Provides a Guaranteed Minimum EV
concepts.summary: Equilibrium strategies are unexploitable: they guarantee at least the game's value regardless of opponent play and beat any non-equilibrium opponent.
concepts.details: In the push/fold game, playing GTO (call 37.4% vs a push) guarantees 10.45 chips no matter what the BN does, whereas guessing wrong about the opponent can drop EV to 8.48. GTO assumes the opponent knows your strategy and best-responds, so you can only break even or profit, and your EV increases as opponents play worse—though a perfect exploit earns more.
concepts.actionable_rule: Default to GTO baseline strategies against unknown or strong opponents to lock in a guaranteed minimum EV, then deviate exploitatively only when you have reads on specific leaks.

concepts.title: The Indifference Principle
concepts.summary: If a hand is played as a mixed strategy at equilibrium, all actions taken with nonzero frequency must have equal EV; your mixing reveals your opponent makes you indifferent.
concepts.details: Mixed-strategy hands sit exactly at the threshold between actions. The opponent's frequencies are set precisely to make the worst hand in your range break even—e.g., BN's bottom shove (43s) is mixed 74/26 because BB calls just enough to make it indifferent, and BB's bottom call (Q6s) is mixed because BN shoves just tightly enough.
concepts.actionable_rule: Set your defending/calling frequency so the bottom of the opponent's value/bluff range is exactly indifferent (break-even); mix marginal hands precisely at that threshold.

concepts.title: Optimal River Bluff-to-Value Ratio (Polarized Bettor)
concepts.summary: To make a bluff-catcher indifferent, bet a polarized range with a bluff frequency equal to the caller's pot odds; an all-in pot bet means betting 2 value for every 1 bluff (67/33).
concepts.details: In the clairvoyance toy game with a pot-sized all-in, the bettor must bluff at a frequency equal to the opponent's pot odds so calling breaks even. This yields a betting range of ~67% value, 33% bluffs (1 bluff per 2 value combos). With P1's polarized range (AA value, QQ bluff), QQ is bet 50% of the time to achieve this mix.
concepts.actionable_rule: On the river when betting polarized, set your bluff fraction equal to the opponent's pot odds—for a pot-sized bet, value:bluff = 2:1 (about 33% bluffs).

concepts.title: Larger Bets Allow More Bluffs; Position Captures Pot Value
concepts.summary: Bigger bet sizes give better pot odds to the caller and thus permit a higher bluff frequency; in the polarized toy game an all-in maximizes value, and the in-position player still captures only the smaller share.
concepts.details: Because bluff frequency equals the caller's pot odds, larger bets (worse pot odds for the caller) let the bettor include more bluffs. P1's optimal size is all-in. Even with 50/50 equity, the polarized OOP bettor captures $75 of a $100 pot while the IP bluff-catcher gets $25, showing equity alone does not equal EV.
concepts.actionable_rule: With a polarized range and the nuts advantage, bet large (up to all-in) to extract maximum value and justify a higher bluff frequency.

concepts.title: Minimum Defense Frequency and Alpha
concepts.summary: To stop the bettor from profitably bluffing any two cards, the defender must call enough that fold frequency does not exceed Alpha = bet/(bet+pot).
concepts.details: The bluff-catcher must call at a frequency that makes the bettor's bluffs break even versus checking—MDF. In the toy game P2 must call KK 50% (fold 50%) against a pot-sized all-in. Alpha = b/(b+pot) is how often a bluff must succeed to break even and equals the bettor's bluff-to-value ratio. Against a pot bet, fold no more than 50%.
concepts.actionable_rule: When facing a bet, defend at least MDF = pot/(pot+bet) of your range (fold no more than Alpha = bet/(pot+bet)) so the opponent cannot profitably bluff any hand.

concepts.title: Eliminate Dominated Strategies First
concepts.summary: Never fold the nuts, never call with a hand that cannot win, and don't bet hands that gain nothing—remove dominated actions before solving for frequencies.
concepts.details: In the toy game, folding AA (always wins) is dominated; calling with QQ (never wins) loses the bet amount and is dominated; betting KK accomplishes nothing since AA never folds and QQ never calls, and loses extra to AA. Strictly dominated strategies cannot be part of any Nash equilibrium.
concepts.actionable_rule: Before computing mixed frequencies, prune dominated actions: always bet the nuts, never call when you can't win, and don't bet a hand that cannot get worse hands to call or better hands to fold.

concepts.title: Polar vs Condensed Range: Bet Maximum Size
concepts.summary: When your range is perfectly polarized (nuts or air) and the opponent's range is condensed (only bluff-catchers), your optimal river bet size is as large as possible, ideally all-in.
concepts.details: In a nuts/air vs bluff-catcher spot, the bigger the bet, the more often you can bluff while remaining balanced, and the more of the pot you capture. The opponent only profits from the branch where you check, so maximizing bet size minimizes that branch. An infinite bet would capture 100% of the pot.
concepts.actionable_rule: On the river with a perfectly polar range against a condensed (bluff-catcher) range, bet all-in or as large as the stacks allow to maximize EV.

concepts.title: Alpha: Required Bluff Success Frequency
concepts.summary: Alpha = bet/(bet+pot) tells you how often a 0%-equity bluff must succeed (get a fold) to break even.
concepts.details: Alpha is the breakeven fold frequency for a pure bluff. It is the complement of MDF (MDF = 1 - Alpha). For example, a half-pot bet gives Alpha = 33%, meaning the bluff needs to work 33% of the time. Useful as a worst-case profitability check assuming zero equity when called.
concepts.actionable_rule: Compute Alpha = bet/(bet+pot); if the opponent folds more often than Alpha, a zero-equity bluff is immediately profitable.

concepts.title: Minimum Defense Frequency (MDF)
concepts.summary: The defender must continue with at least 1 - Alpha of their range to prevent the bettor from profitably bluffing with any two cards.
concepts.details: MDF = 1 - Alpha = pot/(pot+bet). Defending less than MDF lets the opponent profit by bluffing ATC. Note MDF is a theoretical floor; against capped/condensed ranges or in some spots GTO defense can deviate substantially (e.g. BB defending far above MDF in some preflop spots).
concepts.actionable_rule: When facing a bet with bluff-catchers, defend at least 1 - bet/(bet+pot) of your range; deviate only with specific reads.

concepts.title: Polar Range Value/Bluff Ratio by Bet Size
concepts.summary: A polarized betting range should contain value bets and bluffs in a ratio determined by the bet size, making the opponent indifferent to calling.
concepts.details: For a half-pot bet you offer 3-to-1 (25%) pot odds, so the range should be 75% value / 25% bluffs. The bluff frequency that keeps the opponent indifferent is b/(b+p) of value, derived from the indifference principle. Larger bets allow proportionally more bluffs.
concepts.actionable_rule: On the river, set your bluff-to-value ratio so the opponent is indifferent: for a half-pot bet use ~25% bluffs / 75% value, scaling bluffs up with larger bets.

concepts.title: Position Irrelevance in Nuts/Air vs Bluff-Catcher Games
concepts.summary: In a pure nuts/air vs bluff-catcher confrontation, position does not change the equilibrium strategies.
concepts.details: The bluff-catcher will never bet (dominated) and checks 100% regardless of position; the polar player always value-bets the nuts and bluffs at frequency b/(b+p). Position only matters when ranges are not so cleanly polar/condensed.
concepts.actionable_rule: In clean nuts/air vs bluff-catcher spots, apply the same betting and defending frequencies whether in or out of position.

concepts.title: Multiway Bluff Fold Requirement (Combined Folds)
concepts.summary: For a bluff to profit against multiple opponents, the combined fold frequency must exceed Alpha; combined folds equal the product of individual fold frequencies.
concepts.details: With N symmetric opponents each must fold at least Alpha^(1/N) for an ATC steal to profit; the combined required fold frequency is Alpha. For known individual fold rates, multiply them to get combined fold frequency and compare to Alpha. Each opponent's MDF = 1 - Alpha^(1/N).
concepts.actionable_rule: Before bluffing/stealing multiway, multiply each opponent's fold frequency; if the product exceeds Alpha = bet/(bet+pot), the zero-equity bluff profits.

concepts.title: Exploit Over-Tight Blind Defense by Stealing ATC
concepts.summary: If an opponent defends their blind well below MDF, you can profitably open-raise any two cards to steal.
concepts.details: Example: SB opens 2.5bb (Alpha ~43%) and a tight BB folds ~49%, so even with 72o and assuming zero equity when called, the steal yields ~27.4bb/100. The play is only profitable because Villain over-folds; the GTO BB defense in that spot was ~82%.
concepts.actionable_rule: When an opponent folds to your open more than Alpha, raise any two cards to steal; revert to a normal range once they tighten their folding leak.

concepts.title: Passive Exploitation via GTO
concepts.summary: Playing equilibrium automatically extracts EV from weaker opponents without any active deviation, because their mistakes transfer value to you.
concepts.details: In a heads-up subgame, a GTO player cannot lose EV; any deviation by the opponent to a worse strategy lowers their EV and, since poker is zero-sum, that value goes to the GTO player. The weak player self-exploits.
concepts.actionable_rule: When unsure how to exploit or facing capable opponents, default to a sound GTO strategy and let opponents lose EV against you automatically.

concepts.title: Maximally Exploitative Strategy (MES) and Counter-Exploit Risk
concepts.summary: MES maximizes EV against a known leak but creates large unbalanced exposure that can be counter-exploited for far more than it gains.
concepts.details: Example: shoving 100% vs a nit gains ~24.6bb/100 but can be counter-exploited for -62.4bb/100. On average MES gains ~6.4bb/100 over GTO but risks -15.62bb/100 if counter-adjusted. MES requires high read certainty and an opponent unlikely to adapt, since the deviation is easy to spot.
concepts.actionable_rule: Only deploy a maximally exploitative deviation when highly confident in the read and the opponent is unlikely to adapt; abandon it the moment they could counter-exploit.

concepts.title: Minimally Exploitative Strategy (MinES)
concepts.summary: MinES makes a small, robust deviation that captures part of a leak's value while remaining safe from counter-exploitation.
concepts.details: Instead of fully exploiting (e.g. bluffing 0% vs a loose caller), you adjust frequency only enough to bake the leak into the equilibrium (e.g. dropping QQ bluffs from 50% to 45% when Villain calls 55%). It yields less than MES but is unexploitable. Solve it by locking the assumed leak in a solver and letting Villain play optimally elsewhere.
concepts.actionable_rule: Against a small known leak, make a small frequency adjustment that captures extra EV but keeps you unexploitable; use a solver with the leak locked in to find it.

concepts.title: Reactive vs Proactive MinES
concepts.summary: Adjust either after observing a leak occur in the hand (reactive) or in anticipation of the leak before it happens (proactive); use both together.
concepts.details: Example vs a player who overfolds to flop c-bets: proactively increase c-bet frequency, then reactively tighten your read of their range on turn/river since their continuing range is now stronger and your own range is wider than normal.
concepts.actionable_rule: Against a known leak, proactively widen the action that exploits it and reactively re-weight opponent ranges on later streets for the resulting tighter continues.

concepts.title: GTO Reduces to Heads-Up Subgames
concepts.summary: Nash Equilibrium guarantees unbeatability once only two players remain in the pot, even in multiway games.
concepts.details: Common spots reduce to heads-up subgames (e.g. CO opens, BN 3-bets, blinds fold). At that point a GTO player cannot be beaten even if the opponent knows the strategy. With three or more active players, equilibrium offers only near-unexploitable starting points and EV losses from a player's mistakes are distributed unevenly.
concepts.actionable_rule: Apply rigorous GTO play once the pot is down to two players; in genuinely multiway spots treat GTO as a strong baseline, not a guarantee.

concepts.title: Multiway Mistakes Can Cost Innocent Players EV
concepts.summary: In multiway pots, one player's error does not distribute its EV evenly; a third player can lose EV even while playing equilibrium.
concepts.details: Example: a fish under-pushing from the BN causes the SB to lose -4.5bb/100 even playing GTO, and only recover part of it via MES; the BB captures most of the freed EV. Over many hands positional rotation balances this out.
concepts.actionable_rule: In multiway pots don't assume a fish's mistake benefits you; evaluate which seat captures the freed EV and adjust, relying on positional rotation over time.

concepts.title: Normalize Pot and Bets for Quick Math
concepts.summary: Express the pot as 1 and bets as fractions of the pot to quickly compute Alpha, MDF, and required ratios.
concepts.details: A $20 bet into a $60 pot is 1/3 pot. From the fraction you immediately read Alpha = size/(1+size) and MDF = 1-Alpha. This simplifies in-game pot-odds, bluff-frequency, and defense calculations.
concepts.actionable_rule: Convert every bet to a fraction of the pot and compute Alpha = b/(b+p) on the fly to drive bluffing and defending decisions.

concepts.title: Pre-flop Mistakes Propagate Through the Hand
concepts.summary: Pre-flop errors create systematic error that carries through to the flop, turn, and river decisions, compounding losses.
concepts.details: Because each street builds on the previous one, an incorrect pre-flop range introduces a mistake that affects every subsequent decision point and is difficult to compensate for later. Sound pre-flop ranges are the foundation of correct postflop play.
concepts.actionable_rule: Prioritize accuracy in pre-flop range construction since errors there compound into flop, turn, and river mistakes; build hand strategies starting from a solid pre-flop foundation.

concepts.title: Maximize Win Rate by Taking the Highest-EV Action
concepts.summary: Overall win rate is the aggregate EV of every hand in every position, so maximizing it means always choosing the highest-EV action for each hand at each decision point.
concepts.details: Win rate (bb/100) equals the sum of the EVs of all hands dealt across all positions and actions taken. Since the EV of folding is 0, any action with negative EV should be folded. Against a GTO opponent, choosing anything other than the highest-EV action for a given hand can only lower your win rate.
concepts.actionable_rule: For each hand at each decision point, compute the EV of every available action and take the highest-EV one; fold any hand whose best available action has negative EV (worse than the 0 EV of folding).

concepts.title: Win Rate Determined by Opponent Skill — Game Selection Matters
concepts.summary: Your win rate depends on opponents' skill, so a softer lower-stakes game can yield more money and less variance than a tougher higher-stakes game.
concepts.details: If all players are equally skilled, win rates are zero and everyone loses to rake. A 2bb/100 edge in a tough $10/$20 game ($40/100 hands) is worse than a 10bb/100 edge in a softer $2/$5 game ($50/100 hands), and the softer game also has lower variance because higher edge reduces swings. Live games are usually softer than online games.
concepts.actionable_rule: Select games where your edge (win rate) is highest in absolute dollar terms, favoring softer fields even at lower stakes to maximize earnings and minimize variance.

concepts.title: Position Determines Profitability
concepts.summary: Win rate varies by seat: the button is most profitable because it plays the most hands profitably, while the blinds always have negative baseline win rates.
concepts.details: If a 6-max pot's value were split equally, each seat would earn 25bb/100, but win rates decline as position moves away from the button. The BB starts at -100bb/100 and SB at -50bb/100 due to forced posts, so blinds can never match other positions. To break even you must recover -150bb/100 lost to blinds each orbit plus rake.
concepts.actionable_rule: Play wider, more aggressive ranges from late position (especially the button) and tighter from the blinds, accounting for the structural disadvantage of the forced posts.

concepts.title: Verify GTO Proximity Using Nash Distance (Epsilon)
concepts.summary: A strategy's closeness to true equilibrium is measured by Nash distance (epsilon): the maximum EV gain either player achieves by switching to their maximally exploitative strategy.
concepts.details: Compute each player's MES (maximally exploitative strategy) EV gain against the other; the larger of the two gains is the Nash distance. Zero means exact GTO. When epsilon is very small, the strategy is practically unexploitable because an opponent would need perfect knowledge of your exact strategy at every node and flawless execution of their MES to extract it. Practical thresholds: ~0.35% pot for flop solutions and ~3.5bb/100 for pre-flop simulations.
concepts.actionable_rule: When deriving or trusting a GTO strategy, run solver simulations until Nash distance is small (e.g., ~0.35% of pot postflop or ~3.5bb/100 preflop) and treat the result as effectively unexploitable for human play.

concepts.title: Nash Calculator Abstractions Distort Deep-Stack Ranges
concepts.summary: Push/fold Nash calculators only produce correct strategies for shallow stacks; forcing them onto deeper stacks via abstraction biases ranges incorrectly.
concepts.details: Removing the calling option forces tighter defending ranges, making the calculator suggest opening ranges that are too wide and overly blocker-focused while ignoring postflop playability. Allowing calls but checking down postflop lets callers realize 100% equity with marginal hands, producing calling ranges that are too wide. Both distortions limit Nash calculators to genuine push/fold (shallow-stack) spots.
concepts.actionable_rule: Use Nash push/fold calculators only for shallow-stack all-in decisions; for stacks deep enough to have non-all-in bet sizes, rely on postflop-capable solvers instead.

concepts.title: Solvers Provide Core GTO, Not Exploits
concepts.summary: GTO solvers and AI tools output an unexploitable core strategy but cannot compute exploitative adjustments against weak players.
concepts.details: Tools like PioSOLVER, MonkerSolver, and self-play AIs (e.g., Snowie) provide a baseline equilibrium strategy. Self-play AIs reinforce winning lines but don't actually solve for GTO and can't guarantee unexploitability or explain their reasoning. None of these tools deviate to exploit specific opponent leaks, so maximizing EV against weak players requires manually deviating from the solver baseline.
concepts.actionable_rule: Use the solver's GTO output as a baseline default, then deliberately deviate toward exploitative lines when you have a read on an opponent's specific weakness, since solvers won't make those adjustments for you.

concepts.title: Blinds and Antes Force Action
concepts.summary: Forced bets create dead money that incentivizes players to contest pots with hands beyond premiums.
concepts.details: Without blinds/antes, optimal play would be to wait for AA (or hands with correct implied odds against it). The money already in the pot makes a range of hands profitable to play. In ante games an ante of 12.5% of the BB is equivalent to -12.5bb/100 that must also be recovered, widening profitable ranges further.
concepts.actionable_rule: Widen your playable ranges in proportion to the dead money in the pot (blinds plus antes), opening more hands in ante structures than in non-ante games.

concepts.title: +EV Is Not Enough — Compare All Actions
concepts.summary: A play being profitable does not make it correct; the correct play is the one with the highest EV among all available options.
concepts.details: PioSOLVER examples show going all-in with AA is +EV but -136bb/100 worse than raising to 2.5bb, making it a bigger mistake than pushing 72o (-63bb/100). Always evaluate every legal action's EV before choosing.
concepts.actionable_rule: For every decision, compute or estimate the EV of all available actions and choose the maximum-EV option rather than any merely positive one.

concepts.title: Complex Strategies Beat Push/Fold as Stacks Deepen
concepts.summary: Adding limping and multiple raise sizings to a push/fold baseline captures more EV, especially in position and at deeper stacks.
concepts.details: Solver comparison shows a complex strategy gains +7bb/100 (4.62% pot) OOP and +22bb/100 (14.6% pot) IP vs pure push/fold. The gap is small at very shallow stacks but grows as stacks deepen and with positional advantage.
concepts.actionable_rule: Use push/fold only at very shallow stacks (~10bb and under); as stacks deepen and especially when in position, add limping and varied raise sizings to widen your profitable range.

concepts.title: Push More From the SB to Offset OOP Disadvantage
concepts.summary: All-in frequency is much higher in the SB/OOP than on the BN/IP because shoving removes the disadvantage of playing out of position.
concepts.details: Going all-in eliminates post-flop play where being OOP costs equity. BN rarely pushes above 17bb (3.88% at 15bb, 0.69% at 20bb) while SB push frequencies remain high. Limping is dominant for the BN and should never be removed.
concepts.actionable_rule: When OOP and short, prefer pushing over limping to neutralize position; when IP, retain a dominant limping strategy and only shove when very short.

concepts.title: Increase OOP Bet-Size as Stacks Get Deeper
concepts.summary: When out of position the optimal open size grows with stack depth: min-raise when short, larger raises when deep.
concepts.details: SB (3-max) solver: min-raise dominant at short stacks, 2.5x dominant from 15bb, 3x appearing at 20bb and dominant at 25bb. The BN (IP) only ever uses a 2bb min-raise, so larger sizings benefit the OOP player but add little value IP.
concepts.actionable_rule: When opening out of position, scale your raise size up as stacks deepen (min-raise short, ~2.5x mid, ~3x at 25bb); when in position, default to a min-raise.

concepts.title: Simplify Strategies to Minimize Mistakes
concepts.summary: Drop rarely-used, low-EV strategic options because the implementation cost and mistake risk can outweigh their tiny EV gain.
concepts.details: Adding too many low-frequency options can hurt overall expectation by increasing complexity and errors. Example: BN can stop pushing entirely at 15bb+ with negligible EV loss, but removing BN limps would significantly hurt EV. Identify which options carry real EV before pruning.
concepts.actionable_rule: Prune strategic options whose frequency and EV contribution are near zero, but never remove a dominant high-EV option (e.g. BN limping); keep strategies as simple as possible without sacrificing meaningful EV.

concepts.title: Simplify Against Superior Opponents
concepts.summary: Against a stronger player, adopt a simpler strategy to deny them the chance to outplay you with complex options.
concepts.details: Complex multi-option play benefits whoever exploits the options better — usually the stronger player. Reducing decision points (e.g. getting all-in preflop with AJs vs TT, ~50% equity) caps a superior opponent's edge regardless of their skill.
concepts.actionable_rule: When facing an opponent with a clear skill edge, reduce strategic complexity and favor all-in/binary decisions to neutralize their post-flop advantage.

concepts.title: Memorize Preset Preflop Ranges
concepts.summary: Come to the table with preset, well-constructed RFI ranges so brainpower is freed for complex decisions and you recognize standard spots instantly.
concepts.details: Like chess opening memorization, knowing standard ranges (e.g. EP RFI excludes JTo) prevents hesitation and lets you spot when to deviate to exploit weaknesses. Solid balanced ranges also give better board coverage and post-flop playability.
concepts.actionable_rule: Memorize a solid baseline RFI range for each position and use it as default, deviating only deliberately to exploit identified opponent weaknesses.

concepts.title: Absolute Hand Strength Components
concepts.summary: Hand value derives from high card strength, pocket pair rank, suitedness, and connectedness; the best hands have at least two of these.
concepts.details: Higher cards and higher pairs are stronger; suited beats offsuit (more equity, disguised nut flushes, e.g. A5s>A5o); connected beats gapped (T9 makes more and more often nut straights than T8/T7). Hands lacking one trait compensate with others (87s connected/suited, AKo high-card).
concepts.actionable_rule: Rank hands by combining high-card value, pair rank, suitedness and connectedness; require at least two strong components for a hand to be playable.

concepts.title: Position Determines Range Width via 3-Bet Risk
concepts.summary: The more players left to act, the more often you get 3-bet, so earlier positions must open tighter and later positions can open wider.
concepts.details: Roughly each player behind 3-bets ~7%. At 9-max UTG with 8 players behind, expect ~44% chance of facing a 3-bet, making weak hands like Q7s -EV (-26bb/100). With Q7s, opening becomes -EV above ~37.5% 3-bet frequency; only the SB heads-up rarely faces such a high 3-bet rate.
concepts.actionable_rule: Tighten your opening range in early position and widen it in late position in proportion to how often you expect to be 3-bet by the remaining players.

concepts.title: Bet-Size Caps Profitable Range Width
concepts.summary: Larger open sizes risk more on your weakest hands when you face a re-raise, so bigger sizes mean fewer hands can be profitably opened.
concepts.details: The bottom of an opening range is near-indifferent; betting larger increases the loss when steals fail and you must fold to a 3-bet. Smaller sizes let you open wider since failed steals cost less.
concepts.actionable_rule: Match your opening size to your range width — use smaller sizes if you want to open wide, and tighten your range if you choose to open larger.

concepts.title: Exploit Under-Defenders by Opening Wider
concepts.summary: If opponents fold too often (defend below MDF), you can profitably open far more hands, sometimes any two cards.
concepts.details: When villains don't defend or 3-bet enough, your steals succeed too often, making even trash +EV. Against optimal opponents who play back correctly there is a hard cap on profitable opening hands. Q7s open is fine vs a SB BB but unprofitable if 3-bet >37.5%.
concepts.actionable_rule: Against opponents who under-defend their blinds or under-3-bet, expand your opening range well beyond GTO, up to any-two in extreme cases.

concepts.title: Tighten and Raise More as Rake Increases
concepts.summary: Rake reduces every hand's profitability, turning marginal hands -EV, so higher rake demands tighter ranges and more aggression to win pots outright.
concepts.details: Solver comparison (heads-up $5/$10, 4.3% rake): BN raise rises 70.1%→76.4%, limp falls 18.3%→6.9%, fold rises 11.6%→16.7%. BB facing 2.5x: 3-bet 19.9%→22.7%, call 55%→45%, fold 25%→32.3%. Tournaments have no in-game rake so allow more passive play; cash games use larger sizings to discourage calls.
concepts.actionable_rule: In raked games, tighten overall ranges, reduce limping and calling, and favor aggressive pot-taking actions; the higher the rake, the greater the shift toward raising and folding.

concepts.title: Bunching Effect Tightens Late-Position Pushing Ranges
concepts.summary: After many folds, weak hands are removed from the deck, raising the chance remaining players hold strong cards, so late positions must push slightly tighter than naive calculators suggest.
concepts.details: With MonkerSolver (12.5% ante): vs HRC the SB must push ~4.9% tighter, BN 2.2%, CO 1.7%, HJ 0.9%, LJ 0.3%. Effect grows with more prior folds, so it's near zero in early position and largest in the blinds.
concepts.actionable_rule: Tighten push/fold ranges relative to standard calculators in late position (most in the SB, ~5%), and ignore the bunching effect in early position where it approaches zero.

concepts.title: Limping Trade-offs and When It's Viable
concepts.summary: Limping plays more hands cheaply but forces post-flop play OOP, lets opponents realize equity, and splits/caps your range giving away information.
concepts.details: Limping only weak hands lets opponents exploit board hits/misses; limping only medium hands invites aggression since you can't re-raise; balancing requires limping strong hands which weakens your raising range and caps it after limp/calls. Solvers favor limping mainly in rake-free blind-vs-blind spots (tournaments). In modern games where populations under-defend and over-fold to c-bets, raising remains dominant.
concepts.actionable_rule: Default to raising rather than limping; reserve a balanced limping range mainly for rake-free blind-vs-blind situations, and avoid limping against populations that over-fold where raising captures more value.

concepts.title: Isolating Weak-Passive Limpers Wide
concepts.summary: Against limpers who rarely raise and check-fold when they miss, isolation-raise a very wide range and win post-flop with high frequency.
concepts.details: How wide depends on the table: if players behind 3-bet aggressively, iso closer to your normal RFI range; if they call wide leading to multiway pots, prefer hands that play well multiway (suited connectors, pocket pairs, Axs); if players behind are passive/unaware, iso almost anything with playability.
concepts.actionable_rule: When a weak-passive player open-limps, raise to isolate with a wide range; widen toward any playable hand if players behind are passive, and tighten toward your normal open range if they 3-bet often.

concepts.title: Value-Town Against Sticky Limpers
concepts.summary: Against limpers who hate folding, choose hands that flop strong top pairs and value-bet them relentlessly, avoiding pure bluffs.
concepts.details: Any top pair and most second pairs are good enough to value-bet three streets against calling stations. Semi-bluffing is fine but if your draw bricks the river, give up rather than firing stone-cold bluffs—these players call down with bottom pair.
concepts.actionable_rule: Versus a sticky limper, iso with hands that make strong top pairs and value-bet three streets; never run pure river bluffs and give up when draws miss.

concepts.title: Don't Iso Aggressive Limpers Too Wide
concepts.summary: Against limpers who check-raise and lead, tighten your isolation range to strong hands and pot-control medium hands.
concepts.details: Use a range of strong hands that can stand heat. Check your medium-strength hands to control pot size and bluff-catch more efficiently; with a good-but-not-great hand, be willing to play for stacks.
concepts.actionable_rule: Versus an aggressive limper, isolate only with strong hands, pot-control medium holdings by checking, and be willing to stack off with good-but-not-great hands.

concepts.title: Counter Trappy Limp-Raisers by Over-Limping
concepts.summary: Against limpers who limp strong hands to limp-raise, over-limp speculative hands or raise a polarized range built to withstand 3-bets.
concepts.details: The threat of a limp-raise deters others from raising behind, letting you play well postflop against a face-up range. When you do raise, use a polarized range of hands that can withstand a 3-bet plus good-blocker hands you happily raise-fold.
concepts.actionable_rule: Versus a trappy limp-raiser, over-limp suited/connected hands and small pairs, or raise a polarized range of strong stand-the-heat hands plus blocker raise-folds.

concepts.title: Open-Shove Width by Position and Stack
concepts.summary: All-in steals realize 100% equity but risk your stack; shove tighter from earlier position and with deeper stacks.
concepts.details: More players left to act and more chips at risk both demand a tighter pushing range. Example: 10bb 9-max UTG can push 14.4% vs SB 74.7%; at 12bb BN pushes 41.5% but only 37.2% at 15bb. Under ~10bb you can push from any position.
concepts.actionable_rule: With short stacks, open-shove tighter the earlier your position and the deeper your stack; under 10bb you can shove from any position.

concepts.title: Range Shape for Shove vs Raise Strategies
concepts.summary: A pure shoving range should be linear (top equity hands); a split shove/raise/fold strategy uses a condensed shove range and a polar raise range.
concepts.details: When shoving your entire range, use linear top-equity hands. When splitting, shove condensed hands too good to raise-fold but not good enough to raise-call with good equity when called (Axs, Q9s, 87s); keep the non-all-in raise range polar with blocker hands (Axo) you'll fold to a push plus premiums (KK) you raise-call.
concepts.actionable_rule: If shoving your whole range make it linear; if splitting, shove a condensed middling-equity range and raise a polar range of blockers (fold to push) plus premiums (call push).

concepts.title: Position and Range Width Drive Open Sizing
concepts.summary: Use smaller opens from early position and larger opens with wider ranges.
concepts.details: Earlier positions face greater threat of re-raising hands waking up, so size smaller. Wider ranges warrant bigger sizing because more of opponents' hands have correct equity to call a given size against a wide range. Bigger bets faced mean fewer hands needed to defend unexploitably.
concepts.actionable_rule: Size opens smaller from early position and larger as your opening range widens; when facing a larger bet, defend fewer hands.

concepts.title: Never Size by Hand Strength
concepts.summary: Bet sizing should vary by situation (position, stack depth) but never by hand strength, to avoid leaking information about your range.
concepts.details: Changing size based on your holding telegraphs your range and lets opponents exploit your hand distribution. Multiple sizes are fine across different positions or stack depths.
concepts.actionable_rule: Keep one sizing per situation; never change bet size based on whether you hold value or bluffs.

concepts.title: Min-Raise Against Rejam Stacks, Bigger When Deep
concepts.summary: When opponents have good rejamming depth (under ~25bb) min-raise to give them the worst all-in price; size up when stacks are deep.
concepts.details: Min-raising denies short stacks good odds on their all-in re-raises. Deeper stacks get better implied odds with speculative hands, so larger sizing discourages calls, especially from in-position opponents.
concepts.actionable_rule: Min-raise opens when opponents are in rejam range (<25bb); use larger opens against deep stacks to deny implied odds, especially to IP players.

concepts.title: OOP Sizes Up, IP Sizes Down
concepts.summary: Bet larger out of position to reduce SPR and the opponent's positional edge; bet smaller in position since you retain positional advantage.
concepts.details: Larger OOP sizing lowers SPR, blunting the in-position player's later-street edge. In position, smaller bets keep your advantage even when called, but give opponents a better price and let them defend more hands.
concepts.actionable_rule: Size up when out of position to cut SPR; size down in position to retain positional advantage, accepting that opponents defend wider.

concepts.title: Minimum Size for Polar Re-Raise vs Raise-or-Fold Opponents
concepts.summary: When 3-betting a polarized range against an opponent who only re-raises or folds, use the smallest sizing to minimize losses on your raise-folds.
concepts.details: Since the opponent rarely flats, you'll fold your bluff portion frequently; a minimum size reduces the cost of those raise-folds while still applying pressure.
concepts.actionable_rule: When re-raising polar against an opponent who only re-raises or folds, use the minimum legal size to minimize losses on your raise-fold hands.

concepts.title: Pick Sizes That Take Opponents Off Their Comfort Tree
concepts.summary: Among EV-equivalent sizings, choose the one that pushes opponents into unfamiliar branches of the game tree where they make the most mistakes.
concepts.details: Solvers are roughly indifferent between similar sizes when opponents respond optimally, but real opponents respond differently and imperfectly to different sizes. Exploit this by selecting sizes they handle poorly.
concepts.actionable_rule: When sizing options are EV-similar, pick the size your specific opponent responds to worst.

concepts.title: Tighten When Players Have Entered the Pot
concepts.summary: Your range must be strong relative to both random hands yet to act and the distribution of any player who already entered the pot.
concepts.details: If a player limps or enters, the CO's raising range must be tighter than its RFI because it now must beat the limper's distribution too. Always weigh the strength of already-committed ranges.
concepts.actionable_rule: Tighten your entering range when a player is already in the pot so you remain strong against both their range and the random hands behind.

concepts.title: Over-Fold to 3-Bets When Opening Wider Than Standard
concepts.summary: When you've exploitatively widened your open, fold all off-range hands (and the bottom of your normal calling range) to a 3-bet.
concepts.details: You profit because the opponent doesn't 3-bet enough to punish your extra hands; once they do 3-bet, those off-range hands have negative EV, so fold them plus marginal regular continues.
concepts.actionable_rule: After widening opens exploitatively, fold all off-range hands and even the bottom of your normal continuing range when 3-bet.

concepts.title: Widen Opens vs Tight Blinds
concepts.summary: The BN, SB and BB matter most for opening marginal hands; widen steals when those positions are tight.
concepts.details: These positions are most likely to give action. If they are tight and overfold to opens, marginal hands become profitable steals; BN opens can expand to 55-60%+ versus bad passive blinds.
concepts.actionable_rule: Widen your opening range, especially from late position, when the BN/SB/BB are tight and overfold to steals.

concepts.title: Exploit Frequency Leaks by Adding Threshold Hands First
concepts.summary: To exploit overfolders, first push mixed-strategy threshold hands to 100%, then add adjacent borderline hands rather than random junk.
concepts.details: Threshold hands are the first to become profitable against leaks. If A9o is bet 25% baseline, bet it 100% vs an overfolder, then add A8o/A7o (not Q4o). This is harder to detect and the added hands keep useful blockers so they're less -EV if you're wrong or counter-exploited.
concepts.actionable_rule: To attack a leak, first take your mixed threshold hands to 100% of the exploitative action, then add the next-closest borderline hands, never random off-range hands.

concepts.title: Randomize Mixed-Strategy Decisions
concepts.summary: When two actions are EV-equal, use a randomizer to mix at the GTO frequency and stay unpredictable.
concepts.details: For a 50/50 mixed hand, use a coin, RNG, clock seconds, or hole-card suit/color as a randomizer. Randomizing matters more online (HUD samples) than live, where soft games and live reads make decisions more binary.
concepts.actionable_rule: For indifferent hands with a mixed GTO solution, use a randomizer to hit the prescribed frequency; lean toward reads/binary choices live.

concepts.title: Think Ahead to Avoid Tough Spots
concepts.summary: Before acting, plan responses to likely re-raises; if you wouldn't know what to do facing aggression, take the lower-variance line instead.
concepts.details: If 3-betting a medium hand but unsure how to react to a 4-bet, just call. Likewise postflop: if unsure what to do facing a raise, check. Before opening, consider who acts behind, their re-raise tendency, and whether you're happy stacking off; if too good to 4-bet/fold, just call a 3-bet.
concepts.actionable_rule: Plan your response to a raise before acting; if you wouldn't know how to continue against aggression, choose call/check instead of bet/raise.

concepts.title: Use Charts as Guidance, Reason From Principles
concepts.summary: GTO charts are starting points; understand the underlying principles (pot odds, equity, SPR, polarization, MDF, board coverage) rather than memorizing.
concepts.details: The goal is to 'become the solver' by internalizing why hands are played a given way, so you can adapt to specific games. Baseline 6-max 100bb strategies must be adjusted to actual opponents.
concepts.actionable_rule: Treat solver charts as guidelines; derive decisions from core principles (equity, pot odds, SPR, polarization, MDF, board coverage) and adjust to the specific game.

concepts.title: Split SB Range Into Limp and Raise
concepts.summary: From the SB unopened, play a split limp/raise strategy to exploit the discount while keeping raise frequency low and using a larger raise size.
concepts.details: Baseline SB RFI: raise 3x ~24.4%, limp ~37.7%, fold ~37.9%. Limping plays more hands using the price discount while keeping raises infrequent so BB's 3-bets are less effective. The SB uses a bigger open size because it is OOP and wants to discourage calls.
concepts.actionable_rule: From the SB unopened, split into a limping range (~38%) and a larger-sized (3x) raising range (~24%) to use the discount while keeping raises low.

concepts.title: Raise-or-Fold From All Positions Except SB
concepts.summary: In raked cash games, limp only from the SB; from every other position play raise-or-fold.
concepts.details: Rake makes open-limping unprofitable, and non-SB positions get no price discount. Limping invites callers (worse multiway pots) and raises behind that deny equity. Raise-or-fold keeps your range protected and easily defensible against 3-bets.
concepts.actionable_rule: In raked cash games, never open-limp outside the SB; from all other positions play a raise-or-fold strategy.

concepts.title: Opening Ranges Tighten as Players Act Behind
concepts.summary: RFI width shrinks the earlier your position because more players can wake up with re-raising hands.
concepts.details: Baseline 6-max RFI: BN ~43.4%, CO ~27.8%, HJ ~21.4%, LJ ~17%. The CO must worry about the BN's position; HJ has four players behind, two with position; each earlier seat trims small pairs, weak broadways, suited connectors and weak suited Kx/Qx.
concepts.actionable_rule: Open progressively tighter from earlier positions (roughly BN 43% > CO 28% > HJ 21% > LJ 17%), trimming speculative and weak hands as more players act behind you.

concepts.title: 4-Bet Polar With Position, Call More Without
concepts.summary: In position vs a 3-bet, defend mostly by calling with a polar 4-bet range; out of position, 4-bet more and call less.
concepts.details: With position you keep advantage on later streets so flatting is strong and 4-bets are polar (blockers plus premiums). OOP (e.g. CO vs BN 3-bet) you 4-bet more to take it down or force low SPR, since playing OOP postflop realizes equity poorly. Stacking-off ranges vs 5-bets are tight (e.g. 66+, AK+).
concepts.actionable_rule: Facing a 3-bet in position, call most continues and 4-bet a polar blocker/premium range; out of position, 4-bet more, call less, and stack off only with a tight range like 66+/AK+.

concepts.title: Call Wider vs Polarized 3-Betting Ranges
concepts.summary: Your opening range realizes more equity against polarized 3-bet ranges, so call wider against opponents whose 3-bets are polar.
concepts.details: Open ranges have better equity/playability versus polar ranges, making more hands profitable calls. The BN's 3-bets are more polarized than the CO's (since BN has a flat-call range), so defend wider by calling against BN 3-bets than against CO 3-bets.
concepts.actionable_rule: Call wider against more polarized 3-betting ranges (e.g. BN) and tighter against linear/merged 3-bet ranges (e.g. CO) since your opens fare better versus polar ranges.

concepts.title: Tighten RFI ranges in early position due to players left to act
concepts.summary: Open fewer hands from earlier positions because more players remain who can 3-bet or play in position, hurting equity realization.
concepts.details: From the LJ you open ~17% hands vs ~43% from the BN. With five players behind, three of whom have position, you must select high-equity hands with good blockers plus a small portion of suited connectors and small pairs for board coverage. A range you can't defend at least ~48% of versus 3-bets is too wide for the position.
concepts.actionable_rule: Open roughly 17% from LJ, ~21% from HJ/CO, and progressively wider toward the button; never open a range so wide that you cannot defend ~48% of it against 3-bets.

concepts.title: Defend enough vs 3-bets to make villain indifferent
concepts.summary: You must continue against 3-bets often enough that opponents cannot profitably 3-bet the bottom of their range as a bluff.
concepts.details: The only deterrent to relentless 3-betting is your ability to 4-bet plus the chance another player comes over the top. Folding more than your minimum defense frequency allows lets opponents print with bluff 3-bets. Tighter opening ranges (e.g. BN) are easier to defend than wide ones (e.g. UTG), which is another reason to open tighter from early position.
concepts.actionable_rule: When facing a 3-bet, continue (call+4-bet) with enough combos to make villain's bottom-range bluff 3-bets break even; fold no more than your minimum defense frequency requires.

concepts.title: Calling-range vs 3-bet hand selection
concepts.summary: Suited broadways, suited connectors and pocket pairs make good 3-bet-pot calls; offsuit broadways and weak Ax should be folded.
concepts.details: 3-bet pots reward equity realization and good implied/reverse-implied odds. Suited broadways, suited connectors and pairs realize equity well and play well postflop. Offsuit broadways and weak Ax realize poorly and have bad reverse implied odds, so they fold rather than call.
concepts.actionable_rule: Against a 3-bet, call with suited broadways, suited connectors and pocket pairs; fold offsuit broadways and weak Ax rather than call them.

concepts.title: Calling is wider vs polarized 3-bet ranges than vs linear ones
concepts.summary: When villain's 3-bet range is polarized you can call more hands because you are dominated less often.
concepts.details: A polarized 3-bet range contains nut hands and bluffs but few medium hands, so your calling hands face fewer dominating combos and get better post-flop playability and equity. Against a linear 3-bet range you are dominated more often, so you should call less and 4-bet/fold more.
concepts.actionable_rule: Widen your flat-calling range against polarized 3-bet ranges; tighten it (4-bet or fold more) against linear 3-bet ranges.

concepts.title: Choose 4-bet range shape by villain's reaction to 4-bets
concepts.summary: 4-bet polarized if villain folds to 4-bets, linear if they call wide, and 4-bet/call wider if they 5-bet jam wide.
concepts.details: Assess how villain responds to 4-bets before exploiting a high 3-bet frequency. If they fold most of the time, 4-bet a polarized range using good blocker bluffs like A5s. If they call wide and only 5-bet premiums, 4-bet a linear value range to extract value and have a strong postflop range. If they 5-bet jam wide, expand your 4-bet/call-off range to include hands like AQ.
concepts.actionable_rule: Before 4-betting, classify villain's 4-bet response: fold-heavy → 4-bet polarized with blocker bluffs (A5s); call-heavy → 4-bet linear for value; jam-heavy → 4-bet/call-off wider (e.g. AQ).

concepts.title: 3-bet size dictates how much you defend
concepts.summary: Defend more hands against smaller 3-bets and fewer against larger ones.
concepts.details: Minimum defense scales inversely with the price of continuing. Against small 3-bet sizes you get a better price, so call more; against large 3-bet sizes you need to fold more and defend fewer combos to remain unexploitable.
concepts.actionable_rule: Calibrate defense to the 3-bet size: the smaller the 3-bet, the more hands you call; the larger the 3-bet, the fewer hands you defend.

concepts.title: Cold 4-bet rather than cold call after open + 3-bet
concepts.summary: When action reaches you after an open and a 3-bet, 4-bet or fold rather than splitting into a cold-calling range.
concepts.details: Splitting into cold-call and cold-4-bet ranges gives away information and lets active players profitably realize equity by calling hands they'd fold to a 4-bet. Better to cold 4-bet your entire continuing range: ~3% of hands vs tight ranges and ~6% vs wide ranges.
concepts.actionable_rule: Facing an open and a 3-bet, adopt a cold 4-bet-or-fold strategy: cold 4-bet ~3% of hands vs tight ranges and ~6% vs wide ranges, avoiding a cold-calling range.

concepts.title: Standard get-it-in range vs a 5-bet is TT+ and AK
concepts.summary: When facing a 5-bet your default continuing/jamming range is TT or better plus AK.
concepts.details: At 100bb-type stack depths, by the time stacks go in on the 5-bet level only premium holdings retain enough equity to continue profitably. The baseline getting-in range is TT+ and AK.
concepts.actionable_rule: Against a 5-bet, get the stacks in only with TT+ and AK as a default; fold weaker hands.

concepts.title: Match 3-bet bluff strength to villain's range strength
concepts.summary: The stronger the opener's range, the stronger the hands you should pick as 3-bet bluffs.
concepts.details: Against a strong, tight RFI range (e.g. LJ) you need higher-equity bluff candidates because weak bluffs are dominated and realize poorly. Against a weak, wide range (e.g. BN) you can bluff with weaker hands. Bluff hand selection scales with opponent range strength.
concepts.actionable_rule: Pick stronger blocker/equity hands as 3-bet bluffs against early-position (strong-range) opens, and weaker hands as bluffs against late-position (wide-range) opens.

concepts.title: Polarize 3-bets when you have a flat-calling range, otherwise go linear
concepts.summary: With a flatting range (IP/BN) your 3-bet range is polarized; without one (HJ/CO/SB) it is linear.
concepts.details: If you flat your high-equity hands that don't want to face a 4-bet, your 3-bet range becomes your best hands plus a next tier of equity/blocker hands offering board coverage. If you have no flatting range (out of position or 3-bet-or-fold), 3-bet linearly with only your best hands. When splitting into call and reraise at stacks where villain can jam, make the reraise range polarized and put high-equity non-reraise hands in the flatting range.
concepts.actionable_rule: 3-bet a polarized range when you also have a flat-calling range; 3-bet a linear range when you have no flatting range or are playing 3-bet-or-fold.

concepts.title: Use MDF/Alpha and blockers to find profitable 3-bet bluffs vs loose openers
concepts.summary: Estimate villain's defense combos via the Alpha number; if they defend fewer combos than your bluff threshold (further reduced by your blockers) the 3-bet bluff is immediately profitable.
concepts.details: Example: vs a 76% SB open, 3-betting to $45 risking $40 to win $20 requires villain to defend ~334.6 combos for indifference. A fishy SB defends 350 combos (over threshold), so ATC bluff is unprofitable — but holding the K blocks AK, KK, K6s+, KTo+, cutting defense to 324 combos and making the K2-blocker 3-bet bluff profitable. Choose polarized exploit 3-bets vs fold/4-bet players and linear exploit 3-bets vs call-heavy players.
concepts.actionable_rule: Compute villain's break-even defense combos from your 3-bet sizing; if their estimated defending range (after subtracting combos your card blocks) is below that number, 3-bet bluff — preferring hands that block their continuing range.

concepts.title: Beware over-3-betting when other players are active
concepts.summary: When exploiting a weak opener by 3-betting wide, watch out for active players behind who can cold 4-bet you for value.
concepts.details: You can profitably exploit a single weak, over-opening villain by 3-betting more, but if observant players remain behind they can start cold 4-betting wider to punish your inflated 3-bet frequency, even if the original weak player never adjusts.
concepts.actionable_rule: When ramping up exploitative 3-bets against a weak opener, tighten back up if competent players remain behind who could cold 4-bet you.

concepts.title: 4-bet more, call less when out of position to reduce SPR
concepts.summary: Out of position responding to 3-bets, lean toward 4-betting to lower SPR and deny equity rather than calling.
concepts.details: The LJ vs HJ (a linear 3-bet-or-fold range) mostly defends by 4-betting to mitigate its positional disadvantage, reducing SPR and folding out some of villain's equity. With position (e.g. vs SB/BB 3-bets) you don't need to 4-bet as often and can defend more by calling and playing flops in position.
concepts.actionable_rule: When out of position vs a 3-bet, shift defense toward 4-betting to cut SPR; when in position, shift defense toward calling and playing flops.

concepts.title: Hands that get all-in pre-flop tighten in earlier-position confrontations
