concepts.summary: The hands happy to stack off pre-flop depend on opponent range strength: only AA/KK/AKs vs SB, but JJ/TT become get-in hands vs wider late-position ranges.
concepts.details: Vs the CO you can 4-bet wider and are happy getting JJ/TT in pre-flop because the CO 3-bet range is wider than the HJ's. Vs the SB (polar 3-bet, you have position) only AA, KK and AKs want to get all-in, while QQ/JJ prefer to see flops, and suited broadways prefer to call rather than 4-bet.
concepts.actionable_rule: Calibrate your pre-flop stack-off range to villain's 3-bet width: get JJ/TT in vs wider (CO) 3-bet ranges, but only AA/KK/AKs vs tighter polar (SB) 3-bet ranges, letting QQ/JJ see flops.

concepts.title: Button has a flat-calling range and slowplays to protect it
concepts.summary: Only the button needn't fear being OOP postflop, so it has a calling range and protects it by slowplaying strong hands.
concepts.details: The BN protects its flatting range by slowplaying portions of QQ, JJ, TT, 99 and AKo, plus calling good-playability hands (AQs, AJs, ATs, KQs, KJs, etc.) that can withstand squeezes. As you face later-position opens (HJ→CO), the blinds squeeze more, so the BN flatting frequency shrinks and 3-bet frequency rises.
concepts.actionable_rule: On the button, maintain a flat-calling range with good-playability hands and slowplay a fraction of premiums to protect it, but flat less and 3-bet more as the opener's position gets later (more squeeze risk).

concepts.title: SB should play 3-bet-or-fold against most opens
concepts.summary: From the small blind, play 3-bet-or-fold versus opens despite the discount, because OOP cold-calling realizes equity poorly.
concepts.details: Calling from the SB leaves the BB active to squeeze (forcing SB off equity) or to call and realize postflop equity. SB equity realization OOP against two players at high SPR is poor, and rake compounds this, making calling a losing proposition. SB does widen its 3-bet range against later-position opens (e.g. up to ~15% vs the BN).
concepts.actionable_rule: From the SB, adopt a 3-bet-or-fold strategy versus opens (no flatting range), widening the 3-bet range as the opener's position gets later — up to ~15% versus a button open.

concepts.title: 3-bet small pairs and odd hands for board coverage and anti-blocker reasons
concepts.summary: Include some weak pocket pairs and threshold hands in 3-bet ranges for postflop board coverage and to deny opponents clean blocker reads.
concepts.details: The HJ vs LJ 3-bet range carries small weights on 88–22 even though 88 dominates 22, because varied holdings give board coverage to hit sets/strong hands across textures, and mixing prevents opponents from leveraging blockers against a predictable range. GTO outliers like K6s-K5s or 53s are often solver convergence artifacts and can be ignored in practice.
concepts.actionable_rule: Mix small frequencies of weak pairs and threshold hands into 3-bet ranges for board coverage and unpredictability, but ignore tiny GTO outlier hands as convergence noise.

concepts.title: Use suited-wheel Ax as the best bluffs vs very strong, blocker-heavy ranges
concepts.summary: Against strong early-position 4-bet ranges, suited wheel Ax (A5s, A4s) and ATs are the highest-EV jamming bluffs.
concepts.details: EP/MP 4-bet ranges are strong and blocker-heavy, so when bluff-jamming you want hands that block AA and AK and unblock villain's bluffs. Late-position 4-bet ranges vs the blinds are less blocker-centric, which raises the EV of jamming blocker hands like ATs and A5s — the first spot where non-premium hands enter the 5-bet range as bluffs.
concepts.actionable_rule: When bluff-jamming a 5-bet against strong ranges, prefer suited-wheel Ax (A5s, A4s) and ATs because they block AA/AK and unblock villain's bluffs, and prefer calls that unblock bluffs over higher-equity but blocker-bad hands.

concepts.title: Widen 4-bet defense (calling) as your own 3-bet range widens
concepts.summary: When you 3-bet wider against a position, you must call the subsequent 4-bet with a few extra hands to stay unexploitable.
concepts.details: Because a wider 3-bet range means a higher bluff frequency, you need more continuing combos vs the 4-bet to avoid being exploited. E.g. the CO 3-betting wider vs HJ than vs LJ then adds KJs, ATs, KTs to its 4-bet calling range; similar widening occurs for SB and BN as their 3-bet ranges expand.
concepts.actionable_rule: Each time you widen your 3-bet range against a given opener, add a proportional number of calling hands versus their 4-bet to keep your continuing frequency unexploitable.

concepts.title: Slowplay AA more as villain's 4-bet range polarizes
concepts.summary: Increase the frequency of just-calling AA against more polarized 4-bet ranges so you can profitably continue with more hands.
concepts.details: Against more polarized 4-bet ranges (e.g. CO/BN vs blinds), AA is slowplayed more (up to 100% in some BN-vs-CO spots) and you call more hands like AQo, A3s, JTs because the polar range lets these continue profitably. Against tighter blocker-heavy early-position 4-bets, AA is slowplayed less and stacked in more.
concepts.actionable_rule: Slowplay (just-call) AA at higher frequency against polarized 4-bet ranges to protect your calling range, and jam it more against tight blocker-heavy 4-bet ranges.

concepts.title: Respond to Polarized 4-Bets by Calling More, 5-Betting Less
concepts.summary: When an opponent's 4-betting range is polarized (only nutted hands and bluffs), reduce your 5-bet frequency and call more, slowplaying your strongest hands.
concepts.details: Against a polarized 4-bet range you gain little by 5-bet jamming because the opponent's value hands beat you and their bluffs fold; instead you realize more value by flatting and trapping. The SB vs BN 4-bet example slowplays AA 100% of the time and calls 56% while only 5-betting 17.3%. Position amplifies this: in-position defenders (BB vs SB/CO/BN) call even more and slowplay AA/KK because they can profitably play many hands postflop.
concepts.actionable_rule: When facing a 4-bet from a polarized range, lean toward calling rather than 5-betting and slowplay your premium hands (AA often 100%), expanding calls to include hands with good equity and equity realization versus the 4-bet range.

concepts.title: Defend the Big Blind Widely and Profitably
concepts.summary: Folding too much from the BB caps your win rate at -100bb/100 and invites steals, so defend as many hands as can be played profitably given the discount you get.
concepts.details: Most pots involve a raise and a BB defense, so BB defense is among the most important skills. Defending widely both reduces blind losses and deters aggressive stealers. The wider the opener's range, the wider the BB defends: vs LJ fold ~71%, vs HJ ~68.5%, vs CO ~64.6%, vs BN only ~43.2%. Defense frequency scales inversely with opener strength.
concepts.actionable_rule: From the BB, set your overall defense frequency based on the opener's position—defend tightest vs early positions and progressively wider vs late positions—and avoid over-folding to prevent becoming a steal target.

concepts.title: Suited Hands Beat Offsuit Hands for Equity Realization OOP
concepts.summary: Out of position against tight ranges, suited and connected hands outperform stronger-looking offsuit disconnected hands because they realize equity better.
concepts.details: Counterintuitively, K2s is a profitable BB call while A9o is a fold versus a LJ open. Offsuit disconnected hands struggle to realize equity postflop OOP, especially deep-stacked, because they make weak top pairs and rarely flop strong draws or two pair. Suited broadways are the best 3-betting hands, followed by suited Ax, suited Kx, suited connectors and suited gappers. Offsuit broadways (AQo-ATo) make poor 3-bets because they must fold to 4-bets and play poorly in 3-bet pots OOP.
concepts.actionable_rule: Prioritize suited and connected hands for calling and 3-betting OOP; fold offsuit, disconnected hands (e.g. A9o, K8o, Q9o) even when they appear stronger than the suited hands you continue with.

concepts.title: Choose Linear vs Polarized 3-Bet Construction by Opener Range Width
concepts.summary: 3-bet a polarized range (premiums + weak bluffs) against tight openers and a more linear range against wide late-position openers.
concepts.details: Against early-position openers, the BB cannot use many 3-bet bluffs because the opener defends well against 3-bets; offsuit broadways are poor bluffs since they fold to 4-bets. Against the BN, the BB 3-bets a very linear range (13.4%) and calls a huge portion (43.4%) because the BN's wide range dilutes strong hands and downgrades their barreling/overbetting. In position vs the SB, the BB 3-bets a polarized range of value hands that can 5-bet or call 4-bets plus blocker hands (Axo, K4o+) happy to fold to 4-bets.
concepts.actionable_rule: Use a polarized 3-betting range (value plus weak blocker bluffs that don't mind folding to 4-bets) when in position or vs strong/tight openers, and shift toward a linear value-heavy 3-bet range against very wide late-position opens.

concepts.title: Use Blocker Hands as 5-Bet and 4-Bet Bluffs
concepts.summary: Hands like A5s, A4s, and Ax/Kx blockers are used at mixed frequencies to jam or 4-bet as bluffs because they block the opponent's strong continuing range.
concepts.details: Across the ranges, A5s/A4s appear in 5-bet jamming ranges (e.g. A5s 38-74%) precisely because they hold an ace blocker reducing opponent AA/AK combos while retaining nut-flush and wheel-straight equity. Vs SB limp/raise the BB 4-bets only ~7%, mixing strong hands (TT+, AK) with Ax/Kx blocker bluffs. Blocker selection, not raw equity, drives many bluff choices.
concepts.actionable_rule: Select 5-bet and 4-bet bluffs from suited-ace blockers (A5s, A4s) and Ax/Kx hands that block the opponent's value-continuing combos, deploying them at mixed frequencies rather than always or never.

concepts.title: Add Weight to Threshold Hands to Widen Ranges Smoothly
concepts.summary: To adjust defense or 3-bet frequency across positions, increase the mixing weight on borderline hands rather than adding entirely new hand classes.
concepts.details: As opener position moves later, the BB increases its 3-betting frequency (5.8% vs LJ, 7.6% vs HJ, 9.7% vs CO, 13.4% vs BN) chiefly by adding weight to threshold/marginal hands. Minor combo-by-combo singularities (e.g. JJ 5-bet vs HJ but QQ vs LJ due to blockers) are not worth memorizing; the principle is smooth frequency adjustment via mixed strategies on borderline hands.
concepts.actionable_rule: When widening or tightening a range across opponent positions, adjust the frequency on borderline threshold hands first rather than adding or removing whole hand categories, and don't obsess over tiny combo-specific blocker singularities.

concepts.title: Variance Is Driven by Volume and Win-Rate Spread
concepts.summary: Variance equals standard deviation squared; it shrinks with more hands and grows with a wider spread of results around your average win rate.
concepts.details: Dividing a sample into 100-hand chunks yields many local win rates; the more they spread from the average, the higher the standard deviation. Volume is in the denominator of the variance formula, so high-volume players experience less total variance than occasional players. Win rate itself does not change standard deviation but a higher win rate dramatically reduces the probability of going broke (risk of ruin) over a given sample.
concepts.actionable_rule: Use a variance calculator with your tracked standard deviation and win rate to estimate realistic downswings and set bankroll requirements; play more volume to reduce overall variance and prioritize raising win rate to lower risk of ruin.

concepts.title: Tournament Chips Have No Direct Cash Value, Creating Higher Variance
concepts.summary: Because tournament chips only convert to money via finishing position, losing a flip deep in an event destroys far more equity than the same flip in a cash game.
concepts.details: In cash, a 50bb flip costs the same regardless of timing and you can reload to the same stack. In a tournament, losing a 50bb flip after 10 hours—near the final table with 90% of the field gone—can cost hundreds of thousands in equity and cannot be reloaded. Payouts concentrate in the top ~15-18% of the field, so chip accumulation alone doesn't guarantee money, making MTT variance much higher than cash.
concepts.actionable_rule: In tournaments, value chips by their payout equity rather than face value—treat coinflips and marginal spots as more costly deep in the event than early or in cash games—and maintain a much larger bankroll buffer for MTT variance.

concepts.title: Use Average ROI to Measure True Tournament Skill
concepts.summary: Average ROI (computed per tournament then averaged) reflects skill relative to the fields far better than total cashes, profit, or total ROI, which can be skewed by one big score.
concepts.details: Total cashes ignore buy-ins and expenses; total ROI can be identical for a skilled grinder and a luck-box who spiked one big event. Averaging ROI per tournament reveals consistent edge. ITM% should be ~15-18% online for winners—lower means too loose on bubbles/early, higher means too passive on bubbles and passing up stack-building spots. Even high Average ROI does not guarantee profit over a sample due to MTT variance.
concepts.actionable_rule: Evaluate tournament skill primarily by Average ROI and a healthy ITM% (~15-18% online); avoid overly tight bubble play that inflates ITM at the cost of big-stack equity, and don't be too loose early or on bubbles.

concepts.title: Maximize Tournament Profit via ROI Then Volume
concepts.summary: Decrease variance and increase profit in MTTs by first ensuring a positive Average ROI, then adding volume—while accounting for how format and stakes trade off ROI against variance.
concepts.details: It's pointless to add volume in games you cannot beat, so secure a positive Average ROI before ramping volume. Moving up in stakes increases profit potential but lowers ROI (tougher games) and limits volume (fewer high-stakes events), raising variance. Turbos boost volume but lower ROI (less time to exploit weak players, shallow play). Bounty MTTs reduce variance but lower EV (bounty rake captured by weaker players) yet favor weaker players. Online and multi-tabling provide far more volume than live, though live offers higher ROI but more variance from low volume.
concepts.actionable_rule: Confirm a positive Average ROI before increasing volume; choose formats deliberately—use online multi-tabling and turbos for volume, bounties to cut variance, and only move up stakes when the lower ROI and reduced volume are acceptable for your bankroll.

concepts.title: Balance Study and Play Time by Skill Level
concepts.summary: New players should split time roughly 50/50 study/play, while established winners shift toward 80% play and 20% study to maximize earnings without stagnating.
concepts.details: Early on, volume is about gaining proficiency rather than profit, so heavy study (50%) accelerates learning of practical and theoretical aspects only learnable through play. Once a player's ROI is high, additional study yields diminishing financial returns, but stopping study entirely causes skills to stagnate while opponents improve, eroding edge over time—hence maintaining ~20% study.
concepts.actionable_rule: If you are a developing player, allocate about half your poker time to study and half to play; once you are a consistent winner, shift toward 80% play and 20% study but never stop studying entirely to avoid stagnating relative to improving opponents.

concepts.title: GTO Is About Exploitation, Not Balance
concepts.summary: Equilibrium strategies emerge when both players maximally exploit each other; when opponents can't counter-exploit you, balance is unnecessary and you should deviate to exploit them.
concepts.details: The author's key insight: GTO equilibrium is the meeting point of two players maximally exploiting one another. If opponents are unaware of your strategy or incapable of counter-exploiting it, there is no reason to play balanced. Against weaker fields the maximally profitable strategy is heavily exploitative rather than balanced GTO play.
concepts.actionable_rule: Default to GTO only against capable opponents; when opponents cannot counter-exploit you, abandon balance and deviate maximally toward whatever exploits their tendencies.

concepts.title: Small Sample Results Are Dominated by Variance
concepts.summary: Even over hundreds or thousands of tournaments, ROI and money won are poor proxies for skill because variance can make losing players profit and winning players lose.
concepts.details: Simulations show a -25% ROI player can be up $20k over 200 MTTs, a breakeven player can range from -$56k to +$88k over 2,000 MTTs, and a 25% ROI winner loses money 28% of the time over 200 games. Judging skill by money won is unreliable; long-run EV and process matter more than short-run results.
concepts.actionable_rule: Do not judge skill or adjust strategy based on short-term results; evaluate decisions by EV and require very large samples before drawing conclusions about win rate.

concepts.title: MTT Bankroll Sizing in Buy-ins
concepts.summary: Keep at least 200 buy-ins for tournaments, up to 1,000 to minimize ruin risk, plus separate living-expense reserves for professionals.
concepts.details: Tournament variance is far higher than cash, so 200 buy-ins is a baseline and 1,000 buy-ins nearly eliminates ruin risk. Professionals should hold 6-12+ months of living expenses separate from the bankroll. Live tournaments allow smaller bankrolls due to higher ROI and fewer entrants (lower variance), but travel costs must be budgeted.
concepts.actionable_rule: Maintain a minimum of 200 buy-ins for MTTs (more for safety), keep living expenses separate, and only reduce buy-in requirements for lower-variance live events.

concepts.title: Buy-in Spread Increases Variance
concepts.summary: Playing a wide range of buy-ins dramatically raises variance and ruin risk even when total EV and money invested are the same as a tight-spread schedule.
concepts.details: Simulations comparing a wide-spread schedule (mix of $109 to $10,300) versus a uniform $235 schedule with equal total investment and EV show the wide spread has ~10x higher probability of loss, with downside swings far larger (-$262k vs -$36k). Occasionally taking shots at huge buy-ins can cost 150 buy-ins in a couple of events.
concepts.actionable_rule: Keep your tournament buy-ins within a narrow range relative to your average buy-in; avoid sprinkling in events far above your ABI that can swing your bankroll catastrophically.

concepts.title: Game Selection by Edge and Variance
concepts.summary: Choose games where your edge (ROI) is high relative to variance; often smaller stakes with lower variance beat bigger games with thin edges.
concepts.details: Maximizing EV usually means playing against weaker opposition, not the highest stakes you can afford. Unless you are the best player with unlimited bankroll, prefer games where ROI is higher and variance is lower. Ego-driven play against tougher fields lowers ROI and raises ruin risk.
concepts.actionable_rule: Select the games with the highest expected ROI relative to variance—usually weaker, lower-stakes fields—rather than playing as high as your bankroll allows.

concepts.title: Mental Game and Process Habits Drive Long-Term Results
concepts.summary: Winning players take responsibility, control tilt, study constantly, table-select for weaker fields, and maintain health; losing players blame variance and play their B/C game.
concepts.details: Winning mindset traits: positive attitude, accepting responsibility despite variance, strong work ethic, emotional control, openness to feedback, long-term orientation, seeking weaker opposition, tabling only as many games as allow A-game play, good health and sleep, routines, and a study network. Losing traits are the inverse: blame, laziness, tilt, ego-driven tough games, multitabling on autopilot.
concepts.actionable_rule: Take full responsibility for results, control tilt, limit your table count to what preserves your A-game, table-select for weaker fields, and invest continuously in study and health.

concepts.title: Tournament Life and EV of Future Hands
concepts.summary: In tournaments, decisions are not driven by chip EV alone; survival has value because staying alive lets you exploit better future spots and ladder up payouts.
concepts.details: A +cEV call (e.g., J8o with 51.48% equity worth 1,090bb/100 vs a blind shove) can still be wrong because waiting for a premium like AA against the same shover is worth far more (23,500bb/100). Survival preserves the EV of future hands and the EV of gaining higher payouts as others bust. Unlike cash where folding is always 0 EV, folding in tournaments has positive survival value.
concepts.actionable_rule: Do not call off marginal +cEV spots in tournaments if waiting for stronger spots yields far more EV; weight survival value of future hands and payout laddering against raw chip EV.

concepts.title: Diminishing Chip Value and ICM
concepts.summary: Tournament chips are not linearly valued: chips risked are worth more than chips won, and ICM assigns monetary value to stacks based on prize-pool equity.
concepts.details: Winning 100% of chips may pay only 50% of the prize pool, so doubling your stack does not double its value. The Principle of Diminishing Chip Value: the more chips you have, the less each is worth. ICM computes each player's probability of finishing in each paying position from stack sizes and weights by payouts to estimate $EV; FGS extends this to future play. Use calculators for complex spots.
concepts.actionable_rule: Evaluate tournament decisions in $EV using ICM rather than raw chip EV; tighten risk-taking as your stack grows since added chips are worth progressively less.

concepts.title: Base tournament decisions on $EV, not chip EV
concepts.summary: In MTTs chips don't equal money; decisions should maximize monetary expected value ($EV), which differs from chip EV (cEV) because of diminishing chip value.
concepts.details: ICM assigns each stack a monetary value based on prize pool equity and finishing probabilities. A leader with 60% of chips may hold only ~$40 of a $50 first prize because they won't always win. In cash games cEV and $EV are equal (ignoring rake), but in tournaments many +cEV plays are -$EV and must be avoided.
concepts.actionable_rule: In tournaments, evaluate each action by its $EV via ICM rather than raw chip EV, and fold marginal +cEV spots that are -$EV.

concepts.title: Apply risk premium when committing chips
concepts.summary: Tournament players need more equity than in cash games to make a +$EV play; the extra required equity is the risk premium.
concepts.details: Because risked chips are worth more than chips won, the true required equity exceeds the cEV threshold. Example: calling off AKo vs a 100% shove needs ~66.44% equity for +$EV versus only 47% for +cEV, a ~19% risk premium. Risk premium is higher when calling big bets for your tournament life, when many short stacks are present, and with flatter payout structures; it is ~0 in winner-take-all. It applies to making bets too, not just calling.
concepts.actionable_rule: Add the situational risk premium to the cEV equity threshold before calling all-in; require more equity (e.g. ~66% instead of 47%) and tighten calls when stacks risk tournament life or payouts are flat.

concepts.title: Stack-size dynamics dictate ICM pressure
concepts.summary: Medium stacks are forced to play tight near short stacks/bubble, while big stacks can shove very wide because opponents must call off tightly.
concepts.details: ICM pressure compresses calling ranges during the money bubble: a big-stack BN can profitably shove any two cards because blinds can only call with premiums (e.g. AA-TT, then AA-88/AKs/AQs). Conversely, top-heavy payouts reward aggression and flat payouts reward tight play. Short stacks present increase everyone's risk premium.
concepts.actionable_rule: As the big stack on the bubble, shove wide to pressure medium stacks; as a medium stack near short stacks, fold marginal hands and avoid stacking off without a premium.

concepts.title: Only apply ICM pressure to ICM-aware opponents
concepts.summary: ICM equilibrium assumes all players follow ICM; against players who call a wider cEV range, your 'correct' tight shoves lose EV.
concepts.details: Push/fold solvers assume opponents call ICM-tight (e.g. BB calling 6.7%). If a Villain instead calls a regular cEV range (e.g. 23.8%), the EV from your aggression evaporates and transfers to others. Table image, future play, and position are all ignored by ICM.
concepts.actionable_rule: Before applying ICM-based wide shoves, verify opponents are ICM-aware; against players who overcall, tighten your shoving and don't expect them to fold correctly.

concepts.title: Adjust risk based on skill edge (Gambler's Ruin)
concepts.summary: With a skill edge, be risk-averse and avoid marginal all-in gambles; with a skill deficit, be willing to gamble for big chunks of your stack.
concepts.details: In Gambler's Ruin, probability of winning rises linearly with stack only when skill is equal. With a skill edge the value curve is concave, so each added chip is worth less and any 0-cEV flip is -EV in win probability; better to grind and exploit opponent mistakes. With a skill deficit the curve is convex, so even gambles are +EV in win probability—maximize variance. Decreasing variance against a stronger field (like the casino edge) almost guarantees loss.
concepts.actionable_rule: If you are the stronger player, decline marginal/even-money all-ins and keep variance low; if you are the weaker player, take the flips and play for big pots to maximize win probability.

concepts.title: RFI sizing has little EV impact within reasonable ranges
concepts.summary: Open-raise size matters little to your bottom line as long as sizing and range are matched; sweet spot is ~2-2.5bb (BN-UTG) and 2.5-3.5bb blind vs blind.
concepts.details: Bigger opens force tighter ranges or the bottom of your range loses money. Open small from early position and slightly larger toward the button, though the EV gain from position-varied sizing is small and adds complexity. With 100bb+ use 2.3-2.5x; no strong evidence supports larger.
concepts.actionable_rule: Open to roughly 2-2.5bb from BN-UTG (2.5-3.5bb blind vs blind) and tighten your opening range as you increase size; keep one simple consistent sizing.

concepts.title: Min-raise in the rejam region (<25bb)
concepts.summary: With stacks under ~25bb, min-raise to preserve fold equity when facing rejams and to avoid being committed by the bottom of your range.
concepts.details: Raising larger gives short-stack rejammers a better price and commits you when called. Example: open 3x from UTG with 10bb and BB shoves—you must call 7 into 14.6 (>2:1) and are committed with any reasonable hand; min-raising leaves a 1.7:1 call so you can fold the worst hands. Larger raises also reduce the break-even frequency a rejam needs to be profitable.
concepts.actionable_rule: With effective stacks under ~25bb, min-raise your opens so you retain fold equity and can fold the bottom of your range when rejammed; at 30-35bb+ increase to ~2.3x.

concepts.title: 3-bet sizing by position and commitment threshold
concepts.summary: Use bigger 3-bets when deep and OOP, smaller from SB than BB, and never invest over 1/3 of stack with trash—shove instead.
concepts.details: SB 3-bets smaller because it fears the BB waking up and its range is less polarized, so it minds being called less. If a 3-bet commits more than 1/3 of your stack you are pot-committed except with absolute trash, so prefer an open-shove to limit Villain options. Under 40bb all 4-bets are all-in; 50-100bb allows 4-bets to 2.25-2.5x IP and 2.5-3x OOP; all 5-bets are always all-in.
concepts.actionable_rule: 3-bet larger OOP and when deep, smaller from SB than BB; if the 3-bet exceeds 1/3 of your stack, shove all-in rather than make a committing non-all-in raise, and make all 4-bets all-in under 40bb.

concepts.title: Plan your preflop line before raising
concepts.summary: Know in advance whether your open is a raise-fold or raise-call against each opponent and stack depth, and whether to shove or min-raise.
concepts.details: A hand may be able to call a 15bb all-in but not a 20bb one, or call a shove from one position but not another. Decide whether your hand plays better as an open-shove or a min-raise to avoid being stuck when min-raising and getting jammed on. Account for stacks yet to act and their likelihood to call/reraise. Avoid autopiloting, especially when multi-tabling.
concepts.actionable_rule: Before opening, classify the hand as raise-fold or raise-call versus each remaining stack and decide shove vs min-raise, so you never face an unplanned decision after a rejam.

concepts.title: Play push/fold under 10bb
concepts.summary: With effective stacks of 10bb or less, a simple push-or-fold strategy is correct because the EV loss versus complex play is negligible.
concepts.details: Solver/FGS-generated charts give the maximum bb depth at which each hand can be profitably shoved by position (e.g. SB pushes 95o only at ≤5bb but 95s at ≤10bb). Position matters: later positions can shove wider. FGS refines ICM by accounting for blind movement and increases, most affecting UTG, SB and BB at <10bb shallow stacks.
concepts.actionable_rule: With 10bb or fewer, abandon complex play and shove or fold according to position-based push charts, widening shoving range in later positions.

concepts.title: Deep no-ante play resembles tight cash strategy
concepts.summary: In deep no-ante early levels there is less dead money, so ranges tighten and speculative hands gain value, making calling and postflop play more attractive.
concepts.details: With no ante the pot has less dead money, so opening ranges are generally tighter and equilibrium resembles cash games (minus rake). Lower preflop investment relative to stacks increases implied odds, raising the value of speculative/suited connector type hands and favoring calling to play postflop.
concepts.actionable_rule: In deep no-ante early levels, tighten opening ranges but call more with speculative hands to realize implied odds postflop, treating play like rake-free cash.

concepts.title: SB First-In Strategy by Stack Depth: Push/Limp/Fold to Raise/Limp/Fold
concepts.summary: From the SB when folded to you, use a push/limp/fold strategy at 10-15bb and progressively shift toward limping and non-all-in raises as stacks deepen, eliminating the all-in range entirely by 40bb.
concepts.details: The SB can profitably play ~83% of hands when folded to it due to the limp discount and only one player left to act. At 10-15bb push hands with good blockers (Ax, Kx), high-equity-but-poor-postflop hands (66-22), and suited connectors that don't want to call a jam; limp hands strong enough to call all-in (77+, broadways, suited Ax/Kx). At 17bb a non-all-in raise emerges (2.5x), growing to 3.5x by 30bb (bigger sizes give negligible extra EV). At 25bb open-pushing nearly disappears (only 44-22, A9o/A8o). At 40bb the all-in open is gone and most hands play a mixed limp/raise strategy. At 60bb limping frequency peaks (~70%) with no pure-raise hands.
concepts.actionable_rule: In the SB when folded to you, play push/limp/fold at 10-15bb, add a 2.5x-3.5x raise from 17-30bb, drop the open-jam by 25bb, and shift increasingly toward limping as stacks deepen (limp ~50% at 25bb, ~70% at 60bb), never raising larger than 3.5x.

concepts.title: SB Polarized Raising vs Strong Limping Range
concepts.summary: When the SB raises rather than limps, the raising range is polarized into hands strong enough to stack off and bluffs with good blockers, while strong traps are kept in the limping range.
concepts.details: At 25bb the SB raising range comprises stack-off hands (66+, A8o+, A5s+, strong broadways) plus blocker bluffs (A7o-A2o, Kxo) and playable hands (KJo, QTo, J8s, 74s). The limping range hides traps like AKo-A9o and mid pairs that don't want to be forced to fold to a jam. As stacks deepen, the strongest hands raise more often than they limp and weaker hands limp more than raise.
concepts.actionable_rule: When raising from the SB, polarize into stack-off-strong hands plus blocker bluffs, and place strong trap hands (e.g. AKo-A9o, mid pairs) into the limping range rather than always raising them.

concepts.title: Re-Raise Sizing and 4-Bet Selection Depend on Stack Depth
concepts.summary: As stacks deepen, replace limp/shoves and raise/jams with smaller non-all-in re-raises and 4-bets, slowplaying the strongest hands.
concepts.details: After SB limps and faces a raise: at 40bb defend by jamming 5.9% (pairs, AQo/AJo, some weak Axo) plus a 2.75x re-raise; at 60bb stacks are too deep to limp/shove so only a 3.4x re-raise is used. When the SB raises and faces a 3-bet: at 60bb jamming 60bb is bad (only AKo, A5s at low frequency), so use a 2.6x 4-bet with KK/QQ/AK/AQo plus blocker bluffs while slowplaying AA and flat-calling many suited hands.
concepts.actionable_rule: At deeper stacks (40bb+), abandon limp/shove and raise/jam lines: use small non-all-in re-raises (~2.75x) and 4-bets (~2.6x), slowplay AA, and flat strong suited hands rather than jamming.

concepts.title: Button Power: Guaranteed Position Maximizes Equity Realization
concepts.summary: The Button can never be forced out of position by a later player, giving it the highest post-flop equity realization, which widens its opening range as stacks deepen.
concepts.details: Because no one can re-enter behind the BN, its equity realization is highest and increases with depth. BN VPIP grows from 38.9% at 10bb to 55.5% at 80bb. By open-jamming, the BN forsakes its positional advantage, so push frequency falls sharply with depth (3.5% at 20bb, 0% at 25bb). The blinds' best counter—rejamming all-in to deny equity—has poor risk/reward beyond 40bb, so the blinds increasingly cannot prevent the BN from realizing equity.
concepts.actionable_rule: From the Button, widen your opening range as stacks deepen (up to ~55% at 80bb) and reduce open-jamming toward zero by 25bb, since position-driven equity realization rewards seeing flops over forsaking position with a jam.

concepts.title: When to Limp from the Button (and Why Usually Not To)
concepts.summary: The BN has a theoretically valid limping range at 10-30bb, but practical drawbacks make a simpler raise/fold strategy preferable in real games.
concepts.details: With limping allowed, BN prefers limping over min-raising at 10-12bb, adds min-raises at 15-30bb (in-position post-flop play), and stops limping at 40bb for raise/fold. Overall BN limp frequency is only 11.7%. Reasons to avoid BN limps: it adds strategic complexity and balancing difficulty; increases variance and multiway pots (SB gets a good price to come along); the EV gain is small (no call discount, not guaranteed heads-up); and opponents over-fold the BB to steals, making min-raises more profitable.
concepts.actionable_rule: From the Button, prefer a simple raise/fold strategy over limping in practice—min-raise to steal, especially against blinds that over-fold, rather than building a complex limp range.

concepts.title: The Awkward Stack Depth: Folding Small Pairs Around 25bb
concepts.summary: Small pocket pairs (33, 22) should often be folded when first-in at ~25bb because the stack is too deep to open-jam and too shallow for good implied odds.
concepts.details: At 25bb small pairs are too deep to profitably open-shove but too shallow to realize implied odds when called. As min-raises they have two reverse blockers (don't block the blinds' playable rejam hands), so they get re-shoved slightly more often and must fold pre-flop. If called, they play as underpairs—forced to play passively (denied equity) or bluff into bad spots—with few outs. Hence fold them when first in from all positions except the SB. By 40bb improved implied odds and SPR bring these pairs back into opening ranges.
concepts.actionable_rule: At ~25bb effective, fold 33-22 when first in from any position except the SB; re-add them to opening ranges once stacks reach ~40bb where implied odds and post-flop play justify them.

concepts.title: Open-Jam Frequency Decreases as Position Worsens and Stacks Deepen
concepts.summary: The deeper the stack and the earlier the position, the smaller the open-shoving range, because more players left to act increases the chance of running into a premium.
concepts.details: All-in open frequency drops with depth across positions—CO hits 0% at 20bb, HJ all-in disappears by 20bb, LJ by 17bb, and UTG+2's tiny 2.2% jam at 15bb is best replaced by raise/fold because jammed hands are indifferent to a min-raise. From early position you should be hesitant to risk many chips on a jam because someone behind is more likely to wake up with a premium. Open jam frequency therefore declines steadily as position worsens.
concepts.actionable_rule: Shrink your open-jam range as you move toward early position and as stacks deepen; in early position avoid open-jamming for many chips, defaulting to raise/fold once stacks exceed ~15-17bb.

concepts.title: Position-Independent VPIP Peak in Middle/Early Position
concepts.summary: From MP and EP, VPIP does not rise monotonically with stack depth but peaks around 25-30bb and then stagnates or declines, unlike late position.
concepts.details: Late positions (BN, CO) widen as stacks deepen because positional advantage aids equity realization. But MP/EP must play OOP against more opponents, and deeper stacks magnify the positional disadvantage and 3-bet threat, hindering equity realization. So HJ VPIP (~26.9% avg) and UTG+2 (~19.6% avg, peak 21% at 25-30bb) and UTG+1 (~16.75% avg, peak 18.6% at 25bb) peak in the 25-30bb band. Deeper ranges shift from high-card/offsuit-broadway value toward connectedness, blockers, and hands that flop the nuts or nut draws.
concepts.actionable_rule: From middle and early position, peak your opening range around 25-30bb and tighten (not widen) as stacks get deeper, dropping weak offsuit broadways and high-low suited hands in favor of connected, blocker, and nut-potential hands.

concepts.title: No Limping Outside the Blinds and Button
concepts.summary: From the CO and earlier, use a pure raise/fold strategy because the EV gain from limping rarely offsets the complexity and risk of over-limpers or raises behind.
concepts.details: With more players left to act, any limp can be over-limped or raised, undermining the EV of a limping range; the gains hardly compensate for the added complexity. This also matches modern game conditions. CO plays push/fold at 10bb and below, adds min-raises at 12bb, and its all-in frequency reaches 0% at 20bb; total CO VPIP rises from 31.4% (10bb) to 37.5% (80bb).
concepts.actionable_rule: From the cutoff and all earlier positions, never limp first-in; play raise/fold (with push/fold below ~12bb) to avoid over-limpers and raises behind.

concepts.title: Hand Selection Priorities Shift with Stack Depth: Raw Equity vs Playability
concepts.summary: At shallow stacks favor raw high-card equity and blockers; at deeper stacks favor playability, connectedness, and implied-odds hands.
concepts.details: At ~25bb (no jam), high-card value and raw equity matter more than playability—e.g. K7o (king blocker to rejam ranges) beats 74s. As stacks deepen to 40bb+ and SPR rises, post-flop playability gains value: suited gappers, small pairs, and small suited connectors enter ranges while weak offsuit broadways lose value (they struggle to call 3-bets and top pairs are worth less). 4-bet frequency also drops at deeper stacks because higher SPR favors post-flop equity realization, and the in-position player defends 3-bets more by flat-calling.
concepts.actionable_rule: Weight your opening/continuing ranges toward raw equity and blocker hands at ~15-25bb, and toward connected, suited, implied-odds hands at 40bb+; lower 4-bet frequency and flat more 3-bets in position as stacks deepen.

concepts.title: UTG Opens Tightest; Hand Composition Shifts With Stack Depth
concepts.summary: UTG has the tightest opening range (~15% VPIP) that barely widens with depth; instead the type of hands changes — high-equity hands/blockers when shallow, nut-potential hands when deep.
concepts.details: Across all stack depths UTG averages ~15.2-15.4% VPIP. Shallow stacks favor high equity hands and good blockers that can get value/all-in pre. Deeper stacks shift toward suited connectors and small pairs (at low frequency) whose purpose is board coverage and ability to make the nuts/nut draws. VPIP peaks around 20-30bb then decreases slightly deeper. With 10-14bb UTG mixes min-raise and open-jam; with 15bb+ the all-in disappears and it becomes raise/fold only.
concepts.actionable_rule: From UTG open ~15% of hands regardless of depth; with 10-14bb mix min-raises and open-jams, with 15bb+ play raise/fold only, weighting offsuit broadways more when shallow and suited connectors/small pairs more when deep.

concepts.title: Rejam vs Open Shove When Call Exceeds 1/3 of Stack
concepts.summary: When facing an all-in where the call is more than 1/3 of your stack, rejam over the top rather than flat call (except in heavy ICM spots).
concepts.details: If calling costs more than 1/3 of your stack you should re-shove all-in with your continuing range to deny equity and maximize fold equity, except in severe ICM/bubble spots where calling or even folding may be better when other deep stacks remain behind. If the call is less than 1/3 of your stack, just call with your continuing range, or min-reraise if the shove is small and you want to isolate heads-up. There's no need to risk your whole stack when deep stacks remain behind.
concepts.actionable_rule: If the amount to call exceeds ~1/3 of your stack, re-jam all-in with your continuing range; if it's less than 1/3, just call (or min-3bet to isolate) and avoid risking your whole stack when deeper players remain — tighten in heavy ICM.

concepts.title: Calling Range Tightens vs Earlier Position and Deeper Shoves
concepts.summary: Your all-in calling range must be tighter the earlier the shover's position and the deeper their stack.
concepts.details: The hands you can profitably call an all-in with depend on pot odds, your position, and the shover's position. Earlier positions have tighter, stronger shoving ranges, so you need a tighter call. Deeper stacks mean worse pot odds and more post-flop EV foregone, also requiring a tighter call. Adjust further if observation shows a player shoves too tight (call tighter) or too loose (call wider).
concepts.actionable_rule: Tighten your all-in calling range as the shover's position gets earlier and their stack gets deeper; loosen versus players observed to over-shove and tighten versus those who shove too tight.

concepts.title: Overcall Tighter Than When Facing a Lone Raise
concepts.summary: After a raise and a call, enter with a tighter range than vs a lone raiser, and prefer 3-betting over cold-calling marginal hands.
concepts.details: Counterintuitively, even though dead money increased and the caller capped their range (no 3-bet), the caller's range is still strong with many hands that can withstand a 3-bet, so over-3-betting marginal hands is bad against well-balanced post-flop ranges. Because you're forced to play tighter, your range often does better 3-betting than flatting. However, hands that play well multiway and can dominate opponents can be overcalls: suited Ax, suited connectors, suited broadways, medium/small pairs. Offsuit gappers and offsuit high/low combos (K5o, Q7o) are terrible multiway, especially OOP.
concepts.actionable_rule: After a raise and a call, play tighter than vs a lone raise: overcall only with hands that play well multiway (suited Ax, suited connectors, suited broadways, medium/small pairs); avoid offsuit gappers and dominated offsuit combos, and prefer 3-betting to flatting marginal hands.

concepts.title: BB Realizes More Equity In Position vs SB (BvB)
concepts.summary: Blind-vs-blind is the only spot where the BB is in position, allowing it to defend much wider and more profitably than vs other openers.
concepts.details: In BvB the BB is in position the whole hand, dramatically boosting equity realization, so it can defend far more hands profitably against SB raises. Because the BB defends so well, the SB often raises large (or jams) to give worse defense odds, or alternatively limps, giving the BB the option to check behind in position or raise to re-open the betting. The BB checks back ~56% and raises ~44% vs an SB limp.
concepts.actionable_rule: In BvB defend the BB very wide because you are in position; vs an SB limp, check back roughly 56% and raise about 44%, sizing the raise around 2x at 10bb up to ~3.5x at 30bb+.

concepts.title: BB Defense Frequency vs Shove/Raise Scales With Odds
concepts.summary: The more chips the SB jams or raises for, the fewer hands the BB can profitably defend; tighten as the bet/stack grows.
concepts.details: BB's calling range vs an SB push is purely a function of pot odds set by stack size — small shoves let many hands call (12bb: all pairs, Ax, broadways, Kxs, K5o+, Q7s+, J8s+, T8s+), larger shoves shrink it (25bb: 33+, A7o+, A6s+, suited broadways, KQo, QJo). Unexploitable calling ranges can look tighter than push/fold apps suggest due to the bunching effect and the SB having other options (limp, smaller raises).
concepts.actionable_rule: Set your BB defending range by the pot odds offered: call wider against small shoves and tighter against larger ones; at 25bb vs a push call roughly 33+, A6s+/A7o+, suited broadways, KQo and QJo.

concepts.title: BB 3-Bet Strategy Polarizes and Loses All-in Option as Stacks Deepen
concepts.summary: Under ~30bb the BB's only 3-bet is all-in; from 40bb+ it uses non-all-in polarized 3-bets with value plus blocker/board-coverage bluffs, trapping the strongest hands.
concepts.details: At <30bb the only BB 3-bet size is all-in, and the solver traps big pairs (88+) while jamming high-equity/poor-playability hands (small pairs 77-22, offsuit Ax). At 40bb the BB stops jamming and 3-bets polarized: value (TT+, AJ+) plus offsuit bluffs chosen for good blockers (Axo, Kxo) or board coverage (J7o, T4s, 98o). At 60bb 3-bet frequency is similar but composed of more individual combos at lower frequency for board coverage, and against a 4-bet may 5-bet (JJ+/AQ+) while slowplaying AA ~68%.
concepts.actionable_rule: With <30bb make your only BB 3-bet all-in, jamming high-equity/poor-playability hands and trapping 88+; with 40bb+ switch to a polarized non-all-in 3-bet using value (TT+/AJ+) plus blocker/board-coverage offsuit bluffs, occasionally slowplaying AA.

concepts.title: Rejam Blockers With Weak Kickers, Flat Strong-Kicker Versions
concepts.summary: When choosing blocker hands to rejam, prefer weak-kicker versions (K5s-K3s, A5s-A3s) and flat the strong-kicker versions that play better post-flop.
concepts.details: Strong blocker hands like KQs or A9s have high equity but better post-flop playability and more chance to cooler opponents, so the solver calls them. Weak-kicker blockers (K5s-K3s, A4s) lack playability but still block premiums and fare fine vs calling ranges, so they're used as rejams to extract fold equity. Example vs LJ: rejam top (AKs-AJs), flat playable middle (ATs-A6s, A2s), then rejam A5s-A3s. The strongest hands (AKs) are too strong not to jam.
concepts.actionable_rule: When selecting hands to re-jam as blockers, jam the top of range plus weak-kicker suited combos (e.g. K5s-K3s, A5s-A3s) while flatting the high-playability strong-kicker versions (KQs, ATs-A6s) that realize equity better post-flop.

concepts.title: BB All-in Frequency Falls as Opener's Position Strengthens
concepts.summary: As the opener's range gets stronger (earlier position), the BB's rejam frequency drops due to lost fold equity, replaced by more calling and folding.
concepts.details: At 15bb BB all-in frequency goes from 18% vs BN to 7.4% vs UTG, but total VPIP stays roughly constant because calling frequency rises as the all-in frequency falls. At 25bb the all-in drops from 11.4% vs BN to 2.1% vs UTG with a roughly constant ~5% non-all-in 3-bet, while folding rises from 14.6% to 27.2%. Rejam hands are those ahead of the opener's range but with poor post-flop realization; offsuit Ax jam well vs LP (high fold equity) but get replaced by suited Ax vs EP where fold equity is lower.
concepts.actionable_rule: Reduce your BB rejam frequency and increase folding as the opener's position gets earlier; vs late position jam more offsuit Ax/wide blockers, but vs early position replace them with suited Ax and lean on calling instead of jamming.

concepts.title: Don't Over-Defend the BB OOP vs Tight Early-Position Opens
concepts.summary: Defending too many trashy hands OOP vs tight EP ranges in high-SPR pots is unprofitable even if you're the better player; tighten and pick better bluffs.
concepts.details: Equity and equity realization matter even against well-defined ranges. Calling too wide OOP vs tight ranges in high-SPR spots leads to tough call-downs and spew. Against a polarized non-all-in EP range, defend tighter, keep 3-bet frequency low, and use better hands as bluffs. As the value range shrinks (e.g. 99+/ATs+/AJ+ vs BN down to TT+/AK vs UTG), the bluffing range must shrink too and uses entirely different bluff hands vs EP than vs BN. At 40bb folding rises from 24.2% vs BN to 45% vs UTG.
concepts.actionable_rule: Against tight early-position opens, defend the BB tighter (fold ~45% vs UTG at 40bb), keep 3-bet frequency low, shrink your bluff range alongside your value range, and choose higher-quality bluff hands rather than calling with dominated trash.

concepts.title: Deep Stacks: IP Uses Overbets to Suppress OOP Equity Realization
concepts.summary: At deep stacks the in-position player's main weapon to lower OOP equity realization is overbetting the pot, so defend tighter vs opponents capable of it.
concepts.details: At 60bb BB defense rises slightly (65.6% vs 62.9% at 40bb) partly from better implied odds, but the simulations didn't allow overbets. The main lever IP has when deep is overbetting to deny OOP equity realization, so true equilibrium defense would be lower if overbets were permitted. Since most players still underuse overbets, the higher defense frequencies hold up in current games; cut weaker hands vs tough opponents who overbet and apply post-flop pressure.
concepts.actionable_rule: When deep and in position, overbet the pot to reduce opponents' equity realization; when defending the BB deep, trim your weakest defends against opponents who are capable of overbetting and heavy post-flop pressure.

concepts.title: Use Smaller Exploitative Raises vs Unbalanced Limp/Defend Populations
concepts.summary: Against populations that limp in unbalanced ways and over-fold, use smaller bet sizes than the solver's larger theoretical raises.
concepts.details: The solver likes increasingly large raise sizes vs SB limps at deeper stacks, but the EV gain over a flat 3.5x is negligible beyond 30bb. Bigger sizes are overkill in today's games where population limping ranges are highly unbalanced and over-fold to BB raises; even smaller sizes work better exploitatively against weak players who fold too much.
concepts.actionable_rule: Versus weak, unbalanced limpers who over-fold, use smaller raise sizes (around or below 3.5x) rather than the larger theoretically-favored sizes, since the EV difference is negligible and smaller sizes exploit their over-folding.

concepts.title: 3-bet vs Call Mix Shifts With Opener's Range Strength
concepts.summary: As the opener's range gets stronger (earlier position), reduce 3-betting/rejamming frequency and increase flatting, because rejams no longer generate enough folds to be profitable.
concepts.details: Against late-position opens, wide ranges fold often to rejams making them profitable; against EP opens the range is too strong, so the solver shifts hands from rejams to calls. From the SB the rejam frequency drops from ~28% vs BN to ~9% vs UTG at 15bb, while calling frequency rises as position gets earlier.
concepts.actionable_rule: When facing an open, lower your 3-bet/rejam frequency and raise your flat-call frequency as the opener's position gets earlier (range gets stronger); only rejam hands that still generate sufficient fold equity.

concepts.title: Short-Stack Blind Defense Is Jam-or-Fold
concepts.summary: At ~15bb the SB plays a pure jam-or-fold strategy versus opens, with rejam frequency scaling to the opener's range width.
concepts.details: At 15bb the SB VPIPs ~22%, rejamming ~28.2% vs BN, ~22.5% vs CO, ~14.7% vs LJ and ~9.4% vs UTG, with almost no flatting except some calls vs EP where rejams lose fold equity. The CO at 15bb cannot flat at all (no flatting range) because of the risk of the BN calling or squeezing behind, so it rejams its entire playable range (~8.3% vs UTG to ~13.3% vs HJ).
concepts.actionable_rule: With ~15bb facing an open, play jam-or-fold: rejam a linear range whose width tracks the opener's range (wider vs LP, tighter vs EP), and avoid flatting from positions that risk being squeezed behind.

concepts.title: Scrap Tiny All-In Ranges for Simplicity
concepts.summary: When a GTO rejam/all-in range is very small (e.g. ~1-3.5% at 25-40bb from EP-facing spots), drop it and play a cleaner 3-bet/call/fold strategy with negligible EV loss.
concepts.details: At 25bb the SB and BN have tiny rejam ranges vs EP (BN ~1.2% vs UTG); the HJ at 25bb rejams only ~1.45% on average. The author recommends ignoring these and converting mixed strategies to pure actions: a call/rejam mix becomes a pure call, a non-all-in-3-bet/rejam mix becomes a pure non-all-in 3-bet.
concepts.actionable_rule: If the solver assigns a rejam frequency below ~3-4%, ignore the all-in range and play 3-bet/call/fold instead; resolve mixed actions to the dominant pure action.

concepts.title: Deeper Stacks Favor Post-Flop Playable 3-Bets
concepts.summary: As stacks deepen (40-60bb), shift the 3-betting range toward hands with good post-flop playability since most 3-bet pots reach the flop and IP is too deep to 4-bet jam.
concepts.details: At 60bb the SB averages 24% VPIP and prefers 3-betting hands that play well post-flop OOP; because IP can't 4-bet jam, the 3-bettor can call many 4-bets and reach the flop with high-equity hands. The BN warns against 3-betting too much trash deep because you'll play low-equity hands post-flop against a strong calling range.
concepts.actionable_rule: At 40bb+, build your 3-bet range with hands that retain post-flop playability and equity; avoid 3-bet-bluffing pure trash that plays poorly when called deep-stacked.

concepts.title: Polarized 3-Bet Range With Blocker Bluffs
concepts.summary: Non-all-in 3-bet ranges are polarized: strong value hands plus bluffs chosen for their blocker value and decent playability (suited/offsuit Ax, Kx, broadways).
concepts.details: Across positions the 3-bet/fold bluffs are mid-to-low suited Ax and Kx, AJo, ATo, KQo, KJo, with suited Ax preferred vs EP and offsuit Ax/broadways vs LP. At 60bb the CO 3-bet range focuses on blocker hands. Bluffs are picked for card-removal effects against opponents' continuing ranges.
concepts.actionable_rule: Construct 3-bet bluffs from hands with good blockers (suited Ax/Kx, offsuit broadways) and acceptable playability rather than random weak hands; pair them with your value hands to keep the range polarized.

concepts.title: Flat-Calling Range Composition by Multiway/IP Considerations
concepts.summary: Calling ranges favor hands that retain equity multiway and play well post-flop: pocket pairs, suited Ax, suited connectors, and suited broadways, plus occasional slowplayed premiums.
concepts.details: From the SB, suited connectors, small suited Ax and broadways make great calls vs EP because the BB will often call too, creating multiway pots where they retain equity. The BN calls wider including offsuit broadways vs LP since it has position; the CO keeps a capped, fairly constant calling range because it plays OOP post-flop. AA/KK/AKs are slowplayed ~25-33% of the time to protect the calling range.
concepts.actionable_rule: Flat with pocket pairs, suited Ax, suited connectors and suited broadways that play well post-flop; call wider when in position and tighter/capped when you'll be OOP, and occasionally slowplay premiums (~25-33%) to protect the call.

concepts.title: Position Constrains Flatting Width
concepts.summary: Players who will be in position post-flop (BN) can flat much wider than players who will be out of position (CO), even against the same opener.
concepts.details: The BN expands its calling range as the opener weakens (up to ~27% VPIP vs CO at 40bb) because it has position post-flop. The CO's flatting range stays fairly constant (~10% at 25bb) regardless of opener width because it must worry about playing OOP and about players acting behind, limiting how many hands can profitably peel.
concepts.actionable_rule: Widen your flatting range when you'll have position post-flop and the opener is weak; keep it tight and capped when you'll be out of position regardless of how wide the opener is.

concepts.title: 5-Bet vs Call Response to 4-Bets Depends on Range Polarity
concepts.summary: Against a 4-bet, get more of your range all-in (5-bet) when your 3-bet range was polarized; call more when it was more linear/connected.
concepts.details: At 60bb the CO 5-bets all-in ~39% vs an UTG 4-bet but only ~29% vs a HJ 4-bet (calling 22%), because its 3-bet range vs UTG is more polarized so those bluffs play better as 5-bets than as calls. Similarly the HJ 5-bets ~39.2% vs UTG but only ~28.2% vs LJ. As stacks deepen (60bb), a meaningful 4-bet calling range emerges since stacks support post-flop play.
concepts.actionable_rule: When your 3-bet range vs that opener was polarized (more bluffs), respond to a 4-bet by 5-bet jamming more and calling less; when facing a 4-bet from a weaker/wider position with more linear hands, shift toward calling, especially at 60bb.

concepts.title: Small Pairs: Rejam vs LP, Call vs EP
concepts.summary: Small pocket pairs make great rejamming hands against late-position opens (fold equity) but play better as calls against early-position opens (set-mining without fold equity).
concepts.details: At 25bb the SB rejams small pairs vs LP for the fold equity, but against EP opens, where rejams get called too often, small pairs convert to set-mining calls. This reflects the broader principle that fold equity drives the rejam-vs-call decision for marginal pairs.
concepts.actionable_rule: Rejam small pocket pairs against wide late-position opens for fold equity, but flat them as set-mines against strong early-position opens where a shove gets called too often.

concepts.title: Stack Depth Reshapes 3-Bet vs Flat Decision
concepts.summary: As effective stacks deepen, an early-position opener facing or making a 3-bet shifts from rejam/3-bet-fold toward more 3-betting or flatting because equity can be realized post-flop.
concepts.details: At 15bb UTG+1 vs UTG only rejams (~7%). At 25bb rejamming disappears and a flat-call range (JJ-66, AQo+, suited broadways) plus a 5.1% 3-bet appears. At 40bb the 3-bet shrinks and shifts toward suited Ax blockers. At 60bb the 3-bet widens again (5.7%) because UTG defends by calling rather than 4-bet jamming, letting the 3-bettor realize equity OOP-in-position dynamics.
concepts.actionable_rule: Choose your response to or with a 3-bet by stack depth: rejam-only at ~15bb, add a flat-call range around 25bb, use blocker-heavy 3-bets at ~40bb when villain 4-bet-jams, and widen 3-bets at 60bb when villain will call and play OOP.

concepts.title: Number of Active Players Reduces Required Defense vs 3-Bet
concepts.summary: The more players still to act behind a 3-bettor, the more weighted their range is to value and the fewer hands you must defend to stay unexploitable.
concepts.details: Extra active players reduce the chance the 3-bet is a bluff, so the 3-betting range is stronger and you can fold more without being exploited.
concepts.actionable_rule: When facing a 3-bet with multiple players still to act behind the 3-bettor, tighten your continuing range and fold more, since their range is more value-heavy.

concepts.title: Calling vs Rejam = Top Equity Hands by Stack Depth
concepts.summary: When facing an all-in rejam after min-raising, your calling range should be the top X% of hands with the highest equity against the rejamming range, sized to the effective stack.
concepts.details: Average fold after a 2x open vs short-stack rejam (10-25bb) is ~55%, call ~45%. Bigger rejam stacks require less defense (fewer calls). Earlier rejam positions are tighter, so defend tighter against them; SB rejams get called slightly lighter than BB because BB can flat to close action, strengthening its jam range.
concepts.actionable_rule: Against a rejam, call the top-equity portion of your range vs their jamming range; defend tighter vs deeper rejams and vs earlier positions, and slightly lighter vs the SB than the BB.

concepts.title: IP vs OOP Determines 4-Bet vs Flat Balance
concepts.summary: When facing a non-all-in 3-bet, prefer calling and playing post-flop when in position, and prefer 4-betting (or folding) when out of position.
concepts.details: With 25-40bb the only 4-bet size is all-in. IP openers fold less and 4-bet less, choosing to call and realize equity. OOP openers 4-bet more (~22.84% constant) and call less. Realizing equity OOP is harder, so flatting is less attractive there.
concepts.actionable_rule: Facing a 3-bet: when in position, call more and 4-bet less to play flops; when out of position, 4-bet more and avoid flatting since equity realization is poor.

concepts.title: Stack Depth and 4-Bet Frequency Trade-off
concepts.summary: 4-betting frequency falls as stacks deepen; IP openers shift toward calling, while OOP openers shift toward folding rather than flatting.
concepts.details: IP: deeper stacks lower 4-bet frequency and raise calling frequency. OOP: 4-bet frequency stays ~22.84% but calling drops from ~44% at 25bb to ~23% at 40bb because deep OOP equity realization is poor. At 60-80bb all-in 4-bets largely disappear, replaced by smaller non-all-in 4-bets, and calling rises in both cases.
concepts.actionable_rule: As stacks deepen: IP, 4-bet less and call more; OOP, 4-bet at a steady rate but fold more rather than flat; beyond ~60bb replace all-in 4-bets with smaller sized 4-bets.

concepts.title: Hand-Type Selection for 4-Bet vs Call
concepts.summary: 4-bet hands with good equity but poor playability; call with hands that play well post-flop.
concepts.details: The solver 4-bets all-in with mid/small pocket pairs, big offsuit Ax, and small suited Ax (good equity, weak playability, blocker value). It calls with AA, KK, suited connectors, suited broadways, and big suited Ax that flop well and realize equity.
concepts.actionable_rule: When facing a 3-bet, route mid/small pairs and offsuit/small-suited Ax into the 4-bet range, and keep AA/KK, suited connectors, suited broadways, and big suited Ax as calls to play post-flop.

concepts.title: Blinds Should Size Up 3-Bets When Deep
concepts.summary: Because deep IP openers love to flat 3-bets, the blinds must use larger 3-bet sizes to deny cheap equity realization.
concepts.details: With 60-80bb the opener has strong incentive to call and play IP. Small 3-bets let the opener continue with a very wide range and realize equity on hands they would otherwise fold; larger sizing keeps their continuing range honest. Solver frequencies assume sufficiently large 3-bet sizes (e.g. 3.25-3.5x).
concepts.actionable_rule: When 3-betting from the blinds against a deep opener who will have position, increase your 3-bet sizing (around 3.25-3.5x) to prevent them from profitably flatting wide and realizing equity.

concepts.title: Playing vs 5-Bets After 4-Betting
concepts.summary: After your 4-bet gets 5-bet, the strategy collapses to value-or-fold: continue with premiums and fold blocker bluffs.
concepts.details: With deep stacks where smaller 4-bets exist, facing a 5-bet you call any premium hand and fold the blocker-type bluffs used to balance the 4-bet. EP may even adopt a no-4-bet strategy vs the blinds because few hands want to 4-bet IP given how polarized the blinds' 3-bet ranges are.
concepts.actionable_rule: When facing a 5-bet after 4-betting, call only with premium hands and fold your blocker bluffs; consider not 4-betting at all from EP vs polarized blind 3-bets.

concepts.title: ICM and Risk Premium in 3-Bet Defense
concepts.summary: Tournament stack dynamics and risk premium alter how wide you can defend against a 3-bet beyond pure chip EV.
concepts.details: Key factors include how deep you are, your and villain's risk premium, and future game states: losing may cost raise/fold ability or push you into a marginal ICM spot, while winning may make you chip leader to pressure medium stacks. A call near 0 cEV is usually slightly $EV-negative.
concepts.actionable_rule: In tournaments, tighten 3-bet defense relative to chip-EV when you carry a high risk premium or face ICM pressure; treat near-zero cEV calls as folds since they are typically $EV-losing.

concepts.title: Range Morphology Guides Defense
concepts.summary: Whether the 3-betting range is polarized or linear changes which hands you should continue with.
concepts.details: Against a polarized 3-bet range, calling hands need to dominate the bluff portion and realize equity; against a linear range, raw equity and blockers matter more. Consider how your specific hand plays post-flop against villain's range and your relative (post-flop) position.
concepts.actionable_rule: Before continuing against a 3-bet, classify the range as polarized or linear and pick hands that play well against that specific shape, factoring in your post-flop position.

concepts.title: Two Fundamental Reasons to Bet
concepts.summary: Every bet exists to leverage the informational advantage of knowing your own cards and to realize your equity or deny the opponent's equity realization.
concepts.details: Categorizing bets as 'value' or 'bluff' describes only the outcome (called by worse vs folding out better), not the reason. Outcomes depend on the opponent's actual holding, which you don't control. The two true reasons to bet are: (1) leverage that you know your exact cards while the opponent only knows your range, and (2) realize equity / deny villain's equity realization and set SPR favorably.
concepts.actionable_rule: Bet when it leverages your informational edge or improves your equity realization/denies the opponent's — not merely because the hand is good or bad.

concepts.title: Range Diversity Maximizes Informational Advantage
concepts.summary: Build betting ranges containing hand types whose optimal counter-response differs (fold vs call vs raise), so the opponent cannot respond correctly to all of them simultaneously.
concepts.details: Your informational advantage is the gap between your exact holding and your range, and it is valuable only when the opponent's correct decision varies greatly by your actual hand. If your betting range is one type (e.g., only nut/air), the opponent's decision is trivial and betting gains nothing. Mix hands so there is a large EV discrepancy in the opponent's call (or raise) depending on which part of your range you hold; the EV of folding is always 0 so it doesn't constrain you.
concepts.actionable_rule: Construct each betting/raising range with diverse hand types so that no single opponent response is correct against all your holdings.

concepts.title: Board Coverage Across Runouts
concepts.summary: A balanced betting range must be able to make strong hands on a wide variety of turn and river runouts, not just on the flop.
concepts.details: If a betting range is skewed (e.g., heavily flush draws on a two-tone flop), the opponent can call and then attack blank turns. Preserving the informational edge requires runout coverage on both betting and checking ranges across all future streets, otherwise well-built flop ranges still get exploited later.
concepts.actionable_rule: Ensure your betting and checking ranges contain hands that improve to strong holdings across all major runout categories, not just the current street.

concepts.title: Bet EV Scales With Stack Depth (Deeper = More Equity Capture)
concepts.summary: With a polarized range, the deeper the stacks, the more a bettor can over-realize equity and deny the opponent's; shallow stacks let raw equity dominate.
concepts.details: In the clairvoyance toy game, the bettor's EV rises with bet size relative to pot: 10% pot bet gives $54.6, 50% pot $66.7, pot $75, 2x pot $83.5, 10x pot $95.4 (out of $100). Deep stacks and more streets make range balance crucial and raw equity less important; short stacks send money in preflop/flop where raw equity dominates.
concepts.actionable_rule: When deep with a polarized range, use larger bets and rely on balance to over-realize equity; when short, prioritize raw equity since balance matters less.

concepts.title: Never Proactively Fold When Checking Is Free
concepts.summary: Folding when you could check for free is strictly dominated; always check bad hands and wait for a bet before mucking.
concepts.details: Even trash hands retain equity or backdoor equity and can improve or be bluffed later if opponents check. Crucially, proactively mucking weak hands reveals information: if you only check when strong, opponents adjust and only give action with strong holdings. Folding is correct only when facing a bet and neither calling nor raising has positive expectation.
concepts.actionable_rule: Never fold a hand when you can check for free; only fold when facing a bet and both calling and raising are negative EV.

concepts.title: In-Position Checking Guarantees Equity Realization
concepts.summary: Checking back in position immediately realizes equity by seeing a card or reaching showdown, while checking out of position does not because you may face a bet.
concepts.details: Checking back IP removes a betting street from the game tree, benefiting IP's weaker hands. IP's checking range only needs to be balanced for the average turn card. OOP checking guarantees nothing — you may be bet off equity — so OOP's checking range must be balanced on the flop to handle IP bets, demanding greater balance.
concepts.actionable_rule: When IP, freely check weak hands to realize equity cheaply; when OOP, balance your checking range to withstand bets since checking doesn't guarantee equity realization.

concepts.title: Equity Buckets (EQB) Classification
concepts.summary: Classify each hand by its hand-vs-range equity into Strong (≥75%), Good (50-75%), Weak (33-50%), and Trash (<33%) to gauge a range's true equity distribution.
concepts.details: This refines the linear/polarized/condensed morphology categories with finer detail. A hand's bucket is dynamic, depending on board and ranges in play: top pair is 82% EQ (Strong) on AQT but only 60% (Good) on T98; two pair on AQT can beat a set on T98. Use it to assess how well a range fits a morphology.
concepts.actionable_rule: Bucket each hand by hand-vs-range equity (Strong ≥75%, Good 50-75%, Weak 33-50%, Trash <33%) relative to the actual board to evaluate range strength.

concepts.title: IP vs BB Flop Equity Distribution Asymmetry
concepts.summary: Across all flops, the in-position preflop aggressor holds far more strong and good hands while the BB caller holds nearly half trash hands.
concepts.details: Averaged over 1,755 flops for 20-40bb MTT ranges: BB has ~7% strong, ~25% good, ~23% weak, ~46% trash; IP (BN/UTG) has ~22% strong, ~43% good, ~29% weak, only ~6% trash. This range advantage justifies the IP aggressor's high c-bet frequency and the BB's more cautious, capped defense.
concepts.actionable_rule: As the IP preflop aggressor, bet frequently exploiting your range's strength advantage; as the BB defender, recognize your range is trash-heavy and defend selectively.

concepts.title: Pot-Size Bet/Raise Mechanics
concepts.summary: A pot-size bet lays exactly 2-to-1 (33% pot odds); a pot-size raise = match the bet, add the resulting pot, then add that on top.
concepts.details: A simple fraction bet is pot × fraction (e.g., $100 pot, half-pot = $50). For a pot-size raise after a bet: match the previous bet, total the pot including your match, then add that total on top of your match. The size offers the opponent 33% pot odds, the lowest break-even equity threshold for a 'pot' sizing.
concepts.actionable_rule: To make a pot-size raise, call the bet, sum the entire pot after your call, then add that amount on top as the raise.

concepts.title: Alpha and MDF Are Misleading Off the River
concepts.summary: MDF and Alpha assume checking has 0 EV and bluffs always lose the whole pot when called, which is false pre-river where hands retain equity.
concepts.details: Alpha/MDF are derived from the EV equation assuming the bettor checks for 0 EV and loses the pot+bet whenever a bluff is called. On the flop/turn most hands have equity, so the defender need not defend as much as MDF says (they only make IP indifferent to the EV of checking back, not to 0), and bluffs are more profitable because they pick up equity. They only become reliable on the river.
concepts.actionable_rule: Use Alpha/MDF as rough guides only on the river; pre-river, compare actual bet vs check EV instead of relying on these numbers.

concepts.title: Compare EV of Actions, Never in a Vacuum
concepts.summary: Always choose the action with the highest expectation by comparing all available actions, rather than judging one action's profitability in isolation.
concepts.details: A bet being 'profitable' relative to 0 is meaningless if checking is more profitable. EV must be compared across folding, checking, calling, raising, and betting. Don't justify a play just because it 'only needs to work X%' — the real baseline is the next-best action's EV.
concepts.actionable_rule: For every decision, compute or estimate the EV of each legal action and choose the highest, never judging an action against a vacuum baseline of 0.

concepts.title: Actions Convey Information — Tell a Consistent Story
concepts.summary: Every action narrows your possible holdings to that action's range; don't try to represent hands your line cannot contain, and disbelieve opponents whose story doesn't add up.
concepts.details: Once you take an action you can only hold hands in the range that takes that action. Rookies often try to represent hands they cannot credibly have given prior action. This makes hand reading two-sided: track villain's plausible range by their line and keep your own ranges balanced. If an opponent's betting story is internally inconsistent, they likely don't have the hand.
concepts.actionable_rule: Only represent hands consistent with your prior actions, and call down opponents whose betting line cannot credibly contain the strong hand they represent.

concepts.title: Strongest value hands pair with biggest bet-sizes
concepts.summary: In a symmetric-range single-street game, the optimal structure uses larger bet-sizes for stronger value hands, each balanced with bluffs from the weakest hands.
concepts.details: From the [0-1] Toy Game, IP bets the biggest size with the strongest value hand, next size with the second strongest, etc., pairing each value tier with bluffs taken from the bottom of the range so the opponent is indifferent. The solver replicated this: AA used the largest size, KK the next, QQ the smallest, balanced with 55/66 as bluffs; JJ-77 always checked.
concepts.actionable_rule: When constructing a polarized betting range, assign your strongest value hands to your largest bet-size and weaker value hands to smaller sizes, balancing each size tier with bluffs drawn from the bottom of your range to make the opponent indifferent.

concepts.title: Multiple bet-sizes leak information that raises can punish
concepts.summary: Splitting your range across many sizes caps the range tied to each size; if the opponent can raise, they exploit the capped small-size range with a polarized raise.
concepts.details: In the toy game, a 1/3-pot size could only be QQ or 55, so an opponent allowed to check-raise it attacks the capped distribution with AA/KK plus bluffs, picking up EV. Hero adjusts: when x/r is allowed vs the 1/3 size, drop that size and shift QQ to 2/3 pot; when x/r is allowed vs all sizes, collapse to a single full-pot size with value KK+ and check QQ-66.
concepts.actionable_rule: Reduce the number of bet-sizes you use as the opponent's ability to raise increases; if they can profitably raise your smaller sizes, eliminate those sizes and consolidate your value into fewer, larger bets to avoid presenting an exploitable capped range.

concepts.title: All-in size denies opponents exploitation
concepts.summary: Going all-in limits the opponent to call/fold, removing their ability to leverage information via raises, which makes it valuable at low SPR.
concepts.details: All-in is special because it eliminates the raise option. At 2x pot SPR Hero can split between all-in (AA 42%, bluff 55) and pot (KK, protective AA, bluffs). When SPR rises to 3+, all-in stops being used because OOP's range defends effectively and bluffing the bottom becomes too expensive.
concepts.actionable_rule: When SPR is roughly 1 or less, prefer an all-in size to deny the opponent raise-based exploitation; split between pot and all-in for SPR 1-2, and abandon all-in for SPR 3+ where it is no longer effective.

concepts.title: SPR governs optimal bet-size scaling
concepts.summary: As SPR increases, the optimal value bet-size structure shifts from all-in toward larger pot-fraction and overbet sizes.
concepts.details: From the single-street toy game: SPR<=1 -> all-in optimal; SPR 1-2 -> split between pot and all-in; SPR 3 -> split between 75% and 125% pot; SPR 5-10 -> split between 75% and 150% pot. Higher SPR means deeper play where pure all-ins are dominated by sized bets.
concepts.actionable_rule: Scale your bet-size to SPR: shove at SPR<=1, mix pot and all-in at SPR 1-2, use ~75%/125% pot at SPR 3, and ~75%/150% pot at SPR 5-10.

concepts.title: Simplify to one dominant bet-size with negligible EV loss
concepts.summary: Collapsing a multi-size strategy to the single most-used size typically preserves nearly all EV (avg ~0.21% of pot), so humans should use fewer sizes.
concepts.details: Across thousands of postflop sims on all 1755 flops, most flops have one or two dominant sizes. Close sizes (25% vs 33%) have near-identical EV; remove the lower-frequency one. If two chosen sizes are far apart, replace both with a middle size. Removing small sizes lowers betting frequency; removing large sizes raises it. EV gain from splitting against a GTO opponent is rarely worth the complexity.
concepts.actionable_rule: Simplify your strategy to one (or at most two) dominant bet-sizes per node: drop low-frequency sizes that are near a dominant size, and replace two far-apart sizes with a single intermediate size, accepting trivial EV loss for far easier execution.

concepts.title: Exploitative bet-sizing against weak opponents
