concepts.summary: Although splitting sizes adds little EV vs GTO, varying your size by hand type against mistake-prone opponents can be extremely profitable.
concepts.details: Theory and practice agree that multiple sizes don't beat a reacting GTO opponent meaningfully, but an opponent who fails to punish capped ranges or over/underfolds to specific sizes can be exploited by tailoring size to the part of your range you bet.
concepts.actionable_rule: Against opponents who don't react correctly to your sizing, deliberately use different bet-sizes for different parts of your range to extract extra value or fold equity, since they won't exploit the information you reveal.

concepts.title: Geometric bet-sizing for polarized multi-street value
concepts.summary: With a polarized range over multiple streets, betting the same pot fraction each street so the river is all-in (geometric growth) maximizes EV.
concepts.details: Final pot FP = SP * R^S; solve for the growth rate R to get the per-street fraction. This makes equal-fraction bets each street ending in a river shove. It applies only to perfectly polar vs pure bluff-catcher ranges, which never occur in reality, and deep stacks produce huge overbets that real (non-polar) ranges cannot support, so a lower cap applies.
concepts.actionable_rule: When holding a strongly polarized range across multiple streets, size each bet as the same fraction of the pot so the river bet is exactly all-in (geometric sizing), but cap the size below the geometric ideal when stacks are deep and your range is not perfectly polar.

concepts.title: Polarization advantage drives bet frequency and size
concepts.summary: The more polarized your range relative to the opponent's, the more often and the larger you should bet; a depolarized range should mostly check.
concepts.details: Toy games A-E: with a big polarization disadvantage Hero always checks (splits pot 50/50); slight disadvantage allows ~15% betting at 60% pot; symmetric ranges split between 90% and 120% pot; slight advantage introduces all-in with 120% overbet dominant; big advantage makes all-in by far dominant. The small 30% size is never used. Perfectly polar vs bluff-catchers -> only all-in.
concepts.actionable_rule: Bet more frequently and with larger sizes as your range polarization advantage grows; with a depolarized range, check most or all of it, and reserve overbets and all-ins for when you hold a clear polarization advantage.

concepts.title: Check back to preserve range when polarization-disadvantaged in multi-street
concepts.summary: With even a slight polarization disadvantage across multiple streets, the in-position player should never bet and instead check back to keep their full range and remove a betting street.
concepts.details: In the multi-street toy game, unlike single-street, a slight polarization disadvantage stops Hero from betting entirely. Checking back removes a betting street so Hero reaches the river with their whole range, whereas betting forces folding hands to a check-raise. All-in doesn't help because the opponent's range is stronger. Betting and bigger sizes only emerge once Hero gains a polarization (and equity) advantage.
concepts.actionable_rule: In position with a polarization (or range) disadvantage over multiple streets, check back rather than bet, preserving your entire range to the river and avoiding being check-raised off hands.

concepts.title: Range Merging on Early Streets
concepts.summary: Bet a merged (combined polarized + depolarized) range for a small size on the turn rather than a heavily polarized range, to avoid being exploited by the opponent betting into your capped range.
concepts.details: If you over-polarize on the turn (big bets with top and bottom, checking back middling hands like TT-88), the opponent can attack your capped checking range by betting the river, increasing their EV. Betting a merged range for a smaller size raises your betting frequency and minimizes the downside of checking back weak holdings. After the opponent calls, they mostly check to you, letting you check back middling hands and realize equity.
applies_to: situations where opponent can bet future streets
concepts.actionable_rule: On early betting streets without a large polarization advantage, bet a merged range for a small size to protect against being capped, and wait until later streets to polarize.

concepts.title: Polarization Advantage Drives Bet Size
concepts.summary: The more polarized your range is relative to the opponent's, the larger your bet sizing should be; with multi-street betting, prefer smaller sizes early unless your polarization advantage is substantial.
concepts.details: With a strong polarization advantage you can bet 100% of your range and shift toward larger sizes (90% pot, even 120% overbets), approaching the geometric bet size. However, high SPR and the threat of opponent traps reduce profitability of very large bets, so all-in bets are rarely used early unless stacks are shallow.
concepts.actionable_rule: Increase bet size as your polarization advantage grows; with a very large advantage approach the geometric size, but keep bets smaller early and avoid all-ins on early streets unless stacks are shallow or SPR is low.

concepts.title: Flop-Specific Bet Sizing
concepts.summary: Different flops interact differently with ranges' equities and polarization, so GTO play uses flop-specific c-bet sizes; using one size for all flops costs at most ~0.9bb/100 against perfect play.
concepts.details: Across all 1,755 flops in a 40bb BB vs BN SRP, using four sizes (min, 1/3, 1/2, 2/3 pot) vs only 1/3 pot averaged a 0.14% pot (0.9bb/100) EV difference assuming perfect play. The real edge is larger against human opponents who struggle to defend against varied sizing. The solver is usually indifferent between similar sizes (25% vs 33%, 60% vs 67%), so it suffices to identify whether a flop is a 'big bet' or 'small bet' flop.
concepts.actionable_rule: Classify each flop as a small-bet or big-bet board and use at least two c-bet sizes (e.g. 1/3 and 2/3 pot); don't worry about distinguishing very close sizes since they are roughly indifferent.

concepts.title: Exploit Suboptimal Bet Sizing with Check-Raise
concepts.summary: When an opponent uses a non-GTO bet size at full frequency, attack it; e.g. against a 100% 2/3-pot c-bet on a board where GTO says min-bet, switch to a check-raise-only strategy.
concepts.details: On J22 from UTG vs BB, GTO is min-betting 100% (EV 77.05). If UTG instead c-bets 2/3 pot at 100% frequency, BB can x/r-only to crush their EV to 71.01. To stay balanced UTG must drop to 42.45% c-bet frequency, but most players won't, leaving their range unbalanced and exploitable.
applies_to: facing oversized c-bets at high frequency
concepts.actionable_rule: When an opponent bets larger than GTO recommends but keeps a high (near-100%) frequency, deviate toward an aggressive check-raise/folding response to punish their over-betting range.

concepts.title: Simplify Toward 1/3-Pot vs Population
concepts.summary: A single small 1/3-pot c-bet size works well against the general population because it simplifies the game tree, allows high-frequency c-betting, and exploits the tendency to overfold to small bets.
concepts.details: Most online MTT regulars use 1/3 pot across the board. It forces villains to make decisions revealing range information at low cost and exploits population overfolding to small bets. Against tougher players, mix sizes to stay balanced and defend well, while playing exploitatively versus weaker opponents.
concepts.actionable_rule: Against the general population, default to a high-frequency 1/3-pot c-bet to exploit overfolding; add a larger size and balance only when facing tough, adjusting opponents.

concepts.title: Don't Misread Indifference as Free Reign
concepts.summary: Equal EVs between actions in a solver only hold at equilibrium; arbitrarily reshuffling which hands bet vs check while keeping overall frequency the same makes your range exploitable.
concepts.details: If GTO bets all hands at 50%, you are indifferent per combo, but betting the strong half 100% and checking the weak half 100% keeps the aggregate frequency yet creates an exploitable, polarized betting range and a capped checking range. Indifference is created by the opponent's balanced play; against an unaware, unbalanced opponent one action becomes strictly best. Before drastically deviating, re-solve the locked strategy to check EV loss versus a min-exploitative opponent.
concepts.actionable_rule: Maintain balanced range composition and board coverage even when per-combo EVs look indifferent; before major deviations, lock and re-solve to verify minimal EV loss against an adjusting opponent.

concepts.title: Solver Game Tree Must Be Balanced for Both Players
concepts.summary: Solver output depends entirely on the bet-sizing and action options the user inputs; omitting reasonable actions (like OOP check-raise) skews the equilibrium.
concepts.details: A solver cannot discover optimal sizes itself; the user defines the allowed sizes/actions. If OOP cannot check-raise (only call/fold), IP knows equity cannot be denied and bets more often. Too many sizes explode the game tree exponentially and become impractical. Use common fractional sizes (1/2, 2/3 pot) as reasonable approximations unless deliberately modeling an opponent's leak.
concepts.actionable_rule: When solving, give both players realistic bet sizes and response options (including check-raises) to avoid skewed output, and limit the number of sizes to keep trees manageable.

concepts.title: Suit Isomorphism
concepts.summary: Suits are strategically equivalent preflop and on flops, reducing 1,326 combos to 169 hands and 22,100 flops to 1,755 strategically unique flops.
concepts.details: Isomorphic flops (e.g. all four suited-rainbow versions of AKQ monotone) produce identical numbers of flushes, sets, top pairs, etc., and hands play identically regardless of suit. This lets players and solvers study or solve a single representative of each isomorphic class and extrapolate, saving learning effort and computation.
concepts.actionable_rule: Treat suit-equivalent flops as identical and study one representative of each isomorphic class rather than every specific board.

concepts.title: Dynamic vs Static Boards
concepts.summary: Volatile (dynamic) boards let hand equities shift drastically on later streets, while static boards keep good hands good and bad hands bad on most runouts.
concepts.details: Volatility is a property of the flop combined with players' ranges. Low, connected, draw-heavy boards (e.g. 8h7h3d) are dynamic — flushes, straights, and overcards can flip equities. Disconnected high-card rainbow flops (e.g. Ks7d2h) are static. This distinction governs protection betting, bet sizing, and the value of equity realization.
concepts.actionable_rule: Classify the flop as dynamic or static; bet more for protection and charge draws on dynamic boards, and lean toward smaller/thinner value-oriented strategies on static boards.

concepts.title: Flop Classification by Structure, Texture, Rank, and Connectivity
concepts.summary: Group flops by structure (trips/paired/unpaired), texture (monotone/two-tone/rainbow), rank (highest card), and number of possible straights to study similar boards together.
concepts.details: Flop structure (paired rainbow, paired two-tone, etc.) and texture (two-tone subtypes: high-mid, mid-low, high-low) dictate how ranges connect. Higher-ranked flops are more common (Axx = 21.74%; 85% of flops are rank 9+). Straight potential ranges from 0 (AQ7) to 3 (JT9). Cards group into High (K-T), Mid (9-6), Low (5-2), and Ace, allowing flops like A54/A53/A52 to be treated as one 'Ace + two low' family.
concepts.actionable_rule: Categorize each flop by structure, texture, top-card rank, and straight potential, then apply the strategy learned for that family rather than memorizing every individual board.

concepts.title: Representative Flop Subsets
concepts.summary: Even 1,755 unique flops is too many, so select a minimal subset satisfying coverage conditions to represent the whole game for study and simplification.
concepts.details: Tipton's approach defines conditions a good subset must satisfy then finds the minimum set meeting them: any single card appears, any-suit flush draw appears, any-suit monotone appears, paired boards of each rank appear, three-straight boards appear, and boards with each one-gap and two-gap rank structure appear. This produces a manageable representative training set.
concepts.actionable_rule: Study a small representative subset of flops covering all key structural conditions (single cards, flush draws, monotone, paired, straight, and gapped boards) instead of every unique flop.

concepts.title: No betting lead in GTO — bet on range merit
concepts.summary: Game theory has no concept of a 'betting lead'; whether the BB should donk bet or check is determined purely by range composition, equity distribution and SPR, not by who was the preflop aggressor.
concepts.details: Conventional wisdom says OOP should always check to the preflop raiser. But a bet is justified by leveraging informational advantage, range composition and SPR to realize equity or deny opponent's equity realization. Aggregated GTO solutions show overall BB donk frequency is only ~2% and IP c-bets ~84%, broadly agreeing with consensus, but the solver donk bets at high frequency on specific textures where the BB's range merits it.
applies_to: BB vs IP single raised pot
concepts.actionable_rule: Do not refuse to donk bet just because you are not the preflop aggressor; decide between betting and checking based on range vs range equity distribution and SPR rather than the 'betting lead' convention.

concepts.title: Donk bet low/middling connected boards that hit BB range
concepts.summary: The BB should donk bet at high frequency on low connected rainbow boards like 654r and 7xx/6xx textures where the ranges are close in equity and IP is full of weak hands.
concepts.details: On 654r the BB has ~51% equity vs IP's 49%, the BB's good hands rise to 40% and trash drops to 18%, while IP's Ax become weak (49% equity). The ~34 high-donk flops (50%+) are 7xx and 6xx with one to three possible straights. The BB over-realizes equity (103% EQR, capturing ~52% of pot) because its range is more polarized than IP's, resembling the Clairvoyance Toy where the polarized player wants to lead. More flopped straights → smaller size, higher frequency. Rainbow donked more than two-tone; monotone donked least.
applies_to: BB vs IP single raised pot
concepts.actionable_rule: On low connected rainbow boards (7xx, 6xx like 654r) donk bet a polarized-but-wide range at high frequency, using a small (~1/4-pot) size, increasing frequency and shrinking size as more straights are present.

concepts.title: Never donk bet ace-high / IP-favored boards
concepts.summary: On boards like A76r where IP holds a large equity and strong-hand advantage, the BB should check 100% because donking gets raised too often and reverses the equity-denial effect.
concepts.details: On A76r IP has 62% equity vs BB's 38% and 31% strong hands vs the BB's 8%; IP top pairs average 85% equity. IP can c-bet 100% and raise donks 53% of the time, so any BB lead lets IP fold weak hands it would otherwise c-bet and only continue profitably. Forcing the BB to donk top-pair-or-better dropped EV from 25 to 13 and left the checking range vulnerable. Removing the donk option entirely on A76r costs ~0% EV. This category (trips, monotone, high-card-paired, disconnected two-tone, HXX, AXX) averages 39% equity, 76% EQR.
applies_to: BB vs IP single raised pot
concepts.actionable_rule: On A-high, high-card, monotone, paired-high or disconnected boards where IP dominates, check 100% of your BB range and never split your range with a donk bet.

concepts.title: Donk frequency is an effect of range distribution, not a cause
concepts.summary: High donk-bet frequency correlates with high BB equity/EV, but the underlying cause is the favorable range distribution; donking is a downstream response.
concepts.details: Tables subdividing flops by donk frequency show highest-EQ/EV flops are also highest donk-frequency flops. The driver is how ranges interact: when the BB is more polarized (strong+good+trash) and IP is depolarized with many weak hands wanting free cards, leading becomes profitable. Treat range structure as the diagnostic, not the betting frequency itself.
applies_to: BB vs IP single raised pot
concepts.actionable_rule: Before deciding to donk, evaluate equity buckets: only lead when your range is more polarized and the opponent's range is depolarized with many weak free-card-wanting hands.

concepts.title: Donk bet size vs stack depth (SPR)
concepts.summary: At shallow stacks (20bb) prefer a larger (2/3-pot) donk size to deny equity and stack off; at deeper stacks (30-40bb) prefer a small (1/4-pot) size to keep the pot manageable.
concepts.details: At 20bb the low SPR makes the BB happy to get all-in with many good-equity hands, so a bigger bet protects equity, gets folds, and gets money in while equity is high; strongest hands still prefer the small size because they aren't vulnerable. At 30-40bb few hands want to stack off on the flop, so a small size lets the BB call a raise and see the turn without committing. On low-donk-frequency flops the donking range is more polarized, so a larger size is preferred regardless of stack.
applies_to: BB vs IP single raised pot
concepts.actionable_rule: At ~20bb use a larger ~2/3-pot donk size on most donk boards; at 30-40bb default to a small ~1/4-pot donk size, and use larger sizes when your leading range is more polarized.

concepts.title: Bet by vulnerability and blockers within the donk range
concepts.summary: Within a donk-betting range, bet vulnerable and low-blocker hands more and slow down with hands that block the opponent's continuing range or are invulnerable.
concepts.details: On 654r example: low/vulnerable straight 32 bet 91% (unblocks IP continues), 65 two-pair bet lowest (73%, blocks IP continues and is least vulnerable), top set bet 94% but small sets 16-31% (don't block top pair), TT/99 overpairs bet 100% but 88/77 only 38%. Pairs with higher kickers and OESDs are bet more; middle kickers checked. Ace-high and king-high are bet in reverse-linear fashion (A9s 99%, AQs 40%) so the strongest high cards stay in the checking range. Trash with backdoor flush draws is bet more than trash without.
applies_to: BB vs IP single raised pot
concepts.actionable_rule: When building a leading range, bet vulnerable hands and those that do NOT block the opponent's continues at higher frequency, slow-play invulnerable nutted hands, bet draws/high-cards in reverse-linear order, and prefer backdoor-equity combos as bluffs.

concepts.title: Protect the checking range with strong hands
concepts.summary: The more often you check, the more important it is to keep strong and good hands in the checking range so it cannot be attacked.
concepts.details: In the GTO 654r solution the checking range stays protected because the BB does not lead out its strongest hands. When the BB was forced to donk top-pair-plus, the checking range became vulnerable and post-check EV fell to 5.6. Leading only weak hands lets IP raise 100%; leading too many bluffs makes IP call wider and raise more.
applies_to: BB vs IP single raised pot
concepts.actionable_rule: Keep an adequate proportion of strong/good hands in your checking range whenever you check frequently, and never strip all your strong hands out into a leading range.

concepts.title: Donk more vs tighter (UTG) ranges that miss the board
concepts.summary: On boards good for the BB, donk betting occurs more often against tighter opening ranges (UTG, 67%) than wider ones (BN, 53%) because tight ranges miss those boards more.
concepts.details: High-donk boards (7xx/6xx) are missed more often by the narrow, high-card-heavy UTG range, giving the BB a bigger relative advantage and more incentive to lead. On low-donk-frequency flops the BB donks slightly more vs BN (16%) than UTG (14%).
applies_to: BB vs UTG vs BB vs BN single raised pot
concepts.actionable_rule: Increase donk-bet frequency on low connected boards when facing a tighter (early-position) opening range that misses those textures, and lean toward checking against wider button ranges on IP-favored boards.

concepts.title: Simplification: always-check costs little EV
concepts.summary: Because high-frequency donk boards are themselves rare, abandoning donk bets and always checking OOP in single raised pots costs only a small amount of EV.
concepts.details: On 654r (a top donk board) removing the lead option costs the BB ~1.1% of pot, ~6.5bb/100; on A76r removing it costs ~0%. Since donking is high-frequency only on a small set of infrequent flops, the aggregate EV loss from a simple always-check strategy is minor and donk implementation is hard in-game. Reserve donk study for very tough games or exploitable opponents.
applies_to: BB vs IP single raised pot
concepts.actionable_rule: If simplifying, default to checking 100% OOP in single raised pots; only invest in correct donk strategies for the small set of low connected boards when playing tough games or exploitable opponents.

concepts.title: Exploitative donk bets vs predictable opponents
concepts.summary: Deviate to exploitative donk bets based on read: blocking bets vs auto-c-betters who only raise strong, and value leads to induce raises from over-aggressive opponents.
concepts.details: Against a Villain who c-bets at high frequency but only raises donks with strong hands, small donk bets work as blocking bets — seeing a cheap card with weak hands and gathering information. Against a Villain who almost always raises a flop donk, lead out very strong hands to induce raises. Both deviations expose you to counter-exploitation and require strong reads.
applies_to: BB vs IP single raised pot
concepts.actionable_rule: Vs an opponent who only raises donks with strong hands, donk small as a blocking/info bet with weak hands; vs an opponent who reflexively raises donks, lead your strongest hands to induce — but only with reliable reads.

concepts.title: Value of Position is 5-10% of the Pot
concepts.summary: With identical ranges, the in-position player over-realizes equity (capturing ~55% of the pot at 50% equity) while OOP under-realizes, making position worth roughly 5-10% of the pot.
concepts.details: Symmetric range experiments show IP captures an average EQR of 110% (capturing ~55% of a pot they have 50% equity in) while OOP realizes only 90% (capturing ~45%). The information advantage grows with more streets left to play because IP acts last each street, accumulating range information up to the river. Deeper stacks/higher SPR amplify the positional advantage.
concepts.actionable_rule: Treat position as worth 5-10% of the pot: realize equity more aggressively and play wider when IP, and tighten/play more cautiously when OOP, especially on early streets and at deeper stacks.

concepts.title: OOP Uses Larger Bet-Sizes to Reduce Positional Disadvantage
concepts.summary: Out-of-position players prefer larger bet sizes to end hands immediately or reduce SPR, mitigating the equity-realization penalty of acting first.
concepts.details: Because deeper stacks and higher SPR hurt OOP, the OOP player either bets big to fold out opponents and realize equity now, or reduces the SPR so fewer future streets compound the positional disadvantage. When OOP with a range disadvantage, total betting frequency drops sharply (e.g., 9.23% on 654r) and overbet sizes (125%) become the main bet, aiming for a two-street game (bet flop then jam turn).
concepts.actionable_rule: When OOP, prefer larger bet sizes (and overbets) to reduce SPR and play a two-street game; bet rarely but big with a range disadvantage and plan to jam the turn rather than triple barrel.

concepts.title: Protect the OOP Checking Range with Strong Hands
concepts.summary: When checking OOP, include strong check-raising hands so the opponent cannot bet relentlessly and blow your weak hands off their equity.
concepts.details: OOP checking does not guarantee seeing a free card; the opponent can bet and force folds from hands wanting to realize equity. To counter this, OOP must check some strong hands capable of check-raising, which lowers the opponent's betting frequency and lets OOP's weak hands realize equity. Failing to protect the checking range lets the opponent bet at a higher frequency, costing significant EV. OOP checking frequency rises further when OOP has a range disadvantage.
concepts.actionable_rule: When checking OOP, always keep some strong check-raising hands in the checking range so opponents cannot profitably bet your whole range; check more often when you have a range disadvantage.

concepts.title: IP Must C-bet — 100% Check-Back Loses Big
concepts.summary: Unlike the BB OOP, the in-position player cannot profitably check back 100% of the time; always checking the flop costs roughly 26bb/100.
concepts.details: GTO simulations show IP that always checks back loses ~26bb/100 versus an optimal c-betting strategy, because IP has a range advantage and forgoes value, protection, and fold equity. While the BB can play near-pure-check OOP without large loss, IP must develop an active c-betting strategy.
concepts.actionable_rule: As the in-position aggressor, do not default to checking back the flop; build an active c-betting strategy because pure checking forfeits about 26bb/100.

concepts.title: Range Advantage Drives C-bet Frequency
concepts.summary: The more strong hands your range has relative to your opponent's, the higher the frequency you can c-bet and the larger the sizes you can use.
concepts.details: A stronger range protects your betting range, allowing you to bet more hands (including weaker ones) profitably. UTG's stronger range (vs BN's) supports both higher c-bet frequency and bigger sizes. Conversely, when your strong-hand share shrinks and your range becomes depolarized (more good/weak hands), c-bet frequency and sizing drop.
concepts.actionable_rule: Scale c-bet frequency and size to your strong-hand advantage: bet more often and bigger when your range holds more strong hands than the opponent's, less when your range is depolarized.

concepts.title: Bet-Size Selection by Range Polarization
concepts.summary: Use small bets when your range is depolarized (mostly good-but-not-great hands) and larger bets when your range is polarized (more strong, weak, and trash hands).
concepts.details: Small bets on depolarized ranges win the minimum when bet/folding the bottom and force opponents to reveal information, ideal on paired and monotone boards where IP is depolarized and the opponent is polarized. Polarized IP ranges (more strong + trash, fewer medium) favor bigger sizes. Empirically, IP sizes up when OOP has many calling (good) hands and sizes down when OOP has more potential raising (strong) hands.
concepts.actionable_rule: Choose small bets (min/third-pot) when your range is depolarized or the opponent is polarized; choose larger bets (half/two-thirds+) when your range is polarized and the opponent has many calling hands.

concepts.title: Small Bets on Paired and Monotone Boards
concepts.summary: On paired and monotone flops the opponent's range polarizes while IP's depolarizes, so frequent small bets or min-bets are optimal.
concepts.details: Paired boards give the BB strong hands (trips/full houses) and lots of trash, polarizing their range; small bets fold out the trash regardless of size and lose minimum on bet/folds. Monotone flops reduce IP's strong-hand share and increase BB's flushes and weak flush-draw hands, again creating a polarized BB vs depolarized IP. Betting too large on monotone boards isolates yourself against the top of the opponent's range while folding out hands a small bet would keep.
concepts.actionable_rule: On paired and monotone flops, c-bet small (min-bet or 1/3 pot) at high frequency; avoid large bets that fold out worse hands and isolate you against stronger holdings.

concepts.title: Bigger Bets on Rainbow and Higher-Range-Advantage Flops
concepts.summary: Rainbow and high-card unpaired flops give IP a large range advantage, favoring bigger sizes and effective triple-barreling.
concepts.details: On rainbow flops IP holds far more strong hands than the BB (greater advantage than two-tone, where IP ~24% strong vs BB ~5%). Without flush draws, strong flop hands stay strong on later streets and equities shift less abruptly, so IP can bet bigger and triple barrel to get stacks in by the river. Axx, Kxx, and trips boards are c-bet at very high frequencies (Axx ~96%, 222 100%).
concepts.actionable_rule: On rainbow and high-card unpaired flops where you have a strong range advantage, use larger bet sizes and plan to barrel across streets; c-bet near 100% on ace-high and trips boards.

concepts.title: Connected/Low Boards Lower C-bet Frequency
concepts.summary: Flops with more possible straights and lower/middle ranks reduce IP's c-bet frequency because they favor the BB's connector-heavy range.
concepts.details: The BB has more offsuit connectors than IP, so flops with possible straights favor the BB; c-bet frequency falls as straight possibilities rise (zero-straight flops are highest c-bet, three-OESD flops lowest with bigger sizes for protection). Low/middle flops like 6xx (62%) and families MMM, LLL, MML, HMM are the least c-bet; deeper stacks check more.
concepts.actionable_rule: Lower your c-bet frequency on connected, low, and middling boards (multiple straight possibilities); reserve bigger protective sizes for the few strong hands and check more at deeper stacks.

concepts.title: Hand-Class Roles: Trap, Pot-Control, Semi-Bluff, Pure Bluff
concepts.summary: Assign betting roles by hand strength: bet strong/good hands for value and protection but check some to trap or pot-control, semi-bluff weak hands selectively, and bluff trash with fold equity.
concepts.details: Strong hands usually bet but check back when they block continues, are nutted enough to give a free card, or to protect the checking range (trapping). Good hands bet for value/protection but check back when the opponent's range is polarized to stronger-or-trash hands (pot control). Weak hands semi-bluff when the opponent's range is weak and can't check-raise much, otherwise check to avoid being blown off equity. Trash hands rarely improve when checked, so they are bet more often than weak hands as pure bluffs with fold equity, comfortable bet/folding to a raise.
concepts.actionable_rule: Bet strong and good hands for value/protection while occasionally trapping/pot-controlling; semi-bluff weak hands only when the opponent can't check-raise much; bluff trash hands that won't improve and bet/fold them to raises.

concepts.title: Exploit Non-GTO Donking Ranges
concepts.summary: Opponents who donk only-strong or only-weak are highly exploitable once you identify which pattern they use.
concepts.details: Against always-strong donkers, overfold the bottom of your range to their donk bets and bet high-frequency when they check. Against always-weak donkers, bluff-raise their flop donks, trap with strong hands needing little protection, and check back somewhat more often to avoid being check-raised by their strong checking range.
concepts.actionable_rule: Identify an opponent's donk-bet polarity: vs always-strong donkers overfold to donks and attack their checks; vs always-weak donkers bluff-raise their donks, trap strong hands, and check back more to dodge their strong checking range.

concepts.title: Adjust C-betting to Opponent Skill
concepts.summary: Against oblivious calling stations bet big for thin value; against players who never fold, bet small or give up with low-equity hands.
concepts.details: If a weak opponent calls overbets light across streets, take value hands to 'value town' with large sizing whenever ahead of their calling range. If you hold little equity and bad blockers against a station, give up or bet small to try to take the pot now, and abandon when called since size won't induce folds. Against strong, counter-exploitation-capable opponents, rely on balanced GTO frequencies and sizing.
concepts.actionable_rule: Versus calling stations, bet large for thin value with any hand ahead of their range and bet small or give up with low-equity bluffs; versus tough opponents, default to balanced GTO frequencies and sizes.

concepts.title: C-bet Frequency Tiers and Simplification
concepts.summary: Classify flops as high (80%+), mid (60-80%), or low (<60%) c-bet boards; on high-frequency boards you can simply c-bet 100% with negligible loss.
concepts.details: On 80%+ c-bet flops, IP's massive range advantage means betting 100% loses little EV even against a minimally exploitative opponent. On mid-frequency flops the ranges are closer (IP more depolarized, BB stronger) so more mixing/checking is required. C-bet frequency rises as the opponent holds more trash and falls as IP's range depolarizes. Strategy can be simplified (e.g., only 1/3-pot or min-bets on monotone flops) without significant EV loss.
concepts.actionable_rule: On high c-bet flops (80%+), simplify to a 100% c-bet; on mid (60-80%) flops mix and check more as ranges tighten; raise c-bet frequency when the opponent holds more trash and lower it as your range becomes depolarized.

concepts.title: All-in Sizing Increases as Stacks Shorten
concepts.summary: Big and overbet sizes are used less at shallow stacks, but the all-in bet is used more often when stacks are short due to better risk/reward and guaranteed equity realization.
concepts.details: At low SPR there is no need to overcommit large bets to get stacks in over multiple streets, so big bets/overbets decline. The exception is jamming: when all chips go in you are guaranteed to realize your equity and the risk/reward is favorable, so all-in frequency rises as stacks shorten. Deeper stacks make big bets and overbets more relevant.
concepts.actionable_rule: At shallow stacks/low SPR use fewer large non-all-in bets but increase all-in frequency to guarantee equity realization; reserve overbets and big sizes for deeper-stacked situations.

concepts.title: Equity Buckets Over Combo-Precision for C-bet Decisions
concepts.summary: You don't need exact combo-by-combo ranges to c-bet well; estimating the distribution of each player's equity buckets (strong/good/weak/trash) is sufficient for good decisions.
concepts.details: The solver mixes at granular frequencies, but human play is largely binary in-game with one action usually clearly best. Knowing roughly how much of your range and your opponent's range falls into strong, good, weak, and trash buckets drives correct frequency and sizing choices without memorization.
concepts.actionable_rule: Before acting on the flop, classify both ranges into strong/good/weak/trash buckets and choose c-bet frequency and size based on those proportions rather than exact combos.

concepts.title: Bet Size Driven by Opponent Range Composition
concepts.summary: Size up when the opponent has few strong hands relative to you; bet small at high frequency when they fold or raise a lot, and size up when they call a lot.
concepts.details: If villain's range is mostly trash, c-bet at high frequency and expect folds, sizing up because they lack the nutted hands to punish big bets. If you expect many folds or raises, bet small to keep risk low; if you expect many calls, increase size to extract value. Big bet-size flops are best for IP; small bet-size flops favor the BB.
concepts.actionable_rule: Bet big when opponent's range lacks nutted hands and calls; bet small at high frequency when opponent folds or raises a lot.

concepts.title: Split Range Instead of Over-C-betting Strong Boards for Opponent
concepts.summary: When your range isn't strong enough to c-bet 100% without facing frequent check-raises, split your range: c-bet a polarized portion and check back good and weak hands.
concepts.details: On boards that hit the BB's range well, betting a merged range at high frequency costs EV because the BB can defend and x/r profitably. Forcing a 100% c-bet on such boards lets the BB explode their x/r frequency (e.g. from ~4% to ~48% on 984r), costing the bettor large EV. Instead, polarize the c-bet and keep a checking range.
concepts.actionable_rule: If you cannot c-bet 100% without exposing yourself to high-frequency check-raises, split your range into a polarized c-bet plus a checking range of good and weak hands.

concepts.title: Never Bet-Fold High-Equity Hands as 'Information Bets'
concepts.summary: Betting a hand you would fold to a raise just to keep the betting lead is a major -EV mistake; check back hands that hate being raised.
concepts.details: Players make 'information bets' with weak hands that would benefit from pot control, then fold to a x/r or barrel, putting money in only to surrender. Poker is about the highest-EV play, which is sometimes to check or give up rather than win by force. Bet-folding high-equity hands on the flop is especially costly.
concepts.actionable_rule: Before betting, ask what happens if you get raised; if your hand hates a raise and a x/r is likely, check back instead of bet-folding.

concepts.title: Check Back Strong Hands That Block Villain's Continuing Range
concepts.summary: When you have a checking range, trap with strong hands that block the opponent's continue/x-r range, especially when you expect many folds to a bet.
concepts.details: On boards where betting wins the pot uncontested too often, checking back strong hands that block villain's calling/raising combos lets the opponent catch up or start bluffing on later streets, generating more value. Examples: KcKd c-bets more than KsKh when it blocks BDFDs; quads and full houses check back to give villain rope.
applies_to: boards where you fold out villain
concepts.actionable_rule: Trap by checking back some strong hands that block the opponent's continuing combos, particularly on flops where a bet would win uncontested too often.

concepts.title: Protect Your Checking Range to Avoid Stab Exploitation
concepts.summary: If you have a checking range, include some strong hands in it so aggressive opponents can't profitably stab after you check.
concepts.details: A checking range composed only of weak hands is capped and can be attacked by aggressive players betting after your check. Including strong traps balances the checking range, making stabs unprofitable and keeping your range protected on later streets.
concepts.actionable_rule: Always include some strong hands in your check-back range so opponents cannot profitably bet into your checks.

concepts.title: Way Ahead or Way Behind: Check Back at High Frequency
concepts.summary: On boards where the opponent's range is polarized to monsters and trash with little in between, check back at high frequency even when a 100% c-bet would fold out trash.
concepts.details: Example A-T-T BB vs UTG 30bb: IP is 57% strong/37% good but BB is 81% trash/7% strong. IP checks back many good hands for pot control plus a chunk of strong hands as traps, while c-betting all trash and most weak hands balanced with some strong/good. This wins uncontested often with trash and lets IP bluff-catch effectively after checking.
concepts.actionable_rule: On way-ahead-or-way-behind boards (villain polarized to monsters/trash), check back many good hands plus some strong traps and c-bet your trash and weak hands.

concepts.title: Reverse-Linear C-betting of Weak/Marginal Hands
concepts.summary: Bet your weakest reasonable holdings more often than slightly stronger ones, checking back the stronger versions that play well on turns.
concepts.details: Weak hands that cannot call a x/r are c-bet reverse linearly: e.g. K6o c-bet more than K9o more than KQo on 862r, because the stronger Kx wants to realize equity on later streets while the weaker ones serve as bet/folds. Similarly A5o bets more than AQo when no BDFD. Top pair can also be bet reverse-linearly by kicker strength.
concepts.actionable_rule: C-bet your weakest viable hands (poor turn equity) more often as bet/folds, and check back the stronger versions that realize equity well on turns.

concepts.title: Linear C-betting When Facing Strong X-R Ranges
concepts.summary: Bet the stronger versions of a hand type more often when they have better equity and blockers versus the opponent's check-raise range.
concepts.details: When the x/r range is strong, you want better blockers and equity in your c-betting range: on J66r, AKs-AQs c-bet 100%, ATs-A7s 80%, A5s-A2s only 34%, because stronger A-highs block top pair, get called by worse, and fare better versus x/r. With BDFDs c-bet linearly (AKs more than A3s).
concepts.actionable_rule: When the opponent's x/r range is strong, c-bet the higher-equity, better-blocker versions of a hand type more often than the weaker ones.

concepts.title: Adjust C-bet Frequency to Villain's X-R Tendencies
concepts.summary: If the opponent x/r's less than equilibrium, over-fold to their x/r and even fold some normally-strong hands; if they over-x/r, react accordingly.
concepts.details: A villain who x/r's below equilibrium is missing bluffs, so their x/r range is skewed to value and your equity is lower than expected — over-fold and even lay down strong hands. If villain lacks a donk range on good donking flops, c-bet less than equilibrium because you'll get x/r more. If villain's x/r is draw-heavy, 3-bet for protection; if polar (value+bluffs), play your hand as a bluff-catcher and don't raise medium strength.
concepts.actionable_rule: When villain x/r's below equilibrium, over-fold to check-raises; when their x/r is draw-heavy, 3-bet good/strong hands for protection; when it is polarized, call as a bluff-catcher rather than raising medium hands.

concepts.title: Slowplay Overpairs by Strength on Protected Paired Boards
concepts.summary: On low paired boards, c-bet overpairs reverse-linearly — bet smaller pairs more, slowplay bigger pairs that need less protection and make great call-downs.
concepts.details: On 554hh, TT c-bet 76%, JJ 64%, QQ 50%, KK 40%, AA 22%. Bigger pairs need less protection and play better as call-downs across runouts after checking back; full houses checked ~22%, quads mostly checked, trips almost always bet. This balances the checking range and keeps it uncapped.
concepts.actionable_rule: On low paired boards, c-bet smaller overpairs more often than bigger ones, slowplaying the biggest pairs and some full houses to protect your checking range.

concepts.title: Single Bet-Size Simplification Retains EV
concepts.summary: Using one bet-size per flop captures nearly all of the solver's EV; multiple sizes and tiny mixed frequencies are unnecessary for humans.
concepts.details: Examples: on AQ3 c-betting 100% for 2/3-pot retains all EV (vs 1.07% loss at 1/3); on QJTh min-betting 100% loses nothing; on 984r a single 2/3-pot bet loses only ~0.09% of pot. Overbets the solver chooses 14% of the time add no EV. Default to 1/3-pot in short/middle stacks when unsure.
concepts.actionable_rule: Pick one appropriate bet-size per flop texture rather than mixing sizes; default to 1/3-pot when unsure in short/middle-stack spots.

concepts.title: Multi-way Pot Principles: Blockers and Passivity
concepts.summary: In multi-way pots, prioritize blockers over raw hand strength and play passively, betting draws only when they are near the nuts.
concepts.details: With multiple opponents, equity is distributed and someone is more likely to have a strong hand, so blockers reduce the chance of being beaten and improve bluff selection. Overaggression with non-nut draws is punished; passive play preserves EV.
concepts.actionable_rule: In multi-way pots, weight decisions toward blockers, play passively, and only bet draws aggressively when they are to the nuts.

concepts.title: Use Backdoor-Equity Hands Without Showdown Value as Semi-bluffs
concepts.summary: Hands with no showdown value but backdoor equity (BDFD/BDSTD) make ideal semi-bluff c-bets and continuing bluffs.
concepts.details: Combos with a backdoor flush or straight draw can improve on later streets and give equity when called, so they are c-bet more often than identical combos without backdoor equity. They fold out better trash now and can barrel or hit on favorable runouts.
concepts.actionable_rule: Prefer hands with backdoor flush/straight equity and no showdown value as your bluff c-bets, c-betting them more than the equivalent combos lacking backdoor equity.

concepts.title: Bet Flop with Three-Street Value Hands; Don't Bluff Recreationals off Top Pair
concepts.summary: If a hand can extract value across three streets, start betting on the flop; and don't try to bluff recreational players off top pair.
concepts.details: Beginning the value sequence early builds the pot for three streets of value. Against recreational players, top pair rarely folds, so persistent bluffing against them is -EV; size up for value instead when they call too much.
concepts.actionable_rule: Bet the flop with hands that can get value over three streets, and refuse to barrel recreational players off top pair — value bet them instead.

concepts.title: OOP c-betting requires a stronger checking range than IP
concepts.summary: When out of position as the pre-flop aggressor, you must check a stronger, more balanced range than when in position because checking does not guarantee seeing a free turn — the IP player can bet and force folds.
concepts.details: Checking OOP exposes your range to attack: the IP player can bet and deny you equity realization. Therefore your checking range must be balanced both on the average turn after x/x AND immediately, so you can withstand aggression and check-raise at a reasonable frequency. UTG OOP vs BN 40bb checks ~32% on average and checks strong hands ~19% (3x more often than when IP), protecting the check from IP betting too often when checked to.
concepts.actionable_rule: When c-betting from out of position, check a stronger and more balanced range than you would in position, retaining enough strong hands to check-raise and defend against the IP player's bets.

concepts.title: Bet less when ranges are symmetric
concepts.summary: The closer your range is to the opponent's range, the lower your incentive to bet; betting frequency should decrease as equity distributions become symmetric.
concepts.details: IP players c-betting OOP face a caller (e.g. BN cold call 4-20% hands) with a tighter, closer range than blind defenders (50-70%). This symmetry produces a more even post-flop equity distribution and reduces overall optimal betting frequency. On middle and low flops where equity distributions are symmetric, OOP plays much more passively, while on Axx/high-card flops where OOP has range advantage it c-bets most of the time.
concepts.actionable_rule: Reduce c-bet frequency when your range and the opponent's range are close in strength (symmetric equity distribution); bet more aggressively only when you hold a clear range or polarization advantage.

concepts.title: OOP c-bets depolarized (good/weak hands), IP c-bets polarized (trash)
concepts.summary: In position c-bet ranges are polarized and bet trash often; out of position the role reverses — good and weak hands are bet more often than trash, which is checked with intent to fold.
concepts.details: OOP must act first on the turn, revealing information. Betting many low-equity trash hands OOP leaves the average turn range too weak and exploitable, so instead trash is checked and folded most of the time vs a flop bet. This also loads the checking range with more strong hands, increasing the chance the flop checks through so equity is realized for free.
concepts.actionable_rule: When c-betting OOP, bet your good and weak made hands more often and check most trash with intent to fold, rather than barreling air that would weaken your turn range.

concepts.title: Use big sizes when opponent's range is capped on paired/static boards
concepts.summary: On paired boards (trips) and rainbow boards where the caller's range is capped, the uncapped player should use large bet sizes, especially on low and middle boards.
concepts.details: When the BN cold calls, far fewer combos make trips than when the BB defends, so IP's range is capped while OOP is uncapped. This lets OOP use large sizing on paired low/middle flops. OOP also has a polarization advantage on rainbow flops, enabling bigger and more frequent bets. Trips boards are the most c-bet texture.
concepts.actionable_rule: On paired or static rainbow flops where the opponent's range is capped and yours is uncapped, use a large c-bet size; favor large sizes on low and middle paired boards.

concepts.title: Reduce c-bet on draw-heavy and two-tone/monotone boards
concepts.summary: Two-tone, monotone, and straight-connected boards reduce the c-bettor's edge: lower c-bet frequency and smaller sizes because draws and connectors improve the opponent's equity.
concepts.details: On two-tone flops, flush draws reduce the equity and EQR of OOP's strong hands, lowering c-bet frequency. Monotone boards substantially improve IP's equity distribution, so OOP c-bets only ~50% with a small size. Boards with possible straights/straight draws connect well with the BN's suited-connector and small-pair calling range, so the aggressor plays more passively on dynamic boards; static disconnected boards favor the aggressor.
concepts.actionable_rule: Lower your c-bet frequency and size on monotone, two-tone, and straight-connected boards; bet more confidently on static, disconnected, high-card boards.

concepts.title: Check-raise more vs population that auto-bets and over-c-bets
concepts.summary: Most opponents automatically bet when checked to and over-c-bet trash in 3-bet pots; exploit this by checking your whole range to induce and check-raising aggressively.
concepts.details: Equilibrium calls for a CO (weak OOP range) to stab only ~50%, but the population bets nearly always when checked to. Checking all hands lets you run an aggressive check-raise strategy, exploit IP aggression, and reduce effective SPR/positional disadvantage. In 3-bet pots IP profitably c-bets trash because the population under-check-raises; a strong OOP counter is to step up check-raise frequency. Players who OOP-c-bet trash and then x/f the turn can be attacked by floating the flop and firing the turn 100% when checked to.
concepts.actionable_rule: Against a population that auto-bets when checked to and over-c-bets, check your entire weak OOP range to induce, then check-raise at an increased frequency; also float-and-stab when opponents c-bet trash and give up turns.

concepts.title: Pre-flop aggressor has polarization advantage in 3-bet pots
concepts.summary: In 3-bet pots the aggressor's range is polarized (~2:1 strong, ~1.5:1 good hand advantage, with 1/3 of caller's range trash) and the caller's is condensed, favoring small bet sizes.
concepts.details: At 40bb the post-flop SPR is ~1.7-2. The polarized vs condensed structure means small bets are generally preferred, especially IP. IP 3-bet c-bet strategy can be simplified to ~1/4-pot and checks back ~38%. Many strong IP hands (e.g. top set QQ on Q82r) check back ~68% to protect the check-back range, especially when they block the villain's continuing range.
concepts.actionable_rule: As the 3-bet aggressor in position, simplify to a small (~1/4-pot) c-bet and check back ~38% of hands, including some strong hands that block the caller's continues.

concepts.title: OOP 3-bet aggressor c-bets more and bigger than IP
concepts.summary: As the OOP 3-bettor, c-bet at higher frequency and with bigger sizes than IP to deny free turns, reduce SPR, and offset positional disadvantage.
concepts.details: OOP realizes less equity than IP, so it cannot afford to check back weak hands hoping to improve. Bigger sizes prevent giving IP a cheap continue and reduce SPR (and with it the positional disadvantage). E.g. Axx is c-bet 77% OOP vs only 53% IP — OOP bets to avoid giving IP a free turn and being forced to act first on the turn. Low boards are c-bet at high frequency (more overpairs); Qxx/Jxx/Txx are checked most as they favor the caller.
concepts.actionable_rule: As the OOP 3-bet aggressor, c-bet at a higher frequency and with larger sizes than you would in position, especially on Axx and low boards; check more on Qxx/Jxx/Txx that favor the caller.

concepts.title: Defend by equity vs pot odds, not MDF
concepts.summary: MDF ignores equity and range distribution; defend only hands whose equity beats the pot odds offered, folding -EV hands even against tiny bets.
concepts.details: Example: BB vs UTG on AQ3r facing 1/3-pot, MDF says defend 75%, but BB's range is 70% trash with ~16% equity vs UTG while pot odds need 20% — so calling is -EV and raising is worse against a strong range. GTO defense here folds 58%, defending only 42%. UTG can c-bet ATC profitably. Folding (0 EV) beats negative-EV calls/raises; never force the action.
concepts.actionable_rule: When facing a c-bet, compare each hand's equity against the offered pot odds (and the bettor's likely range) rather than defending to MDF; fold low-equity hands even versus min-bets when calling and raising are both -EV.

concepts.title: Read the betting range behind the size
concepts.summary: A given bet size implies a specific range composition; adjust by considering what hands take that line, and overfold against unbalanced betting ranges.
concepts.details: A min-bet offers great pot odds but the villain's min-bet range differs from a pot-sized range, changing your hands' equities. Against a player who always c-bets strong hands and checks back medium ones, your bottom-of-range bluff-catchers have far lower equity than vs a balanced strategy, so you should overfold to exploit the poor range construction.
concepts.actionable_rule: Before defending, infer the opponent's range for that specific bet size; if their betting range is unbalanced toward strong hands, overfold your weak bluff-catchers.

concepts.title: Scale check-raise size inversely to opponent's bet size
concepts.summary: Check-raise larger when the villain bets small and smaller (often a min-raise) when the villain bets big, to keep their weak hands indifferent without over-committing.
concepts.details: A larger raise vs a small bet prices out IP's lowest-equity hands and prevents them from profitably min-betting weak hands. Vs a large bet, a smaller raise (even check-min-raise) suffices and avoids being over-committal — except all-in raises, which get a better risk/reward when IP's bet is large. Smaller IP bets mean a more depolarized betting range, allowing the BB to increase overall x/r frequency.
concepts.actionable_rule: Check-raise to a larger size against small bets and to a smaller size (frequently a min-raise) against large bets; increase your overall x/r frequency the smaller the opponent's bet.

concepts.title: Build protected x/c and x/r ranges by hand class
concepts.summary: Distribute defending hands by class: strong hands mostly x/r but some x/c for protection; good hands mostly call with some x/r; weak hands mostly x/c; trash mostly folds with a few x/r bluffs.
concepts.details: Many strong hands x/c intending to x/r later, protecting the x/c range. Good hands that need protection or unblock the villain's continues (top pair on middle boards, bottom two pair on high boards, combo draws) prefer x/r to get money in or reduce SPR. Weak hands are ~1/3 folded, ~15% x/r, rest x/c. A few trash combos work as x/r bluffs. Avoid splitting your range early unless you have enough strong hands to distribute between x/r and x/c.
concepts.actionable_rule: Distribute defenses by hand class: x/r most strong hands but slow-play some as x/c, call most good/weak hands, fold most trash, and use a few trash combos as x/r bluffs — only split your range when you have enough strong hands to protect both lines.

concepts.title: Check-raise sizing inversely related to c-bet size
concepts.summary: Use large check-raise sizes against small c-bets and small check-raise sizes against large c-bets, with exceptions for all-in bets offering good risk:reward.
concepts.details: The smaller the opponent's bet, the more room and incentive to apply pressure with a large raise; against large bets you risk more for the same pot so a smaller raise is appropriate. All-in bets that give favorable risk:reward ratios are an exception to consider.
concepts.actionable_rule: When check-raising, size up against small c-bets and size down against large c-bets, except when an all-in bet offers a favorable risk:reward ratio.

concepts.title: Polarized check-raise ranges; avoid the middling trap
concepts.summary: Flop check-raise ranges should be polarized: strong hands happy to get in versus a 3-bet and bluffs fine with raise/folding, avoiding medium hands too good to fold but not good enough to stack off.
concepts.details: Raising a hand that is not strong enough to get all-in yet too strong to fold to a 3-bet is a losing proposition because it commits you in awkward spots. Think ahead about what happens when you get raised back.
concepts.actionable_rule: Construct check-raise ranges from clear value (happy to get in) and bluffs (fine to fold); do not check-raise medium hands too good to fold but too weak to stack off.

concepts.title: Raise vulnerable high-equity hands for protection
concepts.summary: Hands with lots of equity but little showdown value, or vulnerable to losing value on later streets, should be played aggressively to get money in while still valuable.
concepts.details: These hands realize equity poorly when checked and can deteriorate as cards come; building the pot now captures their value before it erodes.
concepts.actionable_rule: Play vulnerable high-equity hands with low showdown value aggressively to get the money in while your equity edge is highest.

concepts.title: Deeper stacks require stronger check-raise hands
concepts.summary: The deeper the stacks, the stronger the average hand needed to check-raise; barrel-able draws gain value at depth.
concepts.details: With deeper stacks the implied consequences of getting it in are larger, so you need stronger value to commit. Good draws that can be barreled across multiple streets become more valuable because you can apply pressure over more betting rounds.
concepts.actionable_rule: As effective stacks deepen, require stronger hands to check-raise and prefer multi-street barrel draws over thin value.

concepts.title: Blocker effects in value and bluff check-raises
concepts.summary: For value, prefer hands that do NOT block villain's continuing range; for bluffs, prefer hands that DO block villain's continuing/value range.
concepts.details: Example: 44 on 9h8h4h is a better check-raise than 99 because 44 doesn't block villain's continues, keeping more of their range in. Bluffs should block value and continues rather than blocking bluffs. When a hand blocks both, weigh other variables.
concepts.actionable_rule: Choose value check-raises that unblock villain's calling range and bluff check-raises that block villain's value/continuing combos.

concepts.title: Use bottom pairs as semi-bluff check-raises
concepts.summary: Bottom pair is hard to check-call across multiple streets, especially small pairs, so put some bottom pairs into the check-raise range.
concepts.details: Bottom pairs play poorly as multi-street bluff-catchers but have extra equity (pair outs plus kicker outs) that makes them effective semi-bluffs. Weak-kicker bottom pairs often have more live outs than high-kicker versions.
concepts.actionable_rule: Rather than check-calling small bottom pairs down, mix some into your check-raise range as semi-bluffs, favoring weaker kickers with live outs.

concepts.title: Don't auto-fold A-high and K-high to small bets
concepts.summary: A-high and K-high retain decent value in many spots; do not give up too quickly versus a flop bet, especially a small one.
concepts.details: These hands have showdown equity and overcard outs; the smaller the bet the better the price to continue and the more they outperform marginal pairs sometimes.
concepts.actionable_rule: Continue with A-high and K-high against small flop bets instead of reflexively folding, especially when they have backdoor equity.

concepts.title: Fold trash-heavy ranges regardless of MDF
concepts.summary: If your range contains many trash hands, fold a lot of it versus a c-bet regardless of bet size or what MDF suggests.
concepts.details: MDF assumes defendable hands exist; when a range is mostly unimprovable air there is no obligation to defend to MDF because those hands have no equity. Example: BB on AQ3r folds ~68% of range.
concepts.actionable_rule: When your range is dominated by trash with little equity, over-fold to c-bets rather than defending up to the theoretical MDF.

concepts.title: Don't bluff hoping big hands fold to a small story
concepts.summary: Don't try to represent a small value range expecting opponents to lay down big hands; it won't happen often enough.
concepts.details: Bluffs need credible representation and fold equity; trying to push someone off a strong holding with a thin perceived value range is unprofitable.
concepts.actionable_rule: Only bluff when you credibly represent enough strong hands; don't expect opponents to fold big hands to a narrow represented value range.

concepts.title: Check-raise range built around SPR and blockers, not just strength
concepts.summary: Your flop check-raise range consists of hands that benefit from lowering the SPR and have the right forward and reverse blockers, not necessarily your strongest hands.
concepts.details: Lowering SPR helps vulnerable hands get value/protection; blocker considerations (blocking villain value/bluffs) refine which combos raise. On 9h8h4d, BB only check-raises ~4% with few strong combos, preferring to keep information advantage and donk turns.
concepts.actionable_rule: Select check-raise combos by which hands gain from a lower SPR and have favorable blockers, not simply by raw hand strength.

concepts.title: Don't over-raise with mere draws; keep board coverage in check-call range
concepts.summary: Flush draws and OESDs are strong but not the nuts; you don't need to check-raise every decent draw — keep good board coverage in your check-call range.
concepts.details: Slow-playing some draws and made hands by check-calling maintains a protected, less face-up calling range and balances your strategy.
concepts.actionable_rule: Mix some flush draws and OESDs into your check-call range rather than always check-raising, to maintain board coverage and protection.

concepts.title: Slowplay the effective nuts on blocked monotone boards
concepts.summary: When you hold the near-unbeatable nuts and the board blocks villain making a strong hand, slowplay and let the aggressor do the betting.
concepts.details: On QhJhTh with a straight flush, most flush combos are blocked, so villain rarely has a hand to pay big bets. If villain has the Ah/A-high flush the money goes in regardless, so let IP drive the betting.
concepts.actionable_rule: With the nuts on a board that blocks villain's strong continues, check/slowplay and let the opponent bet into you rather than raising and folding them out.

concepts.title: Reverse-linear flush check-raise by kicker
concepts.summary: On monotone boards, check-raise lower-kicker made flushes more often than nut-blocking high flushes, raising frequency increasing as kicker decreases.
concepts.details: Example: A9s never raises, A5s raises ~57%, A2s ~88%; lower flush combos raise ~88%. High flushes that block villain's continues are better as calls; low flushes don't block continues and protect/value-raise well.
concepts.actionable_rule: Check-raise weaker-kicker flushes more frequently and slowplay/call with nut-blocking high flushes on monotone boards.

concepts.title: Two-pair raise selection by blocker interaction
concepts.summary: Prefer check-raising the most nutted two pair; check-call combos that block villain's top pair, and raise combos needing protection that unblock top pair.
concepts.details: On 9h8h4d, top two is most nutted so raised more; bottom two needs protection and unblocks top pair so also raises; top-and-bottom two blocks villain top pair so prefers check-call. The blocker to villain's continuing range drives the choice.
concepts.actionable_rule: Check-raise your most nutted and protection-needy two pair that unblock villain's top pair; check-call two-pair combos that block villain's top pair.

concepts.title: Overpairs are prime protection check-raises
concepts.summary: On dynamic boards, vulnerable overpairs with good equity are among the most frequent check-raising hands.
concepts.details: On 9h8h4d, JJ check-raises 100% and TT raises mostly with the relevant suit; they have strong equity but are vulnerable to many turn/river cards, so building the pot and protecting is correct.
concepts.actionable_rule: Check-raise vulnerable overpairs on dynamic, draw-heavy boards for value and protection.

concepts.title: Trips: raise more with low kicker, call more with high kicker
concepts.summary: On paired boards, raise trips reverse-linearly and check-call high-kicker trips because they block villain's overcards/overpairs.
concepts.details: On J6 6 board, trips raise ~80% but high-kicker trips work better as check-calls since they block villain's continuing overcards and overpairs, keeping those bluffs/value in.
concepts.actionable_rule: On paired boards, check-raise low-kicker trips more and check-call high-kicker trips that block villain's overcards and overpairs.

concepts.title: Adopt aggressive turn donking when flop check-raise range is thin
concepts.summary: When you lack strong flop combos and keep your range concealed by mostly calling, compensate with an aggressive turn donk-betting strategy on favorable runouts.
concepts.details: On 9h8h4d the BB check-raises only ~4%, waiting until the turn to split range based on runout, preserving information advantage and attacking good turn cards.
concepts.actionable_rule: When you under-raise the flop to conceal a weak range, develop a donk-betting turn strategy on favorable runouts to apply pressure.

concepts.title: Turn decisions reduce to pot, stacks, ranges, and board
concepts.summary: To make educated turn decisions, focus on pot size, effective stacks, the ranges in play (derived from prior action), and the board texture.
concepts.details: GTO ignores history; it only needs ranges, board, stacks, pot and a betting abstraction. Humans use action history to infer ranges. Assess equity distribution and polarization after the line to decide.
concepts.actionable_rule: On the turn, base your decision on pot size, effective stacks, both players' inferred ranges, and board texture rather than on hand history or who was last aggressor.

concepts.title: Checked-back ranges are capped and depolarized
concepts.summary: When IP checks back the flop, their range is capped and more depolarized than a c-betting range because most strong hands would have bet.
concepts.details: This lets OOP develop a turn betting strategy. Against players who check back a flop that should be c-bet at high frequency (e.g. AQ3r), their range becomes face-up made hands with little air, allowing OOP to attack and check-fold accurately versus delayed c-bets.
concepts.actionable_rule: When IP checks back a flop that should be c-bet often, treat their range as capped and made-hand heavy; attack the turn and check-fold confidently against delayed c-bets.

concepts.title: OOP's uncapped polarized range drives turn betting
concepts.summary: After a flop check-back, OOP's preflop calling range is wide and uncapped while IP's is condensed, making OOP more polarized and inclined to bet the turn.
concepts.details: This is reverse of flop dynamics: OOP becomes the polarized/uncapped player and IP the condensed one, so OOP develops a turn betting lead.
concepts.actionable_rule: After IP checks back the flop, build a turn betting range from your uncapped, polarized OOP holdings to leverage your range advantage.

concepts.title: Punish non-GTO check-backs that lack board coverage
concepts.summary: When IP checks back a non-balanced flop range, exploit the resulting capped/over-represented turn range by betting much more frequently.
concepts.details: Example: if IP never checks back 99/88 on 9h8h4h, OOP's turn bet on a blank goes from 27% to 77% and IP's EV drops sharply; if IP never checks back flush draws, a flush turn crushes IP's EV further.
concepts.actionable_rule: Against opponents who check back flops with poor board coverage, bet the turn far more often, especially on cards that complete draws their capped range lacks.

concepts.title: Match turn bet size to board dynamism after double check
concepts.summary: On dynamic boards bet larger when OOP has checked twice (few strong hands); on static boards bet smaller because OOP can profitably slowplay and remains polarized.
concepts.details: On 9h8h4d, IP bets 2/3-pot because OOP wouldn't slowplay strong hands on a dynamic board. On J6 6 (static), IP uses 1/3-pot because OOP can trap and most weak hands don't improve, forcing OOP to a polarized, passive range that folds to small stabs.
concepts.actionable_rule: When checked to on the turn, bet larger on dynamic boards where opponent can't have many strong slowplays, and bet small on static boards where their range is polarized and folds often.

concepts.title: Raise turn bets when your range is condensed-strong vs opponent
concepts.summary: You can raise an opponent's turn bet when their betting range is condensed and you hold relatively more strong hands; avoid raising when they are polarized and you lack strength.
concepts.details: On 9h8h4d IP raises a 1/3-pot bet ~20% because OOP's range is condensed and IP has more strong hands; on J6 6 IP never raises an overbet because OOP is polarized and IP lacks strong combos.
concepts.actionable_rule: Raise turn bets when the bettor's range is condensed and you hold a strength advantage; just call when they are polarized and you lack top-of-range hands.

concepts.title: Bet-Size Affects OOP Continuation and Check-Raise Frequency
concepts.summary: Larger IP bet sizes make it harder for OOP's weak hands to continue, increasing folds; smaller bets and polarized OOP ranges increase check-raising.
concepts.details: On 9h8h4d IP uses a bigger bet, so OOP folds more weak hands. On J6 boards OOP's range is more polarized and IP bets smaller, so OOP check-raises more; if IP overbets instead, OOP only x/r ~3%. Bet sizing changes the pot odds and difficulty of continuation, directly shaping the opponent's response frequencies.
concepts.actionable_rule: Size up c-bets on dynamic boards to deny weak hands the odds to continue, and reduce your check-raise frequency when facing larger/overbet sizing since your bluff-raises become less profitable.

concepts.title: C-bettor Has Polarization Advantage, Caller Range Is Condensed
concepts.summary: After x/b/c, the flop aggressor keeps a polarized range while the caller arrives on the turn with a condensed, capped range.
concepts.details: IP c-bets most strong and trash hands (polarized) and OOP folds trash and raises some strong hands, leaving OOP's calling range condensed/medium. After x/c (flop check-back) equities run much closer. Polarization generally favors the previous street's aggressor.
concepts.actionable_rule: As the previous-street aggressor with a polarized range, keep barreling for value and bluffs; as the caller with a condensed range, default to checking and bluff-catching rather than leading.

concepts.title: Donk Bet the Turn When Aggressor's Range Is Weakened by the Card
concepts.summary: OOP should lead the turn when the board card depolarizes IP's range or hits OOP's range much harder, giving OOP a polarization/range advantage.
concepts.details: On 9h8h4d the best OOP donk-bet turns are 9/8/4 pairing the board, 7/6/5 completing straights, and blank low offsuit cards. Worst donk cards connect with IP's range: aces, high cards, and diamonds bringing IP a BDFD. Solvers donk smaller on flops than they bet turns due to differing range polarization.
concepts.actionable_rule: Donk-lead the turn on cards that pair the board low, complete straights you have, or are low blanks; check turns that bring overcards, aces, or draws favoring the in-position range.

concepts.title: Categorize Turn Cards by Their Range Impact
concepts.summary: Group the 49 possible turn cards into types (paired, flush, straight, ace, overcard, brick) to reason about how each shifts equity and strategy.
concepts.details: Each turn card impacts equity distributions; studying all individually is inefficient. Overcard/undercard categories subdivide by whether they bring a backdoor flush draw. Low straight-completing cards and board-pairing cards often favor the OOP/condensed range; overcards and aces favor the IP/uncapped range.
concepts.actionable_rule: Classify each turn card as paired/flush/straight/ace/overcard/brick (noting backdoor draws) and adjust aggression toward the player whose range that category benefits.

concepts.title: IP Splits Range and Barrels Big After OOP Checks Twice
concepts.summary: After x/b/c/x, IP has a large polarization advantage and c-bets over 65% of the time, mostly 2/3-pot, sometimes overbetting on favorable cards.
concepts.details: IP checks back medium hands wanting a free river and bets strong hands plus bluffs. On cards giving IP many more strong hands than OOP, IP increases size and may overbet, often intending to jam the river. On board-pairing cards (9/8/4) IP still bets small frequently because OOP's checked range lacks strong combos (OOP would have donked).
concepts.actionable_rule: When checked to twice in position with a polarized range, c-bet ~65%+ at 2/3-pot and overbet on cards that heavily favor you; use small sizing on board-pairing cards where the opponent's checking range is weak.

concepts.title: OOP Defense vs Second Barrel: Fold Often, Jam When Raising
concepts.summary: Facing a turn c-bet after x/b/c/x, OOP folds over 40%, calls a protected range, and check-raises ~14% mostly all-in with semi-bluffs that can call a jam.
concepts.details: OOP has ~45% equity but only realizes 77% of it (EV ~21% of pot), while IP over-realizes (EQR ~144%). OOP's strong hands were often raised earlier, weakening the checking range, but some are slowplayed to protect the x/c range even on bricks. Smaller raises would over-commit chips, so x/r is mostly a jam using semi-bluffs with enough equity to be committed.
concepts.actionable_rule: Against a second barrel out of position, fold roughly 40% of weak hands, protect your calling range with some slowplayed strong hands, and check-raise ~14% by jamming with strong hands plus high-equity semi-bluffs.

concepts.title: River Hands Have Fixed, History-Independent Strength
concepts.summary: On the river all hands have 0% or 100% equity versus each other and rank in a fixed linear order regardless of how they were reached.
concepts.details: With no cards to come, hand-vs-range equity equals the fraction of the opponent's range beaten plus half of ties. Any call or IP check ends the hand. This lets solvers ignore history: identical range structures, blockers, pot, stacks and betting tree yield identical GTO solutions.
concepts.actionable_rule: On the river, compute equity simply as (fraction of villain's range you beat + half of ties) and ignore how the hand was reached—rank all hands linearly and play the resulting range structure.

concepts.title: Bucket River Spots into Abstract Range Structures
concepts.summary: Recognize the river situation as a known structure (e.g. polar vs bluff-catcher) and apply its known GTO solution rather than memorizing every runout.
concepts.details: A river is fully defined by the ranges table, blocker relationships, and the game tree (pot, stacks, betting). Different concrete hands producing the same structure (50% nuts/50% air vs 100% bluff-catchers) yield equivalent strategies. Thousands of rivers can be bucketed into a handful of scenario types.
concepts.actionable_rule: Classify each river spot by its abstract range structure (polar vs bluff-catcher, linear, capped, etc.) and apply that structure's known equilibrium strategy instead of memorizing specific runouts.

concepts.title: Polar vs Bluff-Catcher: Jam Nuts, Bluff at Alpha, Call 1-Alpha
concepts.summary: With a perfectly polarized range against pure bluff-catchers, the polar player jams all nuts plus Alpha bluffs; the bluff-catcher calls 1-Alpha and never bets.
concepts.details: The polar player's EV increases with bet size, so all-in is optimal; effective stack size and position don't change the general strategy. Alpha = bet/(pot+bet) sets the bluffing frequency that makes the bluff-catcher indifferent, and the bluff-catcher calls 1-Alpha to make the bluffs indifferent.
concepts.actionable_rule: When you hold a polarized nuts-or-air range against bluff-catchers, jam all value hands and bluff at frequency Alpha = bet/(pot+bet); when you are the bluff-catcher, call 1-Alpha of the time and never lead.

concepts.title: Nut-Heavy Polarized Range Can Bet All Hands to Deny Equity
concepts.summary: When your polarized range has more nuts than air, bet large with your entire range so the opponent's bluff-catchers lack the odds to call and their equity is denied.
concepts.details: If P1 has the nuts 90% and air 10% on the river, a bet large enough to give P2 worse pot odds than their equity forces folds. The minimum size making P2 indifferent is B = EQ/(1-2*EQ) of the pot; with 10% equity that is 12.5% pot. Betting smaller gives a profitable call; betting bigger wins the pot but risks running into an unexpected monster.
concepts.actionable_rule: When your range is polarized but dominated by nuts, bet your entire range at the minimum size that makes villain indifferent (about EQ/(1-2*EQ) of the pot) to deny their equity at minimum risk.

concepts.title: Exploit Players Who Don't Realize They Are Beat
concepts.summary: When your whole range beats a capped opponent, equilibrium says don't bet, but you can bet sizes that induce bad calls from players who don't fold.
concepts.details: If P2's range has 0% equity, GTO says neither player should put money in. But many weaker players will call a tiny bet from a clearly value-only range, or fail to fold a dominated hand. P1 can exploitatively bet (or check/bet by position) to maximize induced mistakes.
concepts.actionable_rule: Against players who don't realize they're drawing dead, deviate from the no-bet equilibrium and make small inducing bets or choose the line most likely to extract a crying call.

concepts.title: Don't Get Attached to a Hand's Earlier Strength
concepts.summary: Strong hands routinely get demoted by later cards; this is mathematically expected and should be planned for, not lamented.
concepts.details: Range morphology changes drastically by runout even after identical action on the same flop; a strong made hand can become a weak bluff-catcher. Players who feel entitled to win with a once-strong hand make errors. Poker is about equity—how much you have, how it's distributed, and how you realize it while denying the opponent's.
concepts.actionable_rule: Re-evaluate your hand's strength relative to both ranges on every card and accept that strong hands get demoted; play the current equity situation rather than the hand's past value.
