concepts.title: Polarized vs Bluff-Catcher: Bet Big to Win the Whole Pot
concepts.summary: When your range is polarized (nuts or air) against a pure bluff-catcher range, betting large enough makes the opponent indifferent and lets value and bluff combos achieve equal EV.
concepts.details: If the bettor has enough stack to make the minimum bet that forces the bluff-catcher to fold their entire range, every betting combo (value or bluff) can win 100% of the pot. The opponent's only equilibrium response is to always fold, since any calling frequency lets the bettor manipulate their value-to-bluff ratio advantageously. Position becomes irrelevant in this pure setup.
concepts.actionable_rule: When your range is polarized against pure bluff-catchers and stacks allow, bet large with all nut hands plus enough bluffs to make the opponent indifferent; against an opponent who folds too much, bet your entire range.

concepts.title: More Air Than Nuts Forces Giving Up Some Bluffs
concepts.summary: When a polarized range contains more than 50% air, you cannot bet your whole range profitably and must give up with some bluffs, betting nuts plus Alpha worth of bluffs.
concepts.details: With over 50% air there is no bet that forces the opponent to always fold. Bet as large as possible to include more bluffs while keeping them indifferent, but the give-up branch still occurs often. Example: with 10% nuts and a pot-sized all-in available, jam a 2:1 value-to-bluff ratio (10% value, 5% air = 15% of range), giving EV of ~15% of pot.
concepts.actionable_rule: When your air exceeds your nuts, bet as large as stacks permit with all nut hands plus the maximum bluffs the value count supports (value-to-bluff per pot odds), and give up the remaining air.

concepts.title: Defend at MDF (1-Alpha) Against Polarized Bettor
concepts.summary: Facing a polarized bet you must call 1-Alpha of the time with bluff-catchers to make the opponent's bluffs indifferent; under-defending invites more bluffing.
concepts.details: Alpha = bet / (bet + pot). If you defend less than 1-Alpha, the bettor will incrementally increase bluffing frequency and profit. When facing a non-all-in bet, the defending player raises traps plus appropriate bluffs rather than just calling.
concepts.actionable_rule: Against a polarized bet, defend exactly 1-Alpha of your range (call bluff-catchers, raise traps with bluffs vs non-all-in bets) to deny the opponent profitable extra bluffs.

concepts.title: Trap with Some Nuts to Cap Opponent's Overbets
concepts.summary: Slowplaying 10-20% of your nutted hands in a bluff-catcher range removes the bettor's incentive to overbet and stops thin value betting and over-bluffing.
concepts.details: In a pure polarized-vs-bluff-catcher model the bettor's EV grows with bet-size (e.g. 4x pot captures ~90% of pot). Adding traps reverses this: with 10% traps, the bettor's EV maxes at SPR ~1.25 and declines thereafter, eventually forcing a 100% check. Just 10-20% traps deters both thin value bets and heavy bluffing at most stack depths. Going all-in for a huge overbet into a range with traps is a major EV mistake.
concepts.actionable_rule: Protect a check/bluff-catcher range by slowplaying roughly 10-20% of your nut hands as traps to cap the opponent's bet-sizing and discourage their overbetting and bluffing.

concepts.title: Optimal Bet-Size Shrinks as Opponent Traps Increase
concepts.summary: The more traps the opponent can have and the deeper the stacks, the smaller the bettor's optimal bet-size becomes, approaching a pure check.
concepts.details: With low SPR the threat of running into the nuts is minor, but at high SPR overbetting into traps is costly. Betting smaller than all-in exposes the bettor to a check-raise where the opponent turns bluff-catchers into bluffs and the bettor's value bets become bluff-catchers; deeper stacks let the opponent raise bigger and capture more EV. There is a trade-off solved by a calculus-derived optimal bet B as a function of stack S and trap% T.
concepts.actionable_rule: Reduce your bet-size as opponent trap frequency and stack depth rise; at high SPR with many possible traps, bet small or check rather than jam to avoid losing EV to check-raises and the nuts.

concepts.title: Leading Traps to Protect a Checking Range
concepts.summary: When stacks are deep enough that the bettor checks back 100%, the trapper should start leading some nuts to extract value, reaching a mixed equilibrium.
concepts.details: If the bettor checks back everything, slowplayed nuts win no extra bets, so the trapper is incentivized to lead some traps. Leading makes the original bettor bet more when checked to, and equilibrium is reached when the EV of leading traps equals the EV of checking them. The defender still calls at MDF.
concepts.actionable_rule: When stacks are so deep the opponent checks back everything, lead a mixed frequency of your trapped nuts for value—just enough to protect your checking range while keeping leading and checking EV equal.

concepts.title: Linear Distribution Threshold Hands
concepts.summary: With continuous ranges, bet the top (value), check the middle, and bluff the bottom; the bottom value hand and best bluff are indifferent between betting and checking.
concepts.details: Categorize hands by equity from 1 (nuts) to 0 (worst). Bet all value above the bottom value threshold and bluff all hands below the strongest bluff; the middle checks because checking EV exceeds betting EV. OOP also checks some value as traps. The defender calls all hands above their indifference threshold and folds the rest (raising traps plus bluffs vs non-all-in bets). Correctly identifying these threshold hands is the key to river play.
concepts.actionable_rule: With a linear range, value-bet the top, check the middle (plus some value as traps if OOP), and bluff the bottom, placing your betting threshold so the marginal value hand and best bluff are indifferent.

concepts.title: Symmetric Range Pot-Bet Threshold (1/4 Rule)
concepts.summary: With symmetric ranges and a pot-sized all-in where checks have zero equity, bet the top 3/4 of hands; the worst quarter of bets are pure bluffs.
concepts.details: For a pot-sized all-in (b=p=s) with symmetric ranges, the betting threshold is 1/4, meaning the bettor bets all hands better than the 25th percentile (3/4 of range). Since the defender gets 2-to-1, 2/3 of betting hands beat the calling threshold and 1/3 are pure bluffs that never win when called. More complex cases require a solver.
concepts.actionable_rule: With symmetric ranges going all-in for pot, bet the top ~75% of your range with the bottom third of those as pure bluffs, and call as the defender getting 2:1 down to your indifference threshold.

concepts.title: Use Multiple Bet-Sizes by Range Overlap and SPR
concepts.summary: Use a large/all-in size with nut hands the opponent cannot have and a smaller size with value hands that overlap the opponent's range; jam more as SPR drops.
concepts.details: When some of your hands beat the opponent's entire range, bet those (e.g. AA-KK) all-in/overbet since the opponent has no traps there, while betting overlapping value (e.g. QQ) smaller. OOP uses smaller sizes (10-25% pot) to mitigate check-raise risk, IP can size larger. As SPR falls below 1, ranges collapse to a single polarized all-in and value ranges expand (e.g. JJ+ at 0.75 SPR widening to 99+ at 0.25). Deep stacks force OOP to bet smaller to avoid being check-raised.
concepts.actionable_rule: Split betting sizes: jam/overbet with nut hands the opponent can't hold and use a smaller size with overlapping value; size up and widen your value jam as SPR shrinks, and bet smaller OOP at deep SPR to limit check-raise exposure.

concepts.title: Use Nut Blockers as Best Bluffs to Eliminate Opponent Traps
concepts.summary: On flush boards, bluff with hands that block the opponent's nut flushes so their range contains zero traps, converting the spot into a clean polarized-vs-bluff-catcher game.
concepts.details: When Hero is polarized on a flush board, the best bluffs are nut-flush blockers (e.g. holding the A of the suit) because they remove the opponent's nut combos, leaving no traps and maximizing fold equity. Bluffing with non-nut blockers loses EV. Note: solvers may show inflated villain calling frequencies because they count 'ghost' nut flushes the villain cannot actually hold; ignoring those, true defense is exactly 1-Alpha.
concepts.actionable_rule: When bluffing into a made-hand range on a flush board, choose nut-flush blockers (hands removing the opponent's nut combos) as your bluffs and avoid non-nut blockers, then jam value plus enough nut-blocker bluffs to keep the opponent indifferent.

concepts.title: Bet Sizing Scales With Nut Blockers in Polarized Spots
concepts.summary: The more nut blockers you hold, the larger you can size (up to all-in); without nut blockers you should size down to about pot.
concepts.details: Holding the nut blocker lets you remove the opponent's trap/nut combos from their continuing range, justifying a large overbet/all-in. Without the nut blocker you cannot remove their traps, so overbetting bleeds EV; pot-sized betting becomes correct. You can split the value range: shove with as many nut combos plus nut blockers as can be accommodated, and bet full pot with the rest.
concepts.actionable_rule: On the river with a polarized range, scale your bet size up toward all-in in proportion to how many nut-blocker combos you hold; if you lack nut blockers, bet around pot instead of overbetting.

concepts.title: Prefer Non-Nut-Blocker Bluffs Over Second-Nut Blockers
concepts.summary: When bluffing without the nut blocker, low non-flush combos are better bluffs than second-best flush blockers like the K-high suited card.
concepts.details: If you bluff with a strong flush blocker (e.g. K-high flush blocker), the opponent can adjust by overfolding king-high flushes and calling more low flushes, neutralizing your blocker. Bluffing with low spade/non-flush combos avoids removing hands you want the opponent to fold. Exception: if your range contains many made flushes beyond the nut flush, then flush blockers become higher-EV bluffs than non-flush blockers.
concepts.actionable_rule: When selecting river bluffs without the nut blocker, bluff with low non-flush combos rather than second-nut flush blockers, unless your range holds many made flushes (then prefer flush blockers).

concepts.title: Make Opponent Indifferent With Blocker-Sized Bluffing Frequency
concepts.summary: At low SPR, shove with enough nut-blocker value to make the opponent indifferent and give up the rest; complete bluff frequency with low combos if needed.
concepts.details: For SPR 1 and lower, size is all-in when you have enough nut blockers. You should shove only enough blocker combos to make the villain indifferent between calling and folding, and give up surplus hands. If nut blockers are insufficient to hit the required bluff frequency, fill the remainder with low spade combos.
concepts.actionable_rule: At SPR 1 or lower, shove enough nut-blocker combos to make the opponent indifferent; if short on blockers, complete the bluffing frequency with low non-flush combos and give up the rest.

concepts.title: OOP Check-Raises River to Deny IP Equity Realization
concepts.summary: OOP should check-raise rivers more when its range has nutted strong hands plus traps, especially when IP bets thinly after a high-frequency check.
concepts.details: The fundamental positional difference is that IP realizes equity by checking back. Betting/raising from OOP prevents free equity realization. A high x/r frequency is favored when OOP has many hands wanting to realize equity plus a small number of nutted strong hands, IP wants to bet often after a check, and x/r protects against IP's thin value. On dry boards after x/c x/c, OOP turns hands like bottom pair (normally x/f) into x/r bluffs.
concepts.actionable_rule: From OOP, raise river check-raises when your range pairs nutted hands with equity-needy hands and IP bets thinly; on dry boards use weak made hands like bottom pair as x/r bluffs.

concepts.title: Bet OOP River After IP Checks Back Turn
concepts.summary: After IP checks back the turn its range is condensed and OOP's is polarized, so OOP should lead the river roughly 20-30% of the time.
concepts.details: IP's turn check-back range is condensed; OOP's is comparatively polarized, justifying river leads at about 20-30% frequency. Calibrate by turn texture: if IP checks back a high-betting-frequency turn its river range is much weaker (bet more); if IP checks back a bad turn its range is stronger (bet less).
concepts.actionable_rule: As OOP after IP checks back the turn, lead the river about 20-30% of the time, betting more when the checked-back turn was a high-bet-frequency card and less when it was a weak card.

concepts.title: OOP River Donk After x/c x/c Is Rare but High-EV
concepts.summary: After check-calling twice, OOP's range is condensed and mostly wants showdown, so donk-betting is rare except when the runout shifts polarization toward OOP.
concepts.details: After IP bets twice, IP's range is very polarized and OOP's is condensed wanting cheap showdown. Donk opportunities arise when the river (or turn+river together) significantly shifts polarization to OOP, e.g. four-flush boards, four-straight boards, river pairing the second-highest card, or runner-runner pairs. In these spots OOP suddenly holds many strong hands and IP wants to check back, so donk frequency can exceed 75%.
concepts.actionable_rule: After check-calling flop and turn, donk the river only when the runout (four-flush, four-straight, second-card pair, runner-runner pair) shifts polarization to your range — then donk at 75%+ frequency.

concepts.title: IP River Betting: Polarized vs Condensed Range Plans
concepts.summary: In position after OOP checks, bet big with a polarized range or bet only the top of a condensed range while checking back middle strength.
concepts.details: OOP's checking range is mostly bluff-catchers. With a polarized range, bet as large as possible and add enough bluffs to make OOP indifferent. With a condensed range, check back middle-strength hands, value-bet the top, and bluff with the weakest. If your range isn't nutted, value-bet small (especially vs possible traps), and add a small frequency of nutted hands to the small size to protect against x/r. Check back when your range is too weak or OOP has too many traps.
concepts.actionable_rule: In position on the river: with a polarized range bet big plus indifference bluffs; with a condensed range bet only the top small while checking back medium hands, and mix some nutted hands into small bets to guard against check-raises.

concepts.title: River Bluff-Catcher Selection by Blockers
concepts.summary: All bluff-catchers are equal except for blocker effects: call more when you block value, fold more when you block bluffs.
concepts.details: On the river the only thing distinguishing bluff-catchers is which combos they remove. Blocking the opponent's value range increases call frequency; blocking their bluffs increases fold frequency; blocking both pushes you to other decision factors; holding no relevant blockers makes the choice irrelevant or slightly negative.
concepts.actionable_rule: When facing a river bet with a bluff-catcher, call more often with hands that block the opponent's value combos and fold more often with hands that block their bluffs.

concepts.title: Never Bluff-Catch Against Insufficient Bluffs
concepts.summary: Anchor river calls to the opponent's value range, always calling hands in it, and never bluff-catch when the opponent lacks enough bluffs.
concepts.details: Use the villain's value range as a starting point and always call hands within it even versus tight players. Never call bluff-catchers when the villain doesn't have enough bluffs. More air in their range means more likely bluffing. Defending close to 1-Alpha (the minimum defense frequency) is a good river approximation in most spots.
concepts.actionable_rule: On the river always call hands that beat the opponent's value range, never bluff-catch when they lack sufficient bluffs, and default to defending close to 1-Alpha.

concepts.title: Adjust Value/Bluff Ranges to Your Table Image
concepts.summary: If perceived as a calling station assume opponents widen their value range; if perceived as weak assume narrower value and wider bluffs.
concepts.details: Perception shapes opponent behavior. When you are seen as a station, expect an expanded (thinner) value range, so call slightly less thin. When you are seen as weak/foldy, expect a narrow value range and a wider bluffing range, so call wider. This is an explicit exploitative adjustment layered on the baseline GTO read.
concepts.actionable_rule: Adjust river calling: if you've been seen as a calling station, assume a wider value range and call slightly tighter; if seen as weak, assume more bluffs and call wider.

concepts.title: Exploit River Betting Frequencies via Flop C-Bet Adjustment
concepts.summary: Versus players who under-bet rivers, c-bet flops more and fold rivers more; versus players who over-bet rivers, c-bet flops less and keep turn check-backs that can raise.
concepts.details: If OOP rarely bets the river, your called hands realize more equity via free showdowns, so you can c-bet the flop much wider and fold more when they do bet. If OOP frequently bets rivers after turn checks, c-bet the flop less to avoid carrying air that must check the turn and fold to a river lead; also check back the turn with some hands capable of raising river bets so OOP can't exploit your bluff-catcher-heavy range.
concepts.actionable_rule: Against rare river-bettors, widen flop c-bets and over-fold to their river bets; against frequent river-bettors, tighten flop c-bets and keep some turn check-backs that can profitably raise rivers.

concepts.title: Plan Early Streets to Reach Favorable River Spots
concepts.summary: Construct flop and turn play to arrive at the most profitable river scenarios with the correct range composition, mirroring how solvers compute equilibria backward.
concepts.details: Solvers solve river situations first, then derive turn strategies that lead to optimal rivers, then flop, then preflop, all maximizing EV by steering toward the most profitable future situations. Players should reason the same way: identify your best possible river outcomes and let earlier-street decisions maximize the likelihood of reaching them with proper ranges. Imbalances created at any street produce exploitable downstream spots.
concepts.actionable_rule: When choosing flop and turn actions, work backward from the river scenarios most favorable to you and pick lines that maximize the chance of arriving there with the correct range composition.

concepts.title: Manipulate Pot Size by Hand Strength
concepts.summary: Build big pots when you hold an edge and keep pots small when vulnerable; this differential is the core source of long-run profit.
concepts.details: All players win and lose pots, but winners ensure the pots they win are larger than average and the pots they lose are smaller. You cannot simply bet big with good hands and small with bad ones because opponents will read the pattern; instead you must plan checks, calls, bets, and raises across all streets to control pot size while disguising your hand strength.
concepts.actionable_rule: Plan the whole hand to grow the pot when you have a strong/big-pot hand and to keep it small when your hand is vulnerable, while varying lines so the sizing pattern is not transparent to opponents.

concepts.title: Hand Strength Is Situational, Not Fixed
concepts.summary: The same holding can be a big-pot or small-pot hand depending on board, opponents, and stack context, so classification must be dynamic.
concepts.details: A given hand on a given flop may warrant building the pot in some circumstances and keeping it small in others. The skill is recognizing which situation applies before deciding whether to pump or control the pot.
concepts.actionable_rule: Before committing to a pot-building or pot-controlling line, evaluate board texture, opponent tendencies, and stack depth to classify whether this specific spot is a big-pot or small-pot situation.

concepts.title: Adjust Decisions to Stack Size
concepts.summary: Correct no-limit play changes fundamentally with effective stack depth; the same hand is played differently with 50, 200, or 1000 in chips.
concepts.details: No-limit is highly situational and stack size is one of the dominant variables. Shallow stacks make theoretical/all-in considerations paramount, while deep stacks elevate the importance of implied odds, hand reading, and post-flop maneuvering. Decisions should be based on the effective stack (the smaller of the relevant stacks that will be all-in).
concepts.actionable_rule: Identify the effective stack size first, then adjust hand selection and bet sizing: prioritize theoretical/shove decisions when shallow and implied-odds, deception, and pot control when deep.

concepts.title: Win the Battle of Mistakes
concepts.summary: Profit in poker comes from inducing opponents to make larger or more frequent mistakes than you make, per the Fundamental Theorem of Poker.
concepts.details: A winning player gets opponents to err (call when they should fold, fold when they should call, misjudge pot odds and implied odds) while minimizing his own errors. Talented players can profit even with imperfect bet sizing because superior hand reading and manipulation win the net exchange of mistakes.
concepts.actionable_rule: Choose lines that maximize the size and frequency of opponents' mistakes relative to your own, rather than playing in a vacuum.

concepts.title: Reading Hands / Assigning Probabilities
concepts.summary: Strong play requires assigning a probability distribution to opponents' possible holdings rather than guessing a single hand.
concepts.details: Mediocre players' notion of hand reading ends at 'putting opponents on a hand.' Experts instead assign probabilities across a range of competing hands and update them with each action, using this distribution to guide bet, call, and fold decisions.
concepts.actionable_rule: Maintain a probability-weighted range of opponent holdings and update it on every action; base decisions on the full distribution, not a single putative hand.

concepts.title: Manipulate Opponents into Playing Badly
concepts.summary: Actively induce opponents to make costly errors through table image, deception, and strategic lines.
concepts.details: A key expert skill is making others play badly via mannerisms, conversation, and strategy—getting pigeonholed, making small obvious errors to induce large costly ones, and using deception. This is a non-theoretical 'talent' skill that complements theory.
concepts.actionable_rule: Cultivate an image and choose plays (including occasional cheap, obvious 'errors') that provoke opponents into larger, more profitable mistakes against you.

concepts.title: Use Effective Stack Size for Analysis
concepts.summary: The effective stack is the amount that will be all-in after full betting—the smaller of the relevant stacks—and it governs the hand's strategic depth.
concepts.details: When one player has 3000 and another 1000, the effective stack is 1000 because betting stops there. Most strategic analysis should be framed in terms of effective stacks rather than absolute chip counts.
concepts.actionable_rule: Always determine the effective stack (smallest relevant stack) before planning sizing and commitment decisions.

concepts.title: Theory vs. Talent Skills Coexist
concepts.summary: Theoretical mastery improves every player, but non-theoretical 'talent' skills (hand reading, gear changes, deception, future-profit setups) are decisive especially in deep-stacked play.
concepts.details: Skills like reading hands, changing gears, using deception, inducing bad play, and setting up future profits often let a talented player beat a theoretically sound but less perceptive one when stacks are deep. As stacks shrink relative to blinds, theoretical considerations dominate.
concepts.actionable_rule: Lean on theory when stacks are shallow relative to blinds, and develop hand-reading, gear-changing, deception, and future-profit skills to win deep-stacked situations.

concepts.title: Adjust Strategy to Effective Stack Sizes
concepts.summary: No-limit strategy changes drastically with stack depth; the effective stacks of all players in the hand must factor into every decision, including preflop.
concepts.details: With very shallow stacks (e.g. 5BB) the only viable decision is shove-or-fold. With deep stacks strategic options multiply. The same holding warrants different plays at different stack depths. You must track your own stack and each opponent's stack and adjust whether to play for stacks, set-mine, bluff multi-street, etc.
concepts.actionable_rule: Before acting, compute the effective stack (smallest relevant stack) and adjust hand selection and bet sizing: with <~15BB favor shove/fold lines, with deep stacks plan multi-street pot-building or pot-control lines for the specific holding.

concepts.title: Win the Battle of Mistakes
concepts.summary: Profit comes from inducing opponents to make larger and more frequent errors than you do, not from playing perfectly.
concepts.details: A 'mistake' is any play that differs from what you'd do with full information. You maximize EV by creating difficult spots and traps for opponents while planning ahead to avoid difficult spots for yourself. Evaluate each action by asking whether it helps or hurts the opponent's ability to respond correctly.
concepts.actionable_rule: For every candidate action, ask 'does this induce an error from my opponent or let them respond correctly?' Choose lines that maximize opponent mistake frequency/cost while minimizing situations where you yourself are likely to err.

concepts.title: Fundamental Theorem of Poker
concepts.summary: Every time you play differently than you would with full knowledge of opponents' cards you lose EV, and vice versa for opponents; this underpins the value of hand reading and deception.
concepts.details: The theorem frames poker as an information game: deduce opponents' holdings while disguising your own. A 'mistake' here is purely informational, not necessarily a bad play (shoving KK into AA you couldn't see is still correct). No-limit lets the theorem 'blossom' because variable bet sizing creates many more opportunities to induce mistakes than fixed-limit betting.
concepts.actionable_rule: Frame each decision by approximating the opponent's likely range and choosing the action that most diverges your opponent from the play they'd make with full information, while keeping your own range disguised.

concepts.title: Bet-Size Targeting to Induce Calling Errors
concepts.summary: In NLHE you can pick a bet size that is incorrect for the opponent to call/fold, targeting the exact amount their style will misplay.
concepts.details: Against a draw the pot odds may make a $20 limit bet automatic, but a $150 bet into $200 changes the math. If you know an opponent calls $100 correctly and folds to $200 correctly but calls in between, bet the in-between amount. Suspicious 'every bet is a bluff' opponents will pay off larger value bets, so size up against them.
concepts.actionable_rule: Estimate the largest bet the specific opponent will incorrectly call (or smallest they'll incorrectly fold to) and size your value bets/bluffs to that threshold rather than to a default fraction of pot.

concepts.title: Bet to Maximize Expectation, Not Call Frequency
concepts.summary: When last to act on the river with the nuts, choose the bet/raise size that maximizes EV = P(called by worse) × size, not the size most likely to get called.
concepts.details: EV is computed across candidate sizes: a small raise gets called often but wins little; a large/all-in raise gets called less but wins more per call. Example: $50 raise called 80% = $40 EV; $150 raise called 40% = $60 EV; $450 all-in called 20% = $90 EV — the all-in wins most. Small 'don't scare them' raises are usually the worst option with a nut hand.
concepts.actionable_rule: With the nuts last to act, estimate P(call) for several sizes, compute size × P(call) for each, and pick the size with the highest product — often a large or all-in bet rather than a small 'milking' raise.

concepts.title: Accept Slightly Lower EV to Limit Risk
concepts.summary: On rare occasions a play with slightly less than maximum EV is correct when it significantly reduces risk, e.g. short bankroll or late tournament stages.
concepts.details: Risk-of-ruin and ICM considerations can justify sacrificing a small amount of expectation to limit variance. This also applies when avoiding giving a losing recreational player a big win that might cause them to quit the game.
concepts.actionable_rule: Default to the max-EV play, but when on a limited bankroll, near tournament money jumps, or preserving a profitable game, accept a slightly lower-EV, lower-variance option.

concepts.title: Pot Size Philosophy: Big Pots for Big Hands
concepts.summary: On average bet more with strong hands and less with weak ones; building big pots with weak hands and small pots with strong hands is a losing long-term pattern.
concepts.details: Many players invert this by slowplaying monsters and making big daring bluffs. A little deception balances normal play, but the baseline should be big pots/big bets with big hands. The biggest pots aren't always made by the biggest preflop/flop bets — a small early bet or check-raise can trigger the avalanche; work backward from stack sizes to plan how the desired pot size is built by the river.
concepts.actionable_rule: Decide early whether you want a big or small pot with this hand/position/opponent, then choose the action at every street (including small bets or check-raises) most likely to produce that target pot size by the river.

concepts.title: Exploit Inverted Bluff-Catchers
concepts.summary: Against players who call big bets thinking they're bluffs but fold to small value bets, bet small when bluffing and big when value betting.
concepts.details: The reasoning 'a big bet must be a bluff because value hands milk' is generally a horrendous, easily exploited strategy. Against such 'perverse callers' you risk little bluffing small and extract maximum value betting big — a double whammy where they lose more to value and snap off cheaper bluffs less often. Normally you must balance this pattern, but not against a clearly perverse caller.
concepts.actionable_rule: Against opponents who call big bets as bluff-catchers and fold to small bets, bluff with small sizings and value bet with large sizings; balance these sizes only against observant opponents.

concepts.title: Hand Reading as Layered Probability and Perspective
concepts.summary: Hand reading involves modeling what the opponent thinks you have and weighting candidate holdings as likely/somewhat likely/unlikely, then translating that into a play.
concepts.details: Beyond guessing the opponent's cards, consider 'given my line, what does he think I have?' and 'is he trying to deceive me?' Conclusions are usually probabilistic categories rather than certainties (e.g. 'either a monster or a bluff, rarely medium'). The final and crucial step is converting that read into the highest-EV action via logical reasoning.
concepts.actionable_rule: Sort the opponent's possible holdings into likelihood buckets given the action so far and their model of you, then select the action that has highest EV against that weighted range.

concepts.title: Manipulate Opponent State of Mind
concepts.summary: Opponents' emotional and mental states shape their play, and table behavior or noteworthy plays can be used to steer them into playing how you want.
concepts.details: Recent winning/losing streaks, tilt, comfort, intoxication, sympathy or fear all influence decisions. Manipulation means behaving (or making image plays) to get opponents into a mindset that makes them play in exploitable ways.
concepts.actionable_rule: Track each opponent's emotional state and image of you, and choose table behavior and showdown reveals that push them toward the exploitable mindset (tilt, ease, fear) you want them in.

concepts.title: Plan the Pot by Working Backward from the Final Bet
concepts.summary: With a big hand, decide how large you want your final bet to be (near the opponent's remaining stack) and construct earlier bets so that money arrives in escalating chunks.
concepts.details: With $500 stacks and a flopped set, the goal is to stack the opponent. Work backward: you want the last bet (~$250 here) to come when the pot is large and the opponent feels pot-committed (e.g. $500 pot, $250 behind) rather than when there's still room to fold cheaply. Break the prior ~$230 into two chunks ($70/$160) or three chunks ($30/$70/$130), each bigger than the last, matching natural escalation of NL betting.
concepts.actionable_rule: With a big hand, pick a target final bet near the opponent's remaining stack, then plan escalating bet 'chunks' across the streets so the big bet arrives only when the pot is large and the opponent feels committed.

concepts.title: Tailor Strategy to the 'Good but Not Great' Hands
concepts.summary: Against non-bluffers, your decisions only matter when the opponent holds good-but-not-great hands (e.g. overpair, AK, flush draw); other holdings produce the same result regardless.
concepts.details: If opponent has a monster you get stacked anyway; if he has air against a non-bluffer you can't win big; if he has two pair you stack him regardless. The only holdings where your line changes the outcome are good-but-not-great hands. Maximize EV against that subset. The way to extract from them is to ensure it's 'too late' (pot-committed) before they suspect they're beaten.
concepts.actionable_rule: When holding a big hand vs a non-bluffer, build your line to maximize value against good-but-not-great hands (overpairs, AK, draws), and arrange betting so they only suspect they're beaten after they are already committed.

concepts.title: Choose Two vs Three Chunks Based on Opponent Tendencies
concepts.summary: Use a two-chunk (overbet) line vs callers who don't raise enough, and a three-chunk line vs aggressive opponents who will put in a raise themselves.
concepts.details: Two chunks ($70/$160) gives the opponent little info and forces tough guesses, but requires overbetting that may scare astute/timid players. Three chunks ($30/$70/$130) avoids overbetting but requires the opponent to raise somewhere so all the money goes in over two streets; ideal if he reliably raises flop and bets turn. If opponent won't raise, you must check-raise (a 'strong-arm' line that risks losing him). Recent caught check-raise bluffs make check-raise lines more attractive.
applies_to: adjusting to caller vs aggressor types
concepts.actionable_rule: Against opponents who call too much but rarely raise, use a two-chunk overbet line; against hyper-aggressive opponents who raise, use a three-chunk line and let them put in the raise.

concepts.title: Consider What the Opponent Thinks You Have
concepts.summary: Effective bet planning requires modeling not just the opponent's hand but how he interprets your bets.
concepts.details: An overbet may look like semi-weakness to one player (inducing a call) and a clear threat to another (inducing a fold). Adept opponents may recognize manipulation toward a big pot and abandon ship. Choose sizing based on the read of how this specific opponent reads your line.
concepts.actionable_rule: Before sizing a bet, estimate how this specific opponent will interpret it (weakness vs threat vs manipulation) and choose the size that produces the response you want.

concepts.title: Against Habitual Bluffers, Check to Induce Bluffs
concepts.summary: When the opponent frequently bluffs weak hands, slow down and check multiple streets to let him barrel into you.
concepts.details: The normal logic (focus only on good-but-not-great hands) flips against a habitual bluffer: his weak hands become the most profitable, so allowing him to bluff earns the most. You shift from betting for value to checking to induce.
concepts.actionable_rule: With a strong hand versus a habitual bluffer, check multiple streets to let him bluff rather than betting for value yourself.

concepts.title: Don't Offer Too High Implied Odds
concepts.summary: Bet/raise enough with strong hands that drawing opponents cannot profitably chase, accounting for the money they can win if they hit.
concepts.details: A small reraise (e.g. $15) lets JJ call vs known AA because flopping a set ~1/9 and winning the ~$125 immediate+implied pot gives ~8.33-to-1 vs the ~8-to-1 draw odds. To deny profit, raise an amount equal to roughly the inverse of the hit frequency times total available win: a ~$65 reraise (about 1/8 of the $520 available) makes the JJ set call break-even at best. Set mining hits ~1/9 with no overset.
concepts.actionable_rule: When betting/raising a strong hand, size it so that an opponent drawing to beat you (e.g. set-mining) cannot show a profit even counting his implied odds — roughly the draw's hit probability times his total stealable stack.

concepts.title: More Hand Transparency Demands Bigger Bets
concepts.summary: The more accurately an opponent can read your exact hand, the larger a fraction of your stack you must bet to deny profitable implied-odds draws.
concepts.details: In the idealized AA example, a fully-known hand forced a relatively large $65 reraise. When your hand is hidden, the opponent risks getting stacked when you both hit (e.g. set-over-set ~1/100, costing ~$5 EV), and you sometimes hold non-AA hands that pay him off less or fold winners — all of which reduce his implied odds, so you can bet less. Symmetrically, the better you can read opponents, the larger the bets you can profitably call to bust or bluff them.
concepts.actionable_rule: Bet a larger proportion of your stack when your hand range is transparent to the opponent, and a smaller proportion when your hand is well-disguised; conversely, call larger bets to chase when you can read the opponent's range precisely.

concepts.title: Implied Odds Calculation Discounts Redraws
concepts.summary: When computing implied odds for a draw, weight the win by the chance the made hand gets redrawn and by the uncertainty over the opponent's exact holding.
concepts.details: With a gutshot vs a known set committing $1,970, you win $2,045 only 77% (avoiding board pair, 34/44) and lose 23%, giving expected win ~$1,132.50, so 11.3-to-1 implied beats 10.25-to-1 draw odds — a call. But add uncertainty (set 75% / flush draw 25%): some catch cards put you only slightly ahead or drawing dead, raising the aggregate outdraw chance to ~27% and dropping expected win to ~$970 (9.7-to-1), which no longer beats 10.25-to-1 — a fold. Uncertainty about the opponent's hand can flip a profitable call into a losing one.
concepts.actionable_rule: When deciding to chase a draw, discount your implied-odds payoff by the probability your made hand gets redrawn and by the chance the opponent holds a hand that has you drawing thin or dead before comparing to your draw odds.

concepts.title: Don't Justify Optimistic Calls
concepts.summary: When you won't go broke with a hand, deny chasers their implied odds by folding before they collect your stack, turning their loose draw-chasing into a losing play.
concepts.details: Players overcall flop bets with longshot draws assuming they'll stack you when they hit. If you fold to the big bet before paying off, their call loses money long-term. Two cases: if you ARE willing to pay off, size your bets to deny implied odds to the most likely draws; if you are NOT willing to pay off, bet an amount that looks callable to the opponent but is actually too much because you won't go broke.
concepts.actionable_rule: Before betting a good hand, decide whether you'll pay off a big bet; if not, refuse to stack off so chasers' optimistic draw calls become losers, and size your bet to look small to them while being mathematically unprofitable for them.

concepts.title: Always Pre-Decide Whether You'll Pay Off
concepts.summary: Whenever you bet or raise, have a plan for whether you intend to call a big bet later or fold.
concepts.details: Knowing in advance whether you're willing to lose a lot with this hand drives both your sizing (deny implied odds when willing to commit; avoid justifying optimistic calls when not) and your later-street discipline. The plan can change as the hand develops, but the question must always be asked.
concepts.actionable_rule: Every time you bet or raise, ask 'Am I willing to pay off a big bet with this hand?' and let that answer guide your sizing and later-street commitment.

concepts.title: Cap protection betting by expected loss, not stack size
concepts.summary: With deep stacks and a vulnerable made hand, don't commit your whole stack to protect a small pot; bet enough to deny the draw profit but base the calculation on how much you'd lose finding out you're beaten.
concepts.details: With $5,000 behind protecting a $100 pot, betting many times pot to deny implied odds invites action only from hands that beat you (sets, two pair). Instead estimate your average loss while discovering your hand is no good (e.g. $684.10), then bet enough so opponents can't profit (e.g. >$85.51) but small enough they might call. Good opponents read your remaining stack to size their draws, so pick an amount too large for draws to call yet tempting.
concepts.actionable_rule: With deep stacks and a good-but-not-nut hand, bet more than the draw's break-even amount but not so much you'd be risking your stack to protect a small pot; size to deny profit while still enticing a call.

concepts.title: Basic protection bet vs a known draw
concepts.summary: When the opponent's hand is clearly worse and identifiable, bet more than he can profitably call given his outs.
concepts.details: With a flush-draw opponent on the turn (9 outs, 3.9-to-1 against), and where you can fold if a third diamond hits so his implied odds equal pot odds, bet enough to offer worse than 3.9-to-1. A $40 bet into $100 offers 3.5-to-1, denying profit. The bet is tied directly to the opponent's out count.
concepts.actionable_rule: When you can identify the opponent's draw and can fold safely if it completes, bet enough to offer pot odds worse than his odds against improving (≈outs/remaining cards).

concepts.title: Bet larger when opponent has multiple possible draws
concepts.summary: When you can't pin down which draw the opponent holds, bet more than against a known draw because his implied odds rise from disguised completions and bluffs.
concepts.details: If the opponent could have a flush draw, straight draw, or backdoor draw, you can no longer safely fold to every scary river card, and he can bluff cards that didn't help him. This means he sometimes makes money on the river, so his implied odds exceed his pot odds. A bet only slightly worse than pot odds no longer denies profit; size up.
concepts.actionable_rule: If the opponent could hold one of several draws, bet a larger amount than you would against a single known draw to offset his higher implied odds and bluffing potential.

concepts.title: Don't blow opponents off their hands (Fundamental Theorem)
concepts.summary: Once you bet more than the opponent can profitably call, you want him to call; avoid overbetting that forces correct folds.
concepts.details: Per the Fundamental Theorem of Poker, you profit when opponents make mistakes. A huge all-in that always blows draws out forces them to play correctly, surrendering EV. Bet within a range: above break-even but below what guarantees a fold, enticing bad calls.
concepts.actionable_rule: Bet more than opponents can profitably call but small enough that they will still often call; never size purely to force a fold when you hold the best hand.

concepts.title: Maximize EV = value of mistake × probability of mistake
concepts.summary: Your expectation from a bet equals how big a mistake the opponent makes times how often he makes it, so choose the size that maximizes that product.
concepts.details: The value of the opponent's mistake is proportional to the EXCESS bet above his break-even point, not the total bet (e.g. betting $600 vs $550 when $500 is break-even doubles your profit). Multiply mistake size by call frequency across candidate sizes (e.g. $150@70%=$35, $200@40%=$40, $500@5%=$20) and pick the max. Larger bets often win even at lower call frequency because each extra dollar over break-even compounds the mistake.
concepts.actionable_rule: For each candidate bet size compute (bet − opponent's break-even amount) × (probability he calls) and choose the size with the highest product.

concepts.title: Maximize EV against the whole range, not one hand
concepts.summary: When the opponent holds a range of draws, pick the size that maximizes total expectation, even if that lets his strongest draw call profitably.
concepts.details: If a weak draw (4-to-1) appears 75% and a strong draw (2-to-1) 25%, a smaller bet that both call may net positive overall: you gain on the frequent incorrect calls more than you lose on the rare correct ones (e.g. +$100×0.75 − $167×0.25 = +$33 vs $0 baseline of betting them all out). Weight each outcome by its frequency.
concepts.actionable_rule: Size against the opponent's entire range: prefer a smaller bet both draws call if the frequent weak draws' losses outweigh the rare strong draw's profitable call, weighted by frequency.

concepts.title: Don't take away their rope when they can make a losing second-best hand
concepts.summary: If the opponent's draw can complete into a strong-but-second-best hand that pays you off, keep him in—sometimes even checking is better than betting.
concepts.details: Holding top set when villain has a flush draw, the cards that make his flush give you a full house, so completion wins you his whole stack. Comparing checking (EV $102.28, occasionally stacking him) versus betting big to fold him ($100), checking is superior. The lower bound of your betting range becomes $0; bet only an amount you're sure he'll call.
concepts.actionable_rule: When the opponent's draw completes into a second-best hand that will pay you off, bet only an amount he's sure to call—or check—rather than blowing him off the draw.

concepts.title: Bet bigger when opponent thinks he already has the best hand
concepts.summary: Against a made hand the opponent believes is good (not a draw), ignore his out count and bet large because he'll call sizable bets.
concepts.details: If villain holds an overpair he thinks is best, his 8 outs are nearly irrelevant—he isn't relying on improvement, so he'll call big. Bet far more than the small protection bet outs would suggest. Still, factor outs at the margin: if he has outs the bigger bet is strictly better since you gain when he folds; with no outs, X@100% and 2X@50% are equal EV.
concepts.actionable_rule: When you think the opponent has a made hand he believes is best, disregard his outs and bet large for value; the call probability, not out-count, drives sizing.

concepts.title: When you might not have the best hand, lean toward checking
concepts.summary: The more likely you're beaten, the less you should bet; in position check, out of position consider a blocking bet.
concepts.details: Bet-sizing math assumes you hold the best hand; you rarely do for sure. As the combined chance you're already beaten or will be outdrawn rises, betting itself becomes a mistake. With marginal hands, check in position; out of position, make a small 'blocking bet' to forestall a large bet from the opponent when you expect him to bet big if checked to.
concepts.actionable_rule: If you're not the favorite (counting both being behind and being outdrawn), check when last to act; out of position make a small blocking bet to prevent facing a large bet.

concepts.title: The hammer of future bets / reverse implied odds
concepts.summary: Bets carry more threat the more money remains behind; a small bet with a deep stack can be stronger than a larger all-in because of the implied threat of future bets.
concepts.details: Calling early commits you to potential future bets. A tough opponent bets the river when ahead (or bluffing optimally) and checks when behind, so calling a turn bet with money behind means risking your whole stack to win only what's currently in play (reverse implied odds: risk a lot to win a little). An all-in turn bet is actually weaker because it caps your risk and gives you straight odds. With a mediocre hand out of position you're effectively laying odds.
concepts.actionable_rule: Recognize that bets with money behind threaten future bets; avoid calling turn bets with mediocre made hands when deep and out of position, since reverse implied odds make you risk a lot to win a little.

concepts.title: Wield the hammer by delaying value with weak hands vs weak opponents
concepts.summary: With a deep stack against a player you read as weak, check the turn so the threat of a river bet doesn't scare him into folding before he pays you off.
concepts.details: A weak-handed opponent often folds a turn bet fearing the river 'hammer,' but will pay off a river bet if you check the turn. Use the hammer's threat to extract value on the river rather than letting it cost you action; conversely avoid betting earlier when the threat would only chase the opponent away.
concepts.actionable_rule: With a deep stack and a hand that beats a likely-weak opponent, check the turn and bet the river so the threat of future betting doesn't drive him off before he pays.

concepts.title: Basic Bluff-Sizing: Get the Job Done
concepts.summary: Size a bluff to be just large enough to fold the specific range you're targeting, and not much more, since extra size adds risk without adding folds.
concepts.details: A bluff targets a specific hand or range, not 'every hand.' No bet folds the nuts, so betting more than needed only risks more money for the same result. The relationship between bet size and folds is non-linear and psychological — sometimes a smaller bet folds more than a larger one. The Fowler/Hoff WSOP example shows betting $190k into a $20k pot was a blunder: any jack made the nuts (never folds) and any non-jack folds to a $15-20k bet.
concepts.actionable_rule: When bluffing, first identify the specific range you want to fold, then bet the smallest amount that folds that range; never bet more than needed to get the job done.

concepts.title: Maximize EV Across Bluff Sizes
concepts.summary: Choose a bluff size by weighing each candidate size against the probability it folds each part of the opponent's range, picking the size with highest expectation.
concepts.details: Different hand strengths fold to different sizes (busted draws fold to tiny bets, pairs need larger bets, sets never fold). Compute EV roughly: for each candidate size, weight the pot won by the chance each holding folds. In the example, a $200 bet (EV $145) beat a $75 bet (EV $60) into a $300 pot because it folded both busted draws and most pairs. You can't solve equations live, but estimate which size folds the most value for the least risk.
concepts.actionable_rule: Estimate the opponent's range distribution, then pick the bluff size that yields the highest weighted expectation across how often each holding folds — generally bet bigger when it folds in additional made hands.

concepts.title: Bet Larger When Planning a Follow-Up Bluff
concepts.summary: If you intend to bluff again on a later street, sizing the earlier bluff larger builds a bigger pot to win with the second barrel.
concepts.details: A planned multi-street bluff gives incentive to oversize the first bet beyond the minimum. Betting $800 instead of $500 into a $1,000 pot means a successful river bluff wins $1,800 instead of $1,500, since the larger turn call grows the pot. This trades off against the basic 'get the job done' rule.
concepts.actionable_rule: When you plan to follow up a bluff on the next street, size the current bluff somewhat larger than the bare minimum to inflate the pot you'll win with the subsequent barrel.

concepts.title: The Threat of the Big Multi-Street Bluff
concepts.summary: In deep-stack NLHE the looming possibility of a large turn/river bluff for stacks constrains opponents with strong-but-not-nut hands.
concepts.details: Most hands the big bluff never happens, but its specter keeps top-pair holders from building big pots, since a $100 flop bet can lead to a hard-to-call $1,000 river bet. Deep-stack proficiency requires being capable of the big turn-and-river bluff. The threat of a bigger bet to come is more powerful than the bet itself.
concepts.actionable_rule: Against capable opponents in deep-stack play, leverage the implied threat of a large later bet to discourage them from building pots with marginal hands, and be willing to execute multi-street bluffs to keep the threat credible.

concepts.title: Save Enough on the Turn for a Credible River Bluff
concepts.summary: Divide remaining stack so your river bet still offers the opponent short enough odds (around 2-to-1) to make folding likely; don't blow the stack on the turn.
concepts.details: If you bet pot on the turn leaving only a small river bet offering 4-to-1, opponents who called the turn with a made hand will call the river too, making it not credible. A bet offering longer than ~2.5-to-1 (less than two-thirds pot) gets called too often. Leaving a credible threat (significantly more than the turn bet) also strengthens the turn bet, because the opponent must fear losing a lot when wrong, not just the current bet.
concepts.actionable_rule: When planning a turn-and-river bluff, ensure the remaining stack lets your river bet offer the opponent roughly 2-to-1 or worse (about a two-thirds-pot to pot-size bet); if you can't leave a credible river threat, don't launch the multi-street bluff.

concepts.title: Maximize the Turn Bluff Within a Credible River Threat
concepts.summary: Bet as much as possible on the turn while still retaining a credible river bluff, because larger turn bets win more often and build a bigger river pot.
concepts.details: Fold equity follows an s-curve: tiny bets and huge bets fold roughly fixed amounts, with the steep change around half-pot to 1.5x pot. The optimal river size is the smallest amount that still folds most hands — found by tracing the fold curve leftward to where it begins dropping. Betting less on the river lets you bet more on the turn, which increases turn success and the reward if called. EV example: $500/$3,500 split gave $580 EV while $1,000/$3,000 gave $600, so shifting money to the turn improved EV even with slightly lower total success.
concepts.actionable_rule: Set the river bluff to the smallest size that still folds most hands, then put as much of the remaining stack as possible into the turn bluff while preserving that credible river threat.

concepts.title: Plan Bet/Pot/Stack Sizes for All Streets
concepts.summary: Effective deep-stack play requires planning the entire sequence of bets, pot sizes, and stacks before acting.
concepts.details: Stack management is central: make no bet or raise without mapping out how the pot and stacks will look on remaining streets. This ensures bluffs and value lines remain coherent and credible to the river.
concepts.actionable_rule: Before making any bet or raise in a deep-stack pot, plan the bet sizes, resulting pot, and remaining stack for every subsequent street.

concepts.title: Information Has Value Only If Specific, Accurate, and Decision-Changing
concepts.summary: Betting 'for information' is only worthwhile when the information is reliable enough and will actually change a decision you'd otherwise make differently.
concepts.details: Information must be specific/accurate and let you make a more profitable decision now or later. Knowing the exact range (AA/KK/AK) is worth far more than 'good hand probably.' If you'll act identically regardless (e.g., calling all-in with aces), the information is worthless. You can quantify value: with KK vs a range containing AA ~11% of the time and a ~$64 cost when facing aces, seeing the cards is worth ~$7. Imperfect information still has proportional value as long as it can ever cause a fold.
concepts.actionable_rule: Before paying (in chips or risk) for information, verify it will be reliable enough and will genuinely change your action; if you'd play the same regardless, don't pay for it.

concepts.title: Paying for Information Is Better in No-Limit Than Limit
concepts.summary: Information-seeking bets are usually dubious in limit but more justifiable in no-limit because the upside (saving your stack) is larger and opponent actions are more reliable.
concepts.details: In limit, pots are large relative to bets and aggressive players respond unpredictably (light three-bets on principle), so information rarely changes profitable decisions much. In no-limit, light raises are punished by huge reraises, so raises and even calls are more reliable signals. A no-limit call typically means a good made hand or strong draw, whereas a limit call can mean almost anything. Top pair getting called on the flop is fine in limit but often a warning sign in no-limit.
concepts.actionable_rule: In no-limit, treat opponents' raises and calls as more meaningful information than in limit, and be more willing to take small risks to gain reliable reads that could save your stack — but still weigh cost versus the decision it enables.

concepts.title: Information Bets to Save Stack When Beaten
concepts.summary: Bet slightly larger than normal to gain reliable information about opponents' hand strength, especially when out of position, so you can fold cheaply instead of bleeding chips across streets.
concepts.details: Small bets and calls reveal little; big bets and calls are telling. If opponents call $15 with many hands but $30 only with good ones, betting $30 lets you fold for one bet when called rather than betting small, getting called multiply, and being forced to commit more out of position under uncertainty. The extra cost is justified by the saved equity, not extra profit. Information bets reduce opponents' positional advantage.
concepts.actionable_rule: When out of position with a mediocre hand against straightforward opponents, bet a little larger than usual so a call reliably signals strength, and fold cheaply if raised or called.

concepts.title: Small Reraise to Read a Straightforward 3-Bettor
concepts.summary: Against a straightforward opponent who only puts in a third raise with AA/KK, make a small reraise to learn his exact strength while keeping worse hands in.
concepts.details: If a tight player will 3-bet only with aces or kings regardless of your sizing and call/fold everything else, a small reraise (e.g., to $80-$100 over a $40 open) extracts information: a third raise means AA/KK. Keep it small so you don't fold out AQ/AJ/KQ and don't risk extra chips to learn you're beaten. The reraise also purifies the remaining players' actions, deterring loose calls and semi-bluff raises since you could hold aces.
concepts.actionable_rule: Versus a straightforward player who 3-bets only AA/KK, make a small reraise; treat a 4-bet as AA/KK and proceed accordingly while keeping dominated hands in.

concepts.title: Information Bet With a Vulnerable Pocket Pair
concepts.summary: With a pocket pair of uncertain rank on an unthreatening flop, bet substantially to induce straightforward opponents to raise bigger pairs and merely call smaller ones.
concepts.details: When preflop action suggests opponent also has a pocket pair but you're unsure whose is higher, a substantial flop bet sorts the situation: straightforward players raise with a bigger overpair but flat with a smaller one. Since you have only two outs when beaten, this read is high value.
concepts.actionable_rule: On an unthreatening flop with a pocket pair of uncertain rank, make a substantial bet and read a raise as a bigger pair and a flat call as a smaller one.

concepts.title: Avoid the Obvious Big Information Raise
concepts.summary: Making an uncharacteristically large preflop raise with a good-but-vulnerable hand like JJ telegraphs your holding and plays poorly out of position deep.
concepts.details: A big raise with JJ to 'scare out riffraff' risks too much out of position with a hand not strong enough, while informing observant opponents you hold roughly jacks/tens/AK. Against capable hand-readers this is disastrous in deep-stack play and invites bluffs or intentional misinformation.
concepts.actionable_rule: Do not make an unusually large preflop raise with a good-but-vulnerable hand to 'find out where you are'; size consistently and avoid telegraphing your range.

concepts.title: Use Information Bets Mainly Against Unaware Players
concepts.summary: Information-gathering bets work best against straightforward, unaware opponents and should be used sparingly and disguised against skilled hand-readers.
concepts.details: Perceptive players may read larger-than-average bets as information attempts and respond with bluffs or false signals. Mix your play so big bets are sometimes strong hands too, and use the tactic most against players who almost never just call or raise deceptively.
concepts.actionable_rule: Deploy information bets primarily against straightforward, unaware opponents; against skilled players use them rarely and balance them with genuine big hands.

concepts.title: Big Bet the Nuts Against Likely-Weak-But-Maybe-Trapping Opponents
concepts.summary: With the nuts on the river when an opponent is probably weak but might be slowplaying a big hand, make a large bet because few hands call small but not large.
concepts.details: If a small/medium river bet won't get called by weak hands anyway, but the only hands that beat-but-don't-fold are the rare slowplayed monsters that will call any amount, a big bet captures maximum value. Selling cheaply only helps when many hands call small but fold to big; here that range is thin.
concepts.actionable_rule: With the nuts on the river, if the opponent is likely weak but could be trapping, assume strength and make a large bet since calling hands will call any size.

concepts.title: Modest Nut Bet to Induce Calls or Check-Raises
concepts.summary: Bet small with the nuts when the opponent likely has little (and may curiosity-call a bet that looks like a bluff) or has a big hand he'll check-raise.
concepts.details: A small river bet on a board where your line looks like a missed draw induces light calls from one pair and lets strong hands or aggressive players check-raise (including bluff-raises), reopening betting. The only loss case is a hand good enough to call big but not check-raise, which is often a remote possibility.
concepts.actionable_rule: With the nuts on the river when your line looks weak, make a modest bet to induce curiosity calls and to let strong/aggressive opponents check-raise.

concepts.title: Overbet the Nuts After a Surprising River
concepts.summary: When the opponent has shown strength all hand and you complete an unlikely nut hand, make an extra-large bet or raise because it looks like a bluff.
concepts.details: If you called along apparently on a draw (e.g., the obvious flush) that missed, then hit a runner-runner straight, an opponent betting his strong hand will read your big raise as a busted-draw bluff and call wider. 'Suspicious' players who view big bets as bluffs warrant extra-large sizing with the nuts.
concepts.actionable_rule: When an opponent has shown strength throughout and you make a disguised/unlikely nut hand on the river, raise extra large since it will be read as a bluff.

concepts.title: Size Up Against Semi-Suspicious Callers
concepts.summary: Choose the bet size that maximizes EV; if a larger bet's drop in call frequency is less than proportional to its size increase, bet larger.
concepts.details: Even if an opponent calls a $600 bet only 40% vs a $300 bet 70%, the larger bet wins more on average (0.40×600 > 0.70×300). Game-theory-based callers behave 'semi-suspiciously,' so against them larger value sizing is correct. Compare EV across sizes rather than maximizing call frequency.
concepts.actionable_rule: Pick the river value size with the highest EV: if call frequency falls less than proportionally as size grows, choose the larger bet.

concepts.title: Shrink Value Bets When You Might Be Beaten
concepts.summary: When you only fairly likely hold the best hand, bet smaller than you would with the nuts because the chance of being beaten penalizes larger sizings.
concepts.details: With a 20% chance of being beaten, large bets get called disproportionately by better hands, dropping EV. In the worked example a $200 bet (EV +$80) beat $500 (+$50) and $1,000 (-$20). The risk of being beaten dramatically reduces optimal sizing toward a thin amount likely called by worse.
concepts.actionable_rule: When last to act with a hand that might be beaten, value bet smaller than you would with the nuts so mainly worse hands call.

concepts.title: Check Behind to Avoid Check-Raise Bluffs
concepts.summary: Last to act, if a decent hand might face a check-raise bluff you must fold to, checking can beat betting in EV.
concepts.details: If betting $200 induces a $2,000 check-raise (part bluff) you can't profitably call, your EV (e.g., $760) falls below simply checking down to win the pot at showdown (e.g., $800). Against opponents who check-raise bluff, fold-vulnerable decent hands should be checked back.
concepts.actionable_rule: When last to act with a decent but bluff-catchable hand against a check-raise bluffer, check behind rather than make a thin value bet.

concepts.title: Out of Position, Bet to Deny the Bluff-Raise
concepts.summary: First to act, size your bet large enough to discourage bluff-raises but small enough to limit losses when beaten.
concepts.details: Checking out of position lets the opponent bet you off the pot with bluffs, lowering EV (e.g., a check wins only 70% for $700 EV). A bet that scares off bluff-raises (e.g., $500 yielding $850 EV) can beat both checking and a thin $200 bet. The optimal first-to-act size balances bluff-deterrence against losses when called by better.
concepts.actionable_rule: When first to act with a value hand vulnerable to bluff-raises, bet an amount large enough to deter the bluff-raise yet small enough to minimize losses when beaten.

concepts.title: Absolute vs Relative Position
concepts.summary: Having the button (absolute position) is not the whole story; relative position to the likely bettor matters, and being just to the right of the bettor is best.
concepts.details: In a multiway raised pot, early players often check to the preflop raiser regardless of strength, so a button player acting right after the raiser is effectively second-to-act and must commit without information. Relative position improves the closer you act before the likely bettor; you can hold both, neither, or one type of position.
concepts.actionable_rule: Evaluate both absolute (button) and relative position; in multiway raised pots, recognize you act effectively early if the likely bettor is on your right and proceed cautiously.

concepts.title: Don't Play Big Pots Out of Position With Moderate Hands
concepts.summary: Calling raises out of position—especially from the player on your right—with moderately big offsuit hands is a major leak.
concepts.details: Moderately strong hands (top pair, shaky kicker) suffer most out of position because you commit chips before learning where you stand, and can get sandwiched by loose players behind. Hands like big offsuit cards become solid dogs out of position despite winning in position.
concepts.actionable_rule: Avoid calling raises out of position (particularly from the player directly on your right) with moderately strong offsuit hands that play poorly without positional feedback.

concepts.title: Small Pairs Play Well Out of Position
concepts.summary: Small pocket pairs are the hands least hurt by poor position because the flop gives instant set-or-no-set feedback.
concepts.details: Unlike moderate made hands, small pairs don't need to see betting to know where they stand—you either flop a set or fold. They profit against loose-aggressive opponents even out of position, though relative position still matters for maximizing winnings on big hands.
concepts.actionable_rule: Set-mine small pocket pairs even out of position against loose-aggressive opponents, but value relative position to maximize payoffs when you hit.

concepts.title: Out-of-Position Play Narrows Your Perceived Range
concepts.summary: Because fewer hands are profitable out of position, observant opponents read your out-of-position continuations as stronger than average.
concepts.details: Good players bet, call, and raise more in position; opponents know hands lose value out of position, so when you do play out of position they assign you a narrower, stronger range—sometimes very narrow. This makes disguising strong hands harder and reduces value extracted from out-of-relative-position holdings.
concepts.actionable_rule: Account for opponents narrowing your range when you play out of position; expect less action on strong hands and consider balancing your out-of-position continuing range.

concepts.title: Relative position can equal or exceed absolute position
concepts.summary: Acting after seeing all opponents respond to a bet (relative position) is often more valuable than having the button, because information about opponents' actions guides your decisions.
concepts.details: Position hurts you two ways: it forces commitment with marginal hands without information (or folding the best hand), and it prevents concealing the strength of big hands. Before entering a pot, anticipate who the likely flop bettor will be and how their position will affect you. Good relative position lets you watch opponents react before acting.
applies_to: out of position vs in position
concepts.actionable_rule: Before entering a pot, identify the likely flop aggressor; prefer entering pots where you act after that bettor (good relative position), and avoid spots where being out of position forces commitment without information.

concepts.title: Out-of-position big hands force premature strength tipping
concepts.summary: A player out of position with a monster is often forced to make strong plays they'd rather delay, and conversely your own OOP monster can't be concealed.
concepts.details: When you hold the nuts out of position in a multiway pot with little money in, any call or raise screams strength to thinking opponents, who fold everything but bigger monsters. Recognize this same dynamic in opponents: when an OOP player shows repeated strength on a drawless board (preflop call, calls a near-pot flop bet, then leads the turn), they likely hold a big hand, not a draw.
concepts.actionable_rule: When an out-of-position opponent shows consistent aggression/strong calls on a drawless board culminating in a turn lead, fold seemingly strong hands like top pair, since their range is sets and strong two-pair, not draws.

concepts.title: An OOP call can signal as much strength as a raise
concepts.summary: Do not assume calls are weaker than raises; an out-of-position call, especially when the caller cannot have merely a strong draw, can represent significant strength.
concepts.details: On drawless boards, a flat call from out of position eliminates draw-based explanations, so the calling range is weighted toward made hands a player wants to trap with. Calls also strengthen YOUR perceived range to opponents, which can let you induce or make laydowns.
concepts.actionable_rule: On drawless boards, treat an opponent's flat call as a potentially strong range and weight your reads toward made hands rather than draws; recognize your own call also looks strong.

concepts.title: Stack depth governs value-raise threshold preflop
concepts.summary: The shallower the stack, the more compelling raising for value becomes; the larger the raise as a percentage of the effective stack, the stronger your hand must be hot-and-cold.
concepts.details: If a raise is ~2% of the stack, you needn't raise all strong hands and needn't have a strong hand to raise (implied odds dominate). If a raise is ~20%+ of the effective stack, you should raise nearly all strong hands and rarely otherwise, because postflop maneuvering room is limited and hot-and-cold equity dominates EV.
concepts.actionable_rule: Scale your value-raising range to effective stack depth: when a preflop raise exceeds ~20% of the effective stack, raise nearly all strong hands and little else; when it's ~2% or less, loosen and don't require strong hands to raise.

concepts.title: Isolation raising is weaker in no-limit than limit
concepts.summary: Raising to isolate is less lucrative and riskier deep-stacked because blind money is a small fraction of expectation and reraises cost your whole equity.
concepts.details: In limit, isolation chops up meaningful blind money and a reraise costs only a fraction of a bet. In deep NL the blind overlay is trivial relative to stacks, and getting reraised usually forces a fold and forfeits your entire pot equity. The exception: when a bad player with a deep stack enters, isolate frequently to get a heads-up, in-position shot at his stack.
concepts.actionable_rule: In deep NL, rarely raise purely to isolate for blind money; instead isolate aggressively only when a bad deep-stacked player has entered, to play heads-up in position against his stack.

concepts.title: Blind stealing and limping the button in no-limit
concepts.summary: Blind stealing pays less in NL because immediate odds are worse, so limping (even on the button) can be correct against weaker blinds you'd rather see flops with.
concepts.details: In limit a $40 raise to win $30 lays 4-to-3; in NL a $60-$80 steal lays only 6-to-3 or 8-to-3, requiring much higher fold equity to profit. If you outplay the blinds postflop, you may earn more letting them see a flop and make expensive mistakes than by shutting them out. With weak hands like J9 you forgo little equity by not raising.
concepts.actionable_rule: On the button against weaker blind players, consider limping marginal hands like J9 rather than always raising to steal, since the immediate odds are poor and you profit more by inducing postflop mistakes.

concepts.title: Preflop semi-bluff raise EV condition
concepts.summary: A preflop semi-bluff raise after limpers is profitable when fold equity plus the residual flop value of getting called outweighs the raise risked.
concepts.details: EV: (chance all fold)(pot + raise) + (chance called without reraise)(value of hand on flop) > raise. Semi-bluff with the best hands you would NOT ordinarily play, because that maximizes the 'value on flop' term. Don't semi-bluff hands strong enough to be profitable calls (calling captures their value without the risk) or hands strong enough to reraise for value.
concepts.actionable_rule: When semi-bluff raising preflop, choose the strongest hands that are NOT profitable calls (e.g., Q8s over both Q9s+ and 72o) so your hand retains the most value the times you get called rather than folded out.

concepts.title: Big blind bluff-raise inversion: use your worst hands
concepts.summary: In the big blind where you'd otherwise see a free flop with every hand, make big bluff-raises that rarely get called with your very worst hands.
concepts.details: Normally you bluff with the best hand you wouldn't play, but in the BB you'd play (check) every hand and see the flop for free. Since a big raise that rarely gets called sacrifices the free-flop value, choose your worst holdings (like 72o) because seeing a flop with them has less value to give up than a decent hand like Q8s.
concepts.actionable_rule: From the big blind facing limpers, when making a large, rarely-called bluff-raise, choose your very worst hands (e.g., 72o) since you sacrifice the least free-flop equity, unlike in other positions where you bluff your best non-playable hands.

concepts.title: Deceptive preflop raises set up stack-winning postflop
concepts.summary: Occasional well-timed small raises with weak/disguised hands exploit deep stacks by mis-weighting your perceived range, enabling huge postflop payoffs.
concepts.details: A timely $20 raise with a hand like 86s can net a full stack when you flop a disguised straight against an opponent holding AK or aces-up, because the raise convinces them you hold premiums. Leverage a tight table image: after playing few hands, a modest raise reads as premium, so action-prone opponents pay you off on low-card flops. Don't overdo it (don't raise every 86 and call every AK).
concepts.actionable_rule: With a tight image and deep stacks, occasionally make small disguised raises with speculative hands (e.g., suited connectors) so that when you flop big on a low board, opponents misread your range and pay off your stack.

concepts.title: Raise to manipulate pot size toward the skill sweet spot
concepts.summary: There's an optimal pot-to-stack ratio that maximizes a skilled player's edge; when the game plays too small you can enlarge pots to engage more skill.
concepts.details: If blinds are too small relative to stacks, money stays unbet and skill goes unused; if too big, hands go all-in early, nullifying turn/river skill. You can't change blinds, but in a too-small game you can make 'sweetener' raises to grow preflop pots, causing larger postflop betting where your edge applies. In a too-big game little can be done.
concepts.actionable_rule: If the game plays too small for the stacks and you have a skill edge, make small sweetener raises (e.g., $20-$30 over a $5-$10 blind) to inflate the pot and produce bigger postflop bets where your edge pays off.

concepts.title: Sweetener Raises to Inflate Small Games
concepts.summary: In games with small blinds relative to stacks, raising marginal hands to make the game play bigger can be profitable despite giving up some immediate equity.
concepts.details: Raising a so-so hand like A5 sacrifices some immediate value (you win less than your share), reopens betting to reraises, and can be read as a sweetener. But the value of making pots 2-3x bigger so a strong player can leverage edge often offsets these drawbacks. An excellent player stuck in a small-blind game may correctly raise nearly every pot.
applies_to: games with small blinds relative to stacks
concepts.actionable_rule: When you are a significantly better player in a game with small blinds relative to stacks, raise marginal hands preflop to inflate pot sizes and leverage your postflop edge.

concepts.title: Vary Raise Size by Hand and Situation
concepts.summary: Reject the advice to always raise a constant amount; different hands and situations call for different raise sizes, and you stay unreadable by occasionally mixing sizes rather than fixing them.
concepts.details: Constant-size raising softens your strategy because different reasons to raise prefer different sizes. To avoid leaking information, occasionally swap a 6x raise for 3x and vice versa, often enough that opponents have significant doubt about which holding maps to which size. Seemingly random sizing is just as unreadable as constant sizing but allows more freedom and profit.
