concepts.actionable_rule: Size preflop raises by hand type and situation rather than a fixed amount, and randomly swap your size occasionally so opponents cannot map a raise size to a hand strength.

concepts.title: Big Raises Make Big Pots
concepts.summary: In deep-stack play, raise size determines eventual pot size; choose your size based on whether you want to play a big or small pot with the hand class.
concepts.details: Big raises build big pots; small raises and limps build small pots. Although you don't know your flop yet, certain hand classes thrive in big pots and others only in small ones. The fundamental deep-stack sizing question is: do you want a big pot or a small pot with this hand?
concepts.actionable_rule: Before choosing a preflop raise size deep, decide whether the hand class wants a big or small pot, then size up for big-pot hands and down for small-pot hands.

concepts.title: Raise Big-Pot Speculative Hands Enough to Brew a Big Pot, No More
concepts.summary: Small pairs and set-mining hands want a larger preflop raise so stacks-to-pot ratio allows getting all the money in postflop, but oversizing only increases reraise risk.
concepts.details: With $1,500 stacks at $5-$10, raising pocket fours to $30 leaves too much behind to stack a tight AK on K94; raising to $60 makes the pot big enough that pot-sized bets and an all-in by the river become near-automatic calls. But bigger raises cost more to a reraise: a $30 raise lets you profitably call a reraise (20:1 stack odds), while a $60 raise forces a fold to a reraise (under 10:1). Raise enough to enable stacking, never more than needed.
applies_to: speculative hands like small pairs and suited connectors
in position vs likely one-pair callers
concepts.actionable_rule: With speculative big-pot hands like small pairs, raise large enough that remaining stacks allow getting it all in by the river, but no larger so you don't overexpose yourself to reraises.

concepts.title: Don't Build Big Pots With Marginal Showdown Hands
concepts.summary: Hands like AJ that win only moderate pots and lose big ones should not be raised large; you don't want to fold out the worse hands you beat.
concepts.details: With AJ on the button you rarely win a big pot but might win a moderate amount against A9 or KT. A large $60 raise makes no sense because it folds out exactly the dominated hands you profit from, while big pots tend to put you on the losing end against stronger holdings.
concepts.actionable_rule: Avoid large preflop raises with marginal showdown hands that win small and lose big; keep the pot small so you keep the worse hands in.

concepts.title: Bigger Value Raises vs Straightforward Players
concepts.summary: Against players who reliably reveal hand strength postflop, you can make larger value raises even out of position because you can fold cheaply when behind.
concepts.details: A straightforward opponent folds flops he misses, calls with pairs/draws, and raises two-pair-plus. Because his actions tell you where you stand, a large preflop raise with AK out of position becomes safe: you extract extra from the small pots you win without getting trapped in a big pot. This differs from raising into unknown blinds.
concepts.actionable_rule: Make larger value raises against straightforward, readable opponents because their postflop transparency lets you escape cheaply when behind.

concepts.title: Bigger Raises vs Players Who Overfold Postflop
concepts.summary: Against timid players who call preflop but fold to later-street pressure, raise larger and more often in position to make their inevitable bad folds more costly.
concepts.details: Many medium-stakes players call raises liberally but fold to big bets on later streets. Since you'll take most pots through position and aggression, those pots might as well be big, magnifying their folding mistakes. Caveats: keep enough behind to bluff later streets, do some hand reading (bluff when they're weak, check down when strong), and don't do it so often they start trapping.
concepts.actionable_rule: Against opponents who fold too much postflop, raise larger and more often in position, then apply pressure with big bets while hand-reading to avoid bluffing into their occasional strong hands.

concepts.title: Smaller Raises vs Players Who Call Too Much Postflop
concepts.summary: Against calling stations, keep pots small preflop because their loose calls are biggest mistakes in small pots and you still stack them postflop on your strong hands.
concepts.details: A calling station's errors are proportionally worse the smaller the pot. Why raise $60 with fours to stack AK when $30 achieves the same goal with less risk and the same payoff? Keep the pot small and let them hang themselves with bad calls of your big postflop bets.
concepts.actionable_rule: Against opponents who call too much postflop, make smaller preflop raises to reduce risk while still extracting their loose calls on later streets.

concepts.title: Short-Stack Raising Has Two Goals
concepts.summary: With a short stack you raise either to steal blinds/antes or to find someone to gamble all-in with; you're not raising to see a flop and proceed.
concepts.details: Short-stack raising lacks subtlety: any raise essentially asks 'anyone want to play for everything?' You can't play for implied odds without money behind, so the best short-stack cash strategy is tight, avoiding small cards and playing high-percentage hands, usually raising preflop and pushing the flop.
concepts.actionable_rule: When short-stacked, raise only to steal blinds/antes or to commit all-in with a strong hand, play tight high-percentage hands, and plan to push the flop rather than play for implied odds.

concepts.title: With Big Hands Short, Raise as Much as Will Still Get Called
concepts.summary: When you want action with a premium short-stack hand, make the largest raise that still gets called and leave little for the flop.
concepts.details: With a big pair or AK short-stacked you usually want action, so the bigger the raise and call the better. Most of the time you raise preflop and push the flop; the bigger the preflop raise and the less left for the flop, the better you perform—just don't size so big you never get called.
concepts.actionable_rule: Short-stacked with a premium hand you want called, raise the maximum amount that still gets action, leaving little behind so you can push the flop.

concepts.title: Don't Size a Raise Into an Indifference Decision
concepts.summary: Size your raise so you're never left unsure how to respond to a reraise; if a smaller raise creates a close (indifferent) call/fold decision, moving all-in is usually better.
concepts.details: With AJ and a $2,400 stack at $100-$200, a $700 raise reraised all-in gives you 2:1, needing 33% equity—but AJ is about a 33% underdog to the reraising range, leaving you indifferent (and your raise mis-sized). Moving all-in instead folds out his marginal reraising hands (e.g., 77, which faces ~47% needed equity), turning small losses into blind-steal profits while you still face KK/AK equally often. This only holds when the smaller raise can't be easily folded; if a $500 raise (vs $3,000 stacks) lets you cleanly fold AJ to a shove, the smaller raise is fine.
applies_to: fairly good but non-premium hands like AJ
concepts.actionable_rule: Don't choose a raise size that leaves you indifferent to a reraise; either size small enough to fold cleanly or move all-in to fold out marginal reraises and pick up the blinds.

concepts.title: Deep-Stack Hand Value Comes From Postflop Extraction
concepts.summary: In deep-stack NLHE, preflop hand value is based on how well a hand extracts money postflop, not on showdown win rate or hand rank.
concepts.details: Hands derive value from their ability to win big pots and stack opponents, not from how often they beat another hand all-in. T9s is a better deep-stack hand than a higher-ranking but less extractive holding even though the latter wins more all-in showdowns. Thinking in terms of 'this beats that' by hand rank leads to wrong conclusions.
concepts.actionable_rule: Evaluate deep-stack starting hands by their postflop money-extraction potential (implied odds, ability to make big disguised hands), not by all-in showdown equity or poker hand rank.

concepts.title: Position-Based Raise Sizing Summary
concepts.summary: Make smaller raises in early position and larger raises in late position, combined with hand class and opponent tendencies.
concepts.details: Consolidated guidance: raise smaller in early position, with small-pot hands, and against players who call too much postflop; raise larger in late position, with big-pot hands, and against players who fold too much postflop. Also consider how opponents read your size and whether you want calls or folds.
concepts.actionable_rule: Raise smaller from early position and larger from late position, adjusting up for big-pot hands/overfolders and down for small-pot hands/calling stations.

concepts.title: Deep-Stack Bread-and-Butter Starting Hands
concepts.summary: The strongest deep-stack hand class is all pocket pairs, AK, suited aces, and no-gap suited connectors down to 54s—hands that play well with deep stacks.
concepts.details: Bread-and-butter hands perform well deep and are usually worth playing: all pocket pairs, ace-king, suited aces, and no-gap suited connectors from KQs down to 54s. Often-playable hands (slightly weaker) include AQ, KQ, any two suited cards jack or higher, and one-gap suited connectors from QTs down to 53s (and 43s). These are flexible categories, not rigid rankings.
concepts.actionable_rule: Prioritize pocket pairs, AK, suited aces, and no-gap suited connectors (down to 54s) as core deep-stack opening hands, treating AQ/KQ/high suited cards and one-gappers as a secondary often-playable tier.

concepts.title: Preflop Hand Tier System (Often/Sometimes/Rarely Playable)
concepts.summary: Starting hands fall into fuzzy value tiers that guide which holdings have intrinsic value, rather than rigid rankings.
concepts.details: Sometimes-playable hands (offsuit broadways, suited kings, gapped suited connectors down to 52s, no-gap offsuit connectors down to 54o) become profitable in late position or against weak opponents. Rarely-playable hands are only used as semi-bluffs, against very bad players, or to balance. The tiers indicate relative value, not absolute superiority.
concepts.actionable_rule: Classify each starting hand into a value tier; expand into lower tiers only in late position or against weak opponents, and use bottom-tier hands mainly as semi-bluffs or balancers.

concepts.title: Mixed Frequency Preflop Actions (UR/UL/UF)
concepts.summary: Rather than always taking one action with a hand, mix raising/limping/folding at roughly 80/20-type frequencies to stay balanced.
concepts.details: UR = raise ~80% / limp ~20%; UL = limp ~80% / raise ~20%; UF = fold ~80% / limp ~10% / raise ~10%. Exact ratios are flexible (70/30 to 85/15) but shifts to 95/5 or 55/45 are real deviations. Balancing matters because predictable preflop play is exploitable in no-limit.
concepts.actionable_rule: Assign each hand a default action (raise/limp/fold) but randomize ~20% of the time to the alternate action to keep your preflop range balanced.

concepts.title: Position-Based Range Promotion
concepts.summary: As position improves, promote borderline hands to more aggressive default actions.
concepts.details: From EP to MP, promote JJ, AQ, and suited broadways from limp to raise, and suited one-gappers from fold to limp. LP first-in is highly read-dependent: strong players vs weak blinds can open almost anything, weak players vs strong blinds stay tight. Limping first-in from LP is acceptable in deep-stack cash games.
concepts.actionable_rule: Widen your opening range and upgrade borderline hands to raises as you move from early to late position; default to MP requirements when uncertain in LP.

concepts.title: Adjusting to Multiple Limpers
concepts.summary: Against two or more limpers, raise larger, play more decisively, and semi-bluff-raise more with bottom-range hands.
concepts.details: Add at least one big blind to your raise size per limper. Convert 'usually' (80/20) plays into 'almost always' (95/5) plays. Increase semi-bluff raises with the best UF hands from ~10% to ~20% because dead money and multiple weak ranges make stealing/building more attractive.
concepts.actionable_rule: When 2+ players limp ahead, increase raise size by one BB per limper, take your default action ~95% of the time, and raise the best fold-tier hands as semi-bluffs ~20% of the time.

concepts.title: Responding to a Raise: Call vs Reraise Thresholds
concepts.summary: Only AA/KK are pure reraises; many strong hands prefer calling, and you tighten as the raise size grows.
concepts.details: Vs an open: UR only AA/KK; flat AK, AQs, QQ-99 and occasional bread-and-butter hands; occasionally reraise the very best of your fold range as a bluff. In LP add all pairs and no-gap suited connectors to the calling range. Tighten as raise exceeds 4x BB; loosen vs loose/wild raisers. Vs a raise plus callers, reraise AK rather than call. Vs a raise and a reraise, shove AA/KK and fold everything else.
concepts.actionable_rule: Against an open, flat most strong hands and reserve reraises for AA/KK plus occasional bluffs; tighten progressively as the raise exceeds 4x BB and loosen against wild raisers; vs a raise and reraise, jam only AA/KK.

concepts.title: Don't Over-Defend the Blinds
concepts.summary: The blind money rarely justifies playing weak hands out of position; defend sparingly.
concepts.details: Play tighter from the blinds than from LP because you'll be out of position postflop. The small blind investment doesn't provide enough incentive to play marginal hands. Call raises sparingly. However, occasionally make a big semi-bluff raise into multiple limpers using your worst hands, not good hands worth seeing a flop with cheaply.
concepts.actionable_rule: From the blinds, call raises sparingly and avoid 'defending' with weak hands; reserve big raises into multiple limpers for your worst (bluff-suitable) holdings, not your decent ones.

concepts.title: Stack Depth Dictates Medium Pair Strategy
concepts.summary: How to play a medium pocket pair changes dramatically with stack depth: limp at medium stacks, raise small when deep, jam when short.
concepts.details: At ~70BB, raising a medium pair risks a reraise from a big pair, applying the Fundamental Theorem of Poker against you by inducing the opponent's correct play and destroying your set-mining value—so limp. At ~200BB, getting reraised isn't disastrous because deep money remains, so a small raise (to maximize set-stacking) is best. At ~10BB (especially with antes in a tournament) focus shifts to stealing blinds, so move all-in.
concepts.actionable_rule: With a medium pair: at ~70BB limp to avoid being reraised off your set-mining equity; at ~200BB make a small raise to build pots for set value; at ~10BB shove to steal blinds/antes.

concepts.title: Set-Mining Value Scales with Stack Depth and Multiway Pots
concepts.summary: Small/medium pairs derive most of their profit from flopping sets, which is worth more multiway and with deeper stacks.
concepts.details: At medium-deep stacks most of a small/medium pair's win comes from set flops; sets are worth more in multiway pots than heads-up. Small pairs perform well against big pairs when preflop betting is a small fraction of stacks, but big pairs pull ahead as preflop investment grows. Limping invites weak hands and keeps pots small, preserving implied odds.
concepts.actionable_rule: Prioritize keeping the preflop pot small and multiway with small/medium pairs to maximize implied odds when you flop a set; avoid bloating the pot, which favors big pairs.

concepts.title: AQ Plays Opposite to Medium Pairs
concepts.summary: AQ-type hands welcome winning the blinds or going heads-up and even welcome a reraise to escape trouble.
concepts.details: Unlike a medium pair, AQ is happy taking the blinds down or playing heads-up, and benefits from a reraise that lets it fold before flopping a second-best top pair. The set-mining limp logic reverses for these high-card hands that dominate or are dominated rather than draw to sets.
concepts.actionable_rule: With AQ-type hands, prefer raising (rather than limping) to win the blinds or play heads-up, and treat a reraise as a useful chance to fold cheaply rather than a disaster.

concepts.title: Blocking Bet to Draw Cheaply (Out of Position)
concepts.summary: An out-of-position player makes a small bet to set a cheaper price for seeing the next card with a draw, avoiding a larger bet if they check.
concepts.details: By betting ~$80 into $180 with a draw, the player risks facing a $180 bet if he checks (assumed 80% of the time). The blocking bet trades occasional folds (10%) and occasional raises that price him out (20%) for the right to see the river for $80 (70%). With a 3-to-1 draw plus implied odds, EV of the blocking bet (~$23) exceeded EV of checking (~$11). Works against opponents who would bet large but won't aggressively raise the small bet.
concepts.actionable_rule: Out of position with a draw against an opponent who bets big when checked to, lead a small blocking bet to set a cheaper price for the next card, provided he rarely raises it.

concepts.title: River Blocking Bet with a Marginal Made Hand
concepts.summary: Lead small on the river with a thin one-pair-type hand to avoid facing a larger value/bluff bet you'd reluctantly call.
concepts.details: If checking leads the opponent to bet ~half pot (3-to-1), you'd call only when winning >25%. With a hand that wins ~35% when called, you'd rather face a smaller bet. Betting ~$80 preemptively (folding to a raise, assuming raises mean you're beat) into a $200 pot can raise EV above check-calling. The play works when the opponent would otherwise bet bigger and won't bluff-raise your lead.
concepts.actionable_rule: On the river with a thin showdown hand against an opponent who bets large, consider a small blocking bet and fold to a raise—do this when it caps your loss while still extracting from worse hands.

concepts.title: Blocking Bet EV Depends on Opponent's Bluff-to-Call Ratio
concepts.summary: A blocking bet only profits when the opponent bluffs about as often as he calls; against habitual bluffers it costs you their bluffs, and against calling stations you should value bet instead.
concepts.details: The standard blocking-bet EV calculation assumes the opponent bluffs with roughly the same number of hands he would call (but not bet) with. If the opponent is a consummate bluffer who bluffs far more than he calls, blocking betting is unattractive because you preempt his bluffs. If he is a calling station who calls far more than he bluffs, you should bet the river for value with weaker-than-normal hands rather than as a blocking bet.
concepts.actionable_rule: Before making a blocking bet, estimate the opponent's bluff-vs-call frequencies: if he bluffs far more than he calls, check instead to capture bluffs; if he calls far more than he bluffs, bet for thin value instead of blocking.

concepts.title: Use Blocking Bets Sparingly and Only vs Unaware Opponents
concepts.summary: Blocking bets work best against unskilled opponents who won't understand the play; against tricky aggressive players who detect and raise them, they backfire.
concepts.details: Overusing blocking bets lets observant opponents catch on and raise them frequently, which is devastating since the whole purpose is to keep betting cheap. Against aggressive players you instead want to check and call with some strong hands to induce and pick off their bluffs (using their aggression against them).
concepts.actionable_rule: Reserve blocking bets for unaware opponents and use them rarely; against aggressive thinking players, replace blocking bets with check-calls to induce and capture their bluffs.

concepts.title: Frequent Blocking Bets Leak Information
concepts.summary: Because blocking bets are small and made with weak-to-medium hands, using them often makes your whole range readable—small bets signal weakness and large bets signal strength or bluffs.
concepts.details: A blocking bet must be smaller than your average bet and is typically made with weak-to-medium holdings. If you do this consistently, opponents learn small bet = medium hand, large bet = strong/bluff, and that NOT making a blocking bet also reveals information. This balance leak lets aggressive players force you to 'play square.'
concepts.actionable_rule: Avoid making blocking bets at a frequency that lets your small bet sizes become readable; occasionally make small bets with strong hands and vary sizing to protect the information content of your bets.

concepts.title: Detect and Raise Blocking Bets
concepts.summary: Against a likely blocking bet, raising is devastating—if you knew for certain a bet was a blocking bet you could profitably raise nearly any weak hand to force a fold.
concepts.details: Blocking bets aim to keep betting cheap; a raise thwarts that and often wins immediately, especially when the opponent's drawing implied odds are poor. Detection cues: the bet is out of position, unusually small relative to pot, and (pre-river) the board offers possible draws the opponent wants to see cheaply. Always verify exact bet size versus pot before acting.
concepts.actionable_rule: When an out-of-position opponent makes an unusually small bet relative to pot, flag it as a candidate blocking bet and raise (large enough to force folds), having first compared bet size to pot and the opponent's normal sizings.

concepts.title: The Call Bluff (Delayed Bluff)
concepts.summary: Instead of raising as a bluff immediately, just call the current street and then bet or raise on the next street, keeping your options open and committing bluff capital only when the opponent shows weakness.
concepts.details: The call bluff is most effective in position against a single opponent; out of position or multiway it becomes risky or prohibitively risky. Its key advantage is informational and flexible: you stay in cheaply, gather information, and only fire when the opponent appears weakest (e.g., checks the turn after betting the flop). If the opponent shows continued strength, you can fold cheaply rather than committing a larger raise-bluff. This converts a $500 raise-bluff loss into a $150 call loss when it doesn't develop.
concepts.actionable_rule: In position heads-up, when you want to bluff a strong-looking spot, just call this street instead of raising, then bet/raise the next street only if the opponent checks or otherwise signals weakness; fold cheaply if he keeps betting.

concepts.title: Combine Independent Profit Sources (Equity + Fold Equity)
concepts.summary: A semi-bluffing call/bet can be correct because the chance of making a big hand and the chance of bluffing the opponent out are independent profit sources that sum.
concepts.details: With a gutshot on the flop and deep stacks, calling can be justified by two simultaneous, non-contradictory hopes: ~40% to stack the opponent when you hit, plus ~60% to bluff him off when you miss. Because the profitabilities sum, the combined play can be correct even if each component alone is marginal or unprofitable. Opponents have a range, so you can exploit their best and worst hands at once.
concepts.actionable_rule: When deciding to continue with a draw, add your equity-when-you-hit EV to your fold-equity-when-you-miss EV; proceed if the combined expectation is positive even when neither reason alone justifies the play.

concepts.title: Exploit Players Who Always Bet Good Hands on the Turn
concepts.summary: Against opponents who rarely check a good hand after betting the flop and being called, call the flop and use their turn action as a perfect read for a profitable bluff.
concepts.details: This is a clear information leak: such players bet the turn with anything decent. So call the flop, then if they bet the turn fold, but if they check the turn they are likely weak and you can bluff profitably. This makes the call bluff 'on air' more profitable the more information the opponent gives away.
concepts.actionable_rule: Against opponents who always bet good turns after a flop bet-and-call, flat the flop; fold to a turn bet but bluff when they check the turn.

concepts.title: Defend vs Call Bluff by Concealing Flop-to-Turn Information
concepts.summary: Since the call bluff is informational, defend by sometimes check-raising the turn and mixing your turn checks/bets so the opponent can't read your flop-bet-then-turn behavior.
concepts.details: After betting the flop and being called, sometimes check-raise the turn—usually with good hands but occasionally as a bluff—and sometimes check your good hands. Keeping opponents guessing makes them reluctant to play back, and they will save call bluffs for more readable players. When out of position, manipulating opponents into playing straightforwardly against you is desirable.
applies_to: after c-betting flop and being called
concepts.actionable_rule: After your flop bet is called, occasionally check-raise the turn (mostly value, sometimes bluff) and occasionally check strong hands, so opponents cannot exploit your turn actions with call bluffs.

concepts.title: Don't Check-Raise Just Because You Can (No-Limit vs Limit)
concepts.summary: Unlike limit poker, in no-limit a near-certain opponent bet is not enough reason to check-raise, because checking lets the opponent set a smaller bet size and the move reveals strength.
concepts.details: Two major drawbacks: (1) check-raising permits the opponent to set the bet size—if he tends to bet small, you collect less than betting yourself; (2) the check-raise is a power move that gives away strength, whereas betting out reveals less. EV example: betting $200 with 80% call = $160 EV beats checking for a $80 bet (90%) then raising $200 more called 40% = $139.20.
applies_to: first to act with strong hands
concepts.actionable_rule: When first to act with a strong hand heads-up on the river, prefer betting out unless you are quite confident the opponent will both bet and call your check-raise; otherwise betting captures more value and conceals strength.

concepts.title: Check-Raise When Opponent Bets More Hands Than He Calls
concepts.summary: The most important reason to check-raise for value is when the opponent will bet (often bluff) worse hands than yours more often than he would call a bet—you profit from the check, not the raise.
concepts.details: In this spot your check-raise rarely gets called, but you still gain because checking induces bets/bluffs from worse hands that would have folded to your bet. This is the same logic as check-calling with a merely good hand, extended to great hands: don't forfeit the induced bet just because your hand is strong. The bigger no-limit river bet makes mediocre hands fold more, so this condition holds more often than in limit.
concepts.actionable_rule: Heads-up on the river, when the opponent bets worse hands more often than he calls, check (planning to raise or call) to induce his bluffs rather than betting out and folding out those worse hands.

concepts.title: Check-Raise Bluff on the River
concepts.summary: Occasionally a check-raise bluff succeeds where a simple bluff bet fails, because many players fold more readily to a check-raise—but it requires the opponent to both bet and then fold.
concepts.details: The daring version is check-raise bluffing when the opponent likely has a good hand, exploiting that players fold more to check-raises than to bets. This needs an accurate read on both his holdings and his betting/calling tendencies. A safer application: when the opponent will often have a decent-but-unbettable hand and sometimes a busted draw he'll bluff—don't bet (you'd be called by the decent hand), but check-raise when he bets to fold out the decent hand. Also use it when the opponent will likely bluff and might beat you at showdown.
applies_to: vs opponents who fold to aggression
concepts.actionable_rule: Reserve river check-raise bluffs for opponents you read as likely to bet then fold to a raise, or who will bluff a busted draw after you check; otherwise remove the play from your repertoire.

concepts.title: Near-Automatic Flop Check-Raise vs Preflop Raiser's C-Bet
concepts.summary: Heads-up on the flop against the preflop raiser, check-raise frequently with any hand you'd otherwise bet, since c-bettors often bet missed flops when checked to.
concepts.details: Because many players auto-continuation-bet when checked to, you can check-raise to grab an extra bet when they missed. Raise with good hands, good draws, and occasionally some semi-junk, adjusting to the opponent. The less likely the opponent is to c-bet, the less automatic this play becomes. Check-raising also traps players in the middle in multiway pots since early-position betting shows too much strength to get multiple callers.
applies_to: out of position vs preflop raiser
concepts.actionable_rule: Heads-up out of position against the preflop raiser, check planning to check-raise with hands you'd otherwise bet; scale this down the less likely the opponent is to continuation bet.

concepts.title: Compare Betting Off vs Drawing With Implied Odds
concepts.summary: Before semi-bluffing a weak hand with a draw, compare the bluff EV to the EV of checking and drawing, factoring in the implied odds of stacking the opponent when you hit.
concepts.details: Example: $100 pot, $1000 stacks, bottom of range with a wheel draw. Semi-bluffing where opponent folds 2/3 yields EV = (2/3)($100) = $33.33. Checking to draw a trey (4/44 ≈ 1/11) wins $1,100 X% of the time when you hit plus $100 otherwise: EV = (1/11)(X)($1,100) + (1/11)(1-X)($100). If X ≥ 1/3, the stacking term alone equals the bluff EV, with the rest as 'gravy,' so checking to draw becomes superior.
concepts.actionable_rule: With a strong draw, compute both the semi-bluff EV (fold equity x pot) and the draw EV (hit probability x stack you can win + showdown value); choose checking-to-draw when implied odds make its EV exceed the bluff, e.g. when you can stack the opponent at least ~1/3 of the time you hit.

concepts.title: Semi-bluff vs check-behind decision with a draw
concepts.summary: When last to act with a drawing hand, weigh the immediate-profit of bluffing against the EV of checking to realize the draw; counterintuitively, the more valuable your draw, the less you should semi-bluff if you'd fold to a check-raise.
concepts.details: The bluff EV doesn't depend on the draw's value, but the checking EV does. Implied-odds boosters (more outs, deeper stacks, calling-station opponent, drawing to the nuts) raise the EV of checking, making semi-bluffing relatively less attractive. Drawing to the nuts is a booster because you win big-hand-vs-big-hand confrontations rather than losing your stack.
concepts.actionable_rule: When last to act with a draw, compare bluff EV against draw-realization EV; if your draw is strong (many outs, deep stacks, calling opponent, nut draw) and you'd fold to a check-raise, lean toward checking, otherwise take the semi-bluff.

concepts.title: Bluff more freely when the draw has less showdown/realization value
concepts.summary: On boards where your straight draw has reduced value (e.g. flush draw and pair on board making your made hand less likely to win or get paid), checking is worth less so semi-bluffing becomes more attractive.
concepts.details: With an OESD, a board containing a flush draw and a pair lowers the value of completing your straight (it may not win or may cost your stack), so the EV of checking drops and bluffing's relative value rises. Against an opponent who'd only check-raise with a full house or better, the check-raise even helps you by signaling you're drawing dead before you invest more.
concepts.actionable_rule: Favor semi-bluffing a draw when the board reduces your made hand's value (flush draw/pair present); a check-raise from a player who only raises monsters is informative, not costly.

concepts.title: Why mediocre hands are checked down on the river
concepts.summary: Mediocre hands win showdowns sometimes but are unlikely to be called by worse and unlikely to fold out better, so betting fails as both a bluff and a value bet.
concepts.details: A bet succeeds either by getting worse hands to call (value) or better hands to fold (bluff). Mediocre hands accomplish neither: callers are usually beating you and folders were already worse. So default to checking these hands down.
concepts.actionable_rule: On the river with a hand that better hands won't fold to and worse hands won't call, check it down rather than betting.

concepts.title: Bluffing with a fairly good hand (fold-equity value bet)
concepts.summary: Betting a hand that would often win at showdown can still gain value by folding out a band of decent-but-beatable hands that you'd lose to less often than you fold them now.
concepts.details: Example: checking wins 30% of a $100 pot ($30 EV). Betting $100 folds out an extra 40% of hands (top pair weak kicker types), winning 70% for $40 EV. Even though the hand often wins showdowns, the additional fold equity makes betting more profitable than checking.
concepts.actionable_rule: Consider betting a 'check-down' hand when a bet folds out a meaningful band of better-than-yours hands; compare bet EV (showdown wins plus added folds) against check-down EV.

concepts.title: Compare all three options: check, value bet, and bluff
concepts.summary: For a bet to be correct it must beat both checking and value betting; bet sizing changes which option is best because size shifts opponent calling ranges.
concepts.details: With 70% best hand: checking nets $70; a big $150 bet (folds 90%, called by best 10%) nets $75; a small $50 bet (called by 80%, mostly worse) nets $80. The small value bet wins because sizing harvests calls from worse hands rather than only folding out hands you already beat. Such cases (e.g. top two pair when a draw completes) are rare but real.
concepts.actionable_rule: Before betting the river, evaluate check, big bet, and small bet separately; choose the sizing that maximizes EV given how the opponent's calling range changes with bet size.

concepts.title: Occasional fairly-good-hand bluffs exploit hand-readers
concepts.summary: Against thinking opponents who assume river bets are polarized to monsters or bluffs and that you check medium hands, occasionally betting medium hands induces big laydowns of hands like two pair or AK.
concepts.details: Skilled opponents discount your value range when you bet, concluding you have a monster or an elaborate bluff. Since you rarely have either, they overweight the monster and make big folds. Use against weak-tight or thinking players prone to ridiculous folds; avoid against calling stations or boards that scream bluff.
concepts.actionable_rule: Against thinking/weak-tight opponents who put you on a polarized betting range, occasionally bet your fairly-good hands to fold out their medium-strong holdings; do not do this versus calling stations.

concepts.title: Move-in vs flat-call with a strong draw on the flop
concepts.summary: With a big draw facing a flop bet, deciding to shove or call depends on fold equity, opponent's turn-betting tendency, and stack depth, not a fixed rule.
concepts.details: Shoving EV = (fold equity * pot won) plus (called equity * net when all-in, often negative since you're an underdog when called). Calling EV depends on realizing the draw cheaply, but is hurt when the opponent barrels the turn and forces a fold getting insufficient odds. Shoving improves with more outs, higher fold equity, higher chance opponent barrels turn, lower chance opponent pays you when you hit, and stacks that aren't exorbitantly deep.
concepts.actionable_rule: With a strong draw facing a flop bet, prefer moving in when you have many outs, high fold equity, the opponent likely barrels the turn if you flat, he's unlikely to pay you when you hit, and stacks aren't very deep; otherwise flat call to realize the draw cheaply.

concepts.title: Balance draw shoves with made-hand shoves
concepts.summary: To keep all-in semi-bluffs with draws profitable, you must also occasionally shove strong made hands on draw-heavy flops.
concepts.details: If you only ever shove with draws, observant opponents fold their marginal hands and you lose fold equity and value. Mixing in big made hands on coordinated boards balances your range so the shoves remain credible and profitable.
concepts.actionable_rule: When you shove draws on coordinated flops, sometimes shove your strong made hands the same way to balance the range and protect your fold equity.

concepts.title: Multiple level thinking framework
concepts.summary: Hand reading proceeds in levels: what you have (0), what he has (1), what he thinks you have (2), what he thinks you think he has (3), and so on; you can think only one level above your opponent.
concepts.details: Level 0 is your own hand. Level 1 reads opponent actions in a vacuum. Level 2 considers what your actions tell him about your hand. Level 3 considers how he expects you to read him. Thinking a level deeper than the opponent is wasted—if he only thinks at level 0, your level 2 is meaningless because he isn't forming reads on you.
concepts.actionable_rule: Identify your opponent's maximum thinking level and operate exactly one level above it; do not over-level against opponents who don't think about what you hold.

concepts.title: Match thinking depth to stack depth and opponent skill
concepts.summary: Use shallow (level 0-1) thinking when decisions are simple—shallow stacks, nut holdings, or push/fold spots—and deeper thinking only when stacks are deep and opponents are sophisticated.
concepts.details: With small stacks relative to blinds/pot, decisions become automatic (shove/fold by hand strength or simple read). Holding the nuts as a caller is level 0. Deep stacks and better opponents demand level 2+ reasoning because bet sizing and lines carry more information and the pots are larger.
concepts.actionable_rule: Default to simple zeroth/first-level decisions when stacks are short or the spot is forced; escalate to deeper levels only when stacks are deep and the opponent is a thinking player.

concepts.title: Reading an overlarge river bet via second-level logic
concepts.summary: When a first-level thinker who should believe you're weak makes an unusually large river bet, the size itself is informative—he likely either wants a fold (big hand vs your perceived weakness) or is overbetting a bluff.
concepts.details: In the example, the line (open, c-bet, check turn) tells a level-1 opponent you're weak. If he had a marginal value hand he'd make a small/blocking bet expecting calls; a pot-sized bet when he thinks you'll fold suggests he isn't betting for thin value, pointing toward a big hand or a deliberately oversized bluff. Combine with pot odds (calling needs ~33% with 2-to-1) to decide.
concepts.actionable_rule: When a player who should read you as weak overbets the river, infer his sizing is polarized to big hands or oversized bluffs, then call only if your bust-down equity exceeds the required pot-odds percentage.

concepts.title: Levels of Thinking and Matching Opponent Depth
concepts.summary: Adjust the depth of your reasoning to the opponent's level rather than always thinking as deeply as possible. Overthinking weak players or underthinking experts both cost money.
concepts.details: Level 0/1: what do I have, what does he have, am I getting odds. Level 2: what does he think I have. Level 3: what does he think I think he has. A bigger-than-average river bet from a first-level player is usually a bluff (he can't get value or fold-outs otherwise), making a call clear. But a third-level player can exploit your level-2 read by making an extra-big bet with a strong hand, knowing you'll read it as weakness. The deepest correct thinker with superior hand reading holds an edge in deep-stack NLHE.
concepts.actionable_rule: Estimate your opponent's thinking level, then reason exactly one level above it; against a first-level player call a suspiciously large river bet as a likely bluff, but against a third-level player do not assume a big bet means weakness.

concepts.title: The Unexploitable Strategy is Defensive
concepts.summary: A perfect (unexploitable) NLHE strategy exists in theory: it respects implied odds, denies draws correct prices, and perfectly balances every action so no opponent can beat it. But it is fundamentally defensive and not maximally profitable.
concepts.details: The unexploitable strategy calls draws only when implied odds justify it, bets enough with strong hands to deny opponents profitable draws, and mixes hands across every check/call/bet/raise so no information leaks. Playing it guarantees you never lose long-term, but it does not win the maximum because it never attacks opponents' specific errors. Understand it as the baseline to fall back on under counterattack.
concepts.actionable_rule: Use balanced, implied-odds-respecting, draw-denying play as your default baseline, and revert toward it when a competent opponent starts attacking your deviations.

concepts.title: Swapping Mistakes
concepts.summary: Maximum profit comes not from perfect play but from deliberately deviating (making 'mistakes') to exploit opponents' larger mistakes, trading small theoretical losses for big gains.
concepts.details: Against a pure calling station you should purge bluffs, value bet far wider, and even check strong hands to the river then bet big, since no card can make you want to not bet and betting early gains nothing when calls are guaranteed (NL-specific; differs in limit/pot-limit). These plays are huge mistakes versus normal opponents but optimal here. Even in multiway games where a savvy short-stacked player exploits your deviations for $100, it's worth it if you're extracting $10,000 from the station. The principle: trade a little for a lot.
concepts.actionable_rule: Identify each opponent's biggest leak and deviate from balanced play to attack it, accepting that your deviation is exploitable, as long as the value you gain exceeds what a third party can take from your exposed weakness.

concepts.title: Never Bluff and Value Bet Wide vs Pure Callers
concepts.summary: Against a player who calls any bet regardless of holding, eliminate bluffing entirely and value bet a much wider range, including hands you'd normally check.
concepts.details: Bluffing has zero value when you're always called. Conversely many marginal/weak hands become +EV bets because they're ahead of the caller's random range. Optimal extraction can mean checking strong hands until the river then betting/jamming, since premature betting in NL gains nothing against a guaranteed call (this depends on it being no-limit so you can get all-in on one street).
concepts.actionable_rule: Versus a player who calls everything, stop bluffing completely and value bet (and overbet) any hand that beats a random holding, often waiting to the river to put in the big money.

concepts.title: Stay Vigilant for Counter-Exploitation
concepts.summary: Deliberate deviations leave exploitable holes; monitor opponents and shut down your deviation the moment a shrewd player starts attacking it.
concepts.details: Example: if opponents over-play raised pots out of position, you loosen up and play more pots in position against them — but a sharp player can now 3-bet you lighter knowing your opening range is weaker. The great player recognizes when his own 'mistake' has become the big mistake at the table and stops making it; the doomed 'maestro' fails to see his deviations as theoretical errors and gets systematically targeted.
concepts.actionable_rule: For every deviation you make, know exactly what weakness it exposes; watch for opponents probing that weakness and revert toward unexploitable play as soon as someone is profiting from it.

concepts.title: Distinguish Truly Loose-Aggressive from Dangerous Loose-Aggressive
concepts.summary: Some skilled players appear loose-aggressive but only gamble for small early bets while playing tightly and skillfully for big turn/river money; do not treat them as live ones.
concepts.details: Truly loose players put too much money in with weak hands at every stage and periodically make enormous big-bet errors (e.g., raising a flush draw into a made full house and stacking off). Dangerous players splash around cheaply preflop and on the flop but ensure they have the upper hand before the big money goes in, using superior hand reading to trap looser opponents. Mistaking one for the other when applying loose-game adjustments can get you fleeced.
concepts.actionable_rule: Before exploiting a 'loose' opponent, confirm their mistakes occur on big bets (turn/river), not just small early-street bets; wait to see at least one (ideally two) major errors for a large bet before adjusting.

concepts.title: Loosen Up in Position vs Entered Loose Players
concepts.summary: When a loose player has already entered the pot and you have position with deep stacks, play a much wider range than baseline, aiming to win big later in the hand.
concepts.details: Mirror the 'dangerous' style for value reasons: play many pots cheaply preflop and on the flop, then leverage post-flop skill and position to win big on the turn and river. The better your post-flop play, the wider you can open. Raise strong hands for value and occasionally weak ones for balance/isolation, raising more when the blinds are tough so you can isolate the bad player. With deep stacks (100bb+) you can flat very wide on the button behind a loose limper.
concepts.actionable_rule: When a loose player limps or raises and you have position with deep stacks, widen your calling/raising range substantially, raise to isolate when blinds are weak, and plan to win the big pots on later streets.

concepts.title: Seek Big Pots with Big Pairs, Not Big Unpaired Cards
concepts.summary: Against loose players, build big preflop pots with big pocket pairs (e.g., KK) but avoid bloating pots preflop with big unpaired hands like AK.
concepts.details: Big pairs are happy to get all-in preflop as favorites against weaker hands a loose player will commit with. Big unpaired hands like AK realize equity worse in large preflop pots and prefer to play smaller pots and outplay post-flop. The asymmetry: pairs want stacks in now; unpaired broadways want to see flops cheaply.
concepts.actionable_rule: Against loose players, push to get a big pot (often all-in) preflop with big pocket pairs, but keep the preflop pot smaller with big unpaired hands like AK and play them post-flop.

concepts.title: Value Bet Top Pair Aggressively, Bluff Less vs Loose Callers
concepts.summary: Against loose callers, value bet top pair and overpairs far more aggressively than normal and reduce bluffing frequency.
concepts.details: Loose players call with many worse hands, so top pair/overpair gain value through repeated betting. Because they call too much, bluffs lose value; when you do bluff, do it mostly on the flop with strong draws so that being called still leaves you with substantial equity (semi-bluff) rather than dead money.
concepts.actionable_rule: Against loose callers, bet top pair and overpairs for thin value on multiple streets, cut your bluff frequency, and confine most bluffs to flop semi-bluffs with strong draws.

concepts.title: Get All-In Preflop with Premium Pairs vs Loose Callers
concepts.summary: When a loose opponent will call all-in with weak hands, get the money in immediately with strong pairs like QQ/AA rather than playing deceptively.
concepts.details: Against loose-aggressive players you can move in preflop with AA because they call big raises with hands that are too weak; with QQ you want to get money in against their wider, weaker range. Against tough players, who only continue with KK+, big all-in raises give easy laydowns and forfeit value, so deception (calling, playing postflop) is better.
concepts.actionable_rule: Against loose/bad players who call too wide, move all-in preflop with QQ+ and AA to get money in vs weaker ranges; against tough players who only call with KK+, just call or make smaller raises with QQ/AA to play deceptively.

concepts.title: Don't Stack Off Deep with QQ vs a Strong 4-Bet
concepts.summary: With deep stacks against a tough player, do not move all-in over a third raise with QQ since you only get called by hands that beat you.
concepts.details: Example: $5-$10, $3000 stacks; you reraise to $100, tough opponent 4-bets to $300. Moving all-in for $2700 more gets called only by AA (maybe KK), which he holds often after the third raise. Stack depth and number of raises determine commitment.
concepts.actionable_rule: With deep stacks facing a 4-bet from a tough/range-aware player, fold or flat QQ rather than shoving, because the calling range crushes you.

concepts.title: Play AK Cautiously Preflop in Position
concepts.summary: With AK in position against a loose player, prefer calling to flopping a pair rather than committing all-in preflop.
concepts.details: AK is a non-made hand; calling lets you fold cheaply when you miss and value-bet top pair when you hit, hoping opponent flopped a weaker pair or draw. Avoids getting stacks in as a coinflip/dog scenario preflop.
concepts.actionable_rule: With AK in position vs a loose player, flat-call preflop, then bet top pair for value on the flop if you pair and fold cheaply if you miss.

concepts.title: Value Bet Top Pair vs Loose Players, Check vs Tough
concepts.summary: Top pair is a big moneymaker against loose calling stations but loses value against tough players who won't pay off three streets without beating it.
concepts.details: Against tough players, three significant bets (e.g., pot, 2/3 pot, 1/2 pot) get called only by hands that beat top pair; you usually lose. Loose players call down with weaker kickers and missed draws turned weak pairs, so multi-street value betting top pair profits.
concepts.actionable_rule: Bet top pair for value across multiple streets against loose calling opponents; against tough players, check or bet thinly since calls usually indicate a better hand.

concepts.title: Bluff Less Against Loose Players
concepts.summary: Loose players call too often, which boosts value betting but undermines bluffing, so reduce bluff frequency without abandoning it entirely.
concepts.details: Keep routine bluffs at reduced frequency to stay unreadable, but avoid big or daring bluffs since loose players don't fold enough. Never bluffing makes you easy to read even for loose players.
concepts.actionable_rule: Against loose callers, cut bluff frequency—keep small routine bluffs occasionally but avoid large/multi-street bluffs, and shift EV toward value betting.

concepts.title: Attack and Isolate Loose Players
concepts.summary: Treat loose players as primary profit sources: isolate preflop, play many pots in position, and make them your seating priority.
concepts.details: Don't play defensively against loose players (defensive advice is meant for tough opponents). Move to the seat on their left (unless they raise habitually), buy in to cover them, isolate with raises, and value bet ferociously. Verify they're genuinely loose for big bets, not just small ones, before fully adjusting.
concepts.actionable_rule: Identify the loosest weak player, take the seat to their left and cover them, isolate with preflop raises, play many pots in position, and value bet aggressively—after confirming they call big bets, not just small ones.

concepts.title: Identify Weak-Tight Players by Bet-Sizing Tells
concepts.summary: Weak-tight players fold too often to big bets, underbet mediocre hands, overbet strong hands, and rarely double-barrel bluffs.
concepts.details: Their strategy is unbalanced and transparent: small bets = moderate hands worried about being behind; huge bets = very strong hands worried about being outdrawn. They misevaluate pot odds with a fold bias, thinking in absolute dollars rather than overlays. Common in live small-stakes (e.g. Las Vegas $2-$5) games.
concepts.actionable_rule: Read weak-tight opponents' bet sizing literally: treat small bets as weak/medium hands and large bets/overbets as monsters, and assume they fold far too much to big turn/river bets.

concepts.title: Build Big Pots Early, Take Them Away Late vs Weak-Tight
concepts.summary: Against weak-tight players, build a pot with a preflop raise in position, then apply big later-street bets to exploit their tendency to fold big pots.
concepts.details: Per the Fundamental Theorem of Poker, create situations where opponents make the biggest errors—bad folds in big pots. Raise the largest amount they'll call without feeling pot-committed (they should still fold middle pair to a pot bet on the flop, top pair/draws to a turn pot bet). Don't make them feel committed relative to stacks.
concepts.actionable_rule: Against weak-tight players, raise preflop in position to build a pot (sized so they call but aren't committed), then fire large flop and turn bets to make them fold for maximum-error folds in big pots.

concepts.title: Play Wide in Late Position vs Limping Weak-Tight Players
concepts.summary: When weak-tight players limp, play very loosely on the button and one off, raising many normally-foldable hands.
concepts.details: Weak-tight players rarely see showdowns, so hand value matters less than fold equity; against terrible players up to 100% of hands may be profitable, though keep some fallback value vs players with a clue (avoid pure trash). Marginal hands like K6s/T8s become profitable raises.
concepts.actionable_rule: When weak-tight players limp, raise a very wide range from the button/cutoff to isolate and take the pot postflop, prioritizing fold equity over hand strength while keeping modest fallback value.

concepts.title: Use Generously Sized Continuation Bets vs Weak-Tight
concepts.summary: Make ~3/4 pot continuation bets against weak-tight players to maximize folds and extract information.
concepts.details: Weak-tight players fold especially too often to big bets (bigger bets = bigger mistakes) and reveal hand strength by which sizing they'll call. A bet they call only with top pair+ or strong draws tells you where you stand.
concepts.actionable_rule: C-bet about three-quarters pot against weak-tight players; their fold/call response to the larger size both wins pots and reveals their hand range for later streets.

concepts.title: Persevere with Later-Street Bluffs vs Weak-Tight Callers
concepts.summary: A flop call from a weak-tight player isn't a reason to give up; their excessive folding to big turn/river bets makes continued bluffing profitable.
concepts.details: Use hand-reading to project their range and how they'll react to various sizings. Sklansky/Miller example: bet flop/turn to fold out draws and weak pairs, then shove a big river bet far larger than prior bets to fold even two pair. They make 'monsters under the bed' laydowns—but don't routinely bluff genuine monsters.
concepts.actionable_rule: Against weak-tight players, don't auto-give-up after a flop call; fire larger turn and river bets (bigger than any prior bet) to exploit their fold-heavy tendencies, guided by hand reads.

concepts.title: Watch for Weak-Tight Tilt
concepts.summary: Weak-tight players who suffer a big beat after folding all night can go on violent mega-tilt, making uncharacteristically reckless plays.
concepts.details: Especially when a bad beat takes most but not all of their stack. They may suddenly shove weak holdings out of frustration—a profitable spot if you have a real hand and they tilt into you.
concepts.actionable_rule: After a weak-tight player takes a brutal beat, expect tilt and be ready to call/value bet their uncharacteristic reckless all-ins with strong hands.

concepts.title: Short Stacks Are Not Disadvantaged in Cash Games
concepts.summary: In cash games, a stack significantly smaller than opponents' carries structural advantages, not disadvantages.
concepts.details: The 'they risk only 1/4 to win all of yours' argument is irrelevant: $50 is $50 regardless of stack percentage. The reduced bluffing ability cuts both ways—opponents can't bluff you either. Stack depth changes the game for everyone equally.
concepts.actionable_rule: In cash games, don't avoid playing a short stack out of fear; evaluate money won/lost in absolute terms, not as a percentage of stacks.

concepts.title: Short Stacks Get Action from Loose Cross-Play
concepts.summary: Deep-stacked opponents play loosely against each other and tailor strategy to the deep bad player, so your short stack gets money in against weaker-than-average ranges.
concepts.details: Example: with $400 vs $4000 stacks, an expert calls your QQ raise with 44 because the bad deep player gives him the implied odds to play, even though 44 is a dog to your range. Both deep players play incorrectly against you while you play well against them.
concepts.actionable_rule: As a short stack at a deep table with weak players, enter pots with strong hands expecting deep opponents to call too loosely (chasing the deep fish's implied odds), getting your money in vs weaker ranges.

concepts.title: All-In Short Stacks Profit from Side-Pot Folds
concepts.summary: Once all-in, opponents continuing to bet each other can fold out hands that could have outdrawn you, helping you at no additional cost.
concepts.details: In cash games (unlike tournaments with check-down 'gentleman's agreements'), players build side pots and force folds. Every player folded out reduces your chance of being outdrawn for free—'free money' available only when all-in short.
concepts.actionable_rule: When all-in short in a multiway cash pot, expect deep opponents to keep betting and fold out live hands, increasing your equity at no extra cost—factor this into shoving with a short stack.

concepts.title: Stack depth determines how much hand strength matters
concepts.summary: The larger a percentage of your stack you commit preflop, the more raw hand strength dominates the decision, so short stacks must play tighter preflop than deep stacks.
concepts.details: When short-stacked, most money goes in preflop and decisions reduce to whether your hand has an edge. Deep stacks allow looser play because postflop skill, implied odds, and maneuverability create profit beyond raw hand strength.
concepts.actionable_rule: Scale preflop tightness to stack depth: with a short stack play premium hands only; with a deep stack you can profitably play a wider, looser range.

concepts.title: Short-stack algorithmic strategy
concepts.summary: With roughly 20bb, a simple strategy of playing only premium hands (AA-77, AK, AQ) and avoiding bluffs beats almost any no-limit game.
concepts.details: Because being all-in forces a showdown, short stacks should concentrate on premium hands and get money in with an edge. Bluffing and multi-street setups lose value when stacks are shallow. This is not optimal for experts but is robust and profitable.
concepts.actionable_rule: On a ~20bb stack, play only premium hands (AA-77, AK, AQ), get all-in when you likely have the edge, and avoid bluffing.

concepts.title: Buy in short when adjusting to a new game
concepts.summary: Buy in short when moving up in stakes or first joining a game to reduce risk and harness the intrinsic short-stack advantage while you learn.
concepts.details: New opponents play differently and better at higher stakes; buying short reduces intimidation, simplifies decisions, and minimizes mistakes from unfamiliarity. You can always add chips later but cannot remove them from the table.
concepts.actionable_rule: When moving up or joining an unfamiliar game, buy in short for the first sessions, then increase your buy-in once confident you can win deep.

concepts.title: Treat near-stack raises as all-in
concepts.summary: If a raise represents most but not all of your stack, treat it as an all-in for calculation purposes because calling commits you to the remainder.
concepts.details: After calling for most of your stack, you'll be getting overwhelming odds to call the remaining bet on a later street, so you are effectively committed. Calculate the call as if it were for your whole stack.
concepts.actionable_rule: When a raise takes most of your stack, evaluate the decision as if it were for your entire stack since you'll be committed to calling the rest.

concepts.title: Calling all-in raises relative to opponent's range and pot odds
concepts.summary: How loosely you call an all-in depends on pot odds: call looser than the raiser's range at 2-to-1, slightly tighter at 3-to-2, and significantly tighter at 6-to-5.
concepts.details: At 2-to-1 you only need ~33% equity, so you can call with hands much worse than the raiser's weakest. At 3-to-2 you need ~40% (about the raiser's worst hand, usually a notch better). At 6-to-5 you need ~45% (better than the raiser's worst hand). Raise sizes of ~3x, ~6x, ~15x BB correspond to these odds.
concepts.actionable_rule: When facing an all-in: at 2-to-1 odds call looser than the raiser's range (any pair, suited connectors); at 3-to-2 call near the raiser's worst hand; at 6-to-5 call only with hands better than the raiser's weakest.

concepts.title: Loose calls are profitable against tight ranges at good odds
concepts.summary: Getting 2-to-1, even weak hands like 54s are profitable calls against a tight raiser because you only need ~33% equity.
concepts.details: Raw EV computation: getting 2-to-1, any hand winning more than one-third of the time against the range is a call. Counterintuitively, against an 'Average' raiser at 2-to-1 you can call with any pair, any suited ace, and suited connectors down to 54s.
concepts.actionable_rule: At 2-to-1 pot odds, call all-ins with hands that have over 33% equity versus the raiser's range, even seemingly weak suited connectors and small pairs.

concepts.title: ICM overrides raw EV near pay jumps
concepts.summary: In tournaments, when prizes are near or on you, fold marginally +EV all-in calls because busting forfeits real money value disproportionately.
concepts.details: Example: with QJ winning ~40% against a loose raiser at 3-to-2, calling caps real expectation around $20 (and less if you don't always win), while folding and letting a short stack bust may yield ~$19+. Chip EV diverges from dollar EV at the bubble and final-table pay jumps.
concepts.actionable_rule: Near pay jumps or on the bubble, fold marginal +chipEV all-in calls when busting drastically reduces your prize equity; only loosen up when you are a chip leader or early in a deep tournament.

concepts.title: Tournament tightness misconception
concepts.summary: You do NOT play tighter in tournaments merely because of a short bankroll; extra tightness is justified only by proximity to pay jumps.
concepts.details: Early in large multi-day events chip values track nominal cash values, so play normally. Near chip leaders also need not tighten when calling a smaller stack's shove. Extra tightness applies specifically when calling drastically increases your chance of a small or no prize.
concepts.actionable_rule: Only tighten all-in calling ranges when near pay jumps or when a call risks a large fraction of your prize equity; otherwise play standard chip-EV strategy.

concepts.title: Bankroll considerations via Kelly Criterion
concepts.summary: A +EV all-in call can still slow bankroll growth if it risks a large percentage of your bankroll, so call more tightly when the call is a big fraction of your roll.
concepts.details: Even positive-expectation gambles reduce long-run growth rate when overbet relative to bankroll, because losing leaves you with too few chips to compound. This is the Kelly Criterion principle applied to poker.
concepts.actionable_rule: When a +EV call represents a significant percentage of your total bankroll, call somewhat tighter than pure EV charts recommend to maximize bankroll growth.

concepts.title: Sklansky-Chubukov number as a worst-case shove threshold
concepts.summary: Each hand has an S-C number: the maximum stack (relative to blinds) for which open-shoving is better than folding even if your opponent sees your cards.
concepts.details: Computed assuming the opponent knows your hand and plays perfectly (calls only as a favorite). The EV equation balances stealing the blinds most of the time against losing to the rare hands that can profitably call. Example: unsuited AK has an S-C number of $332 in a $1-$2 game — you should shove $300 rather than fold even face-up.
concepts.actionable_rule: Open-shove (rather than fold) whenever your stack is below the hand's Sklansky-Chubukov number; you cannot have negative expectation doing so versus folding.

concepts.title: S-C numbers underestimate real shoving power
concepts.summary: Because opponents don't actually see your cards and fold many profitable calls, you can profitably shove with stacks larger than the S-C number.
concepts.details: The S-C calculation assumes perfect opponent play with full information. In reality opponents fold hands that are actually favorites (e.g., folding a marginal hand to a big shove), so your real shove threshold is higher than the S-C number.
concepts.actionable_rule: Treat the S-C number as a conservative floor; against real opponents who fold too much, profitably open-shove with stacks somewhat larger than the S-C number.

concepts.title: Robust vs vulnerable hands for shoving
concepts.summary: Robust hands (e.g., small pairs) get called often but fare okay; vulnerable hands (e.g., A3o) get called rarely but are big underdogs when called — robust hands gain more from opponent folding mistakes.
concepts.details: Pocket deuces is called by 57.9% of hands but wins 46.8% when called; A3o is called by only 18% of hands but wins only 35.1% when called — both have an S-C number of $48. Because opponents fold hands that are actually favorites against deuces (like T7s), their folding errors hurt them more, making robust hands stronger real-world shoves.
concepts.actionable_rule: Prefer robust hands (small/medium pairs) over equal-S-C vulnerable hands (weak aces) for open-shoves, since opponents' overfolding gives robust hands more added value.

concepts.title: Robust hands have more move-in power than S-C numbers suggest
concepts.summary: Suited connectors and other robust hands can be moved all-in profitably with stacks larger than their Sklansky-Chubukov numbers indicate.
concepts.details: S-C numbers assume the opponent calls perfectly with all profitable hands. Robust hands like suited connectors win a decent share (e.g., 87s wins 42.2% when called) even against the calling range, and many opponents fold hands that could theoretically call. This means the true profitable move-in threshold exceeds the S-C number.
concepts.actionable_rule: With robust hands like suited connectors, move all-in even with stacks somewhat larger than their Sklansky-Chubukov number.

concepts.title: Halve the S-C number on the button
concepts.summary: Because there are two possible callers on the button instead of one, your chance of being called roughly doubles, so halve the S-C number.
concepts.details: S-C numbers were derived from a small-blind-versus-big-blind scenario with one opponent. On the button two players remain behind, roughly doubling call probability. As a rough approximation, divide the hand's S-C number by two to find the profitable button move-in threshold. This ignores double-call risk and that you have no money already invested.
concepts.actionable_rule: On the button, halve a hand's S-C number; if your stack (in big-blind-equivalent units) is below that halved value, move all-in.

concepts.title: Convert stack to small-blind units to apply S-C
concepts.summary: Express your stack in terms of a $1-$2 blind structure to compare directly against S-C numbers.
concepts.details: S-C numbers assume a $1 small blind and $2 big blind. To use them at any blind level, scale your stack proportionally (e.g., $1,300 at $100-$200 blinds equals $13 at $1-$2 blinds), then compare to the S-C number.
concepts.actionable_rule: Normalize your stack to $1-$2 blind units, then move in if that normalized stack is at or below the (position-adjusted) S-C number.

concepts.title: Divide S-C number by three to handle antes
concepts.summary: When antes are present, divide the S-C number by three to find the odds you can profitably lay with an all-in.
concepts.details: An S-C number of N means you can profitably lay odds of N-to-3. Dividing by three converts it into a maximum odds figure (e.g., S-C 22.8 lets you lay about 7.5-to-1). Antes increase the dead money in the pot, so you can profitably move in laying worse odds than you could without antes; some move-ins are profitable only because of the ante.
concepts.actionable_rule: With antes, divide the hand's S-C number by three to get the max odds you may lay, and move in whenever the all-in lays fewer odds than that figure.

concepts.title: Best move-in hands have showdown value but play poorly
concepts.summary: Weak hands with one high or medium-high card and little postflop playability are ideal all-in candidates out of position against good opponents.
concepts.details: S-C proves these moves can't be negative EV, and you have no better alternative line: limping invites a raise you can't call, and a small raise gets called and leaves you guessing. Moving in (without showing) is at least as profitable as the proven figure and often more, since opponents fold hands they'd call with if they saw your weak holding. Examples: K4o, K8o-type hands.
concepts.actionable_rule: Out of position with a weak high-card hand (one high/medium card, poor playability) and a stack at or below its S-C number, move all-in rather than limp or make a small raise.

concepts.title: Aces are powerful but vulnerable move-in hands
concepts.summary: Any ace can be moved in profitably near the button with surprisingly deep stacks, often over ten big blinds.
concepts.details: Aces are vulnerable rather than robust, which hurts their S-C value, but S-C still underestimates their move-in power. Even ace-trey has an S-C number of 48 and ace-eight offsuit 71, meaning these are easy move-ins with stacks well above ten big blinds when folded to on or near the button.
concepts.actionable_rule: When folded to on or near the button with any ace, move all-in even with stacks exceeding ten big blinds.

concepts.title: Fold a near-worthless short stack to preserve free hands in tournaments
concepts.summary: With an extremely short stack and a trash hand, folding to see free upcoming blinds can beat a marginally +EV all-in.
concepts.details: S-C may show a tiny positive EV for moving in (e.g., 10-3o, S-C 5.5), but if you'll likely be called and busted, the value of surviving to play the several free hands owed to you before the blind reaches you again exceeds that slight chip EV. This is a tournament-specific survival consideration.
concepts.actionable_rule: In a tournament with a near-worthless hand and a tiny stack, fold to preserve the free hands due before the blinds reach you, even if a move-in is marginally +EV.

concepts.title: True move-in numbers exceed S-C against realistic callers
concepts.summary: Because real opponents fold far more than the theoretically optimal calling range, you can move in profitably with stacks well above the S-C number for mediocre hands.
concepts.details: S-C assumes opponents call with the full profitable range (e.g., 72% for 10-5s, including ugly hands). Real players might call only ~30%, folding many hands you want them to fold. This roughly doubles the practical move-in threshold (10-5s true number ~20 vs S-C 10) for many mediocre hands with S-C numbers below ~20.
concepts.actionable_rule: Against opponents who fold tighter than optimal, treat the practical move-in threshold for mediocre hands as roughly double the S-C number (up to ~20).

concepts.title: Don't move in with playable hands or when deep
concepts.summary: With playable hands or larger stacks, limp or make a small raise rather than waste their postflop value by shoving.
concepts.details: Playable hands (suited connectors, JTs) and in-position situations realize value through postflop play, so moving in (though profitable) is less profitable than limping or a small raise once stacks exceed ~20-30 big blinds. Never fold these, and almost never raise more than 25% of stack (better to shove than make a large non-all-in raise). At high levels with a big stack and S-C number above ~30, the only good move-ins are offsuit aces and kings with weak kickers.
concepts.actionable_rule: With playable hands or a decently sized stack, limp or make a small raise instead of shoving; never raise more than ~25% of your stack short of going all-in.

concepts.title: Play small pairs differently from comparable high-card hands
concepts.summary: Despite similar S-C numbers, small pairs and suited high cards warrant different lines because of how they fare when called.
concepts.details: Pocket deuces (S-C 48) and QJs (S-C 49.5) have near-identical numbers, but deuces frequently lose when a small raise gets called, while QJs wins more often in that spot. This suggests shoving deuces and small-raising QJs, but against most players limping deuces is actually best by a small margin with ~20+ big blinds.
concepts.actionable_rule: With ~20+ big blinds, small-raise suited high-card hands like QJs and prefer limping small pairs like 22 over shoving; when in doubt, fall back on S-C and move in.

concepts.title: Memorize core heads-up all-in matchup odds
concepts.summary: Knowing approximate preflop all-in equities for common hand-versus-hand matchups guides raising and calling decisions in tournaments.
concepts.details: Key approximations: pair vs lower pair ~4.5-to-1; pair vs two overcards ~even (pair gains slightly when overcards are offsuit/unconnected); pair vs one over + one under ~2.5-to-1; pair vs two undercards ~5.5-to-1; pair vs overcard + matching rank ~2.5-to-1; pair vs undercard + matching rank ~9-to-1; non-pair vs two undercards ~9-to-5; non-pair vs in-between + undercard ~3-to-2; non-pair vs two in-betweens ~6-to-5; non-pair vs undercard + matching rank ~3-to-1. Numbers shift with suitedness, connectedness, shared suits, and counterfeiting (especially at low ranks).
concepts.actionable_rule: Commit these approximate heads-up all-in equities to memory and use them when deciding whether to call or shove preflop.

concepts.title: Cultivate and exploit your table image (pigeonholing)
concepts.summary: Opponents reflexively label players; let a label form, then deviate at the precise moment it will profit you.
concepts.details: Players categorize opponents quickly (tight, wild, bluffer). A natural cold run can make you seem tight; aggressive opponents may then bluff at you more (so call lighter to snap off bluffs), while others give your bets too much credit (so bluff them more). Don't overestimate image effects—most players won't drastically change, and don't bluff just because you've been quiet. Only deviate when a specific opponent is likely to change their play this hand due to something recent.
concepts.actionable_rule: Identify the label an opponent has assigned you, then exploit it specifically—call lighter versus those who'll bluff a perceived tight player, and bluff more versus those who'll fold to a perceived strong one—only when that specific player is likely to react this hand.

concepts.title: Make obvious-but-cheap errors to induce costly opponent errors
concepts.summary: Deliberately make small, visibly 'wrong' plays that mislead opponents into bigger, more profitable mistakes later.
concepts.details: Obvious errors (e.g., calling a slightly negative-EV gutshot) are often mathematically tiny mistakes, but when they pay off they brand you a 'chaser' or 'fish.' Opponents then take your calls less seriously, bet weaker hands harder against you (enabling cheap slowplays of big hands), and give you credit for unlikely hands (enabling extra river bluffs). The key is trading small losses for large future gains by befuddling opponents without giving up much.
applies_to: vs competent opponents who remember history
concepts.actionable_rule: Look for cheap, obviously-'wrong' plays that brand you as wild or loose, then cash in by slowplaying big hands and running extra bluffs that opponents will now pay off.

concepts.title: Loose-aggressive image: get out of line cheap, play straight when big
concepts.summary: Raise frequently with marginal hands on cheap streets to provoke opponents, then play orthodox value-oriented poker when the betting gets large.
concepts.details: Frequent small preflop and flop raises with weak hands are clearly wrong but inexpensive, and they unsettle tight players into 'taking a stand'—lowering standards and calling down. Because opponents assume you're equally wild with big bets, they pay off your genuine big hands across the turn and river. The style requires sophistication and is now widely known, so it must be applied selectively, not as a blanket strategy of raising all trash.
concepts.actionable_rule: Apply pressure with frequent cheap small raises on early streets, but revert to straightforward value-heavy play when the betting gets large, letting opponents pay off your strong hands; apply with discretion against observant opponents.

concepts.title: Fake thinking on automatic plays to hide thinking tells
concepts.summary: Occasionally pause to 'think' even when your action is automatic, so opponents can't read genuine deliberation as a signal.
concepts.details: If you only think during genuinely tough spots, opponents learn that hesitation = a marginal hand, leaking information especially in early streets where decoding hurts you. Mixing in fake thinking taints that signal. Don't overdo it or you slow the game and look obvious.
concepts.actionable_rule: Occasionally pause as if deliberating when your play is automatic, and take real time on genuinely big decisions, so your hesitation patterns carry no reliable information.

concepts.title: Reverse your own tells
concepts.summary: Identify your habitual behaviors and intentionally reverse them sometimes to render the information worthless.
concepts.details: Everyone gives off some tells (talking when wanting a call, showing disinterest before folding). You can't eliminate them, but if you sometimes do the same behavior with the opposite intention, opponents can't trust the read.
concepts.actionable_rule: Catalog your own mannerisms and deliberately perform them with the opposite intention part of the time so opponents cannot reliably decode them.

concepts.title: Throw off fake tells in big spots
concepts.summary: Against opponents who know standard tells, fake a tell during a single big decision to induce a mistake.
concepts.details: In no-limit one or two big decisions dominate a session, so a rare fake tell can swing a large pot without opponents catching on (unlike limit, where you'd need to fake repeatedly). E.g., act strong with the nuts against an opponent who believes 'strong means weak' to induce a call.
concepts.actionable_rule: When you have a clear read that an opponent knows a standard tell, occasionally fake that tell during a big decision to induce the call or fold you want.

concepts.title: Use tells only as a tiebreaker proportional to reliability
