concepts.summary: Treat a perceived tell as one factor; the more it would change your normal play, the more certain of it you must be.
concepts.details: Tells may be fakes, misread, or only semi-reliable. It's safe to use a tell to break a close decision, but a tell should only override your standard play when you're highly confident of its reliability.
concepts.actionable_rule: Use a read to break close decisions, but require proportionally higher confidence before letting a tell push you far from your standard line.

concepts.title: When in doubt, bet more
concepts.summary: When unsure of exact bet size, err toward the larger amount across nearly all situations.
concepts.details: A bigger bluff is more likely to get the fold; a bigger value bet rarely costs calls and may gain them; an overbet with cards to come simplifies future decisions (win now or know you're beat) and lets you balance by overbetting big hands too.
concepts.actionable_rule: When uncertain about sizing, choose the larger bet rather than the smaller one.

concepts.title: Don't give action to tight/trapping players
concepts.summary: Avoid big pots against players who only commit with the nuts or near-nuts unless you also hold a near-nut hand.
concepts.details: Nut-peddlers won't loosen up regardless of your image or how many bluffs you show; they wait to trap. Don't try to outplay them in big pots — steal small pots and only play big pots when you have an absolute monster.
concepts.actionable_rule: Against rocks who only stack off with the nuts, refuse to build big pots unless you hold a near-nut hand; freely steal small pots from them.

concepts.title: Randomize your play against good opponents
concepts.summary: Avoid making any play 100% of the time versus perceptive players; mix in the alternative ~5-10% of the time.
concepts.details: Even when one action is clearly best, always taking it makes you exploitable. Sacrificing a little EV in the current hand by occasionally switching protects the profitability of all future hands.
concepts.actionable_rule: Even with a clearly best action, take the alternative line roughly 5-10% of the time against observant opponents to stay unpredictable.

concepts.title: Bluff to stop a bluff
concepts.summary: Out of position on the river with a marginal hand, betting can be better than checking when the opponent bluffs often if checked to.
concepts.details: With a hand barely worth a check-call, checking lets a frequent bluffer bet and force you to fold profitably-priced calls (e.g., getting 3:1 while 5:1 to win). Betting first denies him the chance to bluff and captures the dead money his bluffs would otherwise win.
concepts.actionable_rule: Heads-up OOP on the river with a marginal hand against a frequent bluffer, bet small to deny him a profitable bluff rather than checking and being forced to fold.

concepts.title: Decide big-pot vs small-pot strategy on sitting down
concepts.summary: Identify where your profit comes from based on the worst players' stacks and tendencies, then tailor your game accordingly.
concepts.details: If the worst players have big stacks and play too loose, cover them and target big pots by setting up monster hands. If they're weak-tight, win many small pots with frequent small bets and avoid big pots; possibly limit your buy-in but stay scary.
concepts.actionable_rule: On sitting down, assess the worst players' stacks and mistakes; play for big pots against loose deep stacks and for small pots against weak-tight players, adjusting buy-in to match.

concepts.title: Float to see if opponent fires another barrel
concepts.summary: Call a flop or turn bet with a decent non-drawing hand intending to fold to a second barrel, exploiting the common check-bet-then-give-up pattern.
concepts.details: Because bet-flop/check-turn is so common, calling once to see if the opponent continues is profitable: if he checks, you win or value bet/induce; if he barrels, you fold. This also disguises your made hands and induces future bluffs. Don't feel obligated to reach showdown just because you called earlier.
concepts.actionable_rule: Call one bet with a mediocre hand to see whether the opponent barrels again; fold if he fires, value-bet or induce if he checks, and don't auto-call later streets just because you called earlier.

concepts.title: Disguise one pair when planning to fold to pressure
concepts.summary: Conceal that you hold one pair when you'd fold to a big bet; reveal it when you welcome a bluff.
concepts.details: One pair must be played flexibly. If you'd call a big bet because you expect a bluff, advertising one pair can induce a large bluff. If you'd fold to a big bet, disguise the hand: make it look weaker (induce only a small bluff you can call) or stronger (discourage bluffs entirely).
concepts.actionable_rule: With one pair you'd fold to big pressure, play to disguise it; with one pair you'd happily call, play it transparently to induce a big bluff.

concepts.title: Raise larger from the blinds
concepts.summary: All else equal, make preflop raises from the blinds somewhat larger than your standard open.
concepts.details: Three reasons: (1) playing OOP you value taking the pot down immediately more; (2) bigger raises cut opponents' implied odds when they call OOP-relative with weaker hands; (3) narrowing opponents' ranges is more important when you'll be out of position, which a small raise fails to do.
concepts.actionable_rule: When raising from the blinds, size up beyond your normal open to reduce opponents' implied odds and narrow their range.

concepts.title: Bets matter more than pots in deep NLHE
concepts.summary: With deep stacks, focus on winning/losing future bets rather than protecting the chips already in the pot.
concepts.details: Unlike limit where saving and winning pots dominate, in deep-stack no-limit the money left to bet dwarfs the current pot, so decisions should prioritize maximizing bets won and minimizing bets lost rather than pot protection.
concepts.actionable_rule: In deep-stack no-limit, base decisions on expected future bets won and lost, not on protecting the chips already in the pot.

concepts.title: Check-raise bluff when a bet-out bluff is unprofitable
concepts.summary: Sometimes checking then raising a bluff is profitable even when leading out as a bluff is not, because the opponent's bet narrows his range to mostly weak hands.
concepts.details: If betting gets called too often by made hands, check instead. When the opponent bets, he reveals he likely no longer holds the medium hands he'd check for showdown — so his betting range is skewed toward busted draws and air. A small check-raise then folds out those bluffs profitably and folds many marginal hands too.
applies_to: opponents who bet thin/bluff when checked to
concepts.actionable_rule: When a river bluff-bet is unprofitable but the opponent will bet a polarized range if checked to, check and make a small check-raise to fold out his weak betting range.

concepts.title: A big bet trumps prior reads
concepts.summary: When a reasonable player makes a very large turn or river bet, weight the bet itself above all prior assumptions about their range.
concepts.details: Don't dismiss a scary holding because 'he'd never play that hand' preflop — once a big bet appears, the prior info matters far less than the bet. Unlikely hands deserve serious consideration, though the feared hand won't always be there.
concepts.actionable_rule: Facing a very large turn/river bet, give heavy weight to the bet itself and seriously consider the hands it represents, even ones you'd previously ruled out.

concepts.title: Be wary of overcallers
concepts.summary: An overcall behind a sizable bet and a call usually indicates a very strong hand from a competent player.
concepts.details: To call after a bet and a call (with money behind) a thinking player needs a hand strong enough to overcome two opponents' shown interest, so on a coordinated board the overcaller almost must hold a strong made hand or top pair or better. Don't underrate overcalls just because they weren't raises.
concepts.actionable_rule: Treat a competent player's overcall behind a bet-and-call as representing a strong hand, and narrow their range accordingly before continuing.

concepts.title: Don't raise to a size you can't respond to a shove with
concepts.summary: If you wouldn't know how to react to an all-in reraise, either move in yourself or raise small enough to fold easily.
concepts.details: A medium raise that leaves you indifferent to a shove is dominated: if calling the shove is merely okay (e.g., getting 2:1 as a 2:1 dog), then shoving yourself is better because it folds out the hands you beat (like a smaller pair), while a small raise lets you fold cheaply when reraised. Avoid the awkward in-between size.
concepts.actionable_rule: If you'd be unsure how to respond to an all-in reraise, either shove now or raise small enough to fold easily — avoid an intermediate sizing.

concepts.title: When facing two opponents of unequal stacks, size raise to isolate the short stack while protecting against the big stack
concepts.summary: With one opponent much shorter than you and a deep player behind, raise an amount that still folds out the deep stack's weak hands and effectively puts the short stack all-in, rather than over-committing.
concepts.details: Example: $7,500 stack, $100-$200 blinds, button. Small blind has $15,000, big blind has $1,400. Instead of a big raise putting the big blind all-in, raise to ~$800. This folds out the deep SB's weak hands while still inducing the same all-in/call range from the short BB, saving money when the deep stack wakes up with a real hand you can't call a big reraise with.
concepts.actionable_rule: When you want to commit a short stack but a deeper stack is also in the pot, size your raise just large enough to fold out the deep stack's weak hands and effectively all-in the short stack, rather than over-committing chips you'd be forced to fold to a reraise from the deep stack.

concepts.title: If you can't handle a reraise, bet smaller or move in yourself
concepts.summary: When unsure how to respond to a potential reraise, either bet a smaller amount or move all-in so the betting can't be reopened against you.
concepts.details: Raising in no-limit reopens the betting, which is riskier than in limit. By moving in first, opponents can only call or fold, not reraise you off your equity. Applies most often preflop in tournaments but applies on every street.
concepts.actionable_rule: When facing a decision where a reraise would put you in a tough spot, either reduce your bet size or move all-in yourself to prevent the betting being reopened.

concepts.title: Raise less often than in limit because raising reopens the betting
concepts.summary: Raising in no-limit is riskier than in limit because a reraise can cost you your entire stack/equity rather than a fraction of a bet, so be more judicious with raises.
concepts.details: In limit, the cost of raising with a second-best-but-drawing hand is at most a fraction of a bet via reraise. In no-limit the punishment can be a reraise that forces you off all your pot equity or costs you expectation when you call. The downside is asymmetric and large.
concepts.actionable_rule: Raise less frequently than limit strategy suggests; only raise when the value/protection justifies the risk of being reraised off your equity.

concepts.title: Bet more when opponent thinks his hand may already be best
concepts.summary: The standard 'outs-based' bet sizing assumes the opponent knows he is drawing; if he thinks he might already be ahead, you can bet much larger and still get called.
concepts.details: Outs-based sizing protects against a drawing opponent who knows he needs to improve. When the opponent believes he may not need to improve to win (e.g., he has a made hand he thinks is good), he will call larger bets, so you should bet more for value.
concepts.actionable_rule: When your opponent likely holds a hand he believes might already be best, bet larger than the outs-protection formula indicates to maximize value.

concepts.title: Occasionally overbet with moderate hands to disguise overbets with monsters
concepts.summary: To prevent astute opponents from reading your big overbets as always meaning a monster, occasionally overbet early with moderate hands like top pair.
concepts.details: Big overbets with excellent hands extract maximum, but if you only overbet then, observant players fold their good-but-second-best hands. Occasionally overbetting moderate hands (e.g., bet $150-200 into a $100 pot instead of the normal $80) balances your range. Early overbets also have a multiplier effect: larger flop bets lead to proportionally larger turn and river bets, greatly increasing total value with big hands.
concepts.actionable_rule: Occasionally overbet the flop with moderate hands like top pair so your overbets with excellent hands are disguised and remain credible; don't do it too often.

concepts.title: Check many flops after your preflop raise is called
concepts.summary: Unlike limit, in no-limit you should often check the flop as the preflop raiser when called, including with many strong hands and weak hands alike.
concepts.details: Continuation betting every flop is a limit-style habit. In no-limit, checking back protects your checking range, sets up check-raises (including check-raise bluffs), and avoids bloating pots when you have little. Applies even against a single caller.
concepts.actionable_rule: After your preflop raise is called, check a substantial portion of flops — both weak hands and some good hands — and be willing to occasionally check-raise bluff.

concepts.title: Don't get trapped with turn top pair in multiway checked pots
concepts.summary: In a multiway limped pot that's been checked, hitting top pair on the turn is often not worth calling a bet larger than half pot unless you hold a top kicker.
concepts.details: Example: 6-handed limped pot, you hit top pair on the turn, first limper bets ~$100 into $230. Reverse implied odds dominate: if ahead you win little more, if behind you face further bets. Three ways to lose: already behind, get outdrawn, or get bluffed. With many opponents yet to act, everything must go right to win, so folding is often correct despite likely having the best hand currently.
concepts.actionable_rule: In multiway checked pots, fold turn top pair without a top kicker to a bet of more than half the pot, especially with players still to act behind you.

concepts.title: Don't call in protected pots without a very strong hand
concepts.summary: In a protected pot (many players, an all-in player, or a known loose player still in), a thinking opponent's bet is far less likely to be a bluff, so require a strong hand to call.
concepts.details: A protected pot is one where a bettor reasonably expects at least one caller. If a thinking opponent bets into such a pot anyway, give him credit for a strong hand because he isn't relying on fold equity. The polarization toward value means calls need genuine strength.
concepts.actionable_rule: When a thinking opponent bets into a protected pot (many players in, someone all-in, or a loose player still live), give the bet extra credit for value and only call with a very good hand.

concepts.title: Sometimes limp behind limpers with pocket aces (deep limping)
concepts.summary: With deep stacks and aggressive players behind who like to raise multiple limpers, occasionally limp aces to induce a raise you can reraise, trapping the stealers.
concepts.details: Unlike limit where you'd never do this, deep no-limit allows 'deep limping' with aces to balance play and trap overzealous preflop stealers. You can reraise their raise (especially good if someone calls before you act) and get more action than normal. Caveat: only do it if you can fold the overpair postflop when beaten; if not, raise to protect yourself.
concepts.actionable_rule: With deep stacks and aggressive players behind who raise multiple limpers, occasionally limp pocket aces to induce and reraise their raise — but only if you can fold the overpair postflop when clearly beaten.

concepts.title: Try a deep check-raise with the nuts in limped multiway pots
concepts.summary: After flopping a near-nut hand in a multiway limped pot, you can sometimes check, hoping someone bets and gets a caller or two before you raise.
concepts.details: Analogous to deep limping with aces: e.g., flop a small set in a multiway pot, several players check to you, you check too. This induces action behind you and can build a bigger pot or set up a profitable check-raise with a hidden monster.
concepts.actionable_rule: With the nuts or near-nuts in a multiway limped pot, occasionally check to induce a bet and a call behind you before raising, rather than betting out immediately.

concepts.title: Move in preflop with ace-king
concepts.summary: AK is a strong move-in hand because it's only a huge dog to aces (and you hold one ace, halving that chance) and plays poorly out of position postflop, especially multiway.
concepts.details: AK is favorite vs any non-pair, slight dog vs pairs through queens, moderate dog vs kings, big dog only vs aces. Holding an ace cuts opponent AA chances roughly in half. AK realizes equity poorly OOP and multiway when it misses. Example: $2-$5, $400 stacks, EP raises to $25, three callers, you have AK in BB — moving in for $395 to win $105 usually takes it down. Vs observant opponents who'd then read you for AK, balance by moving in with KK about half the time (KK preferred over AA to avoid wasting aces and to block being outdrawn by an ace).
concepts.actionable_rule: With AK facing a raise and callers when postflop play would be awkward out of position, often move all-in; against observant opponents balance by moving in with pocket kings roughly half the time.

concepts.title: Limping while planning to fold to a raise is fine in no-limit
concepts.summary: With deep stacks against bad players, you can limp a weak high-implied-odds hand intending to fold to a sizable raise — sometimes even when a raise is likely.
concepts.details: In limit this is almost never correct, but deep no-limit implied odds change the math. Example: $1-$2, you limp a hand with position vs a bad limper; a short button raises to $10 and the bad player folds — now you fold without the implied odds. Even when a raise is 60% likely, if your $2 limp averages $6 of value when you see a flop, expectation is +$0.40 (lose $2 sixty percent, win $4 forty percent). Limp-folding also creates a history that can induce aggressive players to raise your limps, letting you trap by limping a strong hand later.
concepts.actionable_rule: Limp speculative hands for high implied odds against bad deep-stacked players intending to fold to a sizable raise; weigh whether the average pot you win when you see a flop outweighs the limps you forfeit.

concepts.title: Make a small raise instead of limping in aggressive games to set the bet size
concepts.summary: In an aggressive game where limping invites a big raise, make a small raise (2-3x BB) yourself to set the price and discourage opponents from making a large raise.
concepts.details: By putting in the first bet, you control the size. Example: instead of limping in a $5-$10 game where someone might raise to $60, raise to $30 — opponents usually just call and you see the flop for $30. Downside is losing more if reraised, but reraising without a strong hand is risky for them; balance by occasionally small-raising big hands so they don't take shots.
concepts.actionable_rule: In aggressive games, when you'd otherwise limp a hand to see a cheap flop, make a small raise (2-3x BB) to set the bet size and prevent a larger raise; balance by sometimes small-raising strong hands.

concepts.title: The button is the bread-and-butter position; play a very wide range there
concepts.summary: Position is paramount in deep no-limit, so you can profitably play an extremely wide range from the button — far wider than from one off the button.
concepts.details: The deeper the stacks and weaker the opponents, the less preflop hand strength matters and the more position matters. Implied odds justify limping or calling small raises with almost any hand (any pair, suited cards, big offsuit, any ace, offsuit connectors down to 54) because any hand can flop two pair or trips against opponents who lose too much with one pair. Rule of thumb for calling raises: if the raise is only a few percent of stacks (e.g., ≤$50 with $1,000 stacks), call wide. Crucially this applies only to the actual button — not one or two off it.
concepts.actionable_rule: On the button (and only the actual button) in deep games with weak opponents, play a very wide range — limp or call small raises (≤ a few percent of stacks) with most playable hands — leveraging position and implied odds.

concepts.title: Increase opening raise size with an ante, but less than proportionally
concepts.summary: With an ante the initial pot is larger, so raise more — but increase the raise by roughly the added ante money, not by the full proportional increase, to keep the big blind's pot odds similar.
concepts.details: Example: 8-handed $100-$200, normal raise $600 (laying 2-1). Add a $25 ante (pot $500): a proportional $1,000 raise over-offers the BB only 13-8 odds, oversizing it. Since the BB is the key caller, keep his odds roughly constant by raising ~$800 (13-6, close to the original 9-4). Rule of thumb in unraised pots: add the extra dead money to your normal bet size (extra $300 in pot → add $300 to your bet). This also makes semi-bluffs more profitable.
concepts.actionable_rule: When there's extra dead money (ante), increase your opening raise by roughly the amount of the extra dead money rather than scaling it proportionally, keeping the big blind's pot odds about the same as without the ante.

concepts.title: Semi-bluff preflop with your best foldable hands, except from the blinds where you use your worst
concepts.summary: Generally turn your best otherwise-folding hands into preflop semi-bluff raises, but when defending the blinds in an unraised pot, semi-bluff with your worst hands instead.
concepts.details: Standard balancing: reraise excellent hands, call good hands, fold the rest, and occasionally reraise as a semi-bluff using the strongest hands you'd otherwise fold (best playability/equity). The exception is being in the blinds in an unraised pot, where you should semi-bluff (raise) with your worst hands — those holdings benefit most from fold equity and have the least value seeing a flop.
concepts.actionable_rule: When semi-bluff raising preflop, choose the best hands among those you'd otherwise fold — except in the blinds in an unraised pot, where you should semi-bluff with your worst hands.

concepts.title: Choose semi-bluff/balancing hands by their fold-value cost
concepts.summary: When randomizing in bluffs, prefer hands you'd fold anyway but which retain some equity, so the balancing play costs nothing in EV.
concepts.details: For reraise/aggressive balancing plays, pick a hand you'd usually fold that still has some chance to make a good hand if you get action (e.g. a marginal suited holding over total trash). Since you'd fold both anyway, you lose nothing by waiting for the better candidate to make your randomizing bluff.
concepts.actionable_rule: When selecting bluff/balancing hands among holdings you'd otherwise fold, choose the one with the most residual equity so the play costs you nothing if called.

concepts.title: In blind unraised pots, balance raises with trash not decent hands
concepts.summary: When your raises here are usually folded to or reraised, use truly terrible hands for balancing raises and check decent hands to see a free flop.
concepts.details: In a limped, multiway big-blind spot where raises rarely get flat-called, raising decent hands wastes their value (you'd profit more checking and flopping a draw/strong hand for free). Use the worst hands to bluff-raise; revert to better hands when reraises are small or opponents are more likely to just call.
concepts.actionable_rule: In a limped multiway pot from the big blind where raises are rarely called, bluff-raise with your worst hands and check decent hands to see a free flop, reverting to better hands only when opponents call more often.

concepts.title: Raise small (pot-building) or large (hand-defining), never in-between
concepts.summary: With strong hands raise either a small pot-building amount or a large hand-defining amount; avoid mid-sized raises that signal strength while still offering correct implied odds.
concepts.details: A small raise (e.g. 3x) is made with a wide range so it conceals strength and lets opponents call. A large raise denies them profitable implied odds even though it reveals strength. A middle-sized raise gives the worst of both: it telegraphs a strong hand yet still leaves opponents implied odds (e.g. ~12-to-1) to draw out. Compute the implied odds your sizing offers before choosing.
concepts.actionable_rule: Choose preflop raise sizes that are either small (disguised, pot-building) or large (denying implied odds); never pick a middling size that reveals strength while still pricing in draws.

concepts.title: Small raises (2-3x) to build pots or set up plays are fine
concepts.summary: Min-raises and small raises are legitimate tools to elevate stakes, especially with hands that play well postflop when stacks are deep.
concepts.details: Many preflop raises exist only to enlarge the postflop pot (doubling preflop pot roughly doubles postflop bets). Make these with 'brave' hands—pocket pairs, suited connectors, suited aces—that flop well. Opponents often react to a min-raise as if you'd limped, so it simply doubles the stakes. Especially valuable when your stack has grown deep relative to the table.
concepts.actionable_rule: With deep stacks and postflop-friendly hands (pairs, suited connectors, suited aces), use small/min-raises to inflate the pot when you want larger postflop bets.

concepts.title: Estimate implied odds per-opponent, not generically
concepts.summary: Different opponents offer different implied odds; calculate based on what a specific player will actually lose, not an average or ideal player.
concepts.details: Aggressive (especially turn/river) and loose-wild players give larger implied odds; weak-tight and tough players give smaller odds. When estimating your draw's implied odds, model the actual opponent's tendencies. Note that opponents who give small implied odds also give more bluffing opportunities.
concepts.actionable_rule: Adjust implied-odds estimates to the specific opponent: assume bigger payoffs vs aggressive/loose players, smaller vs weak-tight/tough players, and bluff more against those who pay off less.

concepts.title: Less obvious draws have higher implied odds
concepts.summary: Stealthy draws (backdoor flushes, small-card gutshots) pay off far more than obvious draws because opponents don't fear them.
concepts.details: A backdoor flush draw or low gutshot is unexpected, so opponents pay you off when it completes. An obvious draw—ace-high one-card draw on a monotone flop, or a big-card open-ender—alerts everyone and gets little action when it hits. Stealth increases implied odds and influences whether to continue.
concepts.actionable_rule: Value your draw's implied odds higher when it is disguised (backdoor, small-card gutshot) and lower when it is obvious to opponents (monotone/big-card draws).

concepts.title: Fold favorites OOP vs good deep-stacked players
concepts.summary: You can correctly fold a hand that's a >50% favorite when out of position against a strong deep-stacked opponent because positional disadvantage erodes its real value.
concepts.details: Being OOP deep against a good aggressive player means calling leads to getting value-bet to death and bluffed off pots on scary cards, while reraising lays too much and wins small/loses big. The positional and informational disadvantage is so large that average best-hand status alone doesn't justify continuing, especially with vulnerable hands the opponent suspects.
concepts.actionable_rule: When out of position against a strong deep-stacked player with a vulnerable, marginal made hand, be willing to fold even when you're likely ahead, since position turns the theoretical favorite into a practical underdog.

concepts.title: Check pairs to keep pot small and induce bluffs
concepts.summary: With one pair against good deep-stacked opponents, frequently check (giving free cards) to control pot size, take free cards, and induce bluffs.
concepts.details: One pair is rarely a big-pot hand, so keeping the pot small avoids playing a big pot with a marginal holding. In position, checking can be 'taking' a free card you'd have lost to a check-raise, sometimes letting you draw out on two pair. Checking weak hands is mandatory (you can't three-barrel everything), so good opponents bet your checks as bluffs—therefore check some good pairs too, planning to call and induce those bluffs.
concepts.actionable_rule: With one pair against good deep opponents, check frequently (behind on flop/turn or facing a check OOP) to control pot size and induce bluffs, planning to call down with your better pairs.

concepts.title: Prefer checking draws that make an overcard
concepts.summary: In a close semi-bluff-vs-check decision, lean toward checking draws that complete with an overcard because they carry higher implied odds.
concepts.details: Higher implied odds make semi-bluffing less attractive (you'd rather get paid when you hit). A draw that can complete while also putting an overcard on board lets an opponent make top pair or two pair simultaneously, increasing your payoff. A flush draw where completing cards are all overcards has better implied odds than one where you block/hold the relevant high card.
concepts.actionable_rule: When deciding between semi-bluffing and checking a draw, check more often if completing cards are overcards to the board, since the higher implied odds favor seeing the next card.

concepts.title: Unusually small bets read as either big hands or bluffs
concepts.summary: A bet that's unusually small for a given player tends to be a suck-in with a monster or a cheap stab as a bluff, rarely a one-pair value bet.
concepts.details: With one pair players usually check or bet a normal/larger amount. An abnormally small bet polarizes toward very strong (inducing a call) or very weak (cheap bluff). This is opponent-dependent and relative to that player's normal sizing—a player who always bets small reveals nothing by doing so.
concepts.actionable_rule: Treat an unusually small bet (relative to that player's norms) as polarized to a monster or a bluff, and discount it as a one-pair value bet when deciding how to respond.

concepts.title: Slowplay near-nut hands more readily than the nuts
concepts.summary: Slowplay very strong but non-nut hands more than the absolute nuts, because the non-nut hand benefits from loss-limiting and induced bluffs that the nuts doesn't need.
concepts.details: Slowplaying a hand just below the nuts induces bluffs, lets opponents catch up to a second-best hand, and limits losses on the rare occasion you're beaten (just call a river bet instead of stacking off). With the absolute nuts, the loss-limiting benefit reverses—now you want action and fast play to extract from second-best hands and avoid letting free cards kill your action.
concepts.actionable_rule: Slowplay strong-but-vulnerable non-nut hands to induce bluffs and limit losses, but play the absolute nuts (or top boat) fast to build the pot and protect your action.

concepts.title: Turn bets should be a smaller fraction of pot than flop bets
concepts.summary: On average size turn bets as a smaller percentage of the pot than flop bets, because with one card to come draws need much less of a price to deny.
concepts.details: Bet sizing derives from denying opponents profitable implied odds. With two cards and two betting rounds to come, the flop favors draws, so made hands must bet large to make drawing unprofitable. On the turn, only one card and one round remain, so made hands deny draws with smaller bets. Exception: if your opponent likely thinks he has the best hand, you can bet big on the turn.
concepts.actionable_rule: Make turn value bets a smaller fraction of the pot than your flop bets, unless your opponent likely believes he's ahead, in which case bet larger.

concepts.title: Semi-bluff non-nut draws more than nut draws (deep stacks)
concepts.summary: When deep, prefer semi-bluffing draws that aren't to the nuts; check nut draws more because their high implied odds and free-card value make checking better.
concepts.details: With a nut draw, checking lets you win money when you hit from hands that would fold to a bet, and (in position) lets you see a free card when opponent has a strong hand, potentially stacking him. These checking benefits are stronger with nut/high-implied-odds draws. With a non-nut or possibly-drawing-dead draw (e.g. on a paired board), implied odds are poor, so semi-bluffing to win immediately is more attractive. NOTE: this reverses with small stacks.
concepts.actionable_rule: When deep-stacked, semi-bluff more with non-nut/low-implied-odds draws to win the pot now, and check nut draws more to realize their higher implied odds—reverse this with short stacks.

concepts.title: Calibrate responses to bet size, not binary bet/no-bet
concepts.summary: Adjust your calling/folding ranges to the actual size of opponents' bets since each size offers different pot and implied odds.
concepts.details: A half-pot bet (3-to-1) and a 1.5x-pot bet (5-to-3) offer very different odds; calling the same range against both is a major leak. Don't treat raises to $40 and $60 the same, or half-pot and overbet flop bets the same. Always compute the odds offered by the specific size.
concepts.actionable_rule: Tighten or widen your continuing range in direct response to bet size—larger bets demand stronger hands or better implied odds; always price each bet rather than reacting in binary terms.

concepts.title: Size flop bets to board texture
concepts.summary: Bet smaller on dry/low-equity flops and larger on draw-heavy flops, regardless of your own holding, to match the implied odds opponents get.
concepts.details: On dry boards opponents behind have little chance to catch up (often drawing dead), so they'd need huge implied odds—bet small with everything (sets, trips, made hands, bluffs) to entice calls/mimic strength while limiting losses. On wet/draw-heavy boards many draws exist and tough opponents bet/bluff completed draws (adding outs), so bet larger with made hands and bluffs alike to deny profitable calls. Don't be rigid (e.g. 'always pot the flop'); let texture dictate size.
concepts.actionable_rule: Bet smaller on dry/low-draw flops and larger on wet/draw-heavy flops, applying the texture-based size across your whole range rather than using one fixed sizing.

concepts.title: With mediocre hands, bet enough that a raise means you're beaten
concepts.summary: Size bets with marginal hands large enough that any raise clearly indicates a better hand, sparing you tough decisions later.
concepts.details: Good play maneuvers opponents into tough spots while avoiding your own. Betting too little with a mediocre hand invites raises that could be bluffs/weaker hands or value, creating a hard guess. Risking slightly more now so that a raise reliably signals strength lets you fold cleanly. Especially relevant against aggressive 'I make reads and act on them' players who raise light when bets look weak.
concepts.actionable_rule: With a mediocre hand, bet enough (but no more) that being raised almost always means you're beaten, so you can fold to raises without a difficult decision.

concepts.title: Bet larger to make opponent's response 'pure'
concepts.summary: When a small bet might tempt a check-raise bluff you won't call, bet larger to discourage bluffing so a check-raise becomes a reliable signal of strength.
concepts.details: On a ragged board with a mediocre made hand, a small bet (e.g. ~$60 into $130) would normally suffice for protection, but it may embolden a check-raise bluff. Since you won't call a check-raise, betting larger (~$100-$120) deters bluffing; if you still get raised you can confidently fold knowing you were beaten, without giving up value.
concepts.actionable_rule: When a small bet invites a check-raise bluff you cannot profitably call, size up your bet to discourage bluffing and make the opponent's actions more 'pure'.

concepts.title: Checking the river polarizes opponent's range
concepts.summary: When you check the river, opponents tend to bet only strong value hands and bluffs, checking down medium hands, so a significant bet is polarized.
concepts.details: A significant river bet (at least ~1/3 pot, more if a check-raise is possible) usually means either a strong value hand or a total bluff. Players check medium-strength hands hoping to win a showdown, so they rarely bet a hand only marginally better than yours.
concepts.actionable_rule: After you check the river and face a significant bet, read the opponent's range as polarized between strong value and bluffs, not medium hands.

concepts.title: Many medium hands become bluff-catchers facing a river bet
concepts.summary: Facing a polarized river bet, your medium-strength hands like top pair only beat bluffs, so their exact strength among that tier barely matters.
concepts.details: Since the opponent rarely bets a slightly-worse hand (he'd check it down), top pair good kicker, top pair bad kicker, or second pair all have similar value against his bet: they beat his bluffs and lose to his value. The bigger the bet, the more hands become mere bluff-catchers; even the second nuts can be a bluff-catcher against an all-in that represents only the nuts.
concepts.actionable_rule: When facing a sizable river bet, treat top pair and similar medium hands as bluff-catchers and base your call on bluff frequency, not on your hand's exact rank within that tier.

concepts.title: Big bets mean big hands
concepts.summary: Don't make or call big river bets often with weak hands; large bets predominantly represent strong holdings.
concepts.details: Big bets are for big hands; an occasional big bluff belongs in your strategy but must remain occasional. Overestimating opponents' big bluffing frequency, or overusing big bluffs yourself, leads to large losses.
concepts.actionable_rule: Don't call large river bets with weak hands as a default, and reserve big bluffs for occasional use rather than a routine play.

concepts.title: Consider what opponents put YOU on (second-level thinking)
concepts.summary: Evaluate a bet not just on your read of the opponent but on what range the opponent thinks you have.
concepts.details: If your prior play makes you look weak (e.g. you checked behind the turn), a big river bet is more likely a bluff because most players won't value-bet big into a perceived weak range — they'd bet small to entice a call. If you've represented strength, a big bet is more credible and dangerous.
concepts.actionable_rule: Before acting, ask what your opponent thinks you hold; if you appear weak and he bets big, weight toward bluff; if you appear strong and he bets big, give it respect.

concepts.title: A raise from a hand worth a call is rarely a bluff
concepts.summary: If the opponent clearly has at least a calling hand but chooses to raise instead, it is almost never a bluff.
concepts.details: When a player has been calling along with a made hand and then min-raises or shoves over your river bet, he would simply have called with a marginal made hand; raising indicates he has a hand stronger than the one that merely calls. Example: facing a check-raise all-in over your river value bet after he flat-called the turn, fold two pair unless his range includes worse value.
concepts.actionable_rule: When an opponent who clearly holds at least a calling hand raises instead of calling, treat the raise as value and fold marginal made hands.

concepts.title: Small either/or bluffs in multiway pots on dry flops
concepts.summary: On ragged or paired flops in multiway pots, make small (~1/3 pot) bluffs when it looks like no one connected, and balance with small value bets.
concepts.details: On a dry board it's an either/or situation: opponents either hit (and call/raise any size) or missed (and fold to a small bet), so a small bet captures the same folds as a large one at lower risk. On coordinated boards, in-between hands can call small but fold large, weakening this play. Mix in small bets with good hands so observant opponents can't resteal against your small bets.
concepts.actionable_rule: In multiway pots on ragged or paired flops, bluff with a small ~1/3-pot bet when no one seems to have hit, and balance by also betting small sometimes with good hands.

concepts.title: Big bet into multiple players = good-but-not-great hand
concepts.summary: A large bet into several opponents typically signals a good but vulnerable hand like top pair, not a monster or a pure bluff.
concepts.details: A big multiway bet says 'I'm not afraid of a caller, I don't want everyone to call, and I'd be happy to win now' — consistent with top pair-type hands. Monsters prefer to check or bet small for action; bluffing big into many players is unprofitable since someone likely connected, so bluffers size down.
concepts.actionable_rule: Read a big bet into multiple players as a good-but-not-great hand (e.g. top pair), not a monster or a bluff.

concepts.title: Respect turn bets after a flop bet-and-multiple-call
concepts.summary: After the flop is bet and called in two or more spots, a significant turn bet indicates real strength because the pot is too protected to bluff profitably.
concepts.details: Firing the turn into a multiway, already-bet pot signals willingness to play a large pot against deep stacks; with mediocre hands most players check hoping to showdown. Bluffing is unlikely because too many players remain for a bluff to succeed often enough. Even top pair out of position should frequently fold to such a bet given implied future river bets.
concepts.actionable_rule: When the flop was bet and called in multiple spots, give significant turn bets credit for a strong hand and fold marginal made hands, especially out of position and deep.

concepts.title: Prefer smaller, more-often-called river value bets in tournaments
concepts.summary: In tournaments choose smaller river value bets that get called more frequently over big bets that win rarely, even at slightly lower chip EV.
concepts.details: Because chips diminish in value (a stack isn't worth proportionally to its size and survival has value), consistent smaller wins are preferred to large infrequent ones. This reverses the cash-game logic that sometimes favors huge bets with the nuts. e.g. prefer winning $1,000 80% of the time to $8,500 10% of the time.
concepts.actionable_rule: In tournaments, size river value bets smaller to maximize call frequency rather than maximizing raw chip EV with rarely-called large bets.

concepts.title: Avoid check-raising to protect/knock out players in no-limit
concepts.summary: The limit tactic of check-raising vulnerable hands to charge or eliminate opponents is rarely worth it in no-limit.
concepts.details: In limit, fixed bet sizes force you to check vulnerable hands and check-raise to apply a double bet for protection. In no-limit you can simply bet an appropriate amount, so the cost-versus-gain of going for a protective check-raise is too high.
concepts.actionable_rule: In no-limit, bet directly for protection rather than checking vulnerable hands to attempt a protective check-raise.

concepts.title: Position changes plays more in no-limit than limit
concepts.summary: Whether you act first or second more often dictates a different action in no-limit than in limit, especially with draws.
concepts.details: With a nut draw, bet when first to act to set the bet size and give a fold chance, but check behind when second to act to preserve a chance at a huge win when you hit, since you no longer control sizing and may not want a fold. In limit you'd usually bet the nut draw from either position.
concepts.actionable_rule: With a nut draw, bet when first to act to control sizing, but check behind when second to act to keep the pot smaller and maximize implied odds when you hit.

concepts.title: Check behind to induce bluffs (stronger in no-limit)
concepts.summary: Checking behind on the turn with decent hands to induce a river bluff is far more valuable in no-limit because bluffs are a larger fraction of the pot.
concepts.details: Checking behind avoids a costly turn check-raise that puts you to a tough decision, and induces bluffs from busted draws on the river. No-limit bluffs are typically at least 1/4 pot (vs 1/6-1/10 in limit), making induced bluffs worth more. Use this play with a wider range than in limit, including strong draws and made hands that would auto-bet in limit.
concepts.actionable_rule: When second to act on the turn against an aggressive opponent, check behind more often with decent hands and strong draws to avoid check-raises and induce river bluffs.

concepts.title: Limping the button can be correct in deep no-limit
concepts.summary: Unlike limit, open-limping on the button is often correct in no-limit because stealing the small blinds matters little compared to implied odds.
concepts.details: In limit, blinds are a large share of expected winnings so blind stealing is near-mandatory. In no-limit with deep stacks, blinds may be 1% of a big pot, so raising is about building pots with good hands and position, not stealing. For hands that flop many draws and play best on later streets (high implied odds), limping preserves implied odds (e.g. raising to $30 cuts $600-to-$10 down to $600-to-$30) and lets big money go in on turn/river.
concepts.actionable_rule: In deep-stacked no-limit, open-limp the button with implied-odds hands that flop draws to preserve implied odds, rather than raising primarily to steal small blinds.

concepts.title: Limp to preserve implied odds with deep stacks
concepts.summary: With deep stacks and a speculative/drawing hand, raising preflop can bloat the pot prematurely and stunt implied odds; limping keeps stacks deep so most betting happens after you make your hand.
concepts.details: If a preflop raise forces the turn betting to be prohibitively large compared to the river money remaining, you lose the ability to keep drawing and to win a big pot when you hit. You want most of the money to go in after you make your straight, not before. Once stacks are deep enough that a raise doesn't compress later-street betting, raising for positional advantage becomes correct again.
concepts.actionable_rule: With a speculative drawing hand in position and stacks deep enough that a raise would force oversized turn betting relative to remaining money, limp to preserve implied odds; only raise once stacks are deep enough that raising doesn't compress later-street betting.

concepts.title: Don't raise out of habit in unopened late position
concepts.summary: Unlike limit hold'em, raising first-in from late position is not an automatic play in no-limit; sometimes limping wins the money.
concepts.details: Blind-steal raises that are automatic in limit are not automatic in NLHE because the blind money is a small portion of total chips at stake. Raising can needlessly bloat the pot or fail to maximize value. (Note: in tournament play with short stacks and antes, blind stealing becomes far more important.)
concepts.actionable_rule: Do not raise first-in from late position automatically; evaluate whether limping captures more value given hand and stack depth, and reserve automatic steals for short-stacked/ante tournament situations.

concepts.title: Pot odds matter little in deep-stack no-limit preflop
concepts.summary: When preflop/early betting is tiny relative to stacks, the immediate pot odds are nearly irrelevant; what matters is how your hand performs across the whole hand.
concepts.details: In a $1-$2 game with $200 stacks, whether the pot is $6 or $10 is trivial compared to the $200 behind. You aren't calling to win the small current pot, you're calling for the stacks. Therefore arguments like 'I'm only a 5-to-1 dog so I should call getting 5-to-1' are absurd deep, because effective odds over the whole hand (with much betting to come) can be far worse than the current pot odds suggest. With short stacks, pot odds regain importance.
concepts.actionable_rule: When preflop/early betting is small relative to effective stacks, ignore immediate pot odds and decide based on full-hand playability; only weight pot odds heavily when stacks are short.

concepts.title: Implied odds, not pot odds, govern deep-stack draws
concepts.summary: In deep no-limit, the relevant calculation for draws is how much you can win when you hit, not just the immediate price.
concepts.details: In limit, comparing the chance of making your hand to the pot price is a useful direct calculation. In deep no-limit the big money lies in the stacks behind, so effective/implied odds dominate. A small immediate pot-odds 'teaser' is no justification for entering with a weak hand or a tough situation.
concepts.actionable_rule: Evaluate draws in deep no-limit by estimating realizable implied odds (likely win when you hit) rather than relying on immediate pot odds, and don't enter weak hands because of a small pot-odds incentive.

concepts.title: Ignore oversized stacks meant to mislead
concepts.summary: Players who buy in for very large amounts often play normally but use the big stack to fake high implied odds and to make their bets seem insignificant.
concepts.details: Outsized buy-ins (e.g., $4,000 in a $2-$5 game) are frequently a psychological ploy: they want you to call draws loosely believing you can win a huge amount when you hit, and to take their preflop/flop bets less seriously. In reality most such players are not trying to win or lose more than a normal-stacked player.
concepts.actionable_rule: Do not inflate your implied odds or discount an opponent's bets just because they have an oversized stack; treat their betting as you would a normally stacked player unless behavior proves otherwise.

concepts.title: Approximate game-theory balance is good enough
concepts.summary: A strategy reasonably close to game-theoretically optimal is essentially as good as optimal; you don't need exact frequencies to be unexploitable.
concepts.details: If GTO says bet all good hands and bluff an extra 22%, bluffing 15% or 30% (even 10%) performs nearly as well; only extreme frequencies like 2% or 80% are exploitable. Computing exact GTO at the table is impossible, so aim for the right ballpark. When you outclass opponents, focus instead on what they put you on and adjust your line/holding mix to stay unpredictable—often beating GTO results.
concepts.actionable_rule: Balance your value bets with bluffs at an approximately correct frequency (avoid near-0% or near-100%); against weaker opponents, deviate to exploit their reads while occasionally mixing the same line with different holdings.

concepts.title: Don't help opponents play correctly; impose tough decisions
concepts.summary: Size bets to deny opponents easy correct decisions—avoid bets that no worse hand calls and no better hand folds, and avoid sizes that invite the raise you don't want.
concepts.details: You profit from opponents' mistakes, so structure bets to create difficult or lose-lose spots for them. River bets that no better hand folds to and no worse hand calls are pure errors. With cards to come, avoid betting so much that a hand you want to call folds, or so little that a hand you don't want to call calls cheaply. Also avoid sizing that entices a raise around the amount you least want to face.
concepts.actionable_rule: Choose bet sizes that maximize opponents' chance of error: ensure river bets get called by worse or fold out better, avoid sizes that fold hands you want calling or price in hands you want gone, and avoid sizes that invite an awkward raise.

concepts.title: Fold modest hands when bet into with players to act behind
concepts.summary: With a hand likely best but unlikely to improve, facing a bet into a multiway pot on a coordinated board with deep stacks, folding is often correct.
concepts.details: Example: deep $5-$10 stacks, small pot, coordinated flop, SB bets and several players remain to act behind you. Raising risks too much versus your chance of being beaten and invites strong draws or being pushed off later. Calling leaves you out of position with a weak holding, lets players behind raise you out or call cheaply, and exposes you to a tough turn bet from a likely-strong bettor. The combination of small pot, deep stacks, multiple opponents, and position against you forces a fold even with a moderately strong made hand.
concepts.actionable_rule: When bet into on a coordinated board in a small multiway pot with deep stacks and players yet to act behind you, fold a modest made hand that is unlikely to improve rather than call or raise out of position (call only versus known habitual bluffers).

concepts.title: Pot-sweetener raises as an exception
concepts.summary: Small raises designed to be called by all limpers ('pot-sweeteners') are a legitimate exception to the limp-don't-raise guidance and can be made with some non-premium hands.
concepts.details: While automatic late-position raises are discouraged, raising to a size you expect every limper to call builds a bigger pot you want to contest; these can be done with some non-excellent hands to add value.
concepts.actionable_rule: When you want a bigger pot and expect all limpers to call, make a small pot-sweetener raise (including with some non-premium hands), rather than a standard isolating/stealing raise.

concepts.title: Always evaluate advice and plays against stack size
concepts.summary: Correct no-limit strategy is contingent on stack depth; what is right at 50bb may be wrong at 500bb, and advice that ignores stacks is suspect.
concepts.details: The five core NLHE skills—manipulating pot size, adjusting to stack sizes, winning the battle of mistakes, reading hands, and manipulating opponents into playing badly—must be applied contextually. Any tip that doesn't specify stack depth, or that has you repeatedly building big pots with weak hands, is questionable.
concepts.actionable_rule: Before applying any guideline, condition it on effective stack depth; reject or adjust advice that ignores stack size or that builds large pots with weak hands.

concepts.title: Poker Is a Game of Skill, Not Luck
concepts.summary: Over the long run all players receive the same proportion of good and bad cards; skill determines who wins.
concepts.details: Variance evens out across the long run. Expert players minimize losses on weak hands and maximize profits on strong hands, and judge correctly when a big hand isn't best and a small hand is best. Good players actually get drawn out on more often because they more frequently have the lead when money goes in.
concepts.actionable_rule: Make decisions based on long-run expected value rather than short-term results; do not let recent good or bad luck change correct play.

concepts.title: The Object Is to Make Money, Not to Win Pots
concepts.summary: The goal is to maximize total profit, which means saving bets as well as winning them—not winning every pot.
concepts.details: Winning $100 in one pot while losing $120 chasing four others is a net loss. Bets saved by folding marginal hands count as much as bets won. Ideal outcomes: pots you win are as large as possible, pots you lose contain only your ante.
concepts.actionable_rule: Optimize for total expected value across all pots; fold marginal and likely second-best hands rather than chasing individual pots, and value bet-sizing to maximize wins and minimize losses.

concepts.title: Release Likely Second-Best Hands
concepts.summary: A good player has the discipline to fold a hand judged to be second-best rather than calling like a weaker player.
concepts.details: Reducing losses by not making calls a weaker player would make adds directly to overall profit. Patience to wait for good situations and discipline to fold beaten hands separate winners from suckers.
concepts.actionable_rule: When your read indicates you are likely beaten and lack sufficient odds, fold rather than make a loose call.

concepts.title: Treat All Sessions as One Continuous Game
concepts.summary: Individual sessions are not separate; think in terms of long-term results, not nightly wins or losses.
concepts.details: You cannot win every session any more than an athlete wins every match. Whether winning or losing on a given night must not affect your play—you must play every hand correctly regardless of results, avoiding tilt or steaming.
concepts.actionable_rule: Play each hand by its correct strategic merits regardless of current session win/loss; never tighten or loosen due to being stuck or ahead.

concepts.title: Game Selection: Stay Only When You Are a Favorite
concepts.summary: The only criterion for playing is whether you are a favorite in the game; quit bad games and stay in good ones regardless of session result.
concepts.details: If you are a significant favorite, stay even when tired; if you are an underdog (too many better players, cheating, or your own poor play), quit whether winning or losing. Never quit a good game just to lock up a winning session, and never stay in a bad game just to get even.
concepts.actionable_rule: Continuously assess whether you have an edge in the current game; remain only while you are a clear favorite and leave when you become an underdog, ignoring your current win/loss.

concepts.title: Diagnose Why You Are Stuck
concepts.summary: When losing, examine whether the cause is luck or a correctable problem such as fatigue, distraction, tilt, or being outclassed.
concepts.details: Being stuck may be bad luck, but may indicate too many better players, cheating, or your own degraded play due to tiredness, emotional distraction, or upset from an earlier bad beat. Identifying the cause informs whether to continue.
concepts.actionable_rule: When losing, audit your conditions and the table; if your edge or focus is compromised, quit rather than continue playing impaired.

concepts.title: Core Concepts Transcend Specific Games
concepts.summary: Underlying concepts like the semi-bluff and slowplaying apply across all poker forms; mastering principles beats memorizing rules of thumb.
concepts.details: The right question is 'What do I consider before acting?' not 'What do I do?' Fixed rules (fold this, call that) won't elevate a player. Principles apply across limit, pot-limit, and no-limit (with proper adjustment), though not always to split-pot games.
concepts.actionable_rule: Base decisions on evaluating all relevant situational factors rather than rigid memorized rules, adjusting fundamental concepts to the specific game structure.

concepts.title: Poker Logic Over Tricks and Ploys
concepts.summary: Sound fundamental play, not gimmicks or table antics, wins against tough competition; mathematics is only a part of poker logic.
concepts.details: Tricks and ploys may work in weak games but fail against strong players. Mathematics helps but is far less important than understanding underlying concepts. Players relying on ploys instead of sound play never succeed against good competition.
concepts.actionable_rule: Prioritize sound conceptual and mathematical play over gimmicks; reserve exploitative ploys for weak opponents only.

concepts.title: Mathematical Expectation as the Basis of Decisions
concepts.summary: Every action has an average value (EV) equal to the probability-weighted sum of its outcomes; you should choose the play with the highest positive or least negative expectation.
concepts.details: EV = sum over outcomes of (probability * payoff). A bet is +EV when you win more on a result than the true odds warrant (e.g., getting 2-to-1 on an even-money coin flip yields +$0.50/bet). Results in any single hand are irrelevant; over the long run cumulative winnings approach the sum of expectations. Among multiple legal actions, the correct one is whichever maximizes positive EV or minimizes negative EV, even if all options lose (e.g., losing $0.75 by playing beats losing $1.00 ante by folding).
concepts.actionable_rule: For every decision, enumerate the candidate actions, compute the EV of each, and choose the action with the highest EV (most positive or least negative).

concepts.title: Taking vs Laying Odds and Bet Profitability
concepts.summary: Compare the price you are getting (or laying) to the true odds of the event; the bet is good only when the price beats the true odds.
concepts.details: You take the odds when you stand to win more than you bet, lay the odds when you stand to win less. Either can be +EV or -EV. Example: laying $50 to win $10 as a 4-to-1 favorite is -$2/bet (win 10 four times, lose 50 once); laying $30 to win $10 as the same favorite is +$2/bet. The structural edge in any wager comes purely from the gap between the price offered and the true probability.
concepts.actionable_rule: Before calling or laying odds, convert your win probability to true odds and only proceed when the pot/payout price is better than those true odds.

concepts.title: Choosing Among Profitable Plays to Maximize Value
concepts.summary: A profitable play is not always the best play; pick the line that extracts the most total value given how the remaining opponents will react.
concepts.details: Sklansky's full-house example: raising wins one bet from the lone bettor but folds out two players behind, while calling keeps both behind in for two extra bets — so calling has higher EV than raising despite raising being +EV. In a seven-card stud flush example, raising can even turn -EV because it folds a worse hand and lets only better hands (a full house) reraise. The optimal action depends on predicted opponent responses across all players still in the pot.
concepts.actionable_rule: With a strong hand, choose between calling and raising by estimating which action keeps the most worse hands in and extracts the most additional bets, not merely whether each action is profitable.

concepts.title: Hourly Rate as Share of Opponents' Mistakes
concepts.summary: Your long-run win rate equals the total value of the mistakes your opponents make against you, minus the rake, divided across the qualified players.
concepts.details: Edge comes not from holding better cards but from situations where opponents would play incorrectly if the hands were reversed. If opponents make a $2 mistake against you five times an hour, that is $10/hour of EV. Estimate your hourly rate by quantifying opponents' errors and the frequency of those errors, then subtract house rake or seat charge. Use this to decide whether a game is worth playing.
concepts.actionable_rule: Assess each game by estimating the size and frequency of opponents' mistakes minus the rake; only sit (or stay) when projected hourly rate is sufficient, and leave when good players quit or start playing well.

concepts.title: Deliberately Suboptimal Play for Bankroll Protection
concepts.summary: When on a short bankroll or against weak opponents with limited funds, reduce variance by not pressing small edges, sacrificing some EV to lock up a win.
concepts.details: It is sometimes correct to play 'incorrectly': avoid maximum raises as a small favorite, fold marginal +EV calls, and decline thin edges when you cannot absorb the variance or when the opponent could otherwise get lucky and quit big or bust you. You still capture most of the value over more hours, but with far less risk of ruin.
concepts.actionable_rule: When bankroll-constrained or up against a small-stack weak player, decline marginal edges and high-variance maximum raises to reduce variance, accepting a lower EV for a more certain win.

concepts.title: The Fundamental Theorem of Poker
concepts.summary: You gain whenever an opponent plays differently than they would with full information, and lose whenever they play the same; conversely you lose EV each time you deviate from your full-information play.
concepts.details: Poker is a game of incomplete information. If all cards were exposed there would be one mathematically correct play; deviations cost the deviator EV. So the goal is twofold: extract maximum information from betting and exposed cards to approximate the full-information correct play, while concealing your own hand to induce opponents to deviate from their full-information correct play. Applies universally heads-up and nearly always multiway.
concepts.actionable_rule: Design every action to (a) come as close as possible to the play you'd make if you saw all opponents' cards, and (b) maximize the chance opponents deviate from the play they'd make if they saw yours.

concepts.title: Make Opponents Fold When They Have Correct Pot Odds to Call
concepts.summary: When an opponent is getting pot odds good enough to correctly call with a drawing or weaker hand, you profit most by making them fold.
concepts.details: By the Fundamental Theorem, you root for the opponent to make the full-information mistake. Example: $80 pot, you bet $10 with two pair, opponent has a flush draw getting 9-to-1 while only a 5-to-1 underdog — calling is correct for him, so you want him to fold. You can induce incorrect folds by representing more strength early (e.g., pairing your board to rep a bigger hand) so a drawing opponent with proper odds folds and forfeits his correct call. Winning the pot immediately beats giving a properly-priced draw a free shot.
applies_to: early streets with cards to come
concepts.actionable_rule: When you hold the best hand but a worse hand is getting correct odds to draw, bet/represent enough strength to make that opponent fold rather than allowing a correctly-priced continuation.

concepts.title: Induce Bad Calls When Opponent Has Insufficient Odds
concepts.summary: When you want a call, slow-play strength early so the opponent makes a poorly-priced call after you have improved or so they continue without correct odds.
concepts.details: Converse of inducing folds: you root for an opponent to call when his pot odds are insufficient. Therefore it can be correct to play a strong hand weakly on an early round so the opponent commits chips with the worst of it on a later round (e.g., calling your bet after you improve when the price is wrong for him). Each insufficiently-priced call he makes is +EV for you.
concepts.actionable_rule: With a hand strong enough to want action, consider underrepresenting its strength on an early street to induce calls later when the opponent will be getting insufficient pot odds.

concepts.title: Profiting From Inferior Hands That Fold Out Better Ones
concepts.summary: Betting a worse hand can be +EV if it induces a stronger hand to fold or merely call when it should raise.
concepts.details: If you bet a hand worse than your opponent's and he only calls (instead of his full-information correct raise) you have gained; if he folds the best hand you gain tremendously. Sklansky's semi-bluff example: betting a draw on the turn to represent aces — if villain knew, he'd raise enough to deny the draw; when he only calls you get a cheap card and he made a mistake. The play's value depends on pot size and the read on the opponent's holding.
concepts.actionable_rule: Bet/represent a stronger hand than you hold to deny better hands their correct raise or to fold them out, sizing the bluff and choosing spots based on pot odds and your read of the opponent's likely holding.

concepts.title: Root for incorrect calls when ahead
concepts.summary: When you hold the best hand and an opponent who would draw out is not getting proper pot odds to call, you want him to call because his call has negative expectation for him and positive for you.
concepts.details: Even though calling gives him a chance to draw out, his play is mathematically incorrect (e.g., a 5-to-1 underdog getting only 3-to-1). Over the long run, every time an opponent makes a -EV call, you gain. Occasional bad beats don't change the underlying profit of inducing the mistake.
concepts.actionable_rule: When you hold the best hand and a drawing opponent is not getting correct odds, size your bet to induce a call rather than to fold him out.

concepts.title: Don't overbet a hand that wants a call
concepts.summary: In no-limit/pot-limit, when you have a made hand that profits from being called by a worse drawing hand, bet a size the opponent will pay, not an exorbitant amount that forces a fold.
concepts.details: Sklansky's nut-straight example: facing the choice to reraise (forcing a fold) or just call (inducing a call), he just called so the opponent with two pair would take 7-to-2 pot odds on a 10-to-1 full house draw. The goal is to give the opponent a chance to make a Fundamental Theorem mistake; raising would deny that opportunity.
concepts.actionable_rule: With a strong made hand that beats a draw, choose a bet/call size that keeps the opponent in at incorrect odds rather than a size that forces him to fold.

concepts.title: Fundamental Theorem of Poker
concepts.summary: Play as you would if you could see opponents' cards; you profit whenever opponents play differently from how they would with full information, and lose whenever they play correctly for your actual holding.
concepts.details: A 'mistake' here means deviating from the perfect-information play, not playing badly. You accomplish the first goal (minimizing your own mistakes) by accurate hand/player reading, and the second goal (inducing opponent mistakes) through deception. Any time an opponent plays correctly given what you actually hold, you have gained nothing.
concepts.actionable_rule: Aim to play each hand as if you could see opponents' cards, and use deception and accurate reading to make opponents deviate from that ideal given your actual holding.

concepts.title: Multi-way exception to the Fundamental Theorem
concepts.summary: In multi-way pots you sometimes WANT an opponent to know your hand so he plays 'correctly' in a way that drives out a third player and improves your equity.
concepts.details: Example: you hold aces (30% equity), Opponent A has two pair (50%), Opponent B has a straight draw (20%). If A raises to force out B's draw, A's equity rises but so does yours (to ~40%) at B's expense. You'd like A to know you only have aces so he raises out the draw, letting you both profit against B.
applies_to: made hand vulnerable to a draw
concepts.actionable_rule: In multi-way pots, welcome an opponent's raise that drives out a drawing hand when doing so increases your own equity, even if it reveals information.

concepts.title: Adjust starting requirements to ante size
concepts.summary: The lower the ante relative to future bets, the tighter you should play; the higher the ante, the looser you should play.
concepts.details: With no ante there's nothing to fight for, so only nut hands are worth playing; with a huge ante, pot odds justify playing almost anything. Sklansky benchmarks: <=5% of average future bets is a small ante, >=15% is large, in between is average. Four reasons to loosen as ante grows: better pot odds, ante cost of waiting, opponents play weaker hands, and tight play earns no action from observant opponents.
concepts.actionable_rule: Estimate the ante/blind size relative to average future bets; tighten your opening range when it's small and widen it when it's large.

concepts.title: Money in the pot is no longer yours
concepts.summary: Antes, blinds, or prior bets you contributed belong to the pot, not to you; base decisions only on current pot odds and total pot size.
concepts.details: It is irrelevant whether you or someone else put the money in; the total pot determines correct play. Avoid the fallacy of making bad calls to 'protect' money already invested. Dealing/anting yourself does not justify looser play.
concepts.actionable_rule: Ignore money you've already committed; decide based solely on current pot size and the odds you're being offered right now.

concepts.title: Play the blind looser due to better pot odds
concepts.summary: From the blind you can call wider because you've already posted part of the bet, giving you better immediate pot odds, not because the posted money is 'yours.'
concepts.details: Example: $5 blind, raise to $10, pot grows to $35. Others getting 3.5-to-1 must pay $10, but you pay only $5 to get 7-to-1. The improved price justifies a wider continuing range. The reasoning is present pot odds, not the sunk blind.
concepts.actionable_rule: When defending the blind, compute your discounted price (cost to you vs. total pot) and widen your continuing range accordingly.

concepts.title: Steal antes against tight players
concepts.summary: When the ante is large or opponents play too tight, raising to steal the antes is profitable even with no hand because it only needs to succeed a fraction of the time.
concepts.details: Example: risking $7 to win $10 in antes needs to work only ~41% of the time to profit; if it works ~60% it's clearly +EV. Players who fold too often relative to the ante give up this edge. As the ante rises, increase steal frequency, especially versus tight opponents.
concepts.actionable_rule: Against tight opponents and in high-ante games, raise to steal antes with any holding when fold equity makes the breakeven success rate easily achievable.

concepts.title: Don't slowplay when the ante is large
concepts.summary: With a large ante, raise immediately with strong hands instead of slowplaying, because cheap entry gives drawing opponents correct odds to draw out.
concepts.details: When opponents are getting 8-to-1 or 10-to-1 on the first round, calling with a mediocre hand is correct even against a suspected big hand. Raising wrecks those odds and forces folds. Conversely, with a low ante, slowplaying becomes profitable to suck in worse hands since the cheap-entry pot odds are not so generous.
concepts.actionable_rule: In high-ante situations, raise with strong hands to deny opponents correct drawing odds; reserve slowplaying for low-ante games where you want to induce action.

concepts.title: Don't play too loose for a small ante
concepts.summary: Playing too many hands in a small/average ante game means playing worse average holdings than disciplined opponents, so even skilled players lose to tight ones.
concepts.details: Even a world champion with kings is an underdog to a tight player's aces; loose play hands a structural edge to those with higher starting requirements. With small antes, play fewer hands, steal fewer antes, slowplay big hands, and let aggressive players gain a false sense of security before you trap them.
concepts.actionable_rule: In low-ante games, tighten starting requirements and avoid frequent stealing; let aggressive players build pots you can take with stronger average hands.

concepts.title: Abandon a steal when called or reraised by a tight player
concepts.summary: If you attempt an ante steal and a known-tight player calls or reraises, give up the bluff immediately because they have a real hand.
concepts.details: Tight players only continue with strong holdings, so their resistance reliably signals a hand far ahead of your steal range. Continuing to invest is throwing good money after bad.
concepts.actionable_rule: After a steal raise, fold to a call or reraise from a tight player rather than firing further bluffs.

concepts.title: Don't over-tighten as the best player in a low-ante game
concepts.summary: When you are clearly the best player, don't tighten so much that you fold every hand; play enough to use your skill edge on later streets.
concepts.details: There is a limit to tightening at very low antes because you need volume to outplay weaker opponents post-flop. The best player should play as many hands as is reasonable to deploy his full arsenal against weaker opposition.
concepts.actionable_rule: If you hold a clear skill edge in a low-ante game, widen slightly beyond pure tightness to create postflop spots where you can outplay weaker opponents.

concepts.title: Call cheap with implied odds when the first bet is tiny
concepts.summary: With a small ante and small initial bet, call marginal hands cheaply to see one more card, justified by implied odds, then fold on the next street if you don't improve.
concepts.details: Example: $3-$6 game with a 50-cent first bet—immediate odds don't justify the call, but implied odds do because making a hand can win a big pot. You can call 20 times without improving and still profit if one made hand gets paid to the end. Crucially, you must fold on fourth street when your hand fails to improve.
concepts.actionable_rule: When the initial bet is cheap relative to potential winnings, call marginal/drawing hands for one card on implied odds, but fold the next street if you don't improve.

concepts.title: Pot odds versus chance of winning
concepts.summary: Call when your chance of winning is better than the pot odds offered, and fold when it is worse.
concepts.details: Pot odds are the ratio of pot size to the bet you must call (e.g., $50 pot, $10 bet = 5-to-1). When all cards are out, the win probability is a judgment/hand-reading problem (gauging bluffs or worse hands). With cards to come, it becomes math: compare your draw odds to the pot odds.
concepts.actionable_rule: Convert the pot and bet into pot odds, estimate your probability of winning, and call only when your winning chance exceeds the price you're getting.

concepts.title: Compute draw odds from outs and unseen cards
concepts.summary: Calculate the odds against making a draw from the number of unseen cards and the number that complete your hand.
concepts.details: In five-card draw with 47 unseen cards, a four-flush has 9 outs (38-to-9 = 4.22-to-1) and an open-ender 8 outs (39-to-8 = 4.88-to-1). Wild cards add outs and shorten the odds (e.g., a bug makes the flush 3.8-to-1). Smaller pot odds relative to your make-odds argue for folding unless implied odds are large, as in no-limit/pot-limit.
concepts.actionable_rule: Count your outs against total unseen cards to get your draw odds, then call only when pot (or implied) odds exceed those draw odds.

concepts.title: Adjust Drawing Odds for Exposed Cards
concepts.summary: In games where opponents' cards are visible (or folded cards are known), the count of needed cards already gone changes your true odds of completing a draw.
concepts.details: With three suited cards in seven-card stud you make a flush ~18% with no other cards seen. Each exposed card you need reduces your chances; each exposed unneeded card slightly increases them by raising the proportion of needed cards among the unseen. A three-flush is strong with no relevant cards out, marginal with two out, and unplayable with four or more out. The same logic applies to low draws: an 8-low is reachable even with many cards out, but a 7-low becomes far harder.
concepts.actionable_rule: Before comparing draw odds to pot odds, subtract dead cards: count how many of your needed cards are already exposed or folded, recompute your completion probability, and fold draws that have too many of their outs gone.

concepts.title: Discount Pot Odds for Raisers Behind You
