concepts.summary: When players remain to act behind you after a bet, your apparent immediate pot odds overstate reality because likely raises force you to invest more.
concepts.details: In a $100 pot with a $20 bet you appear to get 6-to-1, but if a player behind raises and the bettor calls, you must put in $40 to win a larger pot, getting only ~4.5-to-1; a reraise drops you to ~3-to-1. Furthermore, raising between opponents signals big hands, reducing your chance of winning even when you complete your draw. This matters most in positional games like hold'em, draw, and lowball.
concepts.actionable_rule: When facing a bet with live players behind you, recalculate pot odds assuming likely raises and reraises; fold marginal calls that look profitable at face value but lose value once future-round raises are factored in.

concepts.title: Fold Strong-Looking Hands Out of Position vs Strength
concepts.summary: A hand like top pair can be a fold in early/middle position when an opponent shows strength and aggressive players remain behind.
concepts.details: Holding top pair (e.g. aces) when first position bets, you face possible raises from AK, AQ, or sets that shorten your odds, plus calls from flush and straight draws that further dilute your equity. You risk being both currently second-best and outdrawn. In late position the same hand may be playable due to better information and the deceptive value of a hidden pair.
concepts.actionable_rule: Out of position with one pair facing a bet and aggressive players behind, fold when raises and draws threaten you on both sides; in late position be more willing to continue, especially with a disguised hand.

concepts.title: Count Extra Outs to Upgrade Marginal Draws
concepts.summary: Secondary ways to improve add substantially more equity than they appear to, and can turn a fold into a call.
concepts.details: An out is any way to win. A four-flush with two pair has the flush plus a full-house out; adding an inside straight draw gives three outs. Combining a 7-to-1 (12.5%) main draw with a 20-to-1 (5%) backup yields ~17.5% total, improving you to about 4.75-to-1 — enough to call at 5-to-1 or 6-to-1 pot odds. Backdoor flush/straight draws alongside a pair can justify continuing.
concepts.actionable_rule: Sum the probabilities of all your distinct outs (convert each to a percentage, add, reconvert to odds) before comparing to pot odds, so you don't fold combo draws that are actually profitable.

concepts.title: Discount Equity When You May Be Drawing Dead or Reverse-Outed
concepts.summary: Reduce your winning odds when the card completing your draw may also give an opponent a bigger hand, or when you may already be drawing dead.
concepts.details: A four-flush vs trips is a far worse draw than vs two pair because trips often fills to a full house. In community games the same card can make your hand and a better one — a queen completing your straight may fill an opponent's boat; a king-high flush loses to the nut flush. Mathematically, if you make your hand 16% of the time but win only 70% of those, your real equity is ~11% (going from 5-to-1 to ~7.5-to-1), turning an apparent call into a fold.
concepts.actionable_rule: Estimate the chance your opponent beats you even when you hit, multiply your raw completion probability by your win-given-hit rate, and fold close draws once you account for drawing dead or being reverse-outed.

concepts.title: Use Effective Odds, Not Immediate Odds, With Multiple Cards to Come
concepts.summary: When you intend to draw across more than one betting round, compare total money you'll lose if you miss against total you'll win if you hit — not the current pot odds.
concepts.details: A flop flush draw is ~1.75-to-1 to complete over two cards, but seeing the river usually requires calling both the flop and a larger turn bet. Example: calling $10 now plus $20 later means risking $30 to win the $30 pot plus $20 you extract = 50-to-30 (~1.67-to-1), which is below the 1.75-to-1 draw odds, making it a losing call unless you'll get paid on the end. To compute: add all calls you'll make to the end (your loss if you miss), then compare to pot now plus expected future bets won excluding your own (your win if you hit).
concepts.actionable_rule: Before committing to draw to the end, sum all calls you'll make if you miss and compare to the pot plus expected future bets you'll win if you hit; only continue when these effective odds beat your odds of completing.

concepts.title: When Immediate Odds Suffice Instead of Effective Odds
concepts.summary: In certain spots you can use immediate pot odds because no further bets will be required.
concepts.details: Three cases: (1) all-in or near all-in by you or opponent means the next card is effectively free; (2) you expect the opponent to check the next street, giving you a free card; (3) a large bet jump between rounds makes it correct to call for one card only and fold if you miss. Example: in $10-$50 hold'em facing a $10 flop bet expecting $50 on the turn, the all-in effective odds are too poor, but the immediate 5-to-1 on the flop bet beats your one-card draw odds. Note that completing a draw is not the same as winning.
concepts.actionable_rule: Use immediate (not effective) pot odds when you or your opponent is all-in, when you reliably expect a check behind, or when bet sizes jump sharply — in the last case call for one card only and fold to the next bet if you miss.

concepts.title: Implied Odds for Drawing Hands
concepts.summary: Implied odds are the ratio of your total expected winnings when your card hits to the cost of calling now, allowing profitable calls even when immediate pot odds fall short.
concepts.details: Calculate implied odds as (current pot + expected future bets won) : (cost to call). A small pocket pair is roughly 8-to-1 against flopping a set but is playable at much worse immediate odds because you average significant additional profit when you hit. Estimate future winnings based on three factors: size of future bets, how hidden your hand is, and opponent ability.
concepts.actionable_rule: When immediate pot odds are insufficient for a draw, call if (pot + estimated future bets won when you hit) divided by the call amount exceeds the odds against improving; fold the draw on later streets if you miss.

concepts.title: Larger Bet Differentials Increase Implied Odds
concepts.summary: The bigger the gap between current bet size and potential future bets, the higher your implied odds, making implied odds most powerful in pot-limit and no-limit games.
concepts.details: In big-bet formats, a future bet can equal a player's entire stack, so the decision shifts from 'what is in the pot now' to 'how much can be won later.' A call with poor immediate odds (e.g., 3-to-1 on an open-ender) becomes correct if hitting lets you extract a large future bet (e.g., 7-to-1 effective with $40 more to win).
concepts.actionable_rule: In no-limit/pot-limit, weight calling decisions toward how much of the opponent's remaining stack you can win when you hit, not the current pot, and call marginal draws when the future-bet potential is large.

concepts.title: Deny Implied Odds with Oversized Bets
concepts.summary: When an opponent is drawing, bet large enough that even their implied odds don't justify a call, rather than a small bet that gives them a correct price to draw to a hand that busts you.
concepts.details: Brunson's $17,000 flop bet let Ungar profitably draw to a gutshot because Ungar's implied odds (~14.5-to-1) exceeded the odds against hitting (~10.75-to-1). The corrective play is to bet too much for the opponent to call even on implied odds, charging maximum to deny correct drawing prices.
applies_to: when opponent holds a draw to beat you
concepts.actionable_rule: When you suspect an opponent is on a draw that beats you if it hits, size your bet large enough that even generous implied odds make their call unprofitable, rather than betting small.

concepts.title: Implied Odds Adjustments: Hidden Hands and Opponent Quality
concepts.summary: Your true implied odds rise when your hand is disguised and when opponents are weak (more likely to pay you off), and fall against tough opponents who fold and against obvious draws.
concepts.details: If the cards that complete your hand are obvious, opponents won't pay off when you hit, reducing implied odds. Weak players call/raise more when you make your hand. Implied odds disappear when you or opponent is all-in, and are dangerous when you can make your hand but still finish second best.
concepts.actionable_rule: Increase your implied-odds estimate (call wider) when your hand is hidden and opponents are weak/sticky; decrease it (fold) when your draw is obvious, opponents are tough, or you risk making a second-best hand.

concepts.title: Reverse Implied Odds
concepts.summary: With a mediocre made hand that can't improve and limited certainty, your real odds are worse than pot odds because you win the minimum but lose the maximum as the betting opponent continues only with better hands.
concepts.details: You face reverse implied odds when: (1) you're unsure where you stand, (2) you have little chance to improve to beat the opponent's likely hand, (3) calling commits you to calling future bets, and (4) the opponent can back off anytime. Example: pot $50, opponent bets $20—you may be risking $60 to win $70 (close to even money) rather than getting 70-to-20, because the opponent stops betting worse hands and keeps betting better ones.
concepts.actionable_rule: When holding a non-improving marginal hand that wins the minimum and loses the maximum, treat your odds as far worse than the immediate pot offers and often fold immediately rather than committing to call down.

concepts.title: Fundamental Theorem of Poker
concepts.summary: You gain whenever opponents play differently than they would if they could see your cards, and you lose whenever they play the same way they would with full information.
concepts.details: The objective of poker is to induce mistakes. The more your play reveals your holding, the fewer mistakes opponents make and the less you profit. This principle underlies the value of deception and concealment of hand strength.
concepts.actionable_rule: Choose actions that maximize opponents' likelihood of misplaying against your actual hand; avoid lines that telegraph your holding and let opponents play correctly.

concepts.title: Cost of Predictable Play
concepts.summary: Always playing strong hands the same straightforward way gives observant opponents reliable reads that cost more long-term than the immediate value gained.
concepts.details: Berland's consistent early-position slowplay of AA/KK let Brunson deduce his hand and make a profitable hero call. Likewise a razz player who only plays A,2,3 loses to a good opponent who always knows their hand. The information leaked by perfectly consistent play exceeds the value of always playing 'correctly.'
concepts.actionable_rule: Vary how you play premium hands so opponents cannot reliably read you from your betting pattern, even at the cost of occasionally playing a hand sub-optimally on a single round.

concepts.title: Deception Scaled to Opponent Skill
concepts.summary: Use deception more against tough players and hand-readers; play straightforwardly against weak players who won't fold or won't make reads anyway.
concepts.details: Against tough players, decline the last value raise with a strong hand or add extra action with a weak hand to mislead. Against dunces, deception is wasted—just raise with the best hand and don't bluff-raise weak hands since they call regardless. Disguising your hand is especially important against 'super readers' who lock onto an early read.
concepts.actionable_rule: Against skilled opponents or hand-readers, deviate from straightforward play (slowplay, balanced raises) to deceive; against weak/calling-station opponents, play transparently—value bet/raise the best hand and skip deceptive weak-hand raises.

concepts.title: Deception Decreases as Pot Grows
concepts.summary: The larger the pot relative to future bets, the less you should disguise your hand, because neither good nor bad players will fold and protecting your equity outweighs concealment.
concepts.details: In a big pot, good players won't fold to deception and won't bluff much at your shown weakness, so deception loses value. With AA preflop after a large reraise in no-limit, you should reraise all-in and abandon disguise because current pot value exceeds potential future bets.
concepts.actionable_rule: When the pot is large relative to remaining stacks/future bets, play your strong hand straightforwardly for maximum value and abandon deception.

concepts.title: Bet-Size Ratio Governs Slowplay Timing
concepts.summary: When future bets dwarf current bets, slowplay strong hands and add early cheap deception; when early bets are large relative to later, play straightforwardly.
concepts.details: A small raise with a big hand on a cheap early round can put opponents on guard so they fold when bets get expensive—better to slowplay and collect big later bets. Conversely, large bet jumps allow cheap early deceptive bets to set up later misreads. In no-limit you can give more free cards because protecting small pots is too costly with only fair hands.
concepts.actionable_rule: When later betting rounds are much larger than the current one, slowplay monster hands on cheap streets to win big bets later; consider cheap deceptive early bets to mislead opponents for the expensive streets.

concepts.title: Fewer Opponents Means More Deception
concepts.summary: The more players in the pot, the less you gain from disguising your hand; deception is most valuable heads-up or in small multiway pots.
concepts.details: With many opponents you can't make everyone fold with a weak-hand bluff and you cost yourself too many bets by missing value raises with strong hands; you also risk being outdrawn by giving free cards. Heads-up situations reward concealment more than multiway pots.
concepts.actionable_rule: Reserve deceptive lines (slowplays, bluff-raises) for heads-up or one-to-two-opponent pots; in multiway pots play strong hands straightforwardly to extract value and protect equity.

concepts.title: Five Criteria for Using Deception
concepts.summary: Employ deception when facing good players/super-readers, when the pot and current betting round are small versus future bets, when you have only one or two opponents, or when slowplaying a monster.
concepts.details: The first two criteria (good opponents; small pot relative to future bets) are most significant; meeting about three of the five—including at least one of the first two—justifies deception. Avoid deception against bad players, many players, large pots, or large early bets. Sometimes straightforward play is itself the best deception against opponents who expect trickiness.
concepts.actionable_rule: Use deception when at least three of these hold (including good opponents or a small pot vs future bets): tough opponents/readers, small pot relative to future bets, small current bet vs future bets, one-or-two opponents, or a monster to slowplay; otherwise play straightforwardly.

concepts.title: Win Large Pots Immediately
concepts.summary: As the pot grows, your primary goal shifts from extracting value to winning the pot right away, because opponents drawing with good pot odds are correct to call and you gain only when they fold.
concepts.details: When the pot is large in a limit game, a second-best hand is rarely enough of an underdog that the offered pot odds make calling a mistake. Since the opponent's call is profitable for him over the long run, you do not gain from the call even when you win the hand. You gain only when he folds and turns down correct odds, so betting/raising to drive him out is the goal.
concepts.actionable_rule: When the pot is large, bet and raise to force opponents to fold; prioritize winning the pot now over extracting additional value.

concepts.title: Always Bet the Best Hand vs Never Bet (Infinite Odds)
concepts.summary: Even when an opponent is correctly priced to call, betting is superior to checking because checking gives him infinite odds (a free chance to outdraw you).
concepts.details: Betting $20 into $150 offers 8.5-to-1 on a 5-to-1 shot, so the opponent is correct to call—but checking offers infinite odds since he risks zero to win the whole pot. Therefore it is always better to bet the best hand than to check, both to reduce his odds and to retain a chance he folds.
concepts.actionable_rule: With the best hand and cards to come, always bet rather than check—never give a free card that amounts to offering infinite drawing odds.

concepts.title: Size Bets to Deny Correct Odds in No-Limit
concepts.summary: In no-limit/pot-limit you can choose the bet size to make a drawing opponent's call incorrect, so size up to deny proper odds.
concepts.details: With a $150 pot against a 5-to-1 underdog, betting $150 offers only 2-to-1, so the opponent calling is taking the worst of it and you welcome the call. Also account for implied odds: bet large enough that the opponent's implied odds do not make the call profitable.
concepts.actionable_rule: In no-limit, with the best hand against a draw, size your bet large enough that the opponent's pot odds (and implied odds) make calling a mistake.

concepts.title: Raise to Drive Out Opponents
concepts.summary: With a strong but vulnerable hand in a large multiway pot, raise to thin the field and increase your chance of winning, even forsaking future bets.
concepts.details: Example: three-of-a-kind in stud after heavy early betting—raise on fourth street to drive out weaker hands behind you. If everyone folds you win immediately; if it only reduces the field that is still good. The exception is a near-unbeatable hand (e.g. four-of-a-kind) which you keep concealed to collect more bets.
concepts.actionable_rule: In a large multiway pot, raise with a strong-but-beatable hand to drive opponents out; only slowplay if your hand is so strong it cannot realistically be outdrawn.

concepts.title: Compare Pot Odds to Drawing Odds to Decide Fold-vs-Call Preference
concepts.summary: Whether you'd rather an opponent fold or call depends on whether his pot odds exceed the odds against his draw.
concepts.details: Ask whether the opponent would be correct to call given what you hold. If the pot odds you offer beat the odds against his draw, you prefer him to fold. If the odds against his draw exceed the pot odds offered, you prefer the call and accept the small outdraw risk to win an extra bet.
concepts.actionable_rule: Estimate the opponent's drawing odds versus the pot odds you are offering: if he's correctly priced, bet to make him fold; if he's incorrectly priced, bet to induce the mistaken call.

concepts.title: Bet/Raise the Likely Second-Best Hand to Isolate
concepts.summary: In a large pot it can be correct to bet or raise even when you suspect you are second-best, when you're not far behind, to fold out other players and isolate.
concepts.details: Razz example: 8-low raising into a likely 6-low—raising (and a probable reraise) forces out two other players, raising your equity from ~30% to ~45% heads-up, where the dead money more than compensates for being a slight underdog. Applies in stud and hold'em too.
concepts.actionable_rule: In a big multiway pot with a hand you suspect is a slight second-best, raise to isolate to one opponent; the equity gain from thinning the field can outweigh your underdog status.

concepts.title: Delay the Raise Until the Bet Doubles
concepts.summary: In structured limit games, wait to raise on the round where the bet size doubles, making it more expensive and more likely to drive opponents out.
concepts.details: In $10-$20, raising a $10 bet to $20 early may get called by players behind, but raising a $20 bet to $40 on the next round prices them out more effectively. The improved fold equity offsets the cheap card you allowed earlier. This is for thinning the field, not a slowplay.
concepts.actionable_rule: In limit games, consider delaying your field-thinning raise until the betting round where the bet size doubles to maximize fold equity.

concepts.title: Do Not Give a Free Card with the Best Hand
concepts.summary: With the likely best hand and cards to come, bet rather than check even if you expect everyone to fold, to deny opponents a free chance to outdraw you.
concepts.details: Even against a 9-to-1 underdog getting only 6-to-1, bet: you hope for the call but accept the fold, since a fold is better than giving a free ~10% shot at beating you. Example: pair of jacks on the flop should bet so that an overcard doesn't make a better pair or enable a bluff.
concepts.actionable_rule: With a vulnerable best hand and cards to come, bet to deny a free card—do this even when you expect opponents to fold and even when they are getting incorrect odds.

concepts.title: Exceptions That Justify Checking the Best Hand
concepts.summary: Only check the probable best hand when the pot is small with large future potential, when you can set up a check-raise, or when your hand is strong enough to risk a free card.
concepts.details: Three valid reasons not to bet: (1) small pot with deception worth more in future bets (common in NL/PLO), (2) a viable check-raise, (3) a hand so strong (e.g. AA on a dry flop) that one free card is low-risk and deception adds value. Example: AA on a flop where few turn cards beat you, or two kings on an ace-high flop fearing a made pair of aces.
concepts.actionable_rule: Check the probable best hand only if the pot is small with high future value, you can profitably check-raise, or your hand is so strong a free card is nearly harmless.

concepts.title: Hand Strength Determines Free-Card Tolerance
concepts.summary: The fewer cards that can beat you, the more you can afford to check; the more cards that beat you, the more you must bet.
concepts.details: Two jacks face many overcards that beat them, so bet; two aces or two kings (on a non-ace board) fear fewer outs, so checking is more tolerable. Compare the count of dangerous cards remaining in the deck to decide whether a free card is acceptable.
concepts.actionable_rule: Count the cards that can outdraw you: bet hands threatened by many overcards/draws, and only consider checking hands threatened by very few cards.

concepts.title: Get a Free Card with a Small Raise in Position
concepts.summary: When behind with a draw, raise small on an early round so opponents check to you next round, letting you check back and see the next card free.
concepts.details: You must be guaranteed to act last on the following street for this to work, so it is used mainly in fixed-position games like hold'em. The free card can turn a fold into a winner or save a bet on a hand you'd call with anyway.
concepts.actionable_rule: With a draw and last position guaranteed next street, make a small raise now so it checks to you, then check back to take a free card.

concepts.title: Position Dictates Free-Card Dynamics
concepts.summary: The second-to-act player controls free cards; the first-to-act cannot give himself one, so first position must bet more marginal hands.
concepts.details: In position you bet when likely best and check to take a free card when likely worst. Out of position, checking offers your opponent the free card and the option to bet, so you must bet marginal hands you'd check in position—if he's worse he checks behind (you wish you'd bet) and if he's better he bets (so you couldn't get the free card anyway).
concepts.actionable_rule: Out of position, bet marginal hands rather than check (especially if not fearing a raise); in position, bet when likely best and check to take a free card when likely worst.

concepts.title: Outdraw Potential Lowers the Threshold to Bet
concepts.summary: When unsure you have the best hand, more ways to improve to beat a better hand justifies betting even if called only when behind.
concepts.details: Decision factors: chance of being best, chance the next card gives opponent the winner when he'd have folded, pot size, and your chance of outdrawing a better calling hand. Example: A7 (with two sevens) on a flop has five improving outs (three aces, two sevens) versus 88's two outs, so bet A7 more readily. With few outs you must be more sure you're already ahead—bet QQ on a low flop even though it has only two outs because it's likely best.
concepts.actionable_rule: When unsure of being best, factor in your improvement outs: the more ways you can outdraw a better hand, the more freely you should bet; with few outs, only bet when confident you're already ahead.

concepts.title: A Mistake That Costs the Pot Outweighs One That Costs a Bet
concepts.summary: When in doubt, avoid the error of giving a free card that loses the whole pot; being called by a better hand only costs one bet.
concepts.details: Checking and getting outdrawn can cost the entire (large) pot, a catastrophe, while betting into a better hand costs at most one bet. This asymmetry means erring toward betting the probable best hand—giving free cards only when the hand is so strong outdraw risk is minimal and deception sets up larger future profit.
concepts.actionable_rule: When deciding to bet or check a probable best hand, weight pot-losing mistakes far more heavily than one-bet mistakes—default to betting unless your hand is nearly impossible to outdraw.

concepts.title: Definition and Prerequisites of the Semi-Bluff
concepts.summary: A semi-bluff is a bet/raise with a hand that probably isn't best now but has a reasonable chance of outdrawing callers; it can only occur with more cards to come.
concepts.details: It combines two ways to win: opponents folding immediately and improving to the best hand if called. It can be a bet, raise, or check-raise and applies to any game with future betting rounds. It cannot occur on the final street since there are no more cards to come.
concepts.actionable_rule: Only semi-bluff when more cards are to come; classify a betting hand as a semi-bluff when it is likely behind if called but has live outs to become best.

concepts.title: Bet Marginal Hands That Would Call Anyway, Especially First to Act
concepts.summary: If your hand is worth a call when an opponent bets, it is usually better to bet it yourself, particularly out of position.
concepts.details: Betting adds the chance of winning the pot immediately on top of your showdown equity, and represents more strength than you hold. Out of position you cannot guarantee a free card, so betting is preferred over check-calling; in position you may instead take the free card.
concepts.actionable_rule: If a hand is worth a call versus a bet and you are first to act, bet it yourself rather than check-calling, provided there is little fear of a raise and some fold equity.

concepts.title: Semi-Bluff Exploits Opponents' Tendency to Only Call or Fold
concepts.summary: Semi-bluffing makes opponents play incorrectly under the Fundamental Theorem of Poker by inducing calls or folds when raising or calling would be correct.
concepts.details: When you semi-bluff you usually don't have the best hand, so the opponent's correct play would be to raise; instead they typically just call, and sometimes fold the best hand. Either error gains you value.
applies_to: all streets with cards to come
concepts.actionable_rule: Use semi-bluffs to represent strength so opponents merely call (when raising is correct) or fold (when calling is correct), profiting from their suboptimal response.

concepts.title: Scare-Card Deception in Stud-Type Games
concepts.summary: In games where opponents see your cards improve (stud, razz), an early semi-bluff makes later scare cards force folds and disguises the cards that truly help you.
concepts.details: After a semi-bluff raise, moderate-improvement cards look dangerous and induce folds (even of better hands), while the card that actually makes your hand looks harmless, inducing calls. This deception lets you win larger pots and win pots you otherwise wouldn't. It applies far less in hold'em with a shared board and not at all in draw.
concepts.actionable_rule: In stud games, semi-bluff early so that future scary board cards generate folds and your true improvement cards look harmless and get called.

concepts.title: Combined EV of Bluffing Plus Drawing Beats Either Alone
concepts.summary: A semi-bluff can be profitable even when both a pure bluff and a pure value bet would be losing, because fold equity and draw equity add together.
concepts.details: Example: $60 pot, $20 bet, ~20% fold chance, ~30% chance to win at showdown. Pure bluff at 3-to-1 with 20% folds loses. Pure value bet is wrong because you are a 7-to-3 underdog. Combined: 100 tries yield ~$1,200 from folds plus ~$800 from showdowns = $2,000, versus $1,800 by checking — a $200/100 edge. Both the immediate-win and the outdraw paths must be summed to evaluate the play.
concepts.actionable_rule: Evaluate a semi-bluff by adding fold-equity EV (foldP * pot) to called-EV (callP * (winP*(pot+bet) - loseP*bet)); bet if this exceeds the EV of checking to showdown.

concepts.title: Semi-Bluff Raise on Draws
concepts.summary: Raising with a strong draw (e.g., flush draw plus inside straight draw) is correct even with low fold equity because of combined win chances.
concepts.details: With a flush draw and inside-straight draw, even a 20% fold rate makes raising more profitable than calling because of the added immediate-win equity plus high draw equity. Sometimes a hand you think is a semi-bluff is actually the best hand.
concepts.actionable_rule: When facing a bet with a strong draw and any fold equity exists, prefer raising over calling to add immediate-win equity to your drawing equity.

concepts.title: Pot Size and Real-World Bluff Frequency
concepts.summary: In practice, semi-bluffs and bluffs become more profitable as the pot grows because most players don't tighten their calling correctly relative to pot size.
concepts.details: Bigger pots give bigger pot odds, lowering the fold frequency needed for profit. Game theory implies bluffing less into large pots versus experts, but most opponents fail to adjust calling ranges to pot size, so exploitatively you can bluff more into big pots.
applies_to: all streets with cards to come
concepts.actionable_rule: Against typical non-adjusting opponents, increase semi-bluff frequency as the pot grows since the required fold rate drops and they don't widen calls correctly.

concepts.title: Don't Semi-Bluff When Certain to Be Called
concepts.summary: If you are sure the opponent will call, the bluff component vanishes and you're just value-betting a hand that is an underdog, which is incorrect.
concepts.details: The profit of a semi-bluff comes from combining fold equity with draw equity; remove fold equity and you are pouring money in as the underdog. The only exception is stud/razz where the bet sets up scare-card folds on later streets.
concepts.actionable_rule: Do not semi-bluff a hand that is behind if the opponent is certain to call (no fold equity), except in stud/razz where it sets up later scare-card folds.

concepts.title: Semi-Bluff Less in Late Position; Take Free Cards Instead
concepts.summary: Be more inclined to semi-bluff first to act; in last position you can take a free card and avoid being check-raised by a hidden big hand.
concepts.details: In first position you can't guarantee a free card, so betting is preferred. In last position, especially after many checks, a check captures a free card and avoids a possible check-raise from a slowplayed strong hand. A flop raise can also induce a turn check, giving you a free river card option.
concepts.actionable_rule: Favor semi-bluffing from first position; in last position after checks, consider taking the free card rather than betting to avoid check-raises and preserve draw equity.

concepts.title: Use Semi-Bluff Hands to Randomize Bluffing
concepts.summary: Rather than choosing arbitrary spots to bluff, use the cards of natural semi-bluff hands to randomize bluff frequency on early streets.
concepts.details: You must bluff sometimes so opponents can't read you, but you can't form a detectable pattern. Letting semi-bluff holdings dictate when you bet provides natural, deceptive bluff frequency with the bonus of equity when called, and 'advertising' value when caught.
concepts.actionable_rule: Randomize early-street bluffs by betting your semi-bluff hands rather than picking spots arbitrarily, so your bluffing frequency stays unexploitable and carries extra equity.

concepts.title: Defending Against a Possible Semi-Bluff: Often Fold
concepts.summary: Because a semi-bluffer has multiple ways to beat you, folding is frequently best against a possible semi-bluff, especially in small pots.
concepts.details: A bettor who may be semi-bluffing can (1) actually have the best hand, (2) outdraw you, or (3) catch scare cards forcing a later fold. These combined threats mean even a hand currently favored may have poor overall equity. Example: 52% he's semi-bluffing where you're a 6-to-5 favorite, 48% he has it and you're crushed — net you win only ~29%, requiring 7-to-3 pot odds to call.
concepts.actionable_rule: Against a possible semi-bluff, fold unless the pot is large enough to justify your combined win probability across all his ways of winning; in small pots, lean toward folding even when slightly ahead.

concepts.title: Don't Call Marginal Hands Into a Possible Semi-Bluff
concepts.summary: Calling a possible semi-bluff with a marginal hand exposes you to multiple ways of losing: the opponent may already have you beat, may outdraw you, or may catch a scare card that forces you to fold.
concepts.details: When facing a bet/raise that could be a semi-bluff, calling gives the opponent up to three ways to win: a legitimate hand, drawing out, or representing a scare card on a later street to force your fold. A mediocre made hand (e.g. a low pair) is often not even a favorite against the opponent's drawing range with overcards, so a call has poor expectation.
applies_to: any street with cards to come
concepts.actionable_rule: When facing a possible semi-bluff with only a marginal made hand and little chance to improve, fold rather than call, since calling leaves you exposed to being already beat, being outdrawn, and being bluffed off by scare cards.

concepts.title: Semi-Bluff Raise as Defense Against the Semi-Bluff
concepts.summary: When you hold a hand worth a call against a suspected semi-bluff, raising is usually superior to calling because it strips the opponent of his extra ways to win.
concepts.details: A raise forces a semi-bluffing opponent to fold (winning the pot now) or call/reraise with the worst hand, removing his chances to draw out or catch scare cards. It also charges worse hands, gets value when called, and deters future semi-bluffing. Calling is the worst of the three options because it preserves the opponent's outdraw and scare-card equity.
applies_to: hands worth continuing but not slowplay-strong
concepts.actionable_rule: When facing a likely semi-bluff with a hand too good to fold but not strong enough to slowplay, raise (or reraise) rather than call to deny the opponent his extra ways of winning and to charge worse hands.

concepts.title: Reraise to Punish Ante-Stealing Raises in Late Position
concepts.summary: When a late-position opponent raises likely to steal, reraise with a decent hand rather than just call to deny him the semi-bluff's extra winning chances.
concepts.details: An ante/blind-steal raise is a form of semi-bluff: it can win immediately, win by improving, or win by catching scare cards. Flat-calling a decent hand gives the stealer two extra ways to win. Reraising forces him to fold or continue with the worst hand and discourages future steals.
applies_to: you are last or near-last to act
opponent raising from late position to steal
concepts.actionable_rule: When a late-position opponent raises in a likely steal and your hand is too good to fold, reraise rather than call to make him fold or pay with the worst hand and to deter future steals.

concepts.title: Three Criteria for Fold vs Raise Against a Semi-Bluff
concepts.summary: With a medium hand against a possible semi-bluff, decide between folding and raising by weighing bluff likelihood, your outdraw chances, and his outdraw chances.
concepts.details: Three factors govern the decision: (1) the probability the opponent is bluffing/semi-bluffing, (2) your chance to outdraw him if he has a legitimate hand, and (3) his chance to outdraw you if he's betting the worst hand. Higher bluff likelihood and higher own-outdraw equity favor raising; lower bluff likelihood and higher opponent-outdraw equity favor folding.
applies_to: facing a bet or raise that may be a semi-bluff
concepts.actionable_rule: With a medium hand against a possible semi-bluff, raise when bluff likelihood and your outdraw equity are high; fold when bluff likelihood is low and the opponent's outdraw equity against you is high.

concepts.title: Call a Possible Semi-Bluff When the Pot Is Large
concepts.summary: In a large pot, just call a possible semi-bluff rather than fold or raise, since the pot odds prevent folding and a raise won't fold him out.
concepts.details: With a big pot you cannot fold a competitive hand and surrender it to a possible bluff. Raising is pointless because the pot size means a semi-bluffer will call anyway, and if he has the best hand he may reraise. Therefore calling is the optimal middle line.
applies_to: facing a bet that may be a semi-bluff
concepts.actionable_rule: When the pot is large and you hold a competitive hand facing a possible semi-bluff, just call—don't fold (pot too big) and don't raise (he'll call anyway, or reraise with a real hand).

concepts.title: Call (Don't Raise) a Bet on the Come, Then Lead Blanks
concepts.summary: With a good-but-not-great hand against an opponent likely drawing, call rather than raise; then bet out on the next street whenever a blank falls that misses his draw.
concepts.details: If the opponent is legitimate he has you beat (wasted raise); if on a draw he calls your raise easily, defeating the raise's purpose. With two cards to come a 1/3-vs-2/3 split can still make the drawer a favorite, so you can only call. Once one card is out and a blank comes, you revert to favorite—bet to deny a free card. If the card completes the draw, check and fold unless pot odds justify chasing your own draw.
applies_to: facing a bet/raise from a likely draw
good but not great made hands
concepts.actionable_rule: Against an opponent likely on the come, call rather than raise; on the next card lead out when a blank misses his draw, but check-fold (or chase only with proper odds) when a card that completes his draw arrives.

concepts.title: The Delayed Semi-Bluff Raise
concepts.summary: Against tough, semi-bluff-aware opponents, flat-call their first bet then raise on a later blank to disguise strength and force folds even when you may already hold the best hand.
concepts.details: By calling first, you represent a possible draw; raising after both catch blanks makes the opponent fear you've improved to two pair, so he can't profitably continue with overcards or a small pair plus overcard—inducing a Fundamental-Theorem mistake. If he actually has a big pair he likely won't reraise (fearing two pair) and will check the next street, giving you a free card; an open pair you later make can fold even a strong pair.
applies_to: very tough opponents who frequently semi-bluff and know the standard raise response
you hold a modest made hand like a single pair
concepts.actionable_rule: Against tough, semi-bluff-savvy opponents, occasionally just call their first bet and then raise after a blank on the next street to disguise your hand and pressure them into folding hands that are getting correct odds.

concepts.title: Seven Reasons to Raise
concepts.summary: Raising serves seven distinct purposes: value, driving out opponents with the best hand, bluff/semi-bluff, free card, information, driving out worse hands when second best, and driving out better hands when a draw bets.
concepts.details: Every raise should be made to avoid your own Fundamental-Theorem mistake and induce opponents' mistakes. The seven reasons: (1) get more money in with the best hand, (2) drive out opponents when you have the best hand, (3) bluff or semi-bluff, (4) get a free card, (5) gain information, (6) drive out worse hands when you may be second best, (7) drive out better hands when a come hand bets.
applies_to: decision to raise vs call vs fold
concepts.actionable_rule: Before raising, identify which of the seven purposes it serves; if a raise advances none of them (value, fold-equity, bluff, free card, information, protection, or driving out better hands), do not raise.

concepts.title: With Big Hands, Sometimes Decline an Early Raise
concepts.summary: The better your hand on an early street, the more you may prefer not to raise, letting opponents make the mistake of calling a single bet they shouldn't.
concepts.details: If opponents would call a single bet but fold to a raise, and they lack the pot odds to call had they known your hand, decline the raise so they keep making the calling mistake. But if they're getting correct odds to call a single bet (the usual case), raise anyway—even if they still have odds to call the raise—because you profit long-term and may induce folds.
concepts.actionable_rule: On early streets with a big hand, skip the raise when opponents would only call a single bet they shouldn't be calling; but raise when they already have correct odds to call, to build the pot you'll usually win.

concepts.title: Raise More for Value as the Pot Grows
concepts.summary: As the pot gets larger, disguising big hands matters less and getting more money in matters more, so raise with the best hand even if it reveals strength.
concepts.details: In large pots opponents will usually stay to see another card regardless of whether you raise, because they already have the odds. So the deception value of slowplaying drops while the value of extracting bets rises. Raise to build the big pot you expect to win, whether you want folds or calls.
applies_to: you hold the likely best hand
any street with cards to come
concepts.actionable_rule: In a large pot, raise with what you think is the best hand to maximize money in the pot, even when raising gives your hand away, since opponents will stay anyway.

concepts.title: Go for the Overcall Instead of Raising
concepts.summary: When all cards are out and your hand clearly beats players behind you but isn't clearly better than the bettor, just call to extract overcalls and avoid a costly reraise.
concepts.details: Raising risks the bettor reraising (costing you two or three bets) and folding out the players behind you who would have called a single bet. Calling lets those behind players overcall for extra bets while avoiding reraise risk—often gaining as much as a raise would with zero downside. Crucially, only go for the overcall if you are sure you have the players behind you beat; if one might hold a better hand that would fold to a raise, you must raise to protect against losing the pot.
applies_to: you are between a bettor and one or more callers
your hand beats those behind but not clearly the bettor
concepts.actionable_rule: On the river in a multiway pot, when your hand clearly beats the players left to act but not clearly the bettor, just call to collect overcalls and dodge a reraise—unless someone behind could hold a better hand that would fold to a raise, in which case raise.

concepts.title: Raising to Cut Down Opponents' Pot Odds
concepts.summary: Raising forces opponents behind you to invest more for the same pot, reducing their effective pot odds and turning a correct call into an incorrect one.
concepts.details: If a $10 bet into a $100 pot gives the next player 12-to-1, raising to $20 reduces it to ~6.5-to-1. When their drawing odds are 9-to-1, you convert a +EV call into a -EV one. Per the Fundamental Theorem of Poker, you profit whether they fold correctly or call incorrectly. In no-limit you control the exact odds offered via bet size.
applies_to: facing a bet from in front with players left to act
concepts.actionable_rule: When a worse hand or draw behind you is getting odds to continue, raise an amount that drops their pot odds below their drawing odds, making either their call or fold a mistake.

concepts.title: Just Call to Induce a Mistake When a Raise Folds Them Out
concepts.summary: When you hold the best hand and a raise would simply fold out an opponent who would call incorrectly, flat call to let them make the -EV overcall.
concepts.details: You want to give opponents maximum opportunity to err. If raising drives out a player who would overcall with insufficient odds (a mistake you profit from), and your hand is way ahead, just calling captures more EV than the raise. You cannot judge a play by results — a correct play that gets outdrawn is still correct.
concepts.actionable_rule: With a dominant hand, just call rather than raise when raising would fold out an opponent who, given the current odds, would call incorrectly and pay you off.

concepts.title: Raise the Best Hand Only to Cut Odds or Induce Bad Calls
concepts.summary: Raising with the best hand to 'drive out' is justified only when opponents currently get good odds to overcall or when they will incorrectly call a double bet.
concepts.details: Raising to drive people out is really about cutting their odds. If they were already getting bad odds and would fold to a single bet, raising gains nothing extra; if they'll call a double bet they shouldn't, you profit most. Sometimes after raising you actually root for a call.
concepts.actionable_rule: Raise the best hand to drive people out only when opponents are getting good enough odds to overcall, or when you expect them to call a double bet that they shouldn't even call as a single bet.

concepts.title: Semi-Bluff Raise
concepts.summary: Raise with a hand that can improve while cards remain, hoping to win immediately but retaining outs to win when called.
concepts.details: Unlike a pure bluff, the semi-bluff raise always has more cards to come and equity to outdraw the opponent. It can win the pot outright, gain information (a call/reraise signals real strength), and may earn a free card next street if the opponent checks to you out of fear.
concepts.actionable_rule: With a hand that has fold equity plus outs and cards still to come, prefer a semi-bluff raise over calling to win now, gain info, and keep your draw equity.

concepts.title: Semi-Bluff Raise Is +EV Even When a Call Is -EV
concepts.summary: Adding fold equity to a draw can flip an unprofitable call into a profitable raise.
concepts.details: With a 4-to-1 flush draw facing $20 into $40 (3-to-1), calling is -EV (~ -$4/hand). But if the opponent folds ~25% to a raise, the raise becomes +EV (~ +$3/hand). The threshold here is folding more than 4 in 19 times. Fold equity plus draw equity combine to justify the raise.
applies_to: draws facing a bet that gives insufficient pot odds
concepts.actionable_rule: When you have a draw and a call is -EV, semi-bluff raise instead if the opponent will fold often enough (e.g., >~4 in 19) to make the combined fold equity plus draw equity profitable.

concepts.title: Raise for a Free Card Only in Last Position and When Cheaper
concepts.summary: Raising to set up a free card requires being last to act and a raise cost lower than the next street's bet.
concepts.details: You must be guaranteed last position; otherwise checking shows weakness and a better hand bets, denying the free card. The 'free' card costs the price of your raise, so only worthwhile when that raise is cheaper than calling next street (e.g., raise $10 on the flop to avoid a $20 turn call in $10-$20 limit).
concepts.actionable_rule: Raise to obtain a free card only when you are certain to act last next round and the raise costs less than the bet you'd otherwise have to call on the next street.

concepts.title: Raising to Gain Information (Use Sparingly)
concepts.summary: An early heads-up raise can reveal opponent strength and save multiple later bets, but only against honest opponents.
concepts.details: A call suggests a good hand, a reraise a very good hand, a fold confirms weakness and may fold marginal hands. Only valid heads-up in early rounds against opponents whose responses reflect their holdings — never against players capable of a semi-bluff reraise. Risking one bet can save several future bets (especially after the bet size doubles).
concepts.actionable_rule: Raise primarily for other reasons and treat information as a bonus; only raise purely for information heads-up in early rounds against opponents who play face-up and won't semi-bluff reraise.

concepts.title: Raise to Drive Out Worse Hands When You May Be Second Best
concepts.summary: With a possible second-best hand, raising to eliminate weaker drawing hands can increase your overall equity.
concepts.details: Example: bettor 50%, you 30%, two draws 10% each. Folding the two draws shifts the field so the bettor is 60% and you rise to 40%. Driving out hands that could outdraw both of you improves your share even if you can't beat the leader's range entirely.
applies_to: middle-strength made hand vs leader and draws
concepts.actionable_rule: With a likely second-best hand in a multiway pot, raise to fold out the weaker drawing hands, improving your equity share against the leading hand.

concepts.title: Raise to Drive Out Better Hands When a Draw Bets
concepts.summary: When a come hand bets and better made hands sit behind, raise to fold those better hands and isolate the draw as a favorite.
concepts.details: Raising turns the draw's bet into a mistake (it needed multiple callers for proper odds) and induces better pairs behind to fold — also a mistake by them. If you succeed and the draw misses, you win. But if the better hands will call, do not raise — in fact don't even call; raise or fold.
applies_to: better made hands left to act
concepts.actionable_rule: When a draw bets and better made hands are behind you, raise to fold out the better hands and isolate the draw as a favorite — but if those better hands won't fold, fold rather than call.

concepts.title: Raise or Fold — Calling Is the Worst Option
concepts.summary: In many spots the only correct choices are to raise or fold, with calling being clearly -EV.
concepts.details: When your hand needs fold equity to be playable (e.g., two small pair in draw needing to fold out medium pairs, or a marginal made hand vs a draw with better hands behind), a call leaves too many ways to lose. If you can't raise effectively or it won't fold the dangerous hands, fold; never just call. 'A caller in poker is a loser in poker.'
applies_to: marginal made hands needing fold equity
when raising won't accomplish its goal
concepts.actionable_rule: In spots where your hand only plays well by folding opponents out, choose raise or fold — if raising won't drive out the hands that beat you, fold rather than call.

concepts.title: Raise Against a Possible Semi-Bluff When Too Good to Fold
concepts.summary: Against a likely semi-bluffer with a hand too strong to fold, raising beats calling for control, equity protection, and fold equity.
concepts.details: Raising can win the pot now, fold out the semi-bluff, deny a cheap outdraw card, gain information, set up a free card next street, and disguise your hand so scare cards earn you bets. It is so superior to calling that if you can't raise you're usually better off folding (barring the few exceptions noted previously).
concepts.actionable_rule: When facing a likely semi-bluff with a hand too good to fold, raise rather than call to seize control, deny equity, gain info, and enable a free card; if you can't raise, generally fold.

concepts.title: Check-Raising vs Slowplaying Distinction
concepts.summary: Check-raising checks intending to raise the same round to drive opponents out, while slowplaying conceals strength to keep opponents in for later bets.
concepts.details: Check-raising can win the pot immediately or thin the field, so it can be used with merely good hands. Slowplaying gives a free or cheap card and requires a much stronger hand because you want opponents to stay in and develop second-best hands.
concepts.actionable_rule: Use a check-raise with good-but-not-great hands to thin the field; reserve slowplaying for very strong hands where you want to keep opponents in.

concepts.title: Necessary Conditions to Check-Raise for Value
concepts.summary: Only check-raise for value when you likely hold the best hand (not strong enough to slowplay) AND you are nearly certain a player behind you will bet.
concepts.details: If you check and no one bets, you make a double mistake: you give a free card to hands that would have folded to a bet, and you lose value from hands that would have called. Confirm a likely bettor exists before checking.
concepts.actionable_rule: Before check-raising, confirm you probably have the best hand and that a player behind you will almost certainly bet; otherwise bet yourself.

concepts.title: Check-Raise/Bet Choice Based on Bettor Position and Hand Strength
concepts.summary: Whether to check-raise or bet depends on the position of the probable bettor and whether you want to thin the field or keep callers in.
concepts.details: To thin the field with a good-not-great hand (e.g. two pair), you want the probable bettor to your RIGHT so a check-raise forces others to call a double bet; if the bettor is on your LEFT, bet and hope for a raise to create the double bet. With a very strong hand that wants callers (e.g. a set), invert it: with the bettor on your right, bet so others call a single bet then face a raise; with the bettor on your left, check-raise so others call a single bet first.
concepts.actionable_rule: To thin the field, arrange a double-bet by putting the probable bettor on your right (check-raise) or your left (bet for a raise); with a strong hand wanting callers, invert these so opponents call two single bets instead of one double bet.

concepts.title: Check-Raising With a Second-Best Hand to Win the Pot
concepts.summary: It can be correct to check-raise even with a likely second-best hand if the raise drives out other opponents and improves your equity.
concepts.details: With the probable best hand on your immediate right, check and raise after it bets so the rest fold to a double bet. Even as an underdog to the bettor, eliminating others raises your win chance and you collect the dead money already in the pot.
applies_to: when best hand is on your right
concepts.actionable_rule: With a likely second-best hand and the strongest opponent on your right, check-raise to fold out the rest of the field and capture the dead money.

concepts.title: Check-Raising a Draw for Odds
concepts.summary: With a strong draw and many players in, you can check-raise to build the pot when you don't expect to drive others out.
concepts.details: With a come hand like a four-flush and cards to come, you want more callers, not fewer. Make this play with the probable bettor on your immediate left so others call before realizing a raise is coming, keeping them in for correct drawing odds.
concepts.actionable_rule: With a strong draw in a multiway pot and the bettor on your left, check-raise to inflate the pot while keeping opponents in for your draw's odds.

concepts.title: Requirements for a Correct Slowplay
concepts.summary: Slowplay only with a very strong hand when the free card helps opponents make a losing second-best hand and is unlikely to beat you or give a justified draw.
concepts.details: All conditions should hold: very strong hand; the free/cheap card has good chance to make opponents a second-best hand; little chance it makes them a better hand or a properly-priced draw; you'd fold them out by betting but can win big by not; and the pot is still small. As the pot grows, opponents get bigger odds and won't fold anyway, so slowplaying loses value.
concepts.actionable_rule: Slowplay only when your hand is very strong, the pot is small, and a free card cannot give opponents a winning hand or a correctly-priced draw; otherwise bet.

concepts.title: Slowplay Must Beat Immediate-Bet Expectation
concepts.summary: Per the Fundamental Theorem, a slowplay is only correct if its later implied value exceeds what you'd earn by betting now, and opponents still lack proper odds after the free card.
concepts.details: Giving a free card is correct only if deception yields more profit later than betting immediately, and the opponent calling later is still not getting proper odds. If the free card lets him develop a justified hand, slowplaying is wrong.
concepts.actionable_rule: Slowplay only when expected later profit exceeds immediate-bet value AND the opponent will still be priced incorrectly after the free card.

concepts.title: Bet the Pure Nuts, Slowplay Lesser Monsters
concepts.summary: With the absolute nuts you should bet/raise immediately in case someone else also has a big hand; reserve slowplaying for excellent but not unbeatable hands.
concepts.details: A straight flush or pure nut hand should be bet because another player may hold a second-strong hand and pay maximally; slowplaying risks letting two players check it down. With excellent-but-not-nut hands the deception is worth it.
concepts.actionable_rule: Bet and raise immediately with the pure nuts to extract from other strong hands; slowplay only excellent hands that aren't the absolute nuts.

concepts.title: Don't Slowplay With Obvious Strength
concepts.summary: Avoid slowplaying when your board or line shows obvious strength, since observant opponents won't pay you off later.
concepts.details: If your strength is apparent, knowledgeable players will fold to a later bet and unsophisticated ones will call an early bet anyway, so checking gains nothing.
concepts.actionable_rule: When your board shows obvious strength, bet rather than slowplay since opponents won't pay off a delayed bet.

concepts.title: Adjusting Play in Loose Games
concepts.summary: In loose games tighten up on bluffs and semi-bluffs but loosen up on legitimate value hands; play more draws but not marginal made hands in multiway pots.
concepts.details: Loose players rarely fold, so semi-bluffs lose two of their three winning ways (immediate fold, scare-card fold) leaving only improvement. Value hands need not be as strong since opponents call with worse, especially heads-up. Draws gain value from good pot odds and payoffs, but marginal hands like two small pair or one medium pair lose value in multiway pots where someone will outdraw them.
concepts.actionable_rule: Versus loose opponents: bluff and semi-bluff less, value bet thinner and call more, play more draws, but fold marginal made hands in multiway pots.

concepts.title: Adjusting Play in Tight Games
concepts.summary: In tight games loosen up on bluffs and semi-bluffs but tighten your legitimate-hand requirements, since callers will hold strong hands.
concepts.details: Tight players fold often, making bluffs and semi-bluffs profitable. But when they call a value bet they have strong hands, so your good hands are worth less. Play fewer draws since you're rarely priced in and get paid off less.
concepts.actionable_rule: Versus tight opponents: bluff and semi-bluff more, but devalue and bet your legitimate hands more cautiously, call less, and play fewer draws.

concepts.title: Ante Size Determines Looseness
concepts.summary: The higher the ante relative to later bets, the looser you should play; the smaller the ante, the tighter.
concepts.details: A high ante puts more dead money in the pot, improving pot odds for marginal hands. A small ante removes incentive to gamble with marginal holdings, especially when opponents enter only with big hands.
concepts.actionable_rule: Loosen your starting requirements as the ante grows relative to future bets, and tighten them when the ante is small.

concepts.title: Adjust to Individual Players, Not Just the Game
concepts.summary: Apply loose/tight adjustments per opponent: value-bet and reraise against loose raisers, fold or semi-bluff against tight raisers.
concepts.details: Against a tight player's raise you fold marginal hands (he likely has you beat) but can semi-bluff raise with equity since he may fold the best hand. Against a loose raiser you reraise medium hands for value but never bluff since he'll call.
concepts.actionable_rule: Reraise medium hands for value against loose raisers and never bluff them; against tight raisers fold marginal hands but semi-bluff hands with equity to fold out their better holdings.

concepts.title: Last position is the most valuable seat
concepts.summary: Acting last lets you make decisions with maximum information about opponents' actions, which translates into extra bets gained and saved over the long run.
concepts.details: In games with fixed position (hold'em, draw) the dealer acts last each round. Being last means you can call without fearing a raise behind you, get free cards when opponents check, value bet when they check and raise when they bet, and slowplay or raise after knowing how many players remain. The only threat to last position is a check-raise, so position is even stronger in no-check-raise contexts. The edge is not usually winning extra pots but the incremental bets saved/gained — and poker is about winning money, not pots.
concepts.actionable_rule: Prefer playing more hands and more aggressively when last to act; widen your range and use position to call cheaply, take free cards, and value bet/raise after seeing opponents act.

concepts.title: Tighten dramatically when the bettor is on your immediate right
concepts.summary: When you must act first after an aggressor, fold almost all marginal hands because of the threat of a raise behind you and a reraise from the original bettor.
concepts.details: Acting under the gun relative to an early raiser means you face the danger of being raised by players still to act plus a reraise from the original bettor, and you will likely remain out of position for the rest of the hand. Calling with marginal hands forces too many later folds (when raised this round or re-bet next round) to be profitable. Examples: fold two aces in 5-card draw, fold middle pairs in stud against a right-side raiser — hands you'd gladly play if last.
applies_to: facing a raise from immediate right
multiway pots with players still to act
concepts.actionable_rule: When forced to act first directly after an aggressor with players behind, fold marginal and speculative hands you would otherwise play in late position.

concepts.title: Implied odds depend on position, not just price
concepts.summary: A speculative call's profitability changes with position because position determines how much you can win when you hit a big hand.
concepts.details: With a hand like a small pocket pair seeking to flop a set, calling a preflop raise can be correct in last position (bettor to your left) because you can let the bettor drive action and then raise after callers commit, maximizing the pot. The identical hand and price becomes a fold when the bettor is to your right, because you cannot raise to be called by committed players and your implied odds collapse. Position changes a call into a fold even at the same immediate pot odds.
concepts.actionable_rule: Before calling a raise with a speculative hand, require better implied odds when out of position; fold the call if poor position prevents you from extracting value when you hit.

concepts.title: Trap monster hands by letting the left-side aggressor build the pot
concepts.summary: With a strong hand and the bettor to your left, let them bet and gather callers, then raise to win multiple double bets while charging draws.
concepts.details: When the aggressor is on your immediate left, they drive players around to you; the bettor bets, several players call, and you raise. You collect single bets from folders and double bets from callers, while making it expensive for opponents to draw out. If the bettor were to your right, raising would force players to call a double bet cold and yield fewer callers, and just calling lets opponents draw cheaply.
concepts.actionable_rule: With a big hand and the aggressor to your left, smooth-call to let them drive betting and gather callers, then raise after opponents commit to maximize value and protect against draws.

concepts.title: Seat aggressive players to your right, passive players to your left
concepts.summary: Arrange your effective position so loose/aggressive and information-leaking players act before you and tight players act after you.
concepts.details: Having the aggressive player to your right lets you act with knowledge of their action and trap them, while the tight player to your left rarely surprises you with raises behind. Players who tip off whether they're playing should be to your left so you can use that read when deciding to enter a pot.
concepts.actionable_rule: When choosing a seat, sit with loose-aggressive and tell-leaking opponents on your right and tight-passive opponents on your left.

concepts.title: Bluffing keeps opponents guessing on all your bets
concepts.summary: Bluffing with proper frequency disguises your value bets, forcing opponents into tough decisions and preventing them from playing perfectly against you.
concepts.details: Per the Fundamental Theorem of Poker, you profit whenever an opponent misplays relative to your actual hand. If you never bluff, opponents know every bet is for value and fold/call optimally, costing you action and free information. Occasional bluffs disguise both your bluffs and your legitimate hands. The player who never bluffs gets no action; the player who always bluffs goes broke; the correct-frequency bluffer wins most.
concepts.actionable_rule: Mix in bluffs at a controlled frequency so opponents cannot assume your bets are always value; balance your betting range to keep them guessing.

concepts.title: Optimal bluffing frequency makes the opponent indifferent
concepts.summary: Bluff so that the odds against your bluffing equal the pot odds your opponent is getting, leaving them indifferent between calling and folding.
concepts.details: If the opponent is getting 6-to-1 from the pot, set your bluffing frequency so the chances against a bluff are 6-to-1 (bluff 1 time in 7). Then the opponent breaks even whether they always call or always fold, and you average winning the pot regardless of their choice. Bluffs must also be randomized. Mathematically optimal frequency is the unexploitable baseline, but reading when to bluff can earn more.
concepts.actionable_rule: On the final betting round, choose a bluff-to-value ratio so the odds against your bluffing equal the pot odds offered, making the opponent indifferent to calling; randomize which hands bluff.

concepts.title: Exploit opponents' bluffing tendencies when calling
concepts.summary: Adjust your calls based on whether a specific opponent under-bluffs or over-bluffs relative to the pot odds.
concepts.details: Facing $20 into $100 (6-to-1), an opponent who never bluffs is an easy fold, one who frequently bluffs is an easy call, and only an opponent bluffing at exactly the indifference frequency presents a genuinely tough decision. Knowing the player lets you deviate from baseline to capture EV.
concepts.actionable_rule: When facing a bet, fold against known non-bluffers and call against habitual bluffers; only when the opponent bluffs near the indifference frequency should you treat it as a close decision.

concepts.title: Most players bluff too much in limit games
concepts.summary: When it costs an opponent only one small bet to call, bluffs rarely work because they get correct pot odds, so reduce bluffing in cheap-to-call limit spots.
concepts.details: In small limit games and against players who've seen you bluff, the low cost to call gives opponents sufficient pot odds to call with almost anything, making pure bluffs unprofitable. Average players over-bluff and pay for it.
concepts.actionable_rule: In limit or small-bet-to-pot situations and against stations, cut back on pure bluffs since opponents get correct odds to call.

concepts.title: Prefer semi-bluffs over pure bluffs with cards to come
concepts.summary: On early rounds, bet with hands that can improve so you have multiple ways to win rather than relying solely on immediate folds.
concepts.details: A pure bluff wins only if opponents fold immediately. A semi-bluff has three ways to win: immediate fold, a scare card folding them later, or making the best hand. Pure bluffs early are justified only when your fold-equity exceeds the pot odds you're laying yourself (e.g., a $7 bet to steal $10 antes that works ~60% of the time at less than 1.5-to-1 odds is profitable). If a pure early-round bluff is raised, give it up.
concepts.actionable_rule: With cards to come, bluff primarily with hands that retain equity (semi-bluffs); only fire a pure bluff when fold-equity exceeds the price you lay, and abandon a pure bluff immediately if raised.

concepts.title: Use effective (multi-street) odds when planning a multi-barrel bluff
concepts.summary: When a bluff will require betting on more than one street, compute the total risk against the total reward, not just the current street's pot odds.
concepts.details: Example: $100 pot, $10-$20 game, two cards to come, planning to bluff twice. You risk $40 to win $120 (pot plus the $20 first-round call), so you're effectively getting 3-to-1, not 5-to-1. The play needs a better than 3-to-1 chance the opponent folds by the end. This is especially true for pure bluffs with no improvement equity. Each round should still be re-evaluated based on how the new card affects you and your opponent.
concepts.actionable_rule: Before launching a bluff you intend to continue on later streets, sum the total chips risked against the total reward to get your effective odds, and proceed only if your cumulative fold-equity beats that price.

concepts.title: Continue or Abandon a Multi-Street Bluff Based on Relative Card Improvement
concepts.summary: After your bluff is called, decide whether to fire again by comparing how much your hand and the board improved versus how much your opponent's situation appears to improve.
concepts.details: When a first bluff is called, the opponent likely has something. If subsequent cards appear to strengthen the opponent (coordinating cards, draws completing) while you do not improve, give up: check and fold to a bet. If the opponent catches blanks and you catch cards that credibly improve or threaten your perceived range, continue the bluff. Read whether opponent is getting stronger or staying weak, and whether he still believes you are strong.
concepts.actionable_rule: After a called bluff, fire again only if your perceived strength increased and opponent caught blanks; if opponent's cards look threatening and yours did not improve, check and fold to a bet.

concepts.title: Pure Bluff Profitability Threshold vs Pot Odds
concepts.summary: A river bluff is profitable when the opponent's fold probability exceeds the ratio of your bet to the total pot plus bet.
concepts.details: With pot P and bet B, you risk B to win P. Breakeven fold frequency = B/(P+B). Example: $20 bluff into $100 needs folds more than 1 in 6; $20 into $60 needs more than 1 in 4; $20 into $140 needs more than 1 in 8. Larger pots require smaller fold frequency to bluff but also give the opponent better odds to call, so calls become more likely.
concepts.actionable_rule: On the river, bluff only when estimated fold probability exceeds bet/(pot+bet); smaller bets relative to the pot require fewer folds to be profitable.

concepts.title: Bluff Success Depends on Hand Reading and Opponent Type
concepts.summary: The weaker you read the opponent's hand and the tougher/more fold-prone the player, the more likely a bluff succeeds.
concepts.details: Never bluff into a lock or strong hand. It is generally easier to bluff a timid player than a loose one, and easier to bluff a tough player capable of folds than a weak calling-station who calls for any reason including suspicion of a bluff. Prior hand history and table dynamics also inform whether a bluff is currently profitable.
concepts.actionable_rule: Bluff most against opponents whose ranges you read as weak and who are capable of folding; avoid bluffing calling stations and players who hold strong hands.

concepts.title: Bluff First Position vs Tough Players Who Check
concepts.summary: Against tough players, betting a bluff from first position works better than betting after the opponent checks to you.
concepts.details: When a tough opponent checks to you, he knows he revealed weakness and suspects your bet exploits it, so he calls wider; also, with a truly bad hand he likely would have bluffed himself, so his check signals a calling hand. Leading from first position avoids signaling that you are attacking shown weakness.
concepts.actionable_rule: When out of position with a busted hand versus a tough player and you sense weakness, bet first rather than checking and bluffing after he checks to you.

concepts.title: Bet to Fold Out Better High Cards Against Busted Draws
concepts.summary: When you and an opponent both missed draws, betting a weak made hand can fold out higher non-pair holdings, improving your win chance.
concepts.details: Example: with ace-jack high, if there's ~55% chance opponent made a hand, ~15% he beats you 'by mistake' with AK/AQ high, betting folds out those higher highs and raises equity from 30% to 45%. This is a hybrid value/bluff bet that denies equity and folds out dominating air.
concepts.actionable_rule: With a weak high card after both players miss draws, bet to fold out higher unpaired hands that would otherwise win at showdown.

concepts.title: Check-Call Weak Pairs to Catch Bluffs Instead of Betting
concepts.summary: With a small made hand in a board where both missed, checking and calling beats betting because it captures opponent bluffs.
concepts.details: If you bet a small pair, opponents fold worse and call/raise with better, so you only get called when beaten. Checking lets the opponent bet his busted hands as bluffs, which your small pair beats. Either way you lose to legitimate hands, so the difference is capturing bluffs.
concepts.actionable_rule: With a marginal made hand that can't get value betting, check and call to snap off bluffs rather than bet.

concepts.title: Bluffing Multiple Opponents Compounds Fold Requirements
concepts.summary: Bluff EV against multiple players drops because all must fold; individual fold probabilities multiply, often turning a profitable bluff into a losing one.
concepts.details: If each of two opponents folds 1/3 of the time, both fold only 1/9, so 8/9 of the time at least one calls. Even with better pot odds (6:1 vs 4:1), the bluff loses. Fold probabilities aren't fully independent (middle player folds tighter, last player may call expecting others to), but the principle holds: bluffing one player out of pot 2X beats bluffing two out of pot 3X.
concepts.actionable_rule: Rarely bluff into two or more players on the end; require the product of each player's fold probability to exceed bet/(pot+bet).

concepts.title: Bluff-or-Value Dichotomy on the River
concepts.summary: On the end it is almost never right to do neither bluff nor value bet; if you can't profitably bluff a missed hand, value bet your made hands, and vice versa.
concepts.details: Bluffing wants folds; value betting wants calls. If a busted hand can't get folds, then your made fair hands should bet for value; if a fair hand only gets called by better, then your busted hands should bluff. Exception: games where opponent sees your last card (hold'em, five-card stud) and can read whether you improved, making value bets get called only by better.
concepts.actionable_rule: On the river, if you can't bluff profitably with missed hands, value bet your made hands; if value bets only get called by better, bluff your misses instead.

concepts.title: Both Value Bet and Bluff Can Be Correct With a Polarized Plan
concepts.summary: With a large pot, it can be correct to both value bet a fair made hand and bluff your misses from the same betting line.
concepts.details: Example: queens-up best 80% of the time, opponent folds 30% to a bet. You're still 5:2 (5/7) favorite when called, so value betting wins. If you miss, a 30% fold chance still makes a bluff profitable as long as the bet is less than 3/7 of the pot. The hold'em analog: raise preflop in position, check flop, then bet when A/K/Q comes — value betting the two cards that pair you while bluffing the rest, since opponent calls enough for value and folds enough for the bluff.
concepts.actionable_rule: Build a betting plan that both value bets your made hands and bluffs your misses when the opponent calls enough for value yet folds enough for the bluff, sizing bluffs under the breakeven fraction of the pot.

concepts.title: Adjust Bluff vs Value Frequency by Opponent Calling Tendency
concepts.summary: Against calling stations bet thin for value and rarely bluff; against tough folders bluff more and value bet less.
concepts.details: Perpetual callers pay off with worse hands, so value bet any likely-best hand and almost never bluff. Tough players make good folds, so bluff more but be reluctant to value bet fair hands since their calls are usually better. Draw example: vs an opponent who folds unimproved aces, bluff your missed jacks but check jacks-up; vs a never-folder, don't bluff one pair but value bet jacks-up (5:2 favorite when called).
concepts.actionable_rule: Against stations, value bet any likely-best hand and skip bluffs; against tough folders, increase bluff frequency and reduce thin value bets.

concepts.title: Bluffing as Image Advertising
concepts.summary: Deliberately get caught bluffing (or skip bluffs) to manage your future image and extract more value or steal pots later.
concepts.details: An early ill-advised bluff can buy more calls on later legitimate hands; an early loose call may deter future bluffs against you. Conversely, cultivating a tight image by passing marginal bluffs lets you steal pots later with impunity. Effects matter most in no-limit/pot-limit and in long sessions or repeated play against the same opponents.
concepts.actionable_rule: Manage table image by occasionally showing bluffs (or pass marginal bluffs to look tight) when the future-hand value outweighs the immediate cost, especially in NL/PL recurring games.

concepts.title: Bluff Slightly Less Than Optimal to Show a Profit
concepts.summary: Optimal game-theory bluffing breaks even on bluffs; against exploitable opponents, bluff a bit less so your bluffs net a profit.
concepts.details: Game-theory optimal bluffing makes the opponent indifferent, so bluffs break even, with profit coming from value. But because a successful bluff wins the whole pot and takes many extra calls to replace, against all but very tight players bluff slightly less than optimally to make bluffs profitable. A strong tight reputation increases how often you get away with bluffs while still getting paid on value.
