concepts.actionable_rule: Against non-optimal opponents, bluff a little less than the indifference frequency so bluffs themselves show profit, leaning on a tight image to increase fold equity.

concepts.title: Effective Odds for Multi-Street Bluff Plans
concepts.summary: When you intend to keep bluffing on later streets, evaluate the bluff against effective odds, not just current pot odds.
concepts.details: With more cards to come and a plan to continue bluffing, the cost of the full bluffing campaign (this bet plus expected future bets) must be weighed against the pot you can win. A single-street pot-odds calculation understates the risk of a multi-bet bluff plan.
concepts.actionable_rule: When planning to bluff across multiple streets, justify it using effective odds—total expected bluff investment versus the pot—rather than single-street pot odds.

concepts.title: Use Randomized Mixed Strategy to Neutralize a Superior Opponent
concepts.summary: Against an opponent with a judgment edge, randomize your decisions (bluff/call frequencies) so he cannot outguess you.
concepts.details: Game theory finds best strategies against an opponent also playing best. Like flipping a coin in odds-and-evens to capture a price advantage, using a predetermined frequency with a random trigger removes the opponent's ability to read your pattern. Use judgment against weaker opponents; use game-theory mixed strategy against stronger or unknown opponents.
concepts.actionable_rule: Against opponents equal or better than you, execute bluffs and bluff-catches at a fixed optimal frequency using a random trigger so your action is unexploitable; rely on read-based judgment only against weaker players.

concepts.title: Optimum Bluffing Frequency Equals Pot Odds Ratio
concepts.summary: Bluff in such a way that the odds against your bluffing equal the pot odds your opponent is getting to call. This makes the opponent indifferent between calling and folding.
concepts.details: When you bet, the opponent gets pot odds of (pot+bet):bet. To make calling and folding equally bad for them, the ratio of value bets to bluffs in your betting range must equal those pot odds. Example: with 18 value-making cards and a $100 bet into a $200 pot (opponent gets 3:1), bluff with exactly 6 cards so value:bluff = 18:6 = 3:1. This converts a hand that was a 4-to-3 underdog into a 4-to-3 favorite no matter how the opponent responds.
applies_to: situations where bettor either has best hand or is bluffing
concepts.actionable_rule: When betting on the river in a polarized spot, set your bluff frequency so that value-bets:bluffs equals the pot odds the opponent receives (e.g. opponent getting 3:1 means bluff 1 time for every 3 value bets), making the opponent indifferent.

concepts.title: Convert Pot Odds to Bluff Percentage
concepts.summary: Express optimum bluffing as a percentage: bluff frequency should be your value-hand frequency divided by the pot-odds ratio.
concepts.details: If you have a 25% chance of making your hand and the bet gives the opponent 2-to-1, you should bluff 12.5% of the time so value:bluff = 2:1. General method: determine your value frequency, determine the opponent's pot odds N:1, then bluff so value/bluff = N. Example: 20% value chance with opponent getting 5:1 means bluff 4% of the time.
concepts.actionable_rule: Compute opponent's pot-odds ratio N:1, then size your bluffing so that bluff frequency = value frequency / N.

concepts.title: Randomize Bluffs Using a Hidden Source
concepts.summary: Choose specific hidden 'key cards' (or another random device) to decide when to bluff so the opponent cannot detect a pattern.
concepts.details: The power of game-theory bluffing depends on true randomization. By tying bluffs to unseen cards your opponent cannot observe, your decision is as opaque as a coin flip. Even if the opponent knows you are using optimum strategy, they cannot exploit it because they cannot predict any individual bluff. Without randomization, observant opponents will read your pattern and counter you.
concepts.actionable_rule: Tie each bluff decision to a private random source (e.g. hidden cards or a fixed-probability RNG) at the computed frequency rather than bluffing based on feel or pattern.

concepts.title: Adjust Bluff Frequency to Opponent's Calling Tendency
concepts.summary: Deviate from optimum: bluff less against opponents who call too much and more against opponents who fold too much.
concepts.details: Optimum game theory is only ideal against opponents whose judgment matches or beats yours. The math shows bluffing slightly below optimum (5 instead of 6 cards) wins more if the opponent over-calls, while bluffing above optimum (7 instead of 6) wins more if the opponent over-folds. Against a player who always calls, never bluff; against one who always folds, bluff frequently.
concepts.actionable_rule: When the opponent's call/fold frequency is exploitable, shift away from the indifference frequency: reduce bluffs vs over-callers and increase bluffs vs over-folders.

concepts.title: Game Theory Calling to Deter Bluffs
concepts.summary: When your hand can only beat a bluff, call randomly at a frequency that makes the opponent's bluff break even.
concepts.details: If the opponent gets M:1 odds on a bluff (pot:bet), make the odds against your folding equal M:1 by calling M out of M+1 times. Example: opponent betting $20 to win $100 gets 5:1, so call 5 times and fold once. This prevents the opponent from profitably bluffing but, unlike bluffing, does not turn a losing situation into a winning one — it only stops you from being outwitted. Against an optimum bluffer you still cannot gain.
applies_to: hands that beat only a bluff
concepts.actionable_rule: When facing a possible bluff and your hand beats only bluffs, call randomly at frequency pot/(pot+bet) — e.g. opponent getting 5:1 means call 5 of every 6 times — to make bluffing unprofitable.

concepts.title: Maintain a Calling Frequency to Discourage Bluffing
concepts.summary: Never fold so predictably that bluffing becomes automatically profitable; keep enough calls to catch bluffs.
concepts.details: If the opponent assumes you fold often enough (e.g. 1 in 3 to a $20 bet into $100), bluffing earns +EV (lose $20 twice, win $100 once = +$20/bet). If they think you never fold, they never bluff. You want them uncertain, but you must call frequently enough that bluffing does not pay.
concepts.actionable_rule: Avoid folding at a rate that makes the opponent's bluff +EV; if a $X bet into $P pot needs P/(P+X) folds to break even for them, keep your fold rate at or below that threshold.

concepts.title: Scope: Use Game Theory Only in Polarized Spots
concepts.summary: Game-theory bluffing/calling applies cleanly only when the bettor obviously either has the best hand or is bluffing.
concepts.details: The indifference math assumes a binary range (nuts or air). When the bettor may hold a legitimate but non-best hand, the simple ratio breaks down and you need full heads-up-on-the-end analysis comparing your equity plus bluff chance against pot odds. Also, game theory should be reserved for opponents whose judgment equals or exceeds yours, or unknowns; against clearly exploitable players use judgment instead.
applies_to: polarized situations (e.g. obvious draw vs made pair)
concepts.actionable_rule: Only apply pure indifference-based bluff/call frequencies when the opponent's range is polarized (nuts-or-nothing); in spots with merged ranges, use full equity-vs-pot-odds analysis instead.

concepts.title: Lead Opponents Away From Correct Bluffing Frequency
concepts.summary: Against opponents who bluff approximately correctly, take action to push them toward bluffing too much or too little, since correct-frequency bluffers are the most dangerous.
concepts.details: A player bluffing at the game-theory-optimal frequency forces you into indifferent/incorrect decisions. The remedy is to manipulate their behavior: induce more bluffs from those who already over-bluff, and stop bluffs from those who under-bluff. Either way you make them deviate further from optimal, increasing your edge.
concepts.actionable_rule: Identify whether an opponent bluffs more or less than optimal; if more, take actions that induce additional bluffs; if less, take actions that stop bluffs entirely, so they deviate further from correct frequency.

concepts.title: Commit to Calling After Inducing a Bluff
concepts.summary: If you take action designed to induce a bluff, you must call when the opponent bets; folding undermines the entire purpose.
concepts.details: Inducing a bluff increases the proportion of bluffs in the opponent's betting range, making a call profitable. Folding after inducing simply lets the opponent steal more pots than they otherwise would, the opposite of the intended result.
concepts.actionable_rule: Whenever you deliberately induce a bluff (e.g., show weakness), call if the opponent then bets — never fold.

concepts.title: Commit to Folding After Stopping a Bluff
concepts.summary: If you take action designed to stop a bluff, you must fold when the opponent bets; calling means you should never have tried to stop the bluff.
concepts.details: Stopping a bluff removes bluffs from the opponent's range so a bet now mostly represents a made hand. If you would call anyway, you reduced the very bluffs you could have beaten — counterproductive. So a stop-bluff play implies a planned fold.
concepts.actionable_rule: Whenever you deliberately stop a bluff (e.g., represent strength), fold if the opponent then bets; if your hand is worth a call, do not try to stop the bluff in the first place.

concepts.title: Stop Bluffs by Representing Strength on Earlier Rounds
concepts.summary: To prevent an opponent from bluffing, represent more strength than you actually hold on an earlier street so they fear at least a calling hand.
concepts.details: Akin to semi-bluffing in reverse: by betting/raising or standing pat to show a strong line, you convince the opponent that bluffing cannot succeed. Example: raise with two small pair when worried about a draw; if opponent then bets the river you can fold cheaply knowing they have it. Best against players who under-bluff.
applies_to: earlier streets to set up river
concepts.actionable_rule: Against an under-bluffing opponent, raise or otherwise represent strength on an earlier street to discourage bluffs, then plan to fold cheaply if they continue to bet.

concepts.title: Induce Bluffs by Representing Weakness on Earlier Rounds
concepts.summary: To draw a bluff from an over-aggressive opponent, show weakness early (check, take extra cards, slowplay) so they bet hands you beat.
concepts.details: Inducing a bluff resembles slowplaying: by checking behind or feigning a weak hand, you encourage an over-bluffer to bet their air. Example: check behind on the turn with a strong pair to induce a river bluff, accepting the cost of a free card. You only need to push them slightly above correct frequency to profit.
concepts.actionable_rule: Against an over-bluffing opponent, check or otherwise represent weakness on an earlier street to induce a river bluff, then call; weigh this against the cost of giving a free card.

concepts.title: River Bluff Profitability Threshold
concepts.summary: A river bluff is profitable only when the opponent folds often enough that the fold frequency exceeds bet/(pot+bet).
concepts.details: With a $20 bet into $100, you risk $20 to win $100, so you need a fold more than 1 in 6 times to profit. Folding 1/5 yields +$4/hand average; folding only 1/7 yields -$2.86/hand. The break-even fold frequency equals bet divided by (pot plus bet).
concepts.actionable_rule: Before bluffing the river, estimate the opponent's fold frequency; bluff only if it exceeds bet/(pot+bet).

concepts.title: Bluff-Raises Require Far Higher Fold Frequency
concepts.summary: A bluff-raise on the river needs the opponent to fold much more often than a bluff-bet, because you invest a double bet while offering them large pot odds.
concepts.details: Calling $20 and raising $20 into a $120 pot risks $40 to win $120 (3-to-1), so the opponent must fold more than 1 in 4 times. Meanwhile the opponent is getting 8-to-1 to call, so only very tough players capable of big folds will release a legitimate hand. Average players almost always call, so bluff-raises mainly work when you read that they too have nothing.
concepts.actionable_rule: Avoid river bluff-raises against average players who call; only attempt them against tough opponents capable of folding, or when you read the bettor as also having nothing.

concepts.title: Value Bet on the End Based on Equity When Called, Not Best-Hand Probability
concepts.summary: On the final round, bet for value only if you are a favorite to win when called — typically at least 55% — not merely because you likely hold the best hand.
concepts.details: After all cards are out, betting to deny a free card no longer applies. The opponent folds worse hands and calls/raises with better, so your relevant equity is conditional on being called. Example: three-of-a-kind vs a busted flush draw is an 80% favorite overall but a loser when called, so checking behind is correct. The ~55% threshold (vs a raw 50%) compensates for check-raise risk.
concepts.actionable_rule: On the river after the opponent checks, bet for value only if you estimate at least ~55% equity when called; otherwise check behind.

concepts.title: Don't Restrict Value Bets Only to Locks
concepts.summary: You should value bet the river whenever you are a favorite when called, even if not a huge favorite, or you will leave bets uncollected.
concepts.details: A bet with 60% equity when called still profits: over ten such bets you win six and lose four, netting two bets, and even allowing for one called check-raise you still net one bet. Betting only with locks forfeits clearly profitable thin value.
concepts.actionable_rule: Bet thin value on the river whenever your equity when called exceeds ~55%, e.g., bet a queen-high straight when the opponent's range is mostly smaller straights.

concepts.title: River Raising for Value Requires ~55% Equity and a Non-Reraising Opponent
concepts.summary: Raising the river without the nuts effectively lays nearly 2-to-1 on the last bet, so raise only with about 55%+ equity and adjust for the opponent's reraise tendency.
concepts.details: When you raise and get reraised you usually lose two bets, but a called raise gains only one, so you are laying close to 2-to-1 on the extra bet, especially versus opponents who bluff-reraise. Against a player who never bluff-reraises, you can fold to a reraise. Against tough players, raise for value with a stronger hand than versus average players and raise less often on close decisions.
concepts.actionable_rule: Raise the river for value only with roughly 55%+ equity when called; tighten your raising range against tough players who can fold or bluff-reraise, and loosen against average players who always call.

concepts.title: Raise to Fold Out Better Hands
concepts.summary: Against a world-class opponent, a value-light raise can be correct if it makes them fold hands better than yours.
concepts.details: Even with only ~52% equity if you call (and little chance if raised and called), raising can be best when it folds out portions of the opponent's range that beat you. The decisive factor is whether the raise causes better hands to fold, converting an otherwise marginal call into a more profitable line.
concepts.actionable_rule: Consider a raise on the river with a merely decent hand when you believe a tough opponent will fold hands that currently beat you.

concepts.title: River raise only when favored to win the extra bet
concepts.summary: When last to act facing a bet, raise for value only if you are more likely than not to win the additional bet when your opponent calls the raise.
concepts.details: The expectation of a value raise on the end depends on whether you beat the range of hands that will call your raise. Against most players this is the governing rule. The exception (bluff-raising mediocre hands) only applies versus elite players who fold enough better hands to give the raise positive EV.
concepts.actionable_rule: As the last to act facing a bet, raise for value only if you are favored to win the extra bet when called; otherwise just call or fold.

concepts.title: Call when pot odds exceed odds against winning
concepts.summary: You do not need to be a favorite to call; you only need pot odds better than the odds against your hand winning at showdown.
concepts.details: If you have a 30% chance to win and must call $20 into an $80 pot (getting 4-to-1, i.e. needing only 20% equity), the call is correct. Fold only when your win chance is below the equity threshold set by the pot odds.
concepts.actionable_rule: Call a river bet whenever your estimated win probability exceeds the breakeven equity implied by the pot odds offered, regardless of whether you are over 50%.

concepts.title: Choose the action with highest expectation when last to act
concepts.summary: Facing a bet in last position you always have fold, call, and raise available; pick the one with the highest mathematical expectation.
concepts.details: Each option has an EV. Folding is best when equity is below pot-odds threshold, calling when odds are favorable, and raising (even as a bluff vs. very strong players) when it folds out enough better hands. The correct play is simply the maximal-EV branch.
concepts.actionable_rule: When last to act against a bet, compute EV of fold, call, and raise and choose the highest; do not default to fold just because you are an underdog.

concepts.title: Check-raise EV formula on the end
concepts.summary: Check-raise rather than bet out when the value of winning two bets (weighted by how often opponent bets and calls the raise) plus bets-and-folds exceeds the value of betting and being called.
concepts.details: Compute: P(opp calls your bet) versus 2*P(opp bets then calls your raise) + P(opp bets then folds to raise). If the latter sum is larger, check-raise. Example: 70% call-a-bet vs. 2*40% + 10% = 90% favors check-raising, gaining ~20 bets per 100.
concepts.actionable_rule: Check-raise a strong hand instead of betting out when 2*(chance opponent bets and calls your raise) + (chance opponent bets and folds) exceeds the chance opponent calls if you bet.

concepts.title: Simplified check-raise heuristic
concepts.summary: Since most players auto-call a check-raise, check-raise when the chance the opponent bets after your check is at least half the chance he calls if you bet.
concepts.details: Risking the loss of one bet (when opponent checks behind) is justified by the chance of gaining two bets. Check-raising is a long-run play; a single time it fails does not make it wrong, and a busted check-raise can make opponents timid about value-betting behind you later.
concepts.actionable_rule: With a strong hand first to act versus a normal opponent, check-raise whenever you think he will bet at least half as often as he would call your bet.

concepts.title: Limit check-raising vs weak and tough players
concepts.summary: Check-raise less against weak callers (they won't bet enough) and tough players (they fold to raises and bet thin rarely).
concepts.details: Weak players call too much when you bet, so unless you are over 50% sure they will bet after you check, betting out captures the value. Tough players bet fewer hands than they call with and fold to your raise, reducing your chance of collecting the double bet.
concepts.actionable_rule: Against pay-station weak callers, bet your value hands directly; against tough opponents who fold to raises and bet thin rarely, prefer betting out over check-raising.

concepts.title: Go for three bets when reraise is likely
concepts.summary: Deviate from check-raising and instead bet out when you can induce a raise and then reraise, winning three bets.
concepts.details: When your visible hand looks strong enough to be raised by a worse hand (e.g., apparent straight hiding a full house vs. a flush), betting out to get raised and then three-betting maximizes value beyond a simple check-raise.
concepts.actionable_rule: Bet out instead of check-raising when your board lets a worse hand raise you, so you can reraise and collect three bets.

concepts.title: Bet vs callers, check-call vs bettors
concepts.summary: With a fair-to-good hand worth a call, bet if the opponent calls with more hands than he bets, and check-call if he bets with more hands than he calls.
concepts.details: Demonstrated with the 0-100 hand model: against an opponent who bets bluffs and value (more hands than he calls), checking turns you from a 23-to-20 into a 29-to-20 favorite by capturing his bluffs. Against a calling-station who bets few hands, betting captures his loose calls. The right play maximizes wins minus losses, not hand strength.
concepts.actionable_rule: With a callable-strength hand first to act, bet when the opponent calls more hands than he bets, but check and call when he bets more hands than he calls.

concepts.title: Never check-fold when favored if called
concepts.summary: If you are favored to win when called, you must bet rather than check-fold, even against a timid opponent who only bets better hands.
concepts.details: Checking surrenders a positive-EV bet. Even as a 23-to-20 favorite, betting 43 times nets +3 units, better than zero. The only reason to check is uncertainty about being favored combined with fear of a raise you'd have to call.
concepts.actionable_rule: Bet whenever you are favored to win the bet when called; only consider checking if you're unsure you're ahead and fear a raise.

concepts.title: Bet as an underdog when it reduces your underdog status
concepts.summary: Sometimes bet a hand that is an underdog when called because betting picks up worse calls and makes you less of an underdog than checking and being forced to call.
concepts.details: If checking leaves you a 20-to-10 underdog facing a bet you must call (good pot odds), but betting makes you a 20-to-15 underdog by adding worse calling hands, betting has higher EV. Analogous to splitting eights vs a ten in blackjack: still behind, but less behind.
concepts.actionable_rule: Bet an underdog hand when betting adds enough worse calls to make you less of an underdog than checking and being forced to call a bet.

concepts.title: Check-fold underdog when opponent only bets better hands
concepts.summary: When you are an underdog if called and the opponent will only bet hands that beat you, check and fold, saving more bets than you lose.
concepts.details: In the model, opponent calls hands 65+ but bets only 81+. Betting as a 20-to-15 underdog loses money; checking lets you fold to his bets (saving 20 bets) at the cost of missing 15 thin value bets when he checks behind. Saving exceeds sacrifice.
concepts.actionable_rule: Check and fold an underdog hand when the opponent's betting range only contains hands that beat you and you cannot profitably call.

concepts.title: Bet underdog hands for value into wide calling range
concepts.summary: Bet an underdog hand when the opponent calls with many hands you beat but bets only a few you beat, even if you couldn't call his bet.
concepts.details: With $60 pot, opponent calls 65+ but bets only 76+: checking gives you nothing extra (can't call as 5-to-1 underdog vs 4-to-1 pot), but betting collects calls from 65-75. EV of betting ($4,700) beats check-folding ($4,560) by $140 over 100 trials. Pot size and number of second-best calling hands determine this.
concepts.actionable_rule: Bet for thin value even when you'd fold to a bet, if the opponent calls with many worse hands but bets only a few hands that beat you.

concepts.title: Check-call exception: large pot, timid value-bettor, fear of raise
concepts.summary: In a large pot, check and call rather than bet even when the opponent calls with more hands than he bets, if he checks back many better hands and you fear a raise.
concepts.details: With $200 pot and opponent who won't value-bet hands 81-90, checking saves $20 the times he checks back the best hand, turns you from a 4-to-1 to a 2.5-to-1 underdog when he does bet, and avoids a raise you'd be priced in to call. This is the exception to the bet-vs-callers rule.
concepts.actionable_rule: In a big pot versus a timid opponent who checks back many better hands and might raise, check and call instead of betting even though he calls more than he bets.

concepts.title: Bet small edges into pure calling stations
concepts.summary: Against an opponent who calls virtually every time, bet whenever you hold even a small favorite, since even-money wager as a favorite is +EV.
concepts.details: Example: one-paired into a presumed big pair, ~71% (5-to-2) favorite versus a pay station who calls 'to keep you honest'. Wagering even money as a 71% favorite is clearly profitable despite losing 29% of the time.
concepts.actionable_rule: Bet for value against a pure calling station any time you are even a slight favorite over his calling range.

concepts.title: Value bet vs. calling-station who never bluffs
concepts.summary: When an opponent calls with many hands you beat but bets/raises rarely and never bluffs, betting your medium-strong hand for value beats checking because he calls with worse and won't bet those worse hands if checked to.
concepts.details: In first position with a hand that beats more of opponent's calling range than the range that beats it, you must come out betting. A non-bluffing opponent who 'calls too much' adds value because checking would not extract bets from his worse hands. The decision is governed by whether he calls with more hands than he bets with.
applies_to: vs passive players who never bluff
concepts.actionable_rule: On the river out of position, bet for value if the opponent will call with more worse hands than he would bet, especially against a passive player who calls too much and never bluffs.

concepts.title: Check-call vs. aggressive bluffer
concepts.summary: Against an aggressive opponent who bets with more hands than he calls with, check and call rather than betting, so you capture his bluffs in addition to his thin value bets.
concepts.details: A player who bets more hands than he calls with bluffs more than is correct; checking adds his bluffing range to his value range, both of which you can snap off. Betting would make him fold his bluffs and only continue with hands that beat you. The deciding criterion is whether the opponent bets more hands than he calls with.
concepts.actionable_rule: On the river out of position against an aggressive bluffer, check and call instead of betting so you induce and capture bluffs you would otherwise fold out.

concepts.title: Check-fold against non-bluffer when behind his betting range
concepts.summary: If your hand beats only the hands a non-bluffing opponent would not even bet, and he never bluffs, check and fold to any bet.
concepts.details: When your hand is too weak to value bet (it loses to his better calling hands) and the opponent bets only hands that beat you and never bluffs, a bet has negative expectation and a call to a bet has overwhelmingly negative expectation. Folding is correct because the odds you are beaten are overwhelming.
concepts.actionable_rule: On the river, check and fold when your hand beats only hands the opponent would never bet and he never bluffs.

concepts.title: Choosing bet vs. check-raise with very strong hands
concepts.summary: With a near-cinch first to act, choose between betting and check-raising via the check-raise formula; if you fear a raise when you bet, bet anyway to win three bets via a reraise.
concepts.details: With a hand strong enough to check-raise, compare expected value of leading versus inducing a bet you can raise. If the opponent will bet and call a raise more than half as often as he calls a lead, check-raise. If a check-raise won't work often enough, or if a bet may induce a raise that lets you reraise for three bets, just bet.
concepts.actionable_rule: With a near-nut hand out of position, check-raise if opponent will bet-and-call a raise more than half as often as he calls a lead; otherwise bet, especially when you can reraise an aggressive opponent for a third bet.

concepts.title: Bet-vs-check-call decision rule by relative frequencies
concepts.summary: With a favorite hand not strong enough to check-raise, bet if the opponent calls with more hands than he bets, and check-call if he bets with more hands than he calls; never check-fold a favorite.
concepts.details: This is the core last-card decision framework: the action that captures the most value depends on whether the opponent is call-heavy (bet) or bet-heavy/bluffy (check-call). A hand that is a favorite when called should never be folded; only the bet-vs-check-call choice varies with opponent tendency.
concepts.actionable_rule: On the last card with a hand that's a favorite when called, bet if the opponent calls more than he bets, check-call if he bets more than he calls, and never check-fold.

concepts.title: Small underdog when called: extract or capture bluffs
concepts.summary: With a small underdog when called, bet if the opponent calls with more worse hands than he would have bet, or check-call if he bets/bluffs enough worse hands to make calling +EV given pot odds; check-fold only if he almost never bets worse.
concepts.details: Even as a small underdog, betting can be correct when you fold out nothing useful and get called by some worse hands he wouldn't have bet. Check-calling is correct when he checks many better hands behind but bluffs some worse hands, making a call profitable at the pot odds. Check-fold is reserved for opponents who essentially never bet a hand worse than yours.
concepts.actionable_rule: As a small underdog on the river, bet if opponent calls more worse hands than he'd bet; check-call if his betting range contains enough worse/bluff hands to justify the pot odds; check-fold only if he never bets worse than you.

concepts.title: Second-position bluffs work less often than first-position bluffs
concepts.summary: A bluff bet into a checking opponent succeeds less often when you are last to act than when you bet first, so adjust bluff frequency downward in late position.
concepts.details: When the opponent checks to you, his check may be inducing or trapping, and he has already shown he isn't betting, so a bluff is more likely to be called or check-raised relative to a bet that takes initiative from first position. Bluff in second position only if it works often enough for positive expectation.
concepts.actionable_rule: When checked to as the last actor, lower your bluffing frequency relative to leading from first position, and bluff only when it shows positive expectation.

concepts.title: Fundamental Theorem applied to hand reading
concepts.summary: The closer you read your opponent's actual hand, the closer you play to the way you would if you saw his cards, minimizing the mistakes that cost you money.
concepts.details: Per the Fundamental Theorem of Poker, the key error is playing differently than you would with perfect information. Improving hand-reading accuracy directly reduces lost EV and increases won EV, making it arguably the most important skill.
concepts.actionable_rule: Always invest effort in narrowing your opponent's likely holdings so you can choose the action you'd pick if you could see his cards.

concepts.title: Read hands by combining actions and exposed cards
concepts.summary: In open-handed games, combine the meaning of each bet/check/raise across rounds with the visible upcards (and the order they were caught) to determine the most likely holding.
concepts.details: Two universal techniques are interpreting betting actions and, in stud/razz/hold'em, reading exposed cards. Note the sequence in which an opponent caught cards, since order can be the deciding clue (e.g., knowing a player started with A,8 rather than A,6). Synthesizing plays plus upcards yields the conclusion.
concepts.actionable_rule: To read a hand, combine each round's betting action with the opponent's exposed cards and the order he caught them, then deduce his most likely holding.

concepts.title: Use overcalls to deduce strength multiway
concepts.summary: An overcall behind a bet and a call implies a hand strong enough to beat the intervening caller's likely range, so deduce that the overcaller holds a hand stronger than both prior players.
concepts.details: In the three-sevens example, the queens overcalling after aces bet and kings called means the queens player, being competent, must beat kings-up, narrowing his range to three queens or better. Card removal (third ace and king visible) eliminates two-pair combos, confirming a fold is correct.
concepts.actionable_rule: When a competent player overcalls behind a bet and a call, assign him a range that beats the intervening caller's likely hand, and fold weak holdings accordingly.

concepts.title: Avoid premature, irreversible hand reads
concepts.summary: Don't lock an opponent onto one specific hand early; start with a range and eliminate possibilities as the action and cards develop.
concepts.details: An early raise can represent many holdings (e.g., a king-up raise might be two kings, a hidden pair with king kicker, a three-flush, or KQJ). Drawing a narrow conclusion early risks folding the best hand or chasing as a big underdog. Work both forward (eliminate) and backward (reconstruct from later actions).
concepts.actionable_rule: Assign the opponent a range of hands at the start and update it each street, eliminating holdings inconsistent with his later play and cards rather than fixating on one hand.

concepts.title: Less-dangerous boards can be more dangerous on the end
concepts.summary: When an opponent's board shows no missed draws, a final bet is more likely value because nothing suggests he was semi-bluffing; threatening boards with busted draws raise bluff probability.
concepts.details: If a player bets all the way and his board shows a busted flush/straight draw (e.g., caught off-suit blanks after a draw), a river bet may be a missed semi-bluff worth calling at pot odds. If the board never had a draw and he kept betting, eliminate the bluff possibility and treat the bet as value (likely two pair or better) and fold marginal hands.
concepts.actionable_rule: On the end, increase your call frequency when the opponent's board shows a busted draw consistent with semi-bluffing, and fold marginal hands when his quiet, non-drawy board makes a value bet far more likely.

concepts.title: Work backward from a sudden river bet
concepts.summary: When a quiet opponent suddenly bets after a blank river, reconstruct earlier streets to judge whether trips/improvement is plausible or whether it's a bluff.
concepts.details: If there was betting on earlier streets, an opponent wouldn't have called holding only the pair the river paired, so a sudden bet is a bluff or a different made hand. If everyone checked earlier, he may have genuinely caught trips on the river. Combine forward elimination and backward reconstruction each street.
concepts.actionable_rule: When a previously passive player bets after a blank turns up, trace prior action: if there was earlier betting his story for trips is implausible (likely bluff or other hand); if checked through, give weight to the river-improvement holding.

concepts.title: Classify river bets into bad/good/great and respond by tier
concepts.summary: A river bet usually represents a bluff, a good hand, or a great hand but rarely a mediocre one; categorize it and raise vs good hands, call vs possible great hands, and fold great-only.
concepts.details: Players check mediocre hands rather than bet, so a bet polarizes toward bluffs and strong hands. Ask: what is he representing, and could he plausibly have it given how he played? With a very good hand, raise if he likely only has a good hand, call if he might have a great hand, and fold if you're virtually certain he has a great hand and the pot warrants it.
concepts.actionable_rule: Facing a river bet, classify the opponent's likely strength as bluff/good/great; raise your very good hand against a 'good' range, just call when a 'great' hand is plausible, and fold only when a 'great' hand is nearly certain and the pot allows.

concepts.title: Use range math and opening requirements to set calling thresholds
concepts.summary: When you can narrow an opponent to a known range (e.g., raises with trip-deuces or better), compute the hand that is favored to beat his range and call only with holdings that have enough equity plus pot odds.
concepts.details: If an opponent raises with three-of-a-kind or better, the median beating hand works out to about three queens. Calling with three treys is unprofitable, but three fives/sixes can be a call because you beat the few worst hands in his range and can draw out to a full house/quads, and pot odds support it. Bayes-style reasoning compares the probabilities of each holding within his range.
concepts.actionable_rule: Once you've narrowed an opponent to a defined range, calculate which hand is favored against that range and call only with holdings whose equity plus implied/pot odds clears that threshold.

concepts.title: Bayesian Hand Reading via Dealt-Hand Probabilities
concepts.summary: When an opponent's betting range is narrowed to a few hand types, compare the prior probabilities of each being dealt to determine which he most likely holds.
concepts.details: If you know a player bets only certain hands, form a ratio from the base probabilities of being dealt each. E.g., AK is dealt ~1.2% vs ~0.9% for AA or KK combined, making AK a 4-to-3 favorite. Simplify by dividing his range into hands you beat vs hands you don't, then compute the ratio. This is pure card-distribution math independent of his action.
concepts.actionable_rule: When an opponent's range is reduced to a known set of hands, weight each hand by its combinatoric/dealt probability and act based on whether you are favored against the most likely holdings.

concepts.title: Adjust Card-Removal When Reading Hands
concepts.summary: Visible cards (on board or other players' hands) reduce the number of combinations available for a given holding, shifting the relative likelihoods within an opponent's range.
concepts.details: If a player can hold either two kings or a three-flush and another king is visible, only two kings remain unseen instead of three, cutting the probability of a made pair of kings from ~11% to ~7.5%. This raises the relative chance he holds the flush draw, potentially making a marginal call (e.g., two queens) correct.
concepts.actionable_rule: Recount the available combinations for each hand in the opponent's range after accounting for all visible cards, and recompute his likely holdings accordingly.

concepts.title: Math Must Be Combined With Player Tendencies
concepts.summary: Pure probability can be reversed by a player's known behavioral pattern; integrate read-based adjustments with the math.
concepts.details: Some players raise two kings only when another king is showing (to win immediately because their improvement odds dropped). Against such a player, a visible king can increase the chance he actually has kings after raising — the opposite of the naive math. Reads override or modify mathematical priors.
concepts.actionable_rule: After computing the mathematical likelihoods, adjust them with documented player tendencies; if a player's pattern contradicts the math, trust the read.

concepts.title: Tighten Up When a Caller Is Ahead of You
concepts.summary: A caller in front removes the bluff-catching equity that justifies thin calls, so you need a stronger hand to overcall than to call heads-up.
concepts.details: When someone bets and another player calls, both cannot be bluffing; the caller must have a real hand. The extra equity from catching a bluff disappears, so a hand barely worth a heads-up call is not worth an overcall. Multi-way pots demand significantly tighter continuing ranges.
applies_to: facing a bet plus a caller
concepts.actionable_rule: When a player calls a bet ahead of you, fold marginal bluff-catchers and continue only with hands strong enough to beat at least one legitimate holding.

concepts.title: Need a Better Hand to Call a Raise Cold
concepts.summary: A raiser to your right with the same standards as you probably has you beat when you hold a minimum raising hand, so fold rather than cold-call.
concepts.details: If your raising threshold is aces-up-or-better and you hold three deuces, but a same-standard player raises first, his range is on average better than your minimum, so even calling is losing. Cold-calling a raise requires a stronger hand than initiating a raise yourself.
applies_to: facing a raise with a minimum hand
concepts.actionable_rule: When facing a cold raise from a player with standards like yours and you hold a near-minimum raising hand, fold; only continue with hands clearly above your raising threshold.

concepts.title: Multi-Level Thinking (Levels of Thought)
concepts.summary: Against good players, reason about what they have, what they think you have, and what they think you think they have.
concepts.details: Level 1: what opponent holds. Level 2: what opponent thinks you hold. Level 3: what opponent thinks you think he holds. Deception plays (e.g., raising kings to represent kings-up against a known aces holding) only work if the opponent thinks on the corresponding level. Match your thinking level to the opponent's capability — no higher, no lower.
concepts.actionable_rule: Calibrate your level of thinking to the opponent: think to at least the third level versus good players, but stay at level one and play straightforwardly against weak, non-thinking opponents.

concepts.title: A Bet Into Sure Call Is Not a Bluff
concepts.summary: When an opponent bets or raises in a spot where he is certain you will call, he is value betting, not bluffing.
concepts.details: No competent player bluffs when convinced of a call. If your line (betting all the way, your board, pot size) signals you will pay off, an opponent who bets/raises has a real hand. The clearest case is a raise on the end after you've bet every street — almost never a bluff except from very tough players.
applies_to: facing a raise after showing strength
concepts.actionable_rule: Fold routine and bluff-catching hands when an opponent bets or raises into a situation where he is sure you'll call, unless your hand can beat his legitimate value range.

concepts.title: A Bet Into Likely Fold May Be a Bluff
concepts.summary: When an opponent bets where he thinks you are likely to fold, he is more likely bluffing, so call wider.
concepts.details: Corollary to the sure-call principle: if you've shown weakness or the situation looks like a good bluff spot to him, his betting range is more bluff-heavy. This underlies inducing bluffs — show weakness, then call down because he may be betting expecting a fold.
concepts.actionable_rule: When you've represented weakness and an opponent bets into an apparent fold spot, widen your calling range to include mediocre bluff-catchers.

concepts.title: Bet Selection Based on Opponent's Perception of You
concepts.summary: If the opponent thinks you're strong, bluff more but don't value bet fair hands; if he thinks you're weak, value bet fair hands but don't bluff.
concepts.details: When an opponent fears your strong hand he folds everything but hands that beat you, so a fair hand gets no value and only loses — instead bluff because he'll fold. When he thinks you're weak he pays off your fair hands but snaps off bluffs, so value bet and stop bluffing.
concepts.actionable_rule: If opponents perceive you as strong, increase bluffs and stop thin value bets; if they perceive you as weak, value bet fair hands and abandon bluffs.

concepts.title: Intentional Bad Plays to Set Up Future Impressions
concepts.summary: Occasionally make a theoretically incorrect play to create a false impression you can exploit on later hands.
concepts.details: Slowplaying or checking a strong hand in a showdown, or bluffing/folding showily, creates a memorable image. Later you exploit opponents' adjusted expectations (e.g., betting trips after they saw you check trips). Works only against players good enough to adjust but not good enough to realize you're manipulating them. Normally evaluate each play on its standalone EV.
concepts.actionable_rule: Evaluate plays on standalone EV by default, but occasionally make a deliberately suboptimal, memorable play to mislead adjusting-but-not-expert opponents for future profit.

concepts.title: Fall Back on Game Theory When Thought Levels Spiral
concepts.summary: When the leveling war becomes too deep to resolve with reads, switch to an unexploitable game-theory (balanced) strategy.
concepts.details: At expert levels the dialectic of outwitting can extend to so many levels that judgment fails; at that point a balanced, indifference-inducing strategy is the safe default. Game theory is most useful precisely when psychological reads break down.
concepts.actionable_rule: When you cannot reliably resolve the leveling war against a tough opponent, abandon exploitative reads and play a balanced game-theory-optimal strategy.

concepts.title: Match Strategy to Opponent's Reading Difficulty
concepts.summary: Good players are readable through logic, weak players are unreadable through randomness, and tough players are hard via disguise — adjust expectations accordingly.
concepts.details: Weak players have little pattern, so you can't put them on a hand or a thought. Good players follow logical patterns, making them readable. Very tough players deliberately disguise hands. Reading depends on detecting consistent logic, so calibrate confidence in your reads to opponent type.
concepts.actionable_rule: Build reads from logical patterns against competent players, but against unpredictable weak players rely on straightforward value-based play rather than hand reads.

concepts.title: Risk-Reward Framework for All Decisions
concepts.summary: Every poker decision can be framed as comparing the risk (what you can lose) against the reward (what you can gain, including future benefits).
concepts.details: Bluffing risks a bet to win the pot; betting a mediocre hand risks a bet to deny a free card; checking a big hand risks a lost bet and the pot to gain a check-raise or future bets; calling risks a bet to win the pot. The ability to evaluate the risk-reward ratio accurately is the core skill of expert play.
concepts.actionable_rule: For every decision, quantify what you risk (current bet) versus what you stand to gain (pot plus future expected value), and act only when the reward justifies the risk.

concepts.title: Weighted Hand-Range Analysis
concepts.summary: Rather than assuming a single hand, assign your opponent a distribution of possible hands with probabilities, then pick the play best against the most likely hand or group of hands.
concepts.details: Four steps: (1) determine the possible hands the opponent may have; (2) assess the probability of each; (3) determine your best play against each; (4) usually pick the play correct most often. If one hand needs play A but two other hands together (e.g., 60%) need play B, choose play B even though the single most likely hand favors A.
concepts.actionable_rule: Build a probability-weighted range for the opponent, evaluate your best response against each hand, then choose the action that is correct against the largest combined probability of hands.

concepts.title: Call Instead of Reraise to Set Up a Check-Raise
concepts.summary: When you hold the likely best hand against an opponent who will pay you off, just calling and check-raising later can extract more value than reraising immediately.
concepts.details: In the draw example, calling the raise then drawing one card and check-raising after the draw wins $30 when ahead versus $25 by reraising, and loses only $10 instead of $15 when behind. The line is correct against the entire range because it gains value when ahead and saves money when behind.
concepts.actionable_rule: When you likely hold the best hand and the opponent will keep betting, prefer flat-calling to disguise strength and set up a check-raise that wins more bets than an immediate reraise.

concepts.title: Check Back to Induce Calls/Bluffs in Small Pots
concepts.summary: In a small pot, checking behind a marginal made hand can win an extra bet by inducing the opponent to call or bluff later when betting would have folded out his worse hands.
concepts.details: Betting fourth street folds out mediocre hands you beat, gaining nothing. Checking shows weakness, makes it cheaper and easier for the opponent to call on the river, induces bluffs, and is correct when you are behind. Drawbacks: gives a free card and loses value from hands that would call twice. Critical condition: the pot must be small, since you gain only one bet but risk the whole pot to a free-card outdraw.
concepts.actionable_rule: With a marginal made hand in a small pot, check behind to induce a river call or bluff from worse hands, planning to bet if checked to and call if bet into — but only when the pot is small enough that the free card risk is acceptable.

concepts.title: Weigh the Cost of Being Wrong, Not Just Frequency
concepts.summary: The play that is correct most often is not always best; choose the play whose downside when wrong is smaller, even if it is favored to be wrong.
concepts.details: When folding to a river bet is right >50% of the time but folding the best hand costs the whole pot while calling costs only one bet, you call. The general principle: if alternative A has slightly bad consequences when wrong and alternative B has terrible consequences when wrong, choose A even if B is slightly more often correct.
concepts.actionable_rule: Compare not only how often each play is right but the magnitude of the loss when each play is wrong; choose the play with the smaller worst-case cost when frequencies are close.

concepts.title: Folding QQ to a Huge Reraise Despite Being a Favorite
concepts.summary: Being a frequency favorite to have the best hand does not justify calling when the times you are behind you lose much more than you gain when ahead.
concepts.details: Against a range of AA, KK, AK that is 4-to-3 toward AK, QQ is the best hand 4/7 of the time but only a 13-to-10 favorite versus AK, while a 4.5-to-1 underdog versus AA/KK. The large losses when dominated outweigh the small edge when ahead, so calling a giant reraise is unprofitable.
concepts.actionable_rule: When facing a large reraise with QQ, fold against an AA/KK/AK range even though you are a slight favorite to be best, because the dominated losses exceed the marginal wins.

concepts.title: Raise When the Upside of Being Right Is Large
concepts.summary: When raising is wrong only slightly but calling is very wrong, raise even though calling is correct more often.
concepts.details: In the razz example, raising is slightly wrong 55% of the time (opponent has 8,7 made, you still have outs) but calling is very wrong 45% of the time (opponent paired, you are a big favorite to win extra bets). Because the magnitude of gain from raising when ahead exceeds the loss when behind, raising is the superior play despite lower hit frequency.
concepts.actionable_rule: Raise rather than call when the times you are ahead you gain far more than you lose the times you are behind, even if you will be behind more than half the time.

concepts.title: Adjust Strategy to the Ante and Forced-Bet Size
concepts.summary: The size of the ante and blinds relative to betting limits dictates how loose, aggressive, and deceptive you should play.
concepts.details: Large antes require looser play, more steal attempts, and almost no slowplaying; small antes call for tighter play, fewer steals, and more slowplaying. Avoid games where the ante is enormous relative to limits, since the pot is so big it becomes correct to call with nearly anything and skill is reduced. Match game selection to your style: trappers prefer small-ante games, aggressive bluffers prefer large-ante games.
concepts.actionable_rule: Measure ante/blind size relative to bet size; loosen up and stop slowplaying when antes are large, tighten and slowplay more when antes are small, and avoid games with enormous antes relative to limits.

concepts.title: Initial Bet/Raise Ratio Changes Pot-Odds Strategy
concepts.summary: The ratio between the bring-in/first bet and the raise size determines whether to raise or flat-call to manipulate opponents' pot odds.
concepts.details: When the raise is small relative to the first bet (e.g., $5 bring-in, $15 raise), raise with a good hand to cut the next player's pot odds and deny correct draws. When the raise is large relative to the first bet (e.g., $10 bring-in, $25 raise), just call so a later player overcalls without sufficient odds — by calling you disguise strength and induce mistakes (Fundamental Theorem of Poker).
concepts.actionable_rule: If raising materially worsens a later player's pot odds, raise to deny correct draws; if the raise is too large to be worth the deception, flat-call with a strong hand to induce overcalls and disguise your strength.

concepts.title: Play at Limits Your Bankroll Supports
concepts.summary: Never play limits so high relative to your bankroll that fear of going broke prevents correct play, but play the highest limits you can afford when you have an edge.
concepts.details: If stakes are too high you cannot make correct value bets, calls, or bluffs because you are protecting your bankroll, eroding your edge. When you have the best of it, scaling up to the highest affordable limit maximizes earnings.
concepts.actionable_rule: Choose stakes low enough that you can always make the mathematically correct play without fear of ruin, and as high as that constraint allows when you hold an edge.

concepts.title: Adjust looseness to limit escalation / implied odds
concepts.summary: The greater the escalation of betting limits from early to late streets, the higher your implied odds, so you can play speculative drawing hands more loosely early.
concepts.details: When later-round bets are much larger than early bets (as in pot-limit and no-limit), implied odds dominate. Speculative hands that can improve to monster hands (e.g. straight draws, small pairs, suited connectors) gain value because the few times you hit you win a large bet. In steady-limit structures (limits only doubling) you must start with strong made-hand candidates and discard hands that need to get lucky, since the price to draw is too high relative to potential winnings. The key filter: only play a speculative hand if you can be reasonably sure it will be best even when it improves.
concepts.actionable_rule: In deep or escalating-bet structures, widen to play hands that can make the nuts (suited connectors, small pairs, big draws); in steady-limit or shallow structures, tighten to high pairs and high cards that do not depend on implied odds.

concepts.title: Adjust starting requirements to the cost-to-enter ratio
concepts.summary: When the structure makes it relatively more expensive to enter the pot, tighten up and favor hands that don't rely on implied odds.
concepts.details: Compare the entry cost to the size of later bets. In a $15-$30 game with $5/$10 blinds and no ante, calling cost two-thirds of the flop bet and a raise cost almost twice the flop bet, far more than in a $10-$20 game. Higher relative entry cost raises the value of premium hands (AK, big pairs) and lowers the value of speculative hands (76s, baby pairs). Players who fail to adjust to an unfamiliar structure leak money.
concepts.actionable_rule: Compute the ratio of entry/raise cost to later-street bet size; the higher that ratio, the tighter you play and the more you favor premium made hands over implied-odds hands.

concepts.title: Adjust to no-check-raise rules
concepts.summary: When check-raising is disallowed, last position gains power and you should bet more and semi-bluff more since you can't be check-raised.
concepts.details: Without the check-raise tool, the risk of betting is reduced to merely being called rather than raised, so you should bet a wider range, especially in last position, and semi-bluff more freely on early streets. Even in early position you bet more since you can't check-raise; however, against tough players you may still prefer to check-call a very strong hand in early position to induce bets from hands that would fold to a bet.
concepts.actionable_rule: In no-check-raise games, increase your betting and semi-bluffing frequency (especially in last position), but consider check-calling strong hands in early position vs tough players to induce bets.

concepts.title: Beat loose/calling-station players by tightening and not bluffing
concepts.summary: Against players who play too many hands and call too much, play tight solid starting hands and almost never bluff.
concepts.details: The most common opponent leak is playing too many hands and calling too much on every street. Against such players, conservatism and patience win because you'll simply have the better hand more often. Bluffing has no value when you'll be called; bluff far less than game theory prescribes, perhaps once or twice early purely for advertising to ensure your value hands get paid. You can even deliberately play unimaginatively to encourage them to loosen further.
concepts.actionable_rule: Versus loose callers: tighten starting requirements, value bet relentlessly, and cut bluffs to near zero (a couple of advertising bluffs early at most).

concepts.title: Steal more against tight players
concepts.summary: Against players too tight on the first round, steal blinds/antes more often than game theory dictates, but not every single time.
concepts.details: Tight players give away pots, so raise the forced bet roughly two times out of three when a tight player is the only one left behind you. Don't do it every time or the player will notice and loosen up, defeating your edge. Against the rare player who folds too much on all streets, semi-bluff whenever you can represent a good hand and bluff more than game theory indicates.
concepts.actionable_rule: When heads-up against an over-tight player, raise to steal ~2/3 of the time (not always); against players who fold too much on every street, increase bluff and semi-bluff frequency above GTO.

concepts.title: Tight-preflop / loose-postflop opponents: abandon bluffs once called
concepts.summary: Players who play few hands preflop but won't fold them later will pay off value bets but not fold to bluffs, so give up bluffs when called and value bet relentlessly.
concepts.details: Many over-tight preflop players play too loose afterward because they hate folding their good starting cards. If such a player calls your steal raise, abandon the bluff—he won't fold on later streets. Conversely, when you hold a genuine best hand, bet it hard because he'll give you crying calls all the way.
concepts.actionable_rule: If a tight-preflop-but-sticky opponent calls your raise, stop bluffing and check it down; bet thin for value with any likely-best hand since he'll call down lightly.

concepts.title: Exploit players who never bluff
concepts.summary: Against non-bluffers you always know where you stand, so only call when you can beat a legitimate hand or have proper pot odds—never to catch a bluff.
concepts.details: Normally a marginal call wins two ways: by improving or by catching a bluff. Against a player who never bluffs, the bluff-catching equity vanishes, so fold marginal hands and only call/chase when your hand can beat his betting range or pot odds justify a draw. The profit is in bets saved by folding, even though you only 'win' by losing the pot less expensively. Apply the same logic to players who never check-raise-bluff or never bluff-raise: fold to their raises since they always have it.
concepts.actionable_rule: Versus a player who never bluffs (or never bluff-raises), remove all bluff-catching value from calls—only call/raise/chase based on raw hand strength versus his value range or genuine pot odds, and fold otherwise.

concepts.title: Exploit players who never check-raise
concepts.summary: When an opponent never check-raises, bet more hands after he checks because his check reliably signals a weak-to-fair hand.
concepts.details: A check from a non-check-raiser means his hand isn't worth betting—he won't trap you. This is even safer than betting into a check in a normal game, where a player might occasionally check a strong hand to induce. So thinly value bet and bluff more often after such a player checks to you.
concepts.actionable_rule: When a player who never check-raises checks to you, widen your betting range substantially for both thin value and bluffs.

concepts.title: Exploit players who bluff too much by inducing and calling
concepts.summary: Against habitual over-bluffers, check to induce their bluffs and call (or raise) down with mediocre hands rather than betting into them.
concepts.details: Over-bluffers fold to your bets but bet into your checks, so never bet into them—check and let them bluff, then call or raise depending on your hand. You sacrifice some free cards, but the bluff-induced bets more than compensate. Caveat: over-bluffers are dangerous on a limited bankroll because when they do hold real hands you pay them off; on a short bankroll prefer tight non-bluffers as opponents.
concepts.actionable_rule: Versus an over-bluffer, check your marginal and even weak hands to induce a bet, then call or raise; avoid betting into him since he'll just fold.

concepts.title: A bet saved equals money earned
concepts.summary: Folding to avoid a likely-losing call saves bets, and saved bets contribute to your win rate just as much as bets won.
concepts.details: Much of the profit against predictable opponents (non-bluffers, players who never bluff-raise) comes not from winning pots but from not paying off their legitimate hands. Over a session and a year, these saved bets add up substantially. This reframes correct folds as a profit source equal to correct calls and value bets.
applies_to: facing bets and raises from predictable opponents
concepts.actionable_rule: Treat avoided losing calls as profit—fold when expectation is negative; over time saved bets boost your overall win rate as much as bets won.

concepts.title: Player quality outweighs structure in game selection
concepts.summary: Opponent skill matters more than structure when choosing a game; you need only one or two bad players or several mediocre ones to profit.
concepts.details: Rarely will structure deter good players, but if everyone is as good as you, your hourly rate will be poor even if you're not a loser. The classic adage: if you can't spot the sucker, you're it. A game is beatable with one or two weak players or five or six mediocre ones; pure table-of-experts games should be avoided. You can also target good-but-non-theoretical players in unfamiliar structures.
concepts.actionable_rule: Before sitting down, assess opponents; only play if at least one or two clearly weak or several mediocre players are present, and prefer tables where strong players are on unfamiliar structures.

concepts.title: Bet for Value
concepts.summary: Bet to be called by a worse hand, aiming to extract money rather than to fold out opponents.
concepts.details: A value bet is profitable when more than half the hands that call you are worse than yours. The intent is monetary gain from inferior calling hands, distinct from a bluff which seeks folds.
concepts.actionable_rule: Bet for value when you expect to be called by a worse hand more than 50% of the time; size to maximize money extracted from those worse hands.

concepts.title: Pot Odds
concepts.summary: Compare the size of the pot to the bet you must call to determine if a call is mathematically justified.
concepts.details: Pot odds are the ratio of money already in the pot to the amount you must call. Call when your chance of winning exceeds the break-even probability implied by those odds.
concepts.actionable_rule: Compute pot odds as pot:call; call a draw only when your equity exceeds call/(pot+call).

concepts.title: Implied Odds
concepts.summary: Account for future bets you expect to win when calling with a drawing hand, not just current pot odds.
concepts.details: Implied odds are the ratio of total money you expect to win if you complete your hand to the current bet you must call. They justify calls that immediate pot odds alone do not, when stacks are deep and opponents will pay off.
concepts.actionable_rule: When drawing, include expected future winnings in your odds; call marginal draws only if implied odds (future payoff:current call) compensate for the deficit in immediate pot odds.

concepts.title: Effective Odds
concepts.summary: Weigh total expected winnings against the total bets you must call across all remaining rounds to make your hand.
concepts.details: Effective odds extend pot odds across multiple betting rounds: compare what you'll win if you hit to the sum of all calls needed from now to showdown, important when more bets loom before completion.
concepts.actionable_rule: Before chasing a multi-street draw, sum all calls required to reach the end and compare to total expected winnings; continue only if that ratio justifies your draw equity.

concepts.title: Reverse Implied Odds
concepts.summary: Recognize hands that may cost you additional bets when behind, reducing their value.
concepts.details: Reverse implied odds are the money already in the pot versus the money you'll have to call to the end while potentially holding a second-best hand. Hands that make you pay off when beaten have negative future expectation.
concepts.actionable_rule: Discount marginal hands that risk paying off a bigger hand on later streets; play cautiously or fold hands with poor reverse implied odds.

concepts.title: Semi-Bluff
concepts.summary: Bet with a hand that isn't currently best but can improve to the best hand, gaining two ways to win.
concepts.details: A semi-bluff wins immediately when opponents fold, and retains equity to make the best hand if called. It combines fold equity with drawing equity, making it more profitable than a pure bluff.
concepts.actionable_rule: Bet as a semi-bluff with drawing hands that have meaningful outs; you profit from immediate folds plus the chance to hit your draw when called.

concepts.title: Mathematical Expectation
concepts.summary: Evaluate every play by its average long-run profit or loss rather than short-term results.
concepts.details: Expectation is the average outcome of a bet over the long run. Positive-expectation plays win money over time; negative-expectation plays lose. Decisions should maximize expectation regardless of single-hand variance.
concepts.actionable_rule: Choose the action with the highest positive expectation over the long run, ignoring the outcome of any single hand.

concepts.title: Check-Raise / Sandbag
concepts.summary: Check a strong hand intending to raise after an opponent bets, extracting extra value or applying pressure.
concepts.details: Check-raising plays weakly with a strong hand to induce a bet, then raises to build the pot. It is most effective when an opponent is likely to bet behind you.
concepts.actionable_rule: With a strong hand out of position against a likely bettor, check intending to raise to maximize value or charge draws.

concepts.title: Slowplay
concepts.summary: Check or just call with a big hand to disguise its strength and win more on later streets.
concepts.details: Slowplaying conceals hand strength to keep opponents in and induce action on later, larger rounds. Best when the board is unthreatening and giving a cheap or free card won't let opponents draw out profitably.
concepts.actionable_rule: Slowplay a big hand only when the board is safe and disguising strength wins more later than betting now; otherwise bet for value and protection.

concepts.title: Steal the Antes / Blinds
concepts.summary: Raise on the first round to fold out opponents and win the dead money when you likely don't have the best hand.
concepts.details: Stealing targets the antes or blinds by raising to make remaining players fold. It is a positional, frequency-based play that profits from uncontested dead money.
concepts.actionable_rule: From late position with marginal holdings, raise to steal the blinds/antes when the remaining players are likely to fold.

concepts.title: Representing a Hand
concepts.summary: Bet or raise to convince opponents you hold a bigger hand than you actually show.
concepts.details: By betting in a way consistent with strength your board suggests, you can induce folds even without the hand. Effective representation requires a credible story matching the visible cards and prior action.
concepts.actionable_rule: When the board and your action credibly suggest a strong hand, bet to represent it and pressure opponents into folding.

concepts.title: Putting Opponent on a Hand / Hand Reading
concepts.summary: Deduce the range of hands an opponent most likely holds from their actions and exposed cards.
concepts.details: Reading hands means narrowing an opponent's likely holdings using betting patterns, position, and visible cards. Accurate reads drive value-bet sizing, bluff timing, and fold decisions.
concepts.actionable_rule: Continuously narrow your opponent's likely range using their bets, position, and shown cards, and tailor your action to that read.

concepts.title: Exploiting the Calling Station
concepts.summary: Against players who call far too often, value bet relentlessly and never bluff.
concepts.details: A pay station calls bets and raises much more than correct, making them impossible to bluff but highly profitable to value bet. Adjust by maximizing value and eliminating bluffs.
concepts.actionable_rule: Versus a calling station, bet thin for value with legitimate hands and abandon bluffs entirely.

concepts.title: Recognizing Tilt and Steam
concepts.summary: Emotional upset causes worse play and looser pot entry; avoid it in yourself and exploit it in others.
concepts.details: On tilt or steaming players enter too many pots and play hands that don't justify action because they're emotionally upset. This produces negative expectation for them and profit opportunities for disciplined opponents.
concepts.actionable_rule: Stop playing when you go on tilt; against a steaming opponent, tighten up and value bet wider since they will pay off with worse hands.

concepts.title: Game Selection
concepts.summary: Seek good games where you are a substantial favorite and avoid bad games where opponents outclass you.
concepts.details: A good game has enough weaker players to make you a clear favorite; a bad game makes you an underdog. Profit depends as much on opponent quality as on skill, so choosing tables is a core edge.
concepts.actionable_rule: Seat yourself in games containing weak, loose players (live ones) and leave games where opponents are stronger than you.

concepts.title: Positional Awareness
concepts.summary: Acting later in the betting order gives an informational advantage; play more hands in late position and fewer early.
concepts.details: Position determines how much information you have when acting. Early position (under the gun) acts before most players with least info; late position acts last with most info, enabling steals and value extraction.
concepts.actionable_rule: Tighten your starting requirements in early position and widen them in late position to exploit your informational advantage.
